en: General Exposition of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Nanyue. Preface:
Statement of Intent.
In the past, the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai diligently upheld this sutra and attained the Samādhi of the Lotus Sutra.
He personally beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present, never having dispersed.

He then explained the entire body of this sutra through the Three Contemplations (*san guan*), culminating in the principle that the "ten realms and thousand suchnesses" all ultimately return to the contemplation of the mind. His *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) are the most precise and detailed; however—
The text is vast and its meaning profound; those of shallow understanding find it difficult to penetrate. Taking it as overly complex, few have taken it as their primary authority.

Master Wēnlíng composed this *Essential Commentary*, which is concise in expression yet exhaustive in meaning. By employing concrete events to manifest the Dharma, it possesses a refined and clear direction.
Furthermore, its adherence to the principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—establishing a single beginning and a single end—is most appropriate, for its intent lies in brevity and essentiality.

The ultimate source and origin from beginning to end have not yet been fully elucidated; thus, observers have been unable to penetrate the profound intent of tracing the origin and reaching the conclusion, leaving this matter somewhat deficient.

Furthermore, the two masters’ classification of the entire scripture—placing all subsequent chapters under the "Chapter on the Universal Distribution"—seems not to have thoroughly reached the final destination.
Consequently, students regard it as merely ordinary, thereby causing the Buddha’s true intention [to remain obscured].
The meaning of the sutra has not yet been fully elucidated, and its principles remain unclear; thus, there is no lack of redundancy in these written words.
Since my youth, I have entered lecture halls and studied under various masters, yet I have privately harbored doubts. I have long cherished the intent to investigate them deeply.

Previously, while serving under the grace of imperial dispatch to the regions beyond the passes, I was first honored by the encounter with Chan Master Daguan. Upon hearing me raise these difficult questions, he granted me permission to recite this sutra one hundred times.

[He] compiled [the text] to eliminate past transgressions. While stationed among the ranks, he established a *dharma-śālā* within the camp walls and gathered his disciples to chant and recite [the scriptures].

At the request of the assembly, he lectured on it for one full cycle; suddenly, he attained a profound realization. He subsequently categorized the entire scripture according to the four phrases: "Opening, Showing, Awakening, and Entering.
The assembly all rejoiced and approved, whereupon he committed these points to writing as a rhythmic commentary (*ji-jie*). From beginning to end, the work maintains a single, consistent thread.

I have subsumed [the Avataṃsaka] within the four gates of faith, understanding, practice, and realization; it is concise yet exhaustive, with no teaching left out. Having requested instruction from the Great Master, I occasionally received his approval.

Thereupon, I considered that although the general outline had been grasped through the division of chapters and sections, the sūtra had not yet been fully integrated, which was inconvenient for beginners.
Thus, I again composed a detailed analysis of the chapters and sections to manifest the purport of the entire sūtra; yet, this too remains somewhat abbreviated.
In detail: the *Avataṃsaka* school elucidates that the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is for the sake of the "great cause and condition" (*mahāntam artham*).
This is very clear in the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*), where the Tathāgata narrates it himself.

However, because transmitters have been ignorant of its source, students have not failed to sigh at the sight of the vast ocean. Therefore, I now again provide a comprehensive interpretation, honoring the ancient commentaries of the venerable masters.

I dare not venture upon arbitrary exegesis; rather, I shall synthesize the entire scripture to lead back to the Buddha’s revelation of his knowledge and vision—his *jñāna-darśana*—and elucidate the great principle of the *Avataṃsaka*’s beginning and end as a single, unified whole, thereby expressing the Tathāgata’s fundamental intent for appearing in the world.
This is like merging diverse streams into the ocean, prioritizing the essential framework over mere literary phrasing.
This may be abbreviated; therefore, I shall explain its general meaning. Although my composition does not follow the ancients as a teacher, its principles have a source of authority.
May readers be fortunate enough not to discard the words because of the person; thus, my humble crime of overstepping bounds may be excused.
Regarding the Buddha’s teaching throughout his entire life, ancient masters have offered various classifications concerning its depth and breadth; they do not agree on how many levels there are.

The Great Master Xianshou divided them into five: namely, the Small, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect. He classified this sutra as belonging to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*). As for the Flower... [text truncated]

Yan regards [this teaching] as the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Master Zhizhe of Tiantai divided it into four categories—namely, *zang*, *tong*, *bie*, and *yuan*—and considered this sutra to be purely perfect (*chunyuan*), while regarding the *Avataṃsaka* as both distinct and perfect (*biyuan*), meaning that it reveals the perfect while still carrying the distinct.
Thus, these two masters appear to be in disagreement; however, this is likely because each held his own particular veneration. As for Tiantai’s view that it is purely perfect:
The meaning is that this sutra discusses the true reality (*dharmatā*) exclusively; it is like a great white ox—pure, singular, and without admixture.
The three vehicles converge therein, and the five natures enter together. In principle, nothing is not penetrated; in practice, nothing is not exhausted. It is ultimately perfect (*pariniṣpanna*).
As for designating the *Avataṃsaka* as "distinctive-perfect" (*biyuan*), it is because the practices of the forty-two stages are arrayed therein; thus, one uses the distinct to clarify the perfect.

This [Lotus Sūtra] does not yet exhaustively encompass the perfectly interfused ocean of fruition—the ultimate discourse on the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena that accords with the nature of reality.
Therefore, while there is no lack of reason for its singular veneration, it is not without its limitations. This is because Tiantai personally realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra;

thus, he accorded it preeminence based on his own realization to manifest the sūtra’s supreme excellence. It is not intended to disparage Xianshou (Fazang) or to suggest that the *Avataṃsaka* is more "perfect" than this sūtra.

Regarding the "Ultimate": The *Avataṃsaka* is indeed the Buddha of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), residing in the land of actual reward. It is expounded in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

It is the ocean of the perfect fruit, wherein the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused; it is a dharma-gate of sovereign mastery. Within both the primary and secondary environments, down to every speck of dust and hair, each and every thing accords with the nature and is all-pervasive.
Although the various stages are spoken of, their meaning is fully manifest; cause and effect penetrate one another, being without obstruction or hindrance. Therefore, it is called [the Ultimate].
It is perfected, yet concludes with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This is because this sutra was spoken by the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*);
it relies upon the land of skillful means (*upāyabhūmi*) to lead the three vehicles (*triyāna*) through indirect guidance toward the single ultimate goal.

That is to say, the Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of one great causal matter (*ekamahākaruṇāhetu-pratyaya*), desiring to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). However, the Buddha...
That which is known and seen is the one true *dharmadhātu*, the *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
When Vairocana realized it, he termed it the "Ocean-like Wisdom of Universal Radiance" (*dharmadhātu-samudra-prabhāsvara-jñāna*). This is called the one vehicle’s eternally abiding true mind.

Upon first attaining perfect enlightenment at the Bodhimaṇḍa, he immediately designated this mind and expounded the *Avataṃsaka*, suddenly manifesting the perfectly interfused and unobstructed *dharmadhātu*.
Being uniquely endowed with the great capacity (*mahā-yāna*), those of lesser faculties remained in the assembly as if blind or deaf; thus, the conversion was not extensive.

This so-called "single gate" was narrow and limited, failing to fulfill his original intention. Therefore, he observed the trees and practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), contemplating for twenty-one days.

Taking the Dharma of the Single Vehicle, he provisionally taught it as three. Thus, through his great compassion of identical essence (*samatā-karuṇā*), he did not rise from his seat but manifested himself everywhere throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha, manifesting his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), demonstrated descending from Tuṣita Heaven into the royal palace and attaining enlightenment through the eight phases.
At the Deer Park, he preached the Dharma of the Four Truths to deliver all sentient beings.

Yet, although the various *śrāvakas* realized *nirvāṇa*, they remained utterly severed from the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the One Vehicle. Consequently, for forty years, the Buddha employed provisional means.
Through the skillful means of censure and refinement, when one reaches this assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the resolve of the multitude becomes steadfast and pure;

having merely gained faith in the Buddha-mind, they possess the potential for Buddhahood. Therefore, each is granted a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), whereby the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world is finally fulfilled.
As the conditions for benefiting sentient beings are now nearing their end, it is called the "Final Teaching. This is explained in terms of transformation.

The completion of the ritual proceedings constitutes the end. That which is termed "perfect" (*yuan*) refers to the gathering of causes and the fruition of results—the ultimate inclusion within the perfection of the ocean of fruition—not the perfection of abiding in the ocean of fruition through spontaneous interpenetration. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* is the sudden and perfect [teaching].
Just as when the sun first rises it first illuminates the high mountains, this sutra serves as the gradual perfection. It is like the confluence of diverse streams returning to the ocean.
If even a dragon girl can attain Buddhahood, this is also called "Perfect and Sudden. This is the ultimate destination of the two sutras elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
It is as clear as the sun and stars. If one examines the "Chapter on Expedient Means," the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world can be fully perceived.
Thus, we know that the metaphor in the sutra describing the elder’s majestic virtue as uniquely sublime refers to the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body).
The One True Dharma-realm is the elder’s household; the infinite adornments of the Flower Treasury World are...
This is the wealth of such a person. The cause and fruit of the One Vehicle is the Great White Ox-Cart.
Arriving at the treasure site is the place where the Dharma-realm returns to tranquility; it is what is called the Ocean of Wondrous Adornments.
Whatever is established therein all returns to the Dharma-realm. Through these various manifestations, what could remain unilluminated? Therefore, the ancients judged the *Avataṃsaka* to be the root.

The various teachings of expedient means (*upāya*) constitute the provisional dharma-wheels (*śākhā-dharmacakra*). The *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) is the dharma-wheel that subsumes the branches back into the root.
What is revealed within these teachings does not go beyond principle (*li*), practice (*xing*), cause (*yin*), and result (*guo*).

Taking principle and practice as the cause, and realization and entry [into the fruit] as the result—this is what I mean when I say that for forty years prior, [the Buddha] used expedient means to guide and gather [beings], until he spoke [the definitive teaching] at the assembly of the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
The noble wisdom of self-awakening: the *ālayavijñāna* is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*. This reveals the perfection of principle and the subtlety of the mind.

As the sutra says, "My Mahāyāna is a non-vehicle," which already contains the intent of revealing the ultimate by opening the provisional. Upon reaching the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it speaks exclusively of the true reality (*dharmatā*).

Every form and every fragrance all returns to the Middle Way, thereby manifesting the perfection of practice and the subtlety of the objective realm. Since both principle and practice are perfected, the mind...

The objects of perception are all wondrous; the Buddha’s knowledge and vision consist simply in the thorough understanding of this. This is the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world;

there is nothing else. Therefore, for those of the three vehicles, he opens up this knowledge and vision, and thus each and every one receives a prediction of enlightenment and immediately enters nirvana.

Thus, it constitutes the final stage; only by returning to the Dharma-realm can one reach ultimate perfection. Xianshou’s classification of this as the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) based on the ritual of transformation is most thorough in its reasoning.
Wenglun’s assessment that it stands in a relationship of beginning and end with the *Avataṃsaka* is particularly insightful, though he has not yet fully elaborated upon it.
One need only carefully contemplate the intent of the sutra and harmonize the teachings and contemplations to achieve a wondrous accord.
The Buddha-mind is thus fully realized, with no dharma remaining.
Regarding the title of this work, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it directly points to the one true Dharma-realm, the Tathāgatagarbha mind.
This is for the purpose of establishing the name. The *Treatise* says: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings.
This mind universally encompasses all dharmas of the mundane and supramundane worlds, constituting the entire substance of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

All the causes and effects of the defiled and pure states of both the holy and the ordinary are included and subsumed within it. It does not increase in the state of holiness, nor does it decrease in the state of ordinariness; even when abiding in defilement..."
It is not defiled; it emerges from the mundane without being sullied. For this reason, Śākyamuni Tathāgata realized the ultimate nature of this mind;
thus, mind and objects are of one suchness, and the holy and the ordinary are equal. Since this is inherently possessed by all sentient beings, he exclaimed, "How marvelous!
How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata; yet, because of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachments, they do not [realize it]."
Its realization stems precisely from the Buddhas’ awakening to it as the wisdom of universal radiance, which is termed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
Sentient beings, however, are deluded by it, mistaking it for the ignorance of karmic consciousness—the very root of birth and death. Upon seeing this mind even once, one is immediately a Buddha;

such is the wondrous nature of this mind. Within it, the adornments of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang shijie*), both the environment and its inhabitants, are infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
Subtle, wondrous, and perfectly interfused: from the dust motes and blades of grass to the smallest weeds, all arise in dependence upon the mind.

This realm is wondrous in its marklessness within the true reality (*dharmatā*). Mind and object are non-dual; it is purely the one True Reality, and is thus called the "Wondrous Dharma" (*saddharma*).

Yet, when sentient beings are deluded regarding this Wondrous Dharma, they call it the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness); when the Buddhas awaken to it, they call it the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store). It is based upon this single mind.
The Dharma-realm is established and named the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*). Thus, truth and delusion penetrate one another; defilement and purity are interfused; cause and effect are simultaneous;
and beginning and end share a single limit. Therefore, by way of metaphor, it takes the lotus flower as its image; by way of the Dharma, it points directly to the essence of the mind.
Yet this mind, in a Buddha, is the Wisdom of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*), and is also called Reality (*tathatā*).
Wisdom—also termed *sarvākārajñatā* (the knowledge of all modes) and the noble self-awakened wisdom—is therefore called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Within sentient beings, it is the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).

Because sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, yet remain unaware of it due to being shrouded by the weeds of ignorance, the Buddhas appear in the world solely to reveal this mind and enable [its realization].

Those sentient beings, knowing and seeing for themselves, awaken to and enter [this truth]. Therefore it is said that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world solely for the sake of this one great causal matter:
namely, to reveal and show to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Because it brings about complete purification, this alone is the supreme matter; there is nothing else.
This is the fundamental intention for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world. How profound is this mind, yet how difficult it is to awaken to!
Only our Śākyamuni Tathāgata, having first attained perfect enlightenment at the Bodhimaṇḍa, suddenly revealed this mind and expounded the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra, titled "Universal Illumination."
The *Dharmadhātu-sūtra* is called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Only those with superior faculties benefit from seeing or hearing it, while those of inferior faculties and weak understanding remain as if blind or deaf, even though their bodies are seated within the assembly. Therefore, out of great compassion that is identical in essence to theirs, [the Buddha] contemplates the trees and walks in meditation;

he then differentiates and explains the One Vehicle Dharma as three vehicles. Thus, he manifests the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), simultaneously manifesting both.
The two aspects [of the teaching] began simultaneously. At the Deer Park, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and delivered the various śrāvakas.
Yet, considering his original intention, it was specifically to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Since that time, the faculties of sentient beings have remained dull.
For forty years, although the Buddha exerted himself through various and immeasurable skillful means, the multitudes of sentient beings did not awaken;

they were long subject to his reproaches until they finally developed a heart of faith in the Buddha. It was not until the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* that he saw their spiritual faculties had become pure.
Believe this mind with deep conviction; you shall each receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.

That is to say, one knows that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind, and that the realization of the body of wisdom does not depend on another for awakening. The original intent of Śākyamuni’s appearance in the world has finally been fulfilled today;
therefore, I have disclosed everything from the depths of my heart, recounting the bitter hardships we shared throughout our journey, so as to bring you to full understanding and benefit.
The task of his life’s manifestation will not endure for long; he shall soon enter nirvana, which is what is meant by the "conclusion of his manifested traces.
Thus, it is like an elder who, before his death, entrusts his family estate to his heirs. One should know that this sutra is like a testamentary letter for the entrustment of the family estate;
it serves as the means for the circulation of the temporal teachings of a single dispensation. To claim that [the Buddha] never spoke [of this] at all is called "protecting" [the Dharma].
I reflect: it is on this very day that [the Buddha] speaks; this constitutes the entrustment (*parindanā*). Thus, the facts pertain to the past, while the meaning lies beyond words.

Were one not to possess the perfect illumination of the Dharma-realm and a wondrous resonance with the Buddha’s mind, but instead seek this through mere, limited texts, one would find no destination whatsoever.
To fully comprehend this single topic is to have already reflected upon more than half the purport of the entire sutra.
"Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin, by imperial decree.
As for "Yao Qin," this refers to the reign of Yao Xing during the period when the Five Barbarian tribes (Wuh) were in chaos within China under the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Initially, Fu Jian, the ruler of Former Qin, met with Dharma Master Dao’an and honored him as a sage. Dao’an said: "I, a poor monk, am not a sage..."
The Emperor heard that in the Western Regions, in the kingdom of Kucha, there was one named Kumārajīva, who was a sage.
"If you, my benefactor, wish to see him, he should be welcomed here. At that time, Yao Xian dispatched seventy thousand armored troops and appointed Lü Guang as their general.
He campaigned against Kucha to capture Kumārajīva. Upon reaching the siege of the city, the King said, "My kingdom is far removed from the Middle Kingdom;

we have never had prior contact. Why do you attack us? Guṇabhadra replied, "The Celestial King of the Great Qin has heard that your kingdom possesses the sage Kumārajīva and wishes to invite him back to provide for his needs.
It is not for the sake of seizing your land. At that time, Kumārajīva was... [years old].
Fang was twenty years old at the time; he was the nephew of the King of Kucha and possessed extraordinary wisdom and eloquence.

He had already lectured on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the king. The king said, "Kumārajīva is the treasure of my kingdom; how could I bear to lightly abandon him? I shall simply listen to his command.
The king did not understand this for a long time. Kumārajīva then petitioned the king, saying, "To cause suffering to the common people for the sake of this poor monk is not compassionate."
"This is the way of compassion. I pray that you allow me to go; I shall return immediately. The King had no choice but to dispatch him.

Fǎguāng welcomed Kumārajīva into Guān. Hearing that Yao Shì had already passed away and Yáo Cháng had established himself as ruler, Fǎguāng subsequently took up residence in Liángzhōu and ascended the throne.
The state was named Da Liang. Not long after, Guang died. His son Shao ascended the throne but was murdered by Lü Zuan, the Duke of Taiyuan.
Zuan then established himself as ruler, but he was subsequently deposed by Lü Chao. Lü Long was installed for several years; during this time, Kumārajīva was imprisoned in both cases.
In the third year of the Hongshi era of Yao Xing, the latter dispatched an army to attack Long. Long surrendered, and Kumārajīva was consequently escorted to Chang’an. The Qin ruler [Yao Xing]...

He paid him homage. While Kumārajīva was in Liangzhou, he had been humiliated by Daochao and others; there were those who could not endure his words, yet the Master (Sengrui) remained patient and forbearing.
When he met the ruler of Qin, the latter initially held him in great respect. Subsequently, a Dharma master from the Western Regions arrived bearing the *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra*;
as its contents accorded perfectly with those of Kumārajīva, Yao Xing wished to detain the foreign master. However, the master did not remain, and so [the King] abandoned the matter.
He departed. [Fayong] became enraged and secretly dispatched a messenger to assassinate him outside the pass.

Suspecting Kumārajīva, he feared that [Fayong] intended to leave and so bestowed a palace lady upon him, saying it was "to continue the Buddha-seed" as a test of Kumārajīva’s intentions. Kumārajīva perceived this beforehand;
thinking that [Fayong’s] devotion to the Dharma was profound, he accepted her to dispel [Fayong’s] suspicions. When he translated this sūtra, he first resided at the Cottage of Grass.
Precisely at this time of peril and uncertainty, he prioritized the Dharma and, setting aside all personal reservations, brought about these conditions for the propagation of the teachings.
Having seen that the ancients had sacrificed their own lives for the sake of the Dharma and endured every hardship, after Kumārajīva’s body was cremated, a blue lotus grew before his stupa.
When Yao Xing opened the stupa to inspect it, the flower emerged from the base of the Master’s tongue; this was no mere display by a great sage.
Manifestation. Why did this come to pass? Initially, Master Zhao resided together with Kumārajīva at the translation hall, and the Ruler of Qin held him in high esteem.
Before long, Kumārajīva passed away, and Zhao was also put to death. How tragic!

This sutra consists of twenty-eight chapters and is divided into three major sections. The first chapter, the Prologue, clarifies the causes and conditions for the preaching of the Dharma and is designated as the Introductory Section (*nidāna-bhāga*).

The second section, the Main Body (*saddharma-bhāga*), comprises twenty-seven chapters, which are categorized according to the four characters: Opening (*āviṣkaraṇa*), Showing (*darśana*), Awakening (*bodhana*), and Entering (*praveśana*).

From the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*) to the "Chapter on the Dharma-Preacher" (*Dharma-bhāṇaka-parivarta*), these nine chapters constitute the "Opening of the Buddha’s Knowledge" (*buddha-jñānasyāviṣkaraṇam*).
The "Vision" (darśana) is the first chapter, "The Vision of the Jeweled Stūpa," which serves to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
The eleven chapters from the "Devadatta" chapter to the "Entrustment" chapter serve to cause the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The six chapters from the "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter to the "Exhortation of Samantabhadra" chapter serve to lead one into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Revelation, instruction, and awakening constitute faith and understanding (*adhimukti*); entry constitutes practice (*caryā*).
The final few sentences at the end of the chapter constitute the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) section, with which it concludes.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter One: The Introduction (*Nidāna*).
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha... [up to] ...together with his retinue.
This is the ritual for the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka. It constitutes the final instruction bestowed by the World-Honored One upon Ānanda at the time of his parinirvāṇa.
As is commonly understood, this [opening] is placed at the beginning of all sūtras.

However, while the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma always accords with the specific capacities of his audience, the assembly he lists therein is headed by the primary recipient of that teaching. This sūtra belongs to the teaching of the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Regarding the Bodhisattva-dharma, the reason a Śrāvaka is placed at the forefront is that, by now revealing the provisional to manifest the ultimate, he is specifically intended to attract and guide those of the two vehicles into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
thus, he is made the leader so that they may receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. As for the praise of his virtues:
It is said that their outflows (āsrava) have been exhausted and their minds have attained mastery;

this clearly demonstrates that the minds of those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka-yāna) have become pliant and are capable of receiving the Great Dharma. This is precisely the time when their faculties have matured and they are ready to attain the Way.
Those such as the various disciples listed below are such individuals. As for the bhikṣuṇīs in training and others, they are also placed at the head because of the Buddha’s...
Regarding those to be transformed (*vineya*): there is the causal [nature] and there is the proximate [nature]; all others belong to the cause, while this is the proximate.

It is precisely for this purpose that they rely upon the Buddha-nature as the causal condition. Hereafter, each is individually granted a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), which serves as the contributory condition.
Once the Buddha-nature is fully manifested, the task of benefiting sentient beings is completed.
Eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [approached], each bowing at the Buddha’s feet and withdrawing to sit on one side.
This introduction provides a detailed enumeration of the assembly gathered for the Dharma. These great bodhisattvas assist the Buddha in propagating his transformation and serve as his dharma-kin.
The Dharma spoken by the Buddha—the supreme sage who has transcended the world—is a discourse that transcends all worldly talk.
How could anyone other than a Great Being of the Dharma-body be able to strike the harp? Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas and is able to wondrously accord with the Buddha-mind;
therefore, he occupies the foremost position. This sutra establishes its substance through wisdom (*jñāna*), and as such, it is that which is venerated.

As for the kings of devas and humans, the nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits, they constantly follow the Buddha’s transformation and serve as the assembly for protecting the Dharma; thus, they are all [included].
He sat there, his fundamental intention being that the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is for the purpose of transforming sentient beings so that they may all together attain the Buddha-way.
Now, by bestowing individual predictions of enlightenment upon each of those of the two vehicles, he is about to complete the task of benefiting living beings.
This is exactly like an elder, at the point of death, entrusting his family estate to his kinsmen, the king, and the ministers.
The *kṣatriyas* and householders acted as witnesses and entrustments;
this is why not a single person was missing from that assembly on Vulture Peak, allowing us to perceive the excellence of that gathering.

As for the assembly in the *Avataṃsaka*, there were forty-two different types of ordinary bodies, representing that each had attained a specific stage of the Dharma-gate and fully realized the ocean of fruition. Thus we know:
The various sūtras list their assemblies, each according to its own specific tradition.
The preceding portion constitutes the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*); the following portion constitutes the specific introduction (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*).
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly (up to) "rejoicing, they joined their palms and gazed at the Buddha with a single mind."

This introductory section explains the circumstances that gave rise to this sutra. As he was about to discourse on the Sublime Dharma, he first spoke of the *Anantārtha-sūtra* (The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings).
This was because the various dharmas taught for the sake of those of the three vehicles forty years prior were all provisional establishments;
they had not yet transcended the scope of mind, thought, and consciousness. Now, he intends to reveal the true mark of the One Vehicle—the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Therefore, this sutra was preached first to serve as a guide. Its intent is that all people may transcend mind and consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) and emerge from the realm of emotional measures (*sattva-pramāṇa*), so that they may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*).

This sutra is the secret heart-dharma (*hṛdaya-dharma*) of all Buddhas, like the jewel within the topknot of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*); it is not given recklessly to others, and thus it is protected by the Buddhas. This has already revealed the mind.

The Dharma is wondrous. Furthermore, as for "entering the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings," this is to reveal the true realm of the real mark of the single mind of quiescent extinction;
it cannot be perceived by a distracted mind or a scattered intention. One must observe through samādhi before one can penetrate deeply into the boundless.
Therefore, samādhi is also called the "Station of Immeasurable Meanings. This has already revealed the wondrousness of the realm.
Both mind and environment are wondrous; thus, the essential purport of the entire sutra is already manifest herein.

This intends to clarify that only by fully realizing this state of mind and environment does one possess the true cause for attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers, signifying that without entering this state of mind and environment, it is impossible to overturn and shatter ignorance.
Consequently, the earth shook in six ways, manifesting the complete essence and great function of the Sublime Dharma.
This refers to what is called "first moving through meditative concentration. The great assembly at the Dharma-gathering had never before seen such a sight;
therefore, they were all filled with joy. Not knowing the reason for it, they could do nothing but gaze upon the Buddha, hoping that he would bestow some instruction upon them.
At that time, the Buddha emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows (extending to) the construction of stupas made of the seven treasures with the Buddha’s relics.

This fully manifests the true realm of the *dharmadhātu*. The light from the white tuft of hair symbolizes the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way—namely, the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom manifested by one's own mind.
By means of the universally radiant wisdom of the single true *dharmadhātu*, [the teaching is revealed].
The agitated realms of the sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses of all sentient beings are all manifestations of this wisdom according to conditions.
Now, as this wisdom manifests before one, it shines through with total clarity and transparency, free from all obstruction.

Therefore, it universally illumines the eighteen thousand worlds of the eastern direction—the locus of suffering and joy within the three realms, the cycle of transmigration for sentient beings in the six paths, and the sites where all Buddhas attain enlightenment.
The beginning and end of the Buddha’s life, as well as the sublime practices of Bodhisattvas for benefiting sentient beings, are all inseparable from this function of wisdom;

therefore, they all manifest perfectly within the light. To fully comprehend this single light is to forget the distinctions between the pure and the defiled, and to realize the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas.
Thus, the ground of the Buddha-wisdom—the true reality of the One Vehicle—will become vividly clear within the mind and eyes. This is what is meant by "thereafter, by means of..."
This is the one who extracts [the truth] through wisdom. The essential purport of the entire sutra is fully revealed herein.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought... (up to)... he saw all the adornments of that Buddha-land.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to reiterate this meaning, asked in verse:
"O Mañjuśrī, Guide, for what reason [do you remain silent]? ... [you] gaze upon me; what is it that you would speak?"
This is Maitreya’s inquiry regarding the true reality (*tathatā*) and the authentic realm.

The true reality and authentic realm of the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle—the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—has already been fully revealed within a single ray of light. Because the fourfold assembly had never seen this before, they were startled and gave rise to doubt;
it is truly not something that can be reached through the deliberations of the mind or consciousness. Although Maitreya is a sage, his cognitive faculties have not yet [attained this].
Because [the mind] penetrates, it cannot avoid conceptual discrimination; thus, doubts arise. Since Mañjuśrī possesses great wisdom, he must be able to understand the underlying cause of this.
Furthermore, having served many Buddhas over time, he must have witnessed such actual events. Therefore, he must inquire about them to reach a definitive resolution.
As for the states of the sentient beings of the six realms manifested within the light that were asked about, the Buddhas—
The activities for benefiting sentient beings, the beginning and end of the Bodhisattva’s practice,
as well as the various causes and conditions for seeking the Way and the sublime conduct of making offerings to the Buddha’s relics— all these were clearly and vividly perceived. Furthermore,
it was said that within a mere instant while the Tathāgata remained in meditative absorption, he beheld within his light the events and phenomena of many eons, with every detail left unomitted.

For what reason does this exist? It is simply that one does not realize that when Śākyamuni Tathāgata was preaching the *Avataṃsaka* at the site of enlightenment, he entered the Samādhi of the Momentary Boundary of Universal Radiant Wisdom and manifested bodies throughout the ten realms, appearing like stars scattered across the universe to respond universally to all beings.

He preached the Dharma everywhere to benefit sentient beings. Thus, one knows that during the forty years from the Deer Park until now, the deeds he performed were carried out without ever arising from the *kṣaṇa-samādhi*.
How could this be known by the conceptual discrimination of the mind and consciousness of sentient beings with inferior understanding?
This was merely a preliminary account; the matters within the light have not yet been fully exhausted. Today, at last—
It is merely a single fragment of the Dharma-realm revealed. Therefore, by comprehending these marks of light, one penetrates the Buddha’s mind;
this is called awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This cannot be known through the consciousness of the mind, nor can it be reached through verbal expression;

it is truly the entire substance of the wondrous Dharma. The endeavor lies in a wondrous awakening that transcends words. For this reason, when the World-Honored One was about to discourse upon the wondrous Dharma, he said:
First, let a single ray of light serve as the preceding sign. If we can truly behold this manifestation of light, it will be understood without further explanation;
how then could we fall into the tangled thicket of conceptual entanglements?
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Maitreya Bodhisattva... [up to] "...because it is a dharma difficult to believe, he manifested this auspicious sign.
This is Mañjuśrī’s general response to the intent of the question. Indeed, auspicious signs do not manifest without cause; their manifestation must have a reason.
Thus, one knows that the appearance of these signs is a precursor to the preaching of the Great Dharma. Rain moistens what is parched and withered; the conch shell brings about unity.
To stir the resolve of the assembly and to rouse those who are weary or indolent, all these are metaphors for the Great Dharma.

Fearing that because the Great Dharma is so rare it might be treated as commonplace, and wishing to engender the thought that it is difficult to encounter, he first uses auspicious signs to awaken and stimulate them.
Therefore, it is said that he manifested this auspicious sign so that all might hear and know this dharma that is difficult to believe.
O sons of good family, just as in the past, immeasurable and boundless [Bodhisattvas] attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and became possessors of the All-Knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

This introduces the origin of the lamp’s illumination, serving as proof that Śākyamuni followed his predecessors’ teachings and demonstrating that the transmission of the wondrous Dharma has its source.
The Buddha is named Candrasūryapradīpa because the sun and moon pervade both day and night.
Where the light does not reach, the lamp continues it; this eternal, great illumination that is never obscured symbolizes the virtue of the Wisdom of Universal Radiance.
One who can realize this wisdom is named a Buddha, and thus possesses the ten titles in their entirety.
Because the Buddha speaks from the fundamental, ultimate wisdom he has realized, the Dharma he teaches accords with the nature of reality. Therefore, it is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end.

To differentiate according to the capacities of beings, he taught the three vehicles as skillful means for the single vehicle; thus it is said that he causes all to achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Citing the past to verify the present, this demonstrates that Śākyamuni’s transformative ritual is identical [to that of the Buddhas of the ten directions].
Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp), [and so on] up to ten million Buddhas, under whom he planted various roots of goodness.

This is a chronological enumeration of the names of the twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas from the past, all of which were identical. Their preaching of the Dharma was likewise identical, thereby clarifying that the Way of each Buddha is the same.
This reveals that the wondrous Dharma is a mutual seal between mind and mind. [The passage concludes with] their names and what they realized.
Since they are identical, their teaching is likewise identical; thus, it is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.

Because this fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is that which transforms the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*), there were eight sons when the Buddha had not yet left home; this is the symbol of fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) remaining within the entanglements (*saṃkleśa*).
Each of these eight sons governs a four-continent world (*catur-dvīpa*), signifying that their consciousnesses do not depart from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
This refers to the root-body (*mūlakāya*). Because the *ālayavijñāna* has emerged from its entanglements, it hears of the father’s renunciation;

all the consciousnesses (*vijñānas*) then completely abandon defilement and together become wisdom (*jñāna*). Therefore, it is said that they "completely relinquish the royal throne" and likewise follow [the father] into renunciation to constantly cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Since Śākyamuni’s fundamental nature is identical to that of the ancient [Buddhas], his traces (manifestations) are likewise similar. Since both the fundamental and the manifest are identical, there is nothing that is not identical.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [taught] the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.
This Lamp of Wisdom was transmitted through twenty trillion Buddhas; thus we know that the seed of Buddha-nature has no beginning.
When the time arrived, he preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* and entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings.

That each Buddha takes the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as his ultimate discourse—manifesting such events as the raining of flowers, the shaking of the earth, and the emitting of light—is one [aspect of this].
This is the same as now, manifesting that the mind and its objects, from beginning to end, are non-dual in their true reality;
this quiescent, eternally real state is a rare and marvelous dharma. Yet, it has long been difficult for the multitude to believe and understand when they raise doubts about it.

This is not only the case now. That Buddha, immediately upon emerging from meditative concentration, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which serves as sufficient proof for the teaching that reveals the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional.
By this, one may understand the present matter through the ancient, universal standard of how all Buddhas have expounded the Dharma.
When that Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it lasted for sixty minor kalpas, yet the assembly perceived it as [if it were but a short time].

After the duration of a meal, one realizes that the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle, the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, is the Wisdom of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*), which does not depart from the samādhi of the limit of a single instant (*kṣaṇa*).
Once one enters this samādhi, the views of arising and ceasing vanish; the brief and the long become one and the same.
With no further marks of body or mind, the ten ages of past and present—from beginning to end—do not depart from the present thought-moment.
Therefore, not a single person would give rise to weariness or indolence. Having preached this sutra, he immediately entered nirvana.
When the Buddhas have accomplished this great task for the benefit of sentient beings, their fundamental purpose for appearing in the world is fulfilled.
By this, one knows that the time for my Buddha’s imminent nirvana has arrived. As he was about to pass away, he entrusted the record of the *Guṇagarbha* to [Ananda].

I wish to entrust this Dharma to those who shall carry it forward, hoping that it will be transmitted without end. This serves as proof that each disciple of this assembly possesses the destined capacity to attain Buddhahood.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the monk Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for eighty intermediate kalpas and expounded it for others;
this was to manifest the ultimate ground of the One Vehicle—the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

This does not depart from the function of wisdom. As for the eight sons of the Lamp-Light who all took Miaoguang as their teacher, this serves to manifest the wondrous observation wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

In the causal stage, it possesses the merit of transforming defilement into purity; in the resultant stage, it possesses the function of discerning the capacities of sentient beings and preaching the Dharma.
This is why all eight sons were led to attain Buddhahood. The one among the eight sons who attained Buddhahood last was named...
It is said that one achieves fruition by relying on the lamp of the teacher, Dīpaṃkara, and also by depending upon the efficacy of this sutra.
Since Dīpaṃkara was the original teacher of Śākyamuni, the successive transmission of this sublime Dharma has a long-standing tradition.
This is to clarify that the Way is one throughout ancient and modern times.

However, this Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision is by no means an object of conceptualization, deliberation, or discrimination within the realm of ordinary consciousness. Therefore, those who seek fame and crave profit cannot penetrate it.

Furthermore, taking roots of goodness as the true cause for attaining Buddhahood, they have encountered many Buddhas; this is precisely why the Śrāvakas of today receive their predictions of enlightenment.
This is the realization. Therefore, Mañjuśrī joined his fingers and said to that person: "That one named Wonderful Light was my own self;

the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame was you, Maitreya. Since Maitreya once upheld this sutra in the past, yet now harbors doubts regarding the events unfolding before him, it is evident that this Dharma is not an object within the realm of conceptual discrimination by the conscious mind. Having observed this throughout history...

By means of the auspicious signs of entering meditative concentration and emitting light in the distant past, and the causes and conditions for emerging from concentration to preach the sutras and bestow predictions, one knows that today he will surely preach the Mahāyāna *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This constitutes the prologue; it is the very reason for this present Dharma assembly.
First, he reveals the state of mind and its environment—the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and quiescent extinction (*śānti*)—as the total embodiment of great function. One.
The mindfulness [of this] is suddenly revealed. This cannot be reached through verbal expression; therefore, a single ray of light is emitted, manifesting with perfect clarity.
By borrowing the great wisdom of Mañjuśrī as a means for the assembly to understand it comprehensively, they finally perceive the Tathāgata’s fundamental intention in appearing in the world.
This is precisely the Samādhi of the Momentary Realm of Universal Radiance Wisdom, which has not been aroused for forty years. One day, the World-Honored One...
Ascending the seat, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma King; the Dharma of the Dharma King is thus.
Therefore, when later expounding the wondrous Dharma, he simply says, "Thus" (*evam*).
At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to reiterate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke in verse:
"I recall past lives through immeasurable and incalculable kalpas... [omitted] ...in order to seek the unsurpassed path."

This verse and its prose commentary describe entering meditative absorption and emitting light, as well as the manifestation within that light of the phenomena and characteristics of the *dharmadhātu* and the beginning and end of the Buddhas' lives—all of which correspond exactly [to what follows].
However, regarding the proclamation of his passing into extinction (*parinirvāṇa*), it provides detailed words of instruction and exhortation;

furthermore, it details matters such as the construction of stupas after his death and the fourfold assembly’s diligent pursuit of the Way. This, moreover, serves in advance as the most... for the present assembly.
This serves as a model for future generations, demonstrating that the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter.
Thus, the Dharma Master Wonderful Light upheld the treasury of the Buddha-dharma (until) it was exhausted without remainder.

This verse indicates that in assisting with transformation, transmitting the teachings, and manifesting benefits, all are identical; yet for the purpose of certification and realization, one must necessarily preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, using the manifestation of light as a preliminary expedient.
Now, when the Buddha emits radiance to assist in the revelation of the meaning of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), it is for this reason.
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision, being a state of mind in which all is quiescent, is utterly beyond the reach of speech or discursive thought;

I shall therefore briefly demonstrate it through the Samādhi of the Tip of a Hair. As it is said: "When I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal emits light," so that all people may see directly and immediately, without the slightest interval.
For this reason, the patriarchs of the Chan school employ the mutual exchange of staff and shout to manifest [this truth].
The raising of eyebrows and the blinking of eyes—none of these fail to point directly to the meaning of the Western Land’s coming.

This is a skillful means that does not depend on words and speech. If a person can truly understand this radiance, then throughout the twenty-four hours of daily life, even their coughing, spitting, and waving of arms will be nothing other than the Lotus Samādhi.
The second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya*), at the beginning of the formal exposition.
This chapter is titled "Expedient Means" because, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all things are equal and quiescent.
Transcending emotion and departing from views, it is unconditioned and uncreated.

This is that single segment of true wind which, even before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West, was coldly pervasive and perfectly manifest in its primordial wholeness. What is called the "one path above" exists prior to the void kalpa;
only Buddha-to-Buddha knows it by itself. This is what is meant by the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; how could it be contrived?

It is precisely because sentient beings are deluded and do not awaken that it troubles our World-Honored One. He relinquishes the joy of his own Dharma, casts off his precious and noble robes, and dons tattered, soiled garments.
Manifesting his body within the triple world, he specifically acts for the sake of this present age to bring forth and exalt this matter.
Thus, as soon as he emerged from his mother’s womb, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, saying: "Above heaven and below heaven, there is only..."
"I alone am the Honored One. This is the ultimate realization for the sake of humanity; it is the total revelation of one's entire being, wherein great skillful means have long been extended.

From the time he left home to enter the mountains and cultivate the Way, until his attainment of Buddhahood and his preaching of the Dharma, for forty years he has constantly acted for this purpose—whether going or coming, sitting or standing—without ever having any other concern.
Thus, all the various arrangements and manifestations he previously displayed were for this very end.
There is nothing that is not specifically intended to point out to sentient beings the fundamental matter of the upward path.
What, then, is not a skillful means? Alas, sentient beings have heavy defilements and deep-seated attachments; they have consistently failed to awaken.

Fortunately, after a long period of refinement, their faculties have gradually become pure, and the conditions for awakening are now present. Therefore, today the World-Honored One has specifically [acted] for the sake of the great...
The assembly reveals their original intention and manifests what is inherently possessed;
therefore, for this assembly, he preaches the Lotus Sūtra to reveal and instruct others in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby clarifying the causes and conditions for transcending the world.

He enables all sentient beings to each know and see for themselves, to have self-confidence and self-conviction, and only after awakening and entering [this truth] does he finally satisfy his original intention. Thus, for each [being], he...

Regarding the "bestower of prediction": this clearly reveals that simply having faith in one's own mind is itself called "Buddha. Once this mind is awakened to, the dualistic notions of defilement and purity are forgotten;
every phenomenon is wondrous. There is no phenomenon outside of the mind; apart from this mind, not a single thing can be found.
This is what is called the "wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle," the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. By means of this path of quiescent extinction that transcends words—
It cannot be reached by words; therefore, he first entered meditative concentration to demonstrate its subtle and profound nature, and emitted light to manifest its perfect and wondrous character.
Thus, the auspicious signs of light previously displayed were also a skillful means for this present day. Yet the great assembly did not realize it.
They remained in a state of lingering astonishment and doubt; therefore, he provisionally employed Maitreya and Mañjuśrī to provide a lateral thread of connection.
This is the "expedient of expedients. How tragic! The great assembly was ultimately left in utter bewilderment; thus, I, the World-Honored One, once again untangled the vines.
This, however, is a single instance of falling into verbal expression; furthermore, it serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) for this Dharma. Therefore, it is designated by its title and chapter.

These eight subsequent chapters are judged to be the "Opening of the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision" because sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, yet they remain unaware of it due to being shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, the Tathāgata appeared in the world specifically to reveal it.
"Open" (kāi). Now, regarding this character "open": from the perspective of the Buddha, it means to reveal, to open wide, or to eliminate;

thus it is said, "opening the gate of expedient means. As the subsequent scripture states: "It is like removing the bolt and opening the great city gate. From the perspective of the capacity of the sentient beings, it refers to the opening of development;
that is to say, awakening to one's own mind is like the blooming of a lotus flower. Thus, throughout all three cycles [of teaching],...
Regarding the statement that the teaching of the Dharma is universally for the purpose of opening [the way]:

because the provisional means of the three vehicles (triyāna) taught by the World-Honored One some forty years ago were intended so that hearers might realize the wondrousness of the single mind (ekacitta), those of the three vehicles failed to grasp the ultimate intent beyond words.
Instead, they clung to the provisional teachings as being the ultimate reality, and thus did not believe that they themselves could attain Buddhahood. Now, however—

Having opened the previous provisional gates, the secret treasury is revealed, suddenly manifesting the single reality. Therefore, when those of superior faculties hear this teaching, they immediately believe it to be their own mind;
this is not possible for those who lack wisdom. Thus, after one cycle of the Dharma-teachings, only Śāriputra alone attained realization.
As for those of middling faculties, they come to know it only through parables; therefore, there follows one cycle of parables. [The four great disciples...]
Those of inferior capacity will ultimately fail to attain realization. Therefore, by extensively citing past causes and conditions, they only then achieve awakening;
thus, the twelve hundred and others all attained realization through one cycle of causes and conditions.
Although these explanations are lengthy, their essential point is that each person must, according to their own capacity, believe that their own mind is the Buddha. Thus, one by one...
The prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood was bestowed because the Tathāgata has exerted his supreme spiritual power to proclaim this for the sake of the assembly.
Today, the great multitude has finally given rise to true faith; though they are said to have attained realization, it is merely a realization of awakening, not a realization of entry.
In truth, they have only entered the gate of faith. Examining the subsequent text, it is granted that they attain [realization] through faith.
[The text] enters [into this]. It includes the disciples' own accounts of their former lack of faith, as well as Śāriputra’s realization and the narration by the four great disciples;
thus, the chapter is titled "Faith and Understanding" (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). Therefore, the opening of the Buddha's knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*) places primary emphasis on faith.

This is precisely in accord with the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra], which states that knowing all phenomena is the very nature of the mind, and that the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*) is accomplished not by... [external means].
He attained awakening, yet he took faith as the foundation. Therefore, although he received a prophecy of his future enlightenment, he still passed through many kalpas and served many Buddhas;
this precisely corresponds to the forty-two stages, which proceed from faith and understanding toward practice and realization.
If these various stages were not established, how could the ignorance accumulated over kalpas be suddenly purified? How, then, could the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood be attained all at once?
How perfect! Observe the ritual of transformation, and you will understand the intent behind the Tathāgata’s teaching from beginning to end.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi... [up to] ...that which even pratyekabuddhas cannot know.

This World-Honored One has emerged from meditative concentration and extols the profound twofold wisdom of all Buddhas to certify his own wisdom, intending thereby to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas realizes the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm and penetrates to the very end of every speck of dust and hair;

thus, their true wisdom is profoundly deep. Yet, in accordance with the capacities and needs of those following the three vehicles, the ninefold teachings they have proclaimed serve universally to attract and guide them.
Sentient beings enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, this is called entering the gate of wisdom.

Although the words are manifold and their distinctions are not uniform, they all serve to point toward the ultimate ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision within the one mind. Because the words are near while the meaning points to the far, it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter;
thus, it is the profoundness of provisional wisdom. Those of the two vehicles, possessing shallow wisdom and attached to marks, are unable [to comprehend it].
Because he had thoroughly realized the purport that transcends words, he was unable to know [the Buddha's mind]. It was not that his wisdom was insufficient to enter it;
rather, Śāriputra, being the one most suited to the occasion, was moved by the underlying intent to stimulate the two vehicles.

Why is this? Because the Buddha has personally attended [to many Buddhas]—up to and including the fact that the underlying intentions (*abhiprāya*) of his various teachings are difficult to comprehend.
This explains the reason why these two types of wisdom are so profoundly deep. By attending to many Buddhas, one fully attains the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of the Buddhas.
By fully practicing the Dharma, one follows the Buddhas in cultivating the wondrous path and the regulations for benefiting sentient beings.
Thus, he mastered them all. His progress was such that he did not cease until he had penetrated the Dharma thoroughly.
Because of his courageous and diligent exertion, his true virtue was filled within him and his reputation spread far and wide. Such is one for whom both name and reality flourish together.

Because he has accomplished unprecedented dharmas, all the various teachings he expounds for sentient beings according to their needs are intended solely to proclaim the principle of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) of quiescent extinction. Therefore, his underlying intention is difficult to comprehend;
thus, it is not something known by those of the two vehicles.
"Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood until now, [I have] fully perfected the *jñānadarśana-pāramitā* (perfection of knowledge and vision).
This is the Buddha’s own praise of the profundity of his two types of wisdom (*dvividha-jñāna*), which clarifies the reason for his prior skillful means (*upāya*).
Since all Buddhas have realized this, the profundity of their own wisdom can be known. Therefore, from the time he appeared in the world and attained Buddhahood..."

Throughout the forty years since my coming, the ninefold teachings I have expounded—employing various causes and conditions, parables, and countless skillful means and provisional dharma-gates—have all without exception been intended to reveal the One Vehicle.

They were solely for the purpose of guiding sentient beings to leave behind attachment to birth and death and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Although the dharmas differ, the mind is fundamentally one and true. By me...
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with both provisional and ultimate wisdom; therefore, he speaks in accordance with the true nature of reality.

Within his provisional skillful means, the ultimate of knowledge and vision is already complete. Yet, those of the two vehicles grasp at the meaning according to the words and thus do not know the final destination.
For this reason, it is difficult for them to believe and difficult for them to understand. The opening of the provisional to reveal the ultimate has already been disclosed herein.
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision... [up to] ...the unprecedented dharmas; the Buddha has fully accomplished them all.

This praises the profound causes of the two types of wisdom. Because he has drawn near to many Buddhas and practiced all manifold dharmas, the true knowledge and vision he has realized is vast, expansive, and far-reaching;
this is precisely the functional virtue of all Buddhas. If there are the four [immeasurables]...

The immeasurable minds, the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and all other dharmas—each has been deeply realized to its ultimate limit. All unprecedented qualities have been fully accomplished.
Because the realized wisdom of these realizations is profound, their virtuous functions are boundless; this refers to the Buddha as elucidated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The wisdom of the Buddha’s realm, the Buddha’s merits, and so forth—each corresponds to the true *dharmadhātu*.

Only through ocean-like speech can one know their vastness and profundity. Because that which is realized is profound, [the Buddha] skillfully distinguishes and eloquently explains all phenomena according to the capacities and needs of sentient beings.
Observing their faculties and meeting them where they are, his words do not contradict their inclinations; therefore, they are gentle and supple.
He never misses the proper time, and thus the assembly is delighted; this is the profound and wondrous nature of his skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
The meritorious functions of the Buddha cannot be fully described; in brief, he has realized all immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
This is why the followers of the two vehicles (*dviyānika*) are unable to know them.
"Stop, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further [up to] 'thus, from beginning to end, they are ultimately equal.

This correctly reveals the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. The reason it was spoken and then immediately halted is that this Dharma transcends ordinary understanding and must not be discussed lightly.
Fearing that those who hear it might be startled, doubtful, or disbelieving, it can only be..."
It is simply that the words are difficult to understand; I do not dare to speak of the reasons why.
Yet, the reason they cannot be spoken of is that the rare and marvelous dharmas realized by the Buddha are difficult for those of the three vehicles to believe and difficult for them to understand.
Only a Buddha and a Buddha can thoroughly penetrate the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. This is a dharma that transcends speech and is difficult to comprehend; how could it be...?
How light and easy this discourse is! It explains below the reasons why the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) is difficult to understand.

Now, as for all phenomena, they do not exceed their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), nature (*svabhāva*), essence (*bhāva*), function (*kriyā*), causes (*hetu*), conditions (*pratyaya*), fruits (*phala*), and retributions (*vipāka*), from beginning to end; they are exhausted within these ten factors.

All these are easy to see and easy to believe; what difficulty could there be? Because one manifests the true mark (*dharmatā*) by means of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), it is profound, subtle, and difficult to understand.
What is called the true mark of all phenomena? If one speaks of its mark, the mark is itself markless; this is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the mark.
If one speaks of its nature, the wondrous nature is innate; this is the suchness of the nature. If one speaks of...
As for its essence: the essence is itself true and eternal; the essence is suchness (*tathatā*). If one speaks of its power: the functioning of its power accords with the truth;
the power is suchness. If one speaks of its activity: it acts while being without action; the activity is suchness. If one speaks of its cause: arising is fundamentally non-arising;
the cause is suchness. If one speaks of its conditions: their nature is empty yet they accomplish phenomena; the conditions are suchness. If one speaks of its fruit:
The fruit does not depart from the cause; this is the suchness of the fruit. If one speaks of its retribution, the nature of karma is manifest; this is the suchness of retribution.

If one speaks of the beginning and the end, then from start to finish it is a single limit; this is the suchness of the beginning and the end. Among all these dharmas, each and every one is a dharma of suchness.
Therefore, they are ultimately equal, quiescent, and non-dual. This is the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas.
Furthermore, those dharmas that are easy to believe and easy to understand are known by all of the three vehicles; however, those dharmas that are difficult to believe and difficult to understand—
namely, the elucidation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas— can only be fully exhausted by Buddha after Buddha,
and are certainly not something that can be known by the two vehicles.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable... [such people as these] cannot withstand his power."
This verse reiterates that the two wisdoms are profoundly deep and difficult to comprehend, thereby manifesting the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).

To call the Buddha the "Hero of the World" (*loka-vīra*) means that he is called a "hero" because there is no "female" (inferior being) to match him; it is a title signifying that the Buddha transcends both ordinary beings and *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, standing alone as supreme.
When speaking of the fruit attained at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this specifically refers to Vairocana Buddha at the Bodhi-maṇḍa. At first...
Having attained perfect enlightenment, he realizes the ocean-like wisdom that exhausts the Dharma-realm; this is the fruit induced by causes cultivated over vast eons.
As this is the realm of the Buddha’s own self-realization, it is known only by the Buddha.

When it is said that such is the "great fruition," it specifically refers to the infinite adornments of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), the ocean of fruition where all things are perfectly interfused and penetrate one another without obstruction. Therefore, it is so described.
The meanings of the various natures and characteristics can be known only by Buddha after Buddha.

Because the ocean of fruition transcends language and cannot be expressed or demonstrated, it is said that "the characteristics of speech and terminology are quiescent. This path beyond words is not an object of conceptualization or discrimination;
how could it be within the capacity of those of the Three Vehicles? It can only be entered through faith. This is the verse.
This is precisely the ground of the ultimate single reality; it is the supreme culmination to which we now return.
Because the prose account did not exhaust the subject, it is specifically elucidated here in verse.
"Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra (and so forth), they likewise could not know it.
This series of verses demonstrates the profound depth of the two types of knowledge that the three vehicles do not understand. Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom.

Even if the world were filled with Śāriputras, they certainly could not know it. Even if the ten directions were filled with Śāriputras, and the combined wisdom of that assembly of disciples were brought together, they still could not know it.
Although Śāriputra is wise, his wisdom does not equal the sharp intelligence of a Pratyekabuddha;
even if such Pratyekabuddhas were to fill the ten directions as densely as a grove of bamboo, and their collective wisdom were unified into a single mind, [it would still not be able to know].
Even throughout the vast duration of a hundred million kalpas, one could not know it. Although the Pratyekabuddhas are sharp-witted, they do not equal the great faculties of a Bodhisattva.
Suppose there were as many Bodhisattvas as grains of rice or reeds filling the ten directions;

even if they were to unify their minds for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges and contemplate together, they still could not know it. A Bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon enlightenment does not equal those on the bhūmis.
The profound realization of non-retrogression unites the minds of a multitude as vast as the sands of the Ganges; yet even if one were to contemplate it and seek it, one could not know it.

Truly, the Buddha’s wisdom is exceedingly deep and subtle. Because the Buddha’s wisdom is like space, having nothing upon which to rely, it transcends the realm of conceptual thought and consciousness.
Thus, those of the Three Vehicles, using the mind of what is known, attempt to fathom and seek it.

How could such a realm be accessible? The three stages of worthiness and the ten levels of sagehood abide within the retribution of conditioned existence; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.

Just as matters of profound secrecy within the ninefold palace are not permitted for outsiders to know, so too the Buddha’s wisdom is exceedingly deep and cannot be known by any sentient beings of the nine realms.
Again, he addressed Śāriputra: "The untainted and inconceivable [state]... (omitted)... leads them forth so that they may attain liberation.
This verse is an admonition intended to cause one to believe in the wondrous Dharma, and also to believe that the Three Vehicles are provisional means.

Because the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) transcends the path of verbal expression, it is not a realm accessible to the deliberation or discrimination of the mind and consciousness; yet the followers of the Three Vehicles, by means of their minds—
To seek it through conceptual deliberation and measurement is why it is so difficult to know.
Because its Dharma is inconceivable, profoundly deep, and subtle, only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it. All people should simply have faith in it.
If you believe that the present is the reality and the past was a provisional means, then you may abandon your attachments and enter into awakening.

The Great Sutra says: "If a person wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, they should purify their mind until it is like empty space, remaining far removed from discursive thoughts and all forms of grasping, so that wherever the mind turns, there is no obstruction.
How could this be sought through attachment or conceptual deliberation?
At that time, among the great assembly were various śrāvakas [who had heard] the extremely profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
Because the Buddha had previously forbidden it, Śāriputra had not yet expounded this; he now requested it by taking advantage of the doubts of the great assembly.

World-Honored One, in this assembly you have entered samādhi and emitted light, manifesting a rare and wondrous event. There was no one in the great assembly who was not struck with wonder and doubt. Fortunately, Mañjuśrī...

I have already explained this. Now, as I am emerging from meditative absorption, without waiting for the questions of the assembly, I myself deeply exclaim upon the profound depth of the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, I say that the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of the Dharma previously taught is difficult to understand and cannot be known by those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Yet, we have always heard the Buddha teach only the single meaning of liberation; we have already attained it—how could [it be otherwise]?
"I do not know. Yet, that the World-Honored One should suddenly and without cause make such a statement makes my mind deeply suspicious.
This is because those of the Two Vehicles merely believe the Buddha’s words;

they have not yet abandoned their attachment and stinginess, taking what was previously realized as ultimate truth and failing to recognize it as a provisional teaching. Thus, being rebuked, they give rise to doubt"—this refers to Śāriputra.

Although he is wise, he has not yet entirely escaped doubt. I wish to hear the causes and conditions for the praise offered today, and why you have requested this teaching for the sake of the assembly.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, has finally after a long time proclaimed this Dharma... up to "...desiring to hear the complete path.
This is the meaning of the request made in verse. When a Sage does not appear in the world, ten thousand ages are like a long night;
therefore, the Buddha is called the "Sun of Wisdom. For forty years prior, he had never yet praised this profound and inconceivable Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that he spoke of it only after a long time. As for his speaking spontaneously without being questioned:

this is the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), a realm of self-realization by the Buddha that is not known to the multitude; thus, there was no one capable of posing a question.
Even my own wisdom is difficult to fathom, so they were unable to ask. For these reasons, he spoke spontaneously without being questioned.
Moreover, as for the Dharma thus praised, it is the path regularly traversed by the World-Honored One; the assembly all considered it already known.
Yet now, he praises its extreme profundity and subtlety, saying that only the Buddha knows it himself and that it is utterly beyond the reach of the three vehicles.
For this reason, the great assembly has conceived doubts. As everyone in the assembly is in doubt, I too have not yet understood; I venture to ask.
"Is that which the World-Honored One praises the ultimate Dharma? Or is it the path to be practiced?
If it is the ultimate Dharma, then it is what was realized at the site of enlightenment; it is known only by the Buddha himself and is certainly beyond our reach.
If it is the path to be practiced, then for forty years we have all seen and heard it together."
As for what is commonly known, karma has already been realized; what profundity could there be? This is why doubt arises.
Desiring to hear the complete path, we wish that you would ultimately instruct us on the destination of all practices.
Therefore, we venture to make this request.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra—[passage]—“All devas and humans shall be struck with alarm and doubt.

This was a further refusal of the request to preach.
