The reason for this repeated refusal and non-explanation was that on this day he would reveal the provisional means (*upāya*) and completely abolish the three vehicles (*triyāna*), thereby shattering the old nests of those who had followed the previous teachings, like the total ruin of a family or a nation.
I fear they would all be startled and suspicious. When a luminous gem is thrown at people, few do not instinctively draw their swords; how much more so with the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma?
For this reason, I have not yet dared to cast it lightly upon others.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "...upon hearing what the Buddha has taught, one will be able to revere and believe it.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Dharma King, Supreme Honored One, please speak; pray do not hesitate, for among these immeasurable multitudes in this assembly there are those capable of respectful faith.

This is the intent of this repeated request, necessarily urging him to speak. It implies that the reason the World-Honored One had not yet spoken was perhaps because the members of this assembly possessed shallow wisdom and inferior faculties, and thus would not believe.
Now, observing the fourfold assembly, their faculties are sharp and their wisdom is clear.
They will certainly be able to believe with reverence; they will certainly not fail the World-Honored One’s revelation.
The Buddha again stopped Śāriputra, saying: "If one were to speak of this matter... [they] would fall into a great pit."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. Those with overweening pride, upon hearing it, will certainly not show respect or faith."

This is the reason for emerging [from silence] and then ceasing again. The reason I have ceased and not spoken further is not out of secrecy or stinginess, nor is it because there is no spiritual capacity [in others].
Rather, I fear that those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) might hear this and fail to believe;

for such people, who claim to have attained what they have not attained and claim to have realized what they have not realized, will consider themselves sufficient and will inevitably give rise to slander. Thus, it would not only be of no benefit, but...
Yet they would instead harm it and fall into the evil realms; to prevent such things, it would be better not to speak at all.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "...it will bring peace and security for a long night and provide great benefit."
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings, I pray you will explain the foremost Dharma... [until] they shall give rise to great joy."

This expresses the intent of his threefold request. What Śāriputra relied upon in his earnest plea was the observation that the great assembly gathered here had all long been transformed by the Buddha’s teachings;
thus, there would certainly be no one among them who possessed superior [realization].

Yet, as for those in the lower ranks who withdrew from their seats, they were all part of the same Dharma assembly as Śāriputra and had associated with him for a long time, yet they ultimately did not know his [intentions].
As for "people," one can observe their outward appearances and know the difficulty of discerning their minds; this is precisely how one may advance those who harbor increased arrogance.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "...I shall now analyze and explain it for you."

This is because he was earnestly requested to preach. For this assembly, the Buddha had already entered meditative absorption and emitted light that shook the earth, first awakening the latent capacities of all beings. This was no ordinary cause or condition.

As soon as he emerged from concentration, he immediately praised the profound depth of the two wisdoms, speaking of them spontaneously without being asked; thus, it was appropriate for him to speak directly.
Why is it that after beginning to speak, one then stops? Why must one wait for repeated and earnest entreaty before speaking?
For one reason, it is to manifest that the two wisdoms are profoundly deep, difficult to believe, and difficult to understand, and thus should not be discussed lightly.
For another reason, it is to inspire the two vehicles to delight in the Great [Vehicle], to strengthen their sincere faith, and to cause them to conceive a sense of its rarity.

Because those of the Two Vehicles constantly associate with the Buddha and regard him as ordinary, and because the Dharma they preach is easy to believe and easy to understand, they accept it immediately upon encountering it without finding it difficult.
Even if there are those who do not believe, the harm is not great; for their teaching is a provisional device and their realization is but a minor fruit, such that there is still hope for them.

Now, at this time, I reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as the true seed for attaining Buddhahood through the One Vehicle. How much more so, then, regarding that which is subtle, wondrous, and profoundly deep!
If it were explained lightly, people would still grasp at the meaning according to the literal words and fail to enter;

or, out of arrogance and negligence, they would lack faith, thereby forever severing the Buddha-seed and cutting off the true cause for attaining Buddhahood. Or they might even go so far as to slander it.
Falling into the evil realms would result in great harm; therefore, he waited for repeated and earnest entreaties before speaking.
Observe how, when the *Avataṃsaka* was about to expound the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), Vajragarbha required three houses and five entreaties before he spoke.
This was first because he feared that [the listeners] might suffer harm and thus not speak, and second because the dharma of those stages is profound, subtle, and difficult to comprehend.

To explain this without alteration, the ocean-like assembly of the Dharma-realm consists entirely of those with superior faculties; it is therefore fitting that the teaching be as solemn and weighty as it is.
Now, the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is precisely the ground-substance of the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, the inferior understanding of the two vehicles is incapable of bearing its power. If one were to cast it away lightly and fail to believe, then [one would be lost] forever.

If the roots of goodness are severed, there will be no further opportunity for attaining Buddhahood. Moreover, as the Tathāgata’s work of transformation is nearing its end, time does not wait for man;
how could there be the days and months of the past? Therefore, it is essential that the collective will be steadfast and firm, so that through a single transformation one may reach the Way.
How could the meaning of the three pauses be merely incidental?
When these words were spoken, there were bhikṣus in the assembly (up to: who, out of overweening pride, withdrew from their seats;

this was intended to stimulate the faculties of the multitude. At the time when [the teaching] was permitted to be expounded, five thousand people in the assembly prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
That the World-Honored One remained silent and did not restrain them was precisely to awaken and inspire these two types [of individuals].
Those who ride [the vehicle] should abandon their former habits and receive the teachings with an empty mind. As for those of "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*):
they have not actually attained or realized anything, yet they consider themselves to have already attained and realized it; thus it is called "overweening pride.
Furthermore, because they look down upon those who have truly attained and realized, it is termed "overweening pride. Such people consider themselves sufficient; their minds are not empty.
There is no ground for receiving the teaching. If one hears the wondrous Dharma yet does not believe and enter it, the seed of the Buddha will be forever severed.
Such a person sits in the assembly alongside those of the Two Vehicles, all harboring a sense of self-sufficiency.
As was later said by Śāriputra and the four great disciples: "The Buddha has taught the meaning of a single liberation, which we have already attained. Furthermore, he said: "I..."
Having attained what they perceive as nirvāṇa, they no longer advance to seek unsurpassed bodhi; these are all members of the class of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Because they cling to their long-standing habitual views and knowledge, how could they ever enter the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle?

Therefore, those who have now withdrawn do not cease; it is precisely because I wish to rouse these people to abandon their former reputations and habitual tendencies, so that they may purify their own minds and receive the teachings of today.
If I were to allow them to remain and thereby delude the masses, I would greatly fail the profound compassion of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra... (up to) "Yes, World-Honored One, we wish and desire to hear it.
This assembly of joy is pure and fit for teaching; being free from branches and leaves and consisting purely of the essential core, it will further strengthen the resolve of the multitude.
Therefore, it is said that even to withdraw is excellent. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "If there should be even one person who is not pure, then..."
This would cause the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) never to be accomplished, let alone by five thousand people. Therefore, it is better that they withdraw.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma... appears but once in an age, like the udumbara flower."
This is the correct exposition of the sublime Dharma. The Tathāgata, exhausting his supreme spiritual power, has used only these two words: "Thus.
Indeed, it is believed that the quiescent nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) cannot be expressed in words. "Thus" (*tathā*) is a term of direct pointing;
"Dharma" refers to the aforementioned phenomena such as the equality of nature (*dharmatā*). However, while these phenomena have not yet been seen as marvelous, they are nevertheless...
To perceive all phenomena as they truly are (tathatā) is what is called "sublime hearing. If one perceives the sublimity of all phenomena, then there is no phenomenon outside of the mind;
all that is true and eternal is none other than the true mark (dharmatā). To realize this is what is called being a Buddha.
Therefore, it is like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in an age. The udumbara is an auspicious and responsive flower that appears only once every three thousand years. When it appears...

Then a sage appears; this is to manifest in accordance with the timing. This serves as a metaphor for the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle, which is not preached in ordinary times, but is necessarily taught only when the capacity [of beings] has matured and the time for attaining the Way has arrived.
Śāriputra, you and the others should believe that what the Buddha has spoken is not false.
Above, the entire essence of the wondrous Dharma was directly pointed out;

however, because it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand, the following section—what is called the analytical explanation—is taught only as a necessity. Because it is difficult to believe, he first provides this instruction.
"You should believe this. Previously, you both adhered to the teachings of the three vehicles as being real; now that these are suddenly set aside, I fear you may not believe me.
Therefore, I exhort you to trust what the Buddha has spoken, for his words are not false.

This is precisely what the World-Honored One meant when he said that after a long time, the truth must be revealed. With this single phrase, the provisional is opened and the real is fully manifested."
...is the lowest [of the three vehicles]. What follows below is nothing other than the elucidation of this meaning.
"Śāriputra, the Buddhas teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate" (up to) "...there is no other vehicle, whether two or three."

This clarifies that the provisional (*upāya*) is itself the real (*bhūta*). It serves to reveal the subtlety of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). All Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; they all do so by means of the provisional.
Yet, one does not realize that their underlying intent is difficult to understand, for it is because the provisional is identical with the real that it is difficult to believe.

Below, the text investigates and explains this, asking: "How is it that the provisional is itself the real? It answers: "Because [the Buddhas] expound [the Dharma] through countless skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."
All dharmas are entirely beyond the sphere of mind, thought, and consciousness; this reveals the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Originally, it is not a realm of deliberation or discrimination, yet those of the Two Vehicles seek it through deliberation and thus cannot understand it.
Therefore, only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it. Thus, that which is provisional is itself the manifestation of the ultimate, without waiting for—
Therefore, it is said today that the Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of one great causal event (ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya).

That which is called "one" refers to the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*), the eternally abiding true mind (*nitya-citta*). Since there is no phenomenon outside of this mind, it is called "one.
Because it is vast and all-encompassing, and because sentient beings and Buddhas are equal, and the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, it is called "great. All Buddhas have realized...
This constitutes self-benefit and benefit for others; therefore, it is called a "matter.

Taking the inherent endowment of sentient beings as the cause, and the Buddhas appearing in the world to assist in its manifestation as the condition—relying solely on this condition, they appear in the world, and there is no other matter besides this.
Therefore, that which has been revealed through various skillful means over the course of forty years is this very mind. Consequently, the text further inquires and explains below, asking:
"What is meant by the One Great Matter? This is a detailed exposition of the One Great Matter.
That which is called the One Great Matter is the true mind inherently possessed by sentient beings; it is the knowledge and vision of the Buddhas.
Nevertheless, this mind is merely obscured by ignorance;

therefore, when the Buddhas appear in the world, they specifically reveal and point it out for the sake of sentient beings, enabling them to leave behind delusive defilements and attain purity, so that they may awaken and enter [enlightenment] by themselves.
It is for this alone; how could there be any other matter besides? Therefore, it is concluded:

"This is why the Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the one great causal event. Thus we know that the Buddhas act solely to teach and transform bodhisattvas so that they may attain Buddhahood;
this is their only concern. Originally, it was not for the purpose of teaching the two vehicles. How could there be...
Are the Two Vehicles and Three Vehicles real entities? This is where the Tathāgata fully expresses his original intent for appearing in the world:
to completely abolish the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles and uniquely manifest the wondrousness of the One Vehicle; it reaches its ultimate consummation here.
"Śāriputra, among all the Buddhas of the ten directions (up to the point where it says), 'there is not even a second vehicle, much less a third.

This is a sequential citation of the methods by which the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time preach the Dharma, used to prove that Śākyamuni’s words today are not false, as they follow established precedents and ancestral traditions. The Buddha’s intention was to say that I, with my immeasurable..."
When [the Buddha] skillfully expounds that all dharmas are for the sake of the single vehicle of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, this is not something newly created.
Rather, it accords with the fundamental principle of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time.

All Buddhas employ immeasurable skillful means, various parables, and diverse expressions to expound all dharmas, because these teachings are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. Thus, they cause all sentient beings...
Those who hear the Dharma will ultimately all attain the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), continuing until they reach the state of Buddhahood;
this is true for every Buddha. Thus we know that all Buddhas act solely to teach and transform bodhisattvas, leading them directly to awaken to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
this is their primary task. Therefore, I now follow the ritual procedure for the preaching of the Dharma as practiced by all Buddhas.
The reason why the three vehicles were taught first is that [the Buddha] knew sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated attachments;
therefore, having no other choice, he guided them according to their respective natures.
Since the Buddha teaches all dharmas to treat all minds—if there were no such minds, what use would there be for all dharmas? Thus, everything he taught was...
It is solely for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the One Buddha Vehicle and all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā).

Since even in the worlds of the ten directions there are no two vehicles or three vehicles, how could I alone be different from the Buddhas? This is a severe repudiation of the two vehicles and a complete abolition of former provisional teachings;
herein the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is fully revealed.
"Śāriputra, all Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities... [omitted] ...and within the single Buddha-vehicle, they distinguish and teach three.
This passage describes the Buddhas' intention in appearing in the world and teaching the three vehicles out of necessity. Thus do the Buddhas appear in the world, one after another.
The reason why the Three Vehicles must necessarily be taught is that we dwell in an age of turbidity and evil.
Sentient beings are stubborn, their defilements are heavy, and they are difficult to transform; thus, there is no choice but to subdue them according to their individual capacities.

For this reason, immeasurable and innumerable skillful means are exhausted. Therefore, the Dharma of the Single Vehicle is distinguished and taught as three. How could one help it? It is because of the kalpa.
The *kaṣāya* (impurity) refers to a class of sentient beings who collectively commit evil; because they assemble together at one time, it is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya*.
Holding views such as nihilism and eternalism, they possess sixty-two kinds of false views; this is called the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*.

The mental consciousnesses of sentient beings are merely disturbed by deluded thoughts, greed, hatred, ignorance, and so forth; this is called the *kleśa-kaṣāya*. By means of impure seeds, [it] arises...

Karma moistens birth, combining to form sentient beings; this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). Karmic consciousness and the life-faculty follow the karma of birth and death;
thus it is called the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*). At such a time, when the world is at the extreme of corruption and chaos, how could one be taught to attain Buddhahood all at once?
This is why he extensively employs skillful means.

Śāriputra, as for the passage from "If I have disciples" to "there is no other vehicle, only the single Buddha-vehicle," this is a severe rebuke of the two vehicles intended to strengthen their faith in the Single Vehicle. [The name of the Bodhisattvas on the stages in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is...]
A true Arhat—and indeed even Bodhisattvas on the stages who are great Arhats—how could they possibly be unaware of the matter of attaining Buddhahood?

Therefore it is said: "If my disciples claim for themselves to be Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, yet do not know that all Buddhas teach only the path of the Bodhisattva, these are not disciples of the Buddha; they are merely so-called by name."
They were merely Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; thus, upon their subsequent realization, they declared, "We are now truly Śrāvakas and true Arhats.
As for those who previously said we were not true Arhats, it was because they did not believe in this Dharma.
Furthermore, since my disciples have already realized Arhatship and attained liberation from birth and death, they should immediately seek the fruit of Buddhahood above.
This is acceptable. Those who now cling to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and consider themselves sufficient, no longer seeking to advance toward Bodhi, are all people of overweening pride (adhimāna).
If they were truly Arhats, how could they not believe in the matter of attaining Buddhahood?
This is a profound censure, yet it expresses a fervent desire for them to believe. If one were to see this directly before one's eyes...

When the Buddha teaches the Dharma, there is no one who would not believe this matter, except for those after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, who cannot see the Buddha and can only uphold the sūtras—among whom there might be those who do not believe.
Even if they lack faith at present, those who are able to receive, uphold, and understand the meaning of the teaching will also create a distant cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Such persons, if they encounter other Buddhas, will also attain definitive realization. As it is said:
The vajra-seed is not worn away throughout kalpas; it is like a person who, having eaten it, will eventually see it pass through their skin.
This is precisely what is taught in the *Avataṃsaka*: even hearing it without believing still forms the cause for the Buddha-seed.
Since the seed of buddha-nature is the true cause for attaining buddhahood, one must certainly believe in and revere it; therefore, it is said: "You all should believe with a single mind."
This explains the upholding of the Buddha’s words, such as "the speech of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is without falsehood," and so forth; it serves to conclude the introductory remarks.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who harbor overweening pride" (up to) "there are only those who are chaste and true.
This verse refers to the assembly that withdrew from their seats. While the prose section mentions five thousand in general, the verse lists three categories.

Although they are described as having overweening pride (*adhimāna*), self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and lack of faith, in sum they are all *icchantikas*. Lacking the protection of the precepts and possessing blemishes, their faculties—*rūpa*... [text truncated]

If the vessel is impure, or if one possesses but small wisdom and is like dregs and husks—meaning their wisdom is shallow and their mind coarse—and because they lack merit, they are unable to receive the Dharma;
for this reason, they depart. This assembly, however, is steadfast and genuine; therefore, I shall preach it to them.
"Śāriputra, listen well to the Dharma attained by all Buddhas... for this reason I preach this sutra.
This verse clarifies that the provisional is based upon the real. The first stanza is a general summary;

it refers to the Dharma attained by the Buddha—namely, the Great Dharma of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which is the true wisdom of the One Vehicle attained at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Because sentient beings were unable to endure it...
Therefore, he taught it through the skillful means of expedient devices. These three periods of seven days of contemplation are precisely for this purpose.

The verse beginning with "What the minds of sentient beings conceive" eulogizes the reasons why [the Dharma] cannot be borne. This is truly because the mental conceptions of sentient beings regarding the practice of the Path—whether deviant or correct;
their inclinations and preferences—vary according to the good or evil karmic fruits, in all their manifold and diverse ways.
The same applies [to the previous cases]. All of them lack the capacity for the Great [Vehicle]. For their sake, [the Buddha] did not dare to preach the Great [Vehicle].
From the two and a half verses beginning with "The Buddha, having fully known this," the text correctly clarifies the employment of skillful means (*upāya*).

That is to say, since he knows that their capacities are insufficient, he cannot help but transform them through expedient and skillful means. These ninefold teachings were all preached for the sake of such people.
*Sūtra* is called "Scripture in Accordance with Reality" (*kīya-sūtra*). *Geya* is called "Verses Standing Alone.

*Itivṛttaka* refers to accounts of the Buddha’s past conduct, such as those of Devadatta and the Ascetic Kṣānti. *Jātaka* refers to accounts of the Buddha’s previous causes, such as those of the sixteen princes.
*Adbhutadharma* refers to marvelous and rare events. *Nidāna* refers to various causal conditions, teachings, and parables.
As in the "Burning House" and other such [parables]. *Geya* means "Verses to be Chanted. *Upadeśa* means "Exegesis.

These describe the provisional teachings of the nine divisions (*navāṅga*) of the Hīnayāna, which were specifically taught for the sake of the two vehicles (*dvyāyānika*). If one adds *Vaipulya*, *Udāna*, and *Vyākaraṇa*, they become the twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga*).
In total, these are teachings given according to the capacities of sentient beings. [The following] four verses concern those of dull faculties.
The second half of the verse clarifies the meaning of the provisional as being the real.

This means that although those of dull faculties who delight in the Lesser Vehicle may have been near many Buddhas, they do not practice the wondrous path and are thus afflicted by the manifold sufferings of birth and death.
Out of compassion for such people, he teaches the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle; while this is a skillful means (*upāya*), its true intent is to lead them into the Buddha-wisdom, as follows:
The establishment of the "transformed city" (nirmita-pura) was intended to lead [beings] to the place of treasure.

It was merely a teaching through esoteric intent for the sake of discipline; it was never explicitly stated that "you shall all become Buddhas. That it was not said at all until now is because the time for such a teaching had not yet arrived. Now is precisely that time; therefore, the Mahāyāna will be definitively taught.
Yet, the "Great" (Mahāyāna) does not exist as something separate from outside the ninefold division of scriptures (navāṅga-śāsana). One need only know these nine.

The teaching of "expedient means according to the faculties" has as its primary intention solely the induction [of beings] into the Mahāyāna. Because they thereby enter the Great Vehicle, this sutra was preached;
it is not that there exists a separate Mahāyāna apart from this. Thus, the meaning of revealing the provisional in order to clarify the real is fully disclosed herein.
"There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, supple, and sharp-witted... (omitted)... they will all attain Buddhahood without doubt.
This verse now clarifies the reality for those of great capacity. With pure minds and sharp faculties, they practice the profound and wondrous Way;

thus, unlike those of dull faculties mentioned above, they are capable of bearing the Great Dharma. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is taught to them—namely, "the straightforward abandonment of expedient means."

Therefore, the records state that such a person will attain Buddhahood in a future life. Because they recite the Buddha’s name with such great roots of goodness and profound resolve, their mind merges with the Buddha;

because they maintain the pure precepts, they do not crave or cling to birth and death. Upon hearing for the first time that they shall attain Buddhahood, great joy pervades their entire body—what is called the pores of the skin radiating with bliss.
Since the seed of the Buddha-nature is so exceptionally sublime, the Mahāyāna is preached for them.
If one has not yet heard the sublime Dharma, there still remains a distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties;
however, if one is able to hear this Great Dharma, then regardless of whether one is great or small, it is certain that all shall attain Buddhahood.

This is because the rain of the Dharma is showered equally upon those of sharp and dull faculties, such that all are fully satisfied. This precisely demonstrates the great benefit of the ultimate reality.
"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma" (up to) "because [the Buddha] speaks of the Buddha’s wisdom.

This verse concludes by revealing the single reality. That is to say, although there are three vehicles as provisional names for guidance, in truth they only reveal the One Vehicle—the Buddha’s wisdom.
Thus, the provisional is itself the real. It is known that all phenomena are thusness (*tathatā*).
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is solely for this one reality" (up to) "causing all to enter the Buddha-way.
This verse describes the intent behind the Buddhas' appearance in the world, which is to teach only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The first five lines praise how the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is solely to realize the single reality; therefore, they do not deliver beings by means of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). The subsequent twenty lines provide a detailed enumeration.
It is not by means of the Lesser Vehicle that one delivers others; rather, the Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle, practicing impartial compassion to benefit all beings.
The Dharma attained is the true essence of the Dharmakāya realized at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Adorned with meditative concentration and wisdom, it manifests as the Saṃbhogakāya for the enjoyment of others. Because the Dharma-body and the Enjoyment-body are in profound unity, it is called "equality."
Since one possesses the Great Dharma of self-realized equality, how could one transform others through the Lesser Vehicle?
To transform even a single person by causing them to fall into stinginess and greed would already be improper; how much more so when it concerns many?

Whenever there is anyone who places their faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Buddha treats them with singular sincerity. It would be wrong to deceive them by pretending they are incapable, or to mislead them by pretending they are ignorant.
To covet profit and to envy excellence—these are all evils among all phenomena. The Buddha has severed them all;
therefore, throughout the ten directions, he has no fear of ill repute, nor does he have any dread of the great assembly.

Thus, with a body adorned by the primary and secondary marks, he manifests the sign of light universally illuminating, and for their sake, he expounds the Great Dharma of the true reality of the One Vehicle. This [is] the darkness...

This passage describes the events at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The "Seal of the Single Reality" (*eka-lakṣaṇa-mudrā*) is what is known as the Ocean Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
All teachings expounded by the Buddha are sealed and confirmed by this Seal of the Single Reality; therefore, they are not confused with those of Māras or externalists.

The first verse concerning the *śarīra* relics describes the original intent for appearing in the world. The first verse beginning with "As I... describes how the present fulfillment of vows now accords with that original intent.
Furthermore,
if I were to encounter sentient beings and teach them all the Buddha-way [until] they attain Buddhahood in a future life—
this verse describes the reason for the provisional opening of the way (*upāya*). Since the Buddha’s fundamental vow was to transform all sentient beings into Buddhas...
"Buddha, why then do you speak of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles? It is because I encounter multitudes who lack wisdom;
fearing that they might fall into confusion, delusion, or refuse to accept [the truth], I therefore preach according to their capacities. This is not my original intent.
Below, [the text] extensively praises the five turbidities of this evil world, wherein sentient beings are difficult to save. Thus, one cannot help but employ skillful means. I—
The first eight lines below describe the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (defilement of afflictions). The next four lines describe the *jāti-kaṣāya* (defilement of birth).
The following eight lines describe the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (defilement of views). The final four lines describe the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (defilement of the eon).
In this world of such turbid evil, sentient beings are submerged in suffering and distress; therefore, as an expedient means, he first expounds the path for escaping suffering.
The Dharma reveals the path to Nirvana for the extinction of suffering;

however, this merely extinguishes all suffering and brings one out of the *pariccheda* (segmented) birth-and-death, rather than being the true extinction that brings one out of the *parināma* (transformative) birth-and-death. The four lines following "all dharmas" reveal the reality.
How, then, is there true extinction? Because all dharmas are from the beginning truly, eternally, and quiescently extinguished; this is the One Vehicle.
This is the wondrous Way. When the sons of the Buddha practice this, they shall attain Buddhahood in a future life.

Because those of the Two Vehicles perceive only the dharmas of the Four Truths of arising and ceasing, [the Buddha] now specifically reveals it; only then will the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world be fully realized.
"I possess the power of skillful means to reveal and teach the three vehicles, up to the single, non-dual vehicle.
This verse describes the manifestation of the ultimate reality. The Tathāgata has fully perfected the pāramitās of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.
Therefore, it is said that there is the power of skillful means. For this reason, the three vehicles are taught;
yet since all Buddhas preach only the One Vehicle, I now teach only the One Vehicle. You all should believe this with earnest clarity and without doubt.
"Throughout countless kalpas of the past, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa... [and so forth]... cause [beings] to enter the Buddha-way.
This verse shows that the Way is identical throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time. First, it clarifies the Buddhas of the past;
since all those Buddhas of the past expounded the ultimate truth by relying on provisional means, I, Śākyamuni, follow and reiterate their path.
Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords know all worlds [up to] assisting in the manifestation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This verse extensively clarifies how they assist in manifesting the ultimate truth. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, by means of other skillful expedients" (*anyaiḥ punar upāyakauśalyaiḥ*), this refers to the passage in the Introductory Chapter where Mañjuśrī says:
"Now the Buddha has emitted a radiance, coming to assist in the development of the meaning of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is the intended meaning.
That is to say, the wondrous Dharma of the true mark cannot be proclaimed by words. The Buddha first emitted a single ray of light to fully manifest his wondrous essence;
thus, the true realm of the true mark appears in its equality, and one may awaken to it without words.

This serves as the primary expedient means, for all Buddhas employ countless expedients to preach the teachings of the Three Vehicles. What is now said is that these provisional means reveal the ultimate reality. Indeed...
Because this Dharma is subtle and difficult to believe, I fear that those of the three vehicles might cling exclusively to expedient means, being stingy and unwilling to relinquish them;
if they cannot transcend words to grasp the meaning, then the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) will be difficult to clarify. Although light was previously emitted to manifest it equally, [it remains so].
It is a pity that these people do not realize it; they have already missed the mark face-to-face.

What was said previously—that "the sons of the Buddha, having practiced the Way, shall become Buddhas in a future age"—was intended for those of the Two Vehicles who, fearing the long duration of the Buddha-way, still harbor a mind of hope and waiting, and might not fully believe it.
Thus, they were unwilling to relinquish their provisional [attainments], and thereby they have failed this [teaching].
The auspicious assembly has lost its proper time. Now, [I] manifest the wondrous Dharma of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the primary ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*):

the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas. Regardless of whether one is a sage or an ordinary person, or possesses merit or lacks it—even for the minor good deeds of humans and devas—if one can simply follow the Buddha with single-minded faith, then one is a Buddha at that very moment, without waiting for further accomplishment. This is what my World-Honored One most urgently desires.

Because those of the Two Vehicles have initiated faith, [the Buddha] cites the various Buddhas who further employ diverse skillful means (*upāya*) to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, the following passage cites bodhisattvas, humans, and devas, even down to those with minute causes and minor virtues, such as raising a hand or bowing the head.

If merely reciting the name of the Buddha once causes all to have already attained Buddhahood—without waiting for it to be further accomplished—how much more so must this be true for the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles and Nine Divisions; are they not indeed the very foundation for attaining Buddhahood?

Thus, when the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) reveals that which transcends [conventional reality], whether through a staff or a shout, a raised brow or a blink, or amidst sarcasm, rebuke, anger, or abuse, it enables people to suddenly cast off birth and death.
Regarding the root of the faculty of death: is it not the case that by merely raising a hand or bowing the head, one has already become a Buddha?

Fearing that they might overlook this because a single light had previously manifested with impartiality, [the Buddha] further stated that the teaching of the Dharma through various causes and conditions is all for the sake of the One Vehicle.
Therefore, they are now further revealed by means of various minor practices. Thus it is said: "Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful means, I reveal the ultimate truth.
Viewed in this light, how could the provisional teachings of the three vehicles not be the one true dharma?
Hence it is said: "These ninefold teachings of mine have the Great Vehicle as their foundation. This is precisely what that refers to.
"If there are sentient beings who encounter the various past Buddhas... (up to) "...they have all already attained the Buddha-way.

This verse sequentially recounts the diverse skillful means (*upāya*). Here, regarding these diverse skillful means, the Bodhisattvas are mentioned first, followed by humans and devas, while the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) are not mentioned;
this is because the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-dharma*) currently available serves only as the vehicle for the two vehicles to attain Buddhahood.

This is a skillful means (*upāya*). Fearing that [the audience] might not believe, he cites practices that are beyond the scope of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to assist in its manifestation, so that they may certainly believe without doubt. Furthermore, a bodhisattva is one who has not yet attained Buddhahood;

that it is now said to have been "already accomplished" is intended to reveal that the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are indeed the practice of the true mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*). As for ordinary beings...

Such a person is not one who has already attained Buddhahood. Now, if it is said that they possess a virtuous and gentle mind, this means they are not a person of rigid temperament or stubborn resistance to transformation.
Rather, they are able to accord with the Buddha-dharma, possessing faith that does not rebel against it.

Since ordinary beings can possess such a supple and gentle mind, even though they have not yet seen the Buddha after his parinirvāṇa, they are nonetheless able to resolve their minds toward enlightenment because of the Buddha, or for...
Making offerings to the *śarīra* by sincerely constructing stūpas using the seven treasures— even children gathering sand—
or by sincerely offering the seven treasures to images— even children’s drawings made with grass, wood, fingernails, or playthings—
or by sincerely making offerings to the Buddha even with scattered thoughts, such as raising one's hands or bowing one's head with respect.

Whether one pays homage with a distracted mind and calls upon the Buddha’s name but once, or performs various such practices through subtle causes and minor virtues—these all originate from the initial resolve for enlightenment directed toward the Buddha. This is why each and every one of them has already attained Buddhahood.
Sentient beings are precisely the sentient beings within the hearts of all Buddhas; they merely go through their daily lives without knowing this existence.

Now, by giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta) following the Buddha, one comes to know that the Buddha exists. Once this existence is known, one’s own entire mind is itself the Buddha.
Therefore, whatever single practice one performs is entirely the practice of the Buddha. Thus it is said: "The moment of a single thought of faith is the attainment of Bodhi. For this reason:

"Every single word has already brought them to the path of Buddhahood; this is no empty speech. Regarding the statement that they have "already become Buddhas," according to the Tiantai doctrine of the six stages of realization (*liu ji*):

if it refers to the stage of "principle-identity" (*li ji*), they simply possess [the Buddha-nature] inherently. If it refers to the stage of "name-identity" (*mingzi ji*), they merely know the names and recognize the characters.
The meaning of "already accomplished" (*siddha*) is clear. The reason these various practices are cited as aids for clarification is this:

if those of the Two Vehicles can believe that the Bodhisattva’s six perfections and the manifold virtues of ordinary beings have all already resulted in Buddhahood, then how could the ninefold teachings of expedient means not be the wondrous Dharma of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and how could the nirvāṇa of the Two Vehicles not be [the realization of] accomplishment?

The true practice of the Buddha lies in the upright and faithful realization of one’s own mind; by not doubting the Buddha’s words, one directly realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*) in this very moment.

This is the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) in revealing the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*) through provisional teachings, which awakens the urgent and earnest resolve of those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), a state difficult to describe in words. An observer who merely follows the literal expressions...
Without deeply comprehending their minds, it is difficult to fathom the profundity of the wondrous Dharma.
As for those who, during the lifetimes or after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas of the past, heard this Dharma, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
This verse concludes by showing that the paths of the past were identical. Those of the three vehicles all personally witnessed the practices taught by the Buddha.
As for ordinary people making offerings at stupas and the like, these are all practices initiated after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, arising from the Buddha’s residual influence.
If even such incidental practices can lead to Buddhahood, how much more so the specifically established Dharma!
"The future World-Honored Ones shall be immeasurable in number" (up to) "the Guides explain through skillful means.

This verse is identical to that regarding the path of the future. The four lines concerning the original vows of all Buddhas state that the reason the future Buddhas follow the example of the present one is because of Śākyamuni’s original vow: he desires to cause all sentient beings to be like himself.
They are equal and without difference; therefore, all future Buddhas likewise share this very vow.

The eight lines following "All Buddhas" state that the Dharma attained by the Buddhas is profoundly deep; because they preach in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), their skillful means (*upāya*) are also profoundly deep.

Regarding "the Dharma is eternally without self-nature," etc., this refers to the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*), which is the primordially abiding Dharma—namely, the eternally abiding reality.
Because the mind is thus, it is called "constant. However, since the Dharma-realm takes dependent origination as its fundamental principle, it is said to be "without intrinsic nature.

Ignorance and the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the Wisdom of Universal Radiance; according to whether they encounter conditions of defilement or purity, these conditions immediately become the fundamental principle.

Defiled conditions are the seeds of the karma of birth and death, while pure conditions are the seeds of Buddhahood. Our Buddha realized this wisdom to its ultimate extent, and therefore spoke of the One.
It serves as the condition for sentient beings to attain Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that "one vehicle is taught.

Regarding the passage beginning with "This Dharma abides in its own station," it means that the Buddha preaches the Dharma in accordance with his true nature, which is called the eternally abiding function of the Sea-Seal (Sāgara-mudrā) that reflects all phenomena.
The Dharma he teaches all remains unmoved from the primordial limit (*koṭi*); therefore, it abides in the station of phenomena (*dharmapada*).

Because it abides in the station of phenomena, the characteristics of the world are themselves the eternally abiding true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Thus, there is not a single phenomenon that is not real.
This is precisely what is realized at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), namely, the primordially abiding Dharma, which is true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*). By means of this foremost...

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is quiescent and beyond words; it is only through the provisional wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that it is expounded for the sake of the multitudes.
Therefore, every teaching spoken accords with reality, and thus the provisional is itself the real. This refers to what is called the profound depth of the two types of wisdom.
This specific account concerning those among the future Buddhas is intended as a model to be transmitted to those who are to receive their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).
"The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions, who are honored by devas and humans" (up to) "expounding according to appropriate skillful means.
This verse indicates that the path of the present is the same [as the past]. The first eight lines clarify that the provisional (*upāya*) is itself the real (*bhūta*).
The subsequent eight lines, beginning with "knowing the multitudes," clarify the various methods used to assist in its manifestation.
Now I am likewise thus, for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings (up to) causing them all to attain joy.
These verses describe the ancestral practice of the three periods of time. The first four lines clarify that the provisional is identical to the real;
the subsequent four lines beginning with "I" clarify assisting in manifestation according to the capacities of beings—what is called "delighting the hearts of the multitude."
"Śāriputra, you should know that with my Buddha-eye I observe [the world]... and preach the Dharma of non-discrimination.
This verse is based on observing how the six realms of existence are muddied by the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*); it sequentially recounts the causes and conditions for transcending the world.

The first sixteen lines recount the observation of the five turbidities. The Buddha is endowed with the five eyes; were it not for the Buddha-eye, one could not exhaustively fathom the realm of sentient beings.

Therefore, observing with the Buddha-eye: that sentient beings are impoverished and lack merit and wisdom is the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*); that they enter the suffering of birth and death is the turbidity of life (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*);
that they are deeply attached to the five desires is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); that they do not seek the Buddha-dharma is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*);

and that they have deeply entered into false views is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Because he observes these sentient beings of the five turbidities, he gives rise to great compassion of identical essence (*sahaja-mahākaruṇā*). Thus it is said.
This gives rise to the mind of salvation. The first ten phrases below describe the causes and conditions for his appearance in the world, thereby clarifying the three-week period of contemplation.
When Śākyamuni Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment at the Bodhimaṇḍa, the Dharma-body and the Reward-body were in profound unity as he enjoyed the bliss of the Dharma within himself.
However, upon seeing sentient beings suffering in affliction, he was moved by the power of his unconditional compassion; thus, at the beginning—
Seventh is the contemplation on deliverance. Furthermore, he contemplates that the subtle and supreme wisdom realized by himself is not something that those of dull faculties can endure;
thus, he reflects upon the means for their deliverance, asking, "How may they be delivered? This refers to the following eight lines.

This section describes the mutual resonance between the path and its response. It refers to the time when, while he was correctly contemplating transcendence, the various devas came to request his teaching;

this was the moment when the true capacity for awakening met with its corresponding response. This corresponds to what is later referred to in the text as "hearing someone say. The eight lines beginning with "I immediately" describe his twenty-eight days of contemplation.
Fearing that those of dull faculties would be unable to withstand the Great Dharma and might suffer harm, he chose instead to enter nirvana.
"I dare not venture to expound it lightly. He then contemplated the four lines below; for twenty-one days he reflected that he should follow the ritual for preaching established by all Buddhas:
to use the Dharma of the One Vehicle to distinguish and teach the Three Vehicles.

The eighteen lines following "He made this [thought]" describe how the various Buddhas exhorted Śākyamuni. Having well grasped the intention of the Buddhas, he manifested the provisional through skillful means (*upāya*).
This is indeed so. Therefore, it is said that [the teaching] is intended solely for the instruction of bodhisattvas.
The eight phrases following "Śāriputra" describe how Śākyamuni, having heard the exhortations of the various Buddhas, followed their instructions and practiced accordingly.

The ten phrases following "contemplating" correctly describe the manifestation of the two forms—the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*—hanging down like twin banners, whereby he preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for his present disciples. Prior to this, the Buddha had not yet...
He appeared in the world. Previously, the Three Jewels did not exist; it is only today that the names of the Three Jewels have come into being.

The four lines following "From long ago" clarify that although the three vehicles were taught, the original intention was solely to reveal the ultimate reality. *Nirvāṇa* refers to the unsurpassed Great *Nirvāṇa*.
It means that the suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted and the two types of death are eternally extinguished. This is because the Buddhas, throughout kalpas of long antiquity...

Regarding those things that have been praised and shown, they are all expedient means employed to reveal the ultimate reality. Therefore, as I have always taught in accordance with what the Buddhas have said:

"Although the Three Vehicles are spoken of, it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas. The twelve phrases following "Śāriputra" describe the original intent of my appearance in the world.
Because I must wait for the proper capacity [of beings], this is now precisely the time when the capacity has matured and the Buddha-wisdom should be proclaimed.

Such a wondrous Dharma is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at certain times. That is to say, if one wishes to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, one must observe the conditions of time and season.
Once the faculties and capacities have matured, the moment of the chick pecking from within and the parent pecking from without coincide; then, no further effort is required.

Therefore, regarding both mundane and supramundane dharmas, one must value the proper timing. The applications of the Buddhas and Patriarchs do not deviate from the season or miss the opportune moment;
thus it is said, "Now is precisely that time. The eight lines following "Śāriputra" describe the assembly that withdraws from their seats.

It means that once those of inferior faculties have departed, they will no longer disturb the minds of the assembly; therefore, there is joy and no fear, as there is nothing to be withheld or diverted.
Because of his compassionate and flexible mind, he has set aside straightforwardness and expedient means to preach only the Unsurpassed Way.
The four lines following "the Bodhisattvas" state that those of the former Small Vehicle, upon hearing this present Dharma, are all Bodhisattvas; their former doubts are now resolved.
Now all these [defilements] have been eliminated. Each one has gained self-confidence in their attainment of Buddhahood; thus, the twelve hundred people shall all become Buddhas.
This does not require that each be granted a prediction (vyākaraṇa) individually, for it has already been clearly determined and resolved for the assembly.
The four lines beginning with "As in the three periods" serve as a general conclusion, showing how Śākyamuni reverently follows the ritual protocols of the Buddhas of the three periods.
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world occurs at vast intervals; it is difficult to encounter them [until] there are no longer disciples of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
This verse highly praises the rarity of encountering the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), thereby strengthening the faith of those following the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). It begins by stating:
"Such a wondrous Dharma is preached by the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, only from time to time; it appears but once in a long while, like the Udumbara flower."
Therefore, I have recounted its difficulties in detail. The Buddhas appear but once throughout vast eons; how could they be easily encountered?

Although they appeared in the world, they did not immediately preach this Dharma, but rather waited patiently for the right time. Forty years passed before it was finally spoken—how could this Dharma be easily proclaimed?
Even as it is being preached today, there are still those who withdraw from their seats; thus, those who listen with faith and conviction are even more difficult to find.
One finds such a person. Therefore, this Dharma appears but once in a great while, like the udumbara flower. It is as you have correctly understood.
Although a Buddha is difficult to encounter, one has now encountered him; although the Dharma is difficult to expound, it has now been expounded.
Even though these things are difficult, they are not yet the most difficult; only those who hear and believe are exceedingly rare. Thus, there are those who rejoice upon hearing the Dharma.
Not only those who shoulder the burden with their entire being, but even those who utter a single word of praise are exceedingly rare, surpassing the udumbara flower in rarity;
this is an extreme expression of how difficult it is for faith to arise. From "You all" onwards, he exhorts them not to doubt, but to believe in the Buddha.
Having now universally addressed the great assembly, I have clearly shown that I teach and transform beings solely by means of the One Vehicle.
"You are Bodhisattvas! You followers of the Two Vehicles must by no means continue to regard yourselves as Śrāvakas.
Out of my profound compassion, I fear that you may not believe this; therefore, I have exhorted and instructed you with such earnestness."
"O Śāriputra, you śrāvakas and bodhisattvas... [up to] "...extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle.
This verse describes the intent of entrustment and protection. It means that this wondrous Dharma is the secret heart-essence of all Buddhas, which they have never dared to speak of lightly;
therefore, he earnestly exhorts Śāriputra and the others that, having now obtained this Dharma, [they must uphold it].
In this world of the five turbidities, one must not lightly explain [this teaching] to others, for fear that they might fail to believe it and thereby suffer the loss of falling into evil destinies.
If there truly are those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, such individuals are difficult to find; yet, one must not let such persons pass by.
Therefore, one should explain it to them. Hence it is said: "Extensively praising" means that one will not be reproached for speaking at length.
"Śāriputra, you should know that the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus" (up to) "knowing for themselves that they shall become Buddhas.

This verse summarizes the preceding meaning. "The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus" refers to what was stated above regarding the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—all of whom preach the Dharma that reveals the ultimate reality through provisional means.
Since you now understand that the Buddhas act according to what is appropriate, [you should likewise realize this].
Regarding the matter of skillful means, one should know that from the beginning there have been no three vehicles. One need not further doubt that śrāvakas lack the potential for Buddhahood;
rather, one should joyfully believe in oneself as a Buddha. How profound it is that the mind is so difficult to clarify!
The seed of Buddha-nature is not separated from sentient beings and Buddhas by even a hair’s breadth; it depends solely on whether one believes or does not believe.
Listen. Formerly, there was a monk who asked an ancient worthy, "What is the Buddha? The worthy said, "I say it, fearing you will not believe.
The monk said, "Since the Master speaks with such gravity, how would I dare not believe? The worthy said, "It is you yourself. The monk was left utterly bewildered.

Therefore, it is difficult to have confidence [in this teaching]. Thus, after the World-Honored One had expounded this Dharma, fearing that it might be treated as something ordinary, he charged them to cherish it and charged them to believe it resolutely. This is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood;
it takes faith as its foundation.
The General Meaning of the Lotus Sutra, Volume One;
The General Meaning of the Lotus Sutra, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Exposition by the Śramaṇa of Nanyue, Han-shan Shi Deqing.
The third chapter, titled "The Parable" (*Upamā*), is so named because it compares events and categorizes circumstances;
hence, it is called a parable. The purpose for the inclusion of this chapter arises from the Buddha’s...
The Dharma teachings have completely set aside former expedients to manifest the present reality. Those of the Two Vehicles were previously and entirely cut off from the hope of attaining Buddhahood;
however, Śāriputra, being of superior capacity, upon hearing the Buddha’s wisdom, felt great joy in his heart and gained self-confidence that he would become a Buddha.

Thus, he recounted his state of realization, and the World-Honored One specifically bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon him. As for those of middling and inferior capacities who had previously adhered to the provisional vehicle—

Because they were unwilling to abandon [their attachments] all at once, the Buddha preached the Parable of the Burning House to grant his children the provisional and ultimate truth of the three carts and the one cart;
it was only then that those of middling capacity attained realization. Therefore, this chapter follows. Together with the nine subsequent parables, each has its specific purpose.
Since it was previously stated that the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is for the sake of the single great cause and condition, now, by means of...
The elder’s sudden entry into the burning house to rescue his children is also a parable for the One Great Matter.
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy (until the passage: "born from the transformation of the Dharma, he obtained a portion of the Buddha-dharma."
This is Śāriputra’s own account of his present joy and his remorse for the faults of his past ignorance. "Leaping up" refers to celebrating his present attainment;
"sinking down" refers to grieving over his past loss. "I have always... expresses his regret and resentment toward the Buddha's [past] failings.
Although Śāriputra followed the Lesser Vehicle, he has certainly been under the Buddha’s grace and receiving the Buddha’s teachings for no fewer than a single day.

They do not yet know the Buddha’s mind and thus assume it to be partial; how much more so for others? Thus we know that the relationship between teacher and disciple is as difficult to harmonize as water and milk has been since antiquity.
From "If we [are inferior]" below, I describe how knowing the Buddha’s mind is not partial is merely the fault of being misled by greed for the small.
From "I [follow from below]" onward, I rejoice in my present attainment. As stated previously: "If my disciples do not believe..."
This dharma is not for one who is not a true arhat; therefore, Śāriputra, with self-assurance, considered himself a true son.
A true son emerges by hearing the Buddha preach the true dharma; hence it is said he was "born from the Buddha’s mouth.
He transformed my mind, which was solely characterized by attachment and stinginess; hence it is said he was "born through transformation by the dharma. Now, this great treasure of the Dharma King—
It arrived spontaneously; therefore, it is said that one has attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before... [until] teaching and transforming all bodhisattvas."
This verse records Śāriputra’s realization. He recounts his own past errors and doubts, expressing his feelings repeatedly and at length, rejoicing in his present attainment with great joy.
The ten lines beginning with "I have heard" describe his current attainment;
knowing that he had not lost [his potential] in the past, he removes his sorrow. The twenty-four lines beginning with "I was situated" describe his remorse and reproach for his past failings.
"Faults. The first eight lines, "I have always... and so forth, describe how he habitually harbored doubts and could not reach a resolution. The next twenty lines, "Now that I have heard...
and so forth, describe how he now understands his error upon hearing the Dharma, and repents for his past self-delusion in adhering to heterodox views.

The final four lines, "The Buddha... and so forth, describe the joy of having now eliminated his doubts. This concludes the verse summary of the prose section. "Having first heard what the Buddha taught... [and so on].
The following thirty-six sentences restate the circumstances of his doubt in order to explain the reason for his lack of uncertainty. How profound is the difficulty of awakening the human mind!
Even when the Buddha’s clear teaching is presented, he still doubts and does not believe; he would take the *amṛta* (clarified butter) for poison.
Initially, when Śāriputra requested that [the Dharma] be taught, the World-Honored One stopped him, saying: "There is no need to speak further. If this were spoken..."
All gods and humans will surely be struck with alarm and doubt. At first, they would have thought there was nothing to cause alarm or doubt;

yet now, Śāriputra himself reveals his own state, saying: "When I first heard the Buddha’s teaching, my mind was greatly struck with alarm and doubt, even to the point that I considered the Buddha to be a Māra.
This means that he had nearly severed his connection to the path forever. Thus, the nature of his alarm and doubt can be understood.
I understand. If it were not for the Buddha’s subduing of me through various causes and conditions, this doubt could not be resolved, and my mind would never find peace.
By citing the protocols of the Buddhas of the three periods, I have finally come to believe in the Buddha’s heart;
thus I know that Pāpīyān has no such power. It was because I had fallen into the net of doubt that I took the Buddha to be Māra.
Regarding those who are "pliant and subtle": they are moved by the Buddha’s teaching of various causes and conditions to reveal the reality.

Furthermore, the Buddha entrusted them, saying: "In your hearts arise great joy; know for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas. Therefore, my heart rejoices, and I know for certain that I shall surely become a Buddha.
The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of these two vehicles, regardless of their past causes and conditions. That is to say—
Now that forty years of arduous effort have already been expended, it is only today that I have finally found one person who accepts my teaching with faith and without doubt.
From this, we know that the harmonious union between teacher and disciple is rare; how could the work of benefiting sentient beings ever be considered easy?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra... [up to] "the Dharma for teaching Bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.
This passage recounts the causes and conditions by which Śāriputra had long been transformed by the Buddha, manifesting that his conditions have now matured and he has received his prediction.

The Dharma-realm takes dependent origination as its fundamental principle; therefore, the Buddha-nature possesses both the direct cause and the conditional cause. As it is said, "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions.

Thus, although sentient beings possess the direct cause of Buddha-nature, if they do not encounter the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and virtuous friends appearing in the world to provide the conditions for teaching and transforming them, then that nature will ultimately be difficult to manifest. As it is said, "The Buddha [acts] through one great..."
Phenomena appear in the world due to causes and conditions; this sutra emphasizes the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Although Śāriputra now believes he will become a Buddha, the text retrospectively recounts his former doubts, as if he had already lost the opportunity to attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke of the original causes for his past transformations and taught the conditions and seeds for attaining Buddhahood;

it was merely that [the disciples] had forgotten them, not that they were lost. Thus, although he now speaks of the Śrāvakas attaining Buddhahood, he does so only to cause them to know their inherent nature and gain self-confidence;
there is nothing else added to them. This Lotus Sūtra is, indeed, the cause for attaining Buddhahood.

The conditions [for this] were never previously mentioned; thus it is called "protective mindfulness. Now that they have been explained, because the conditions are seen to be ripe—namely, the act of entrustment—it is therefore given as a prediction (vyākaraṇa).
The predictions bestowed upon the various disciples below are all of this same intent.
"Śāriputra, in a future age, until the Semblance Dharma (śeṣa-dharma) remains in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.

This explains the matter of the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). "Prediction" (*ji*) is also called "bestowal of a prophecy" (*jibie*). "Prophecy" (*bie*) refers to the seeds of grasses and vegetables.

This clearly demonstrates that the relationship between cause and effect is unfailing. Although Śāriputra knew for himself that he would become a Buddha, the bestowal of his prediction was delayed by many more kalpas.
This is because those who have already performed much service for the Buddhas and possess the path of a bodhisattva will subsequently achieve fruition;

whereas śrāvakas, who abide exclusively in the Hīnayāna, have already severed their portion of attaining Buddhahood, which is not the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s teaching. Therefore, regarding the forty... [text truncated]
Over the years, through various causes and conditions, I have repeatedly given rise to the aspiration to abandon the small for the sake of the great, yet I have ultimately failed to achieve it.
This is because I do not believe that my own mind is the Buddha.

Because I do not believe it is the Buddha, all the bodhisattva paths, dharmas, and activities for benefiting sentient beings are not within my own domain; therefore, throughout kalpas, ignorance remains entirely unextinguished.

[The Buddha] said, "Broken! This is merely a withered sprout and a ruined seed. For many skillful means, the World-Honored One has sought to subdue him, yet it is only until this day that he is finally willing to believe for himself.
However, what he believes in is the mind that is neither born nor extinguished; this mind is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, from this point forward, he may advance in the practice to achieve Buddhahood. As for the practices cultivated by a Bodhisattva—
The practice for attaining Buddhahood takes the Four Great Vows as its foundation:
to deliver boundless sentient beings, to sever inexhaustible afflictions, to study immeasurable Dharma-gates, and to realize the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha.
How could those of the Two Vehicles—who harbor fear regarding the long duration of the path to Buddhahood—ever be willing to give rise to such a great resolve? Since they now possess faith...
One’s own mind is precisely that which can be taught through the Great Practice—namely, the teaching of the Bodhisattva Dharma.
This involves making offerings to many Buddhas to cultivate merit, and perfecting all practices to cultivate wisdom. When both merit and wisdom are fully complete, the Four Great Vows are fulfilled;

thus, they serve as the cause for attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, after passing through many kalpas, one finally attains the fruit, wherein name and reality are both fully realized, and the primary and secondary bodies are perfected.
It is indeed fitting that both are exquisite. As for Śāriputra’s becoming a Buddha named Puṣpārāma (Flower-Light), this is a name derived specifically from his individual causes:
"flower" represents the cause, and "light" represents wisdom. Because Śāriputra possessed the wisdom of past causes, his fruition was likewise so;
the ten titles and various explanations are very detailed. This is the general name of that Buddha. His land is named Vimalā (Free from Defilement); thus it is not comparable [to others].
In this Sahā world, the Three Vehicles are also taught; this is in accordance with his original vow. The kalpa is named Mahāratna, and thus it is not a time of the five turbidities.
There are countless bodhisattvas, all of whom possess exclusively superior faculties. The lifespan is twelve minor kalpas, and thus it is not a kalpa of extinction.
When he is about to enter extinction, he will transmit the prediction of supreme fulfillment to another, thereby ensuring that the Sublime Dharma continues in succession without end.

As for the fact that the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma shall abide in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas: this is because the time is not one of the five turbidities and beings are free from the three evil states;
thus, it is fitting that the Dharma should endure for such a long duration. This refers to what is known as a future Buddha. However, regarding the disciples who receive [the prediction]...

Regarding the records of their attainment of Buddhahood, the adornment of their external environments, the excellence of their retinues, and the long duration of their Dharma’s abiding—why is it that each of these surpasses those of Śākyamuni?
It is because within the twenty layers of Buddha-fields in the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*), those that are exceptionally sublime and wondrous are many;
whereas the single land of Sahā alone is defiled and unbearable, being of the same category as evil karma.
The land of retribution experienced by sentient beings due to their shared karma and afflictions is the realm where the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha subdues them;
it is not the subtle realm of actual retribution. Now, when the various Śrāvakas attain Buddhahood, this directly points to the adornment of their actual retribution.
Because every Buddha has completely severed all afflictions, they possess a purely singular pure cause; therefore, what they experience is as follows:
The retribution for causes is likewise incomparably pure. Although this is most excellent, it is but a single speck of dust upon a hair within the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha);
how could it exhaust the measure of the entire Dharma-realm? Only our Vairocana has realized the ultimate extent of the Dharma-realm;
therefore, he takes the entire Flower Treasury as his field of transformation. This Buddha-wisdom is profoundly deep and inconceivable.
This is precisely what is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. Later, it is said that the elder’s household was immensely wealthy, yet his son was able to inherit the family estate;
however, what he required did not exceed the capacity of his own person.
How could he possibly exhaust all that the elder possessed? By observing this, one can discern the ultimate intent of this sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Śāriputra, in a future age you shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom... (omitted)... you ought to rejoice within yourself."
This is the matter of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) given in verse. As for the statement in the verse that Puṣpārāma also became a prince and left the household life:
his original name was Dīpaṃkara-jñānavijaya, who is none other than our Śākyamuni Buddha. Both [Puṣpārāma and Śākyamuni] left the household life as princes;
thus we know that there is not a single Buddha who does not transform consciousness into wisdom (vijñāna → jñāna) and realize the three bodies (trikāya). Therefore, it says "abandoned."
The kingdom has abandoned its splendor. How could it be that Maitreya was born by heaven or Śākyamuni appeared spontaneously, such that they were accomplished without cultivation?
At that time, the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus... [up to] now he has once again turned the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"In the past at Vārāṇasī, he turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths... [up to] ...dedicating it all toward the Buddha-way."
This passage describes how the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings present at the gathering, upon seeing Śāriputra receive his prediction of enlightenment, each gave rise to joy.
Because the Tathāgata dwells in the world as the refuge for the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, they have followed the Buddha exclusively and heard the Dharma,
yet they did not know its ultimate goal— just as generals and followers of Han all longed to obtain even a few inches of fiefdom.
Thus it was. When they first saw the Tathāgata emit light and manifest auspicious omens, everyone was filled with doubt, not knowing what he intended to do.

Moreover, through Mañjuśrī, they already knew that he was about to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Yet, when he emerged from meditative absorption and preached the sutra, he merely extolled the profound depth of the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*), stating that they were beyond the comprehension of all devas, humans, and those of the three vehicles. This, in turn, gave rise to further [doubt].
This refers to being perplexed and distressed. Yet Śāriputra was the eldest son of the Buddha and one whom the fourfold assembly and the devas alike revered;
thus, he first experienced shock and doubt, but ultimately attained realization and received the prediction of his own future buddhahood.
It is therefore like a patriarch who, upon obtaining a son, entrusts the family estate to him, so that all his dependents and kinsmen have someone to rely upon and follow. Thus it is said:
The fourfold assembly rejoiced and their bodies attained liberation; thus they removed their robes to offer them to the Buddha.
From this moment on, each person knew for themselves that they would surely become Buddhas, and so all gave rise to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
This Dharma King governs the world and battles against all Māras; now, having rewarded one merit, the kingdom of the Dharma-realm is secured. How could this be a minor cause?
Ah! The World-Honored One appeared in the world for the sake of the single great cause and condition; now his original aspiration has been fulfilled.

Yet there remain those who have not yet attained faith, and these may be addressed one by one in succession. Therefore, the discourse that follows will proceed with the momentum of a vessel sliding down a slope;
those who hear it will collapse before its influence without the need for further exertion.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [and so on], requesting that the causes and conditions be explained so as to free him from doubt and regret.

This was because Śāriputra, rejoicing in his own realization and having received the prediction of his future enlightenment, yet for the sake of those who had not yet realized it, requested the Buddha to resolve their doubts;
thus he initiated this discourse through parables.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra (up to the point where it says): "Those who possess wisdom gain understanding through parables.

This is precisely the teaching of the parable of hearing.
