It means that previously, through various causes and conditions and by means of parables and words, all were for the purpose of revealing the unsurpassed bodhi of the One Vehicle and the Dharma taught to Bodhisattvas; it was stated explicitly that my Dharma has no [dual] vehicles.
As for the two vehicles, every person should know that they possess the potential to attain Buddhahood; why, then, should there be any doubt?
Nevertheless, since they have not yet awakened to this through causes and conditions, it must be further elucidated by means of parables.

The reason the "One Great Matter" (ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya) was difficult to clarify in the previous discourse is that, at the end of the "Expedient Means" chapter, it was explained directly as the manifestation of the response-body of Vairocana.
The Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body) distinguishes and expounds the One Vehicle Dharma as three; this clearly indicates that there exists the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya Buddhas therein.

Yet those of the Two Vehicles have consistently recognized only the Śākyamuni of the Nirmāṇakāya, wandering extensively through the defiled realms of the Three Worlds and clinging to the fruits of the Two Vehicles they have realized, no longer knowing that there is a matter of further transcendence.

Although the matter of manifesting in the three realms through seven days of contemplation was previously explained, because the śrāvakas possess inferior understanding, there remains that which they have not yet fully comprehended;
therefore, it is necessary to further clarify the causes and conditions for manifesting in the three realms by means of parables.
Thus, the subsequent parables are extremely clear.

"Śāriputra, if in a kingdom, city, village, or [town]... [the mind] does not feel weary or distressed and lacks the intent to seek liberation—this is precisely describing that there is no peace within the three realms.
It is spoken of as being like a burning house by way of analogy.

As for the Sahā world, it dwells within the ocean of the Flower Treasury World-System (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu-samudra), occupying but a single speck of dust or a single hair; it is like a single cluster within a kingdom or city."
It falls upon the village house. "Elder" (*gṛhapati*) refers to the Buddha, the Lord who manifests transformation from the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*.

"Advanced in years" is a metaphor for the state where the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are merged in mystery—the ground of experiencing the bliss of the Dharma for oneself. This is like the time when an elder has reached advanced age, a period of peaceful tranquility.

By contrast, the stages of cultivation and progress are likened to the vigor of youth and the achievement of meritorious deeds; if one forgets these merits and ceases their practice, it is compared to [the decline of that vigor].
The old man’s mind being at ease and having no affairs represents wealth and so forth; this is a metaphor for ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*).
The servants represent expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), which serves as attendants and messengers—what the Zen school calls "the matters of slaves and maids.

That his house is vast yet has but a single gate is a metaphor for the Buddha-knowledge and vision of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); it refers to what the Tathāgatas of the ten directions call "the one path."
This refers to transcending birth and death. Within the three realms, there are sentient beings belonging to the five destinies; hence it is said that "five hundred people dwell therein.

That the halls and pavilions are decayed and dilapidated is a metaphor for the two types of retribution—primary and secondary—of sentient beings within the three realms, characterized by impermanence and ruin.
Within the cool hearts of sentient beings, the fire of the five desires arises without cause; hence it is said:
"Suddenly" refers to the sons of the elder, which is a metaphor for those in the three good realms.

To say that "beings among the five paths who are capable of receiving transformation are but one in ten" means that when the elder saw this great fire below, it was a metaphor for the Buddha’s eye observing the beings of the six paths.
Because they are impoverished and lack merit and wisdom, they do not perceive or know; thus, they abandon suffering only by means of further suffering, and so they have no seeking [for liberation].
The underlying intention: The Buddha, seeing the suffering of sentient beings to be such as this, gave rise to a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to rescue and deliver them.
Śāriputra, this elder thought thus... (until)... he merely ran back and forth playing, looking for his father.
The following passage is a metaphor for the seven-times-seven reflections; it expresses the intention of relying on the ultimate truth to manifest provisional means.

"The strength in his hands and body" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s possession of both supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) and the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*). "The garment-bag (*kośa*) and the small table (*mañca*).

A "garment-bag" is like the lap or breast of a robe in this region, which can be grasped and lifted. A "small table" is like a chair or a sedan chair in this region, which can be carried and supported. These serve as metaphors for...

This is also an inclusion. "One gate" is a metaphor for the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Because it does not extensively reach all capacities, it is called "narrow and small. That is to say:

"If I were to rely solely on the power of my supernatural faculties and the power of my wisdom, abandoning skillful means (*upāya*) to praise the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge and vision and his fearlessness, sentient beings would be unable to attain liberation thereby. [Therefore,] one must have faith in the Dharma of the One Vehicle.
[Such people] are rare; thus, those who attain deliverance are few. [The Buddha’s] intention was to employ skillful means (*upāya*) so that sentient beings might believe and consent for themselves;
had he done so, those transformed by the teaching would have been numerous. This illustrates the first seven days of contemplation while newly seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

If he had merely praised the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would not have been able to believe this Dharma. Therefore, during the second seven days of contemplation, he taught based on [the capacity of] beings.
This is a provisional [expedient] (upāya). Therefore, it is said that "the single gate is narrow and small," meaning that one must intentionally establish a separate expedient.

When the Buddha employs his supernatural powers (ṛddhi) to gather, support, and uplift sentient beings, they cannot be so reached; those who must necessarily attain self-confidence and self-conviction are precisely those for whom one cannot walk by taking their hand.

Only when others act for them and they themselves attain conviction do they finally become intimate with the teaching. If a person does not believe and does not attain conviction, [they remain distant].
"Then they would be those whom even the Buddhas could not transform. "The children are young and small" below serves as a metaphor for sentient beings who, being ignorant, are difficult to transform.
Intending to employ skillful means, [the father] first describes their perils so that they may become aware of fear and dread, and thus be willing to come out of their own accord.

This is the beginning of the three turnings, wherein he first demonstrates the miserable conditions of the triple world. "Although the father... below serves as a metaphor for sentient beings' delusion and confusion.
Having received these teachings, they did not seek the Buddha Mahāsthāmaprāpta nor the Dharma for the cessation of suffering;
thus, they regarded him merely as a father, lacking any heart of intimacy or trust.
At that time, the elder had this thought... [omitted] ...they vied with one another to run and rush out of the burning house.

These words describe the elder’s rescue from the conflagration; they are a metaphor for the Buddha’s seven days of contemplation, manifesting his body within the triple world and initially preaching the Three Vehicles.
Now, although the Buddha has already transcended the triple world, the statement that he and his sons would all be consumed by the fire is as follows:
This illustrates how the Buddha-nature exists within the five desires and afflictions of sentient beings.
If it is not revealed through skillful means, the seeds of Buddhahood will inevitably be severed and extinguished; thus, it is said to be "like burning.

That which was previously cherished by the mind illustrates how sentient beings, through attachment to various desires, fall into the cycle of birth and death; now, likewise, by means of various desired objects...
To guide them, he taught the various expedient means of the Three Vehicles; that is to say, first using the hook of desire to draw them in, and later leading them into the Buddha’s wisdom.
The phrase "pushing and shoving one another to compete for escape from the burning house" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s residence at the Deer Park.
The various non-Buddhists, such as Śāriputra and others, each leading their own followers, vied with one another to take refuge in the Buddha.
This "pushing and shoving" serves as a metaphor for the manner in which the disciples at the beginning of their practice abandon the heterodox for the orthodox;
it is sufficient to demonstrate that the provisional skillful means (*upāya*) of the Three Vehicles possess great power.
At that time, the elder saw his sons [and so forth], attaining what they had never experienced before and which was not what they had originally expected;
this is a metaphor for the intent of abandoning the three vehicles to reveal the one.

The passage stating that "the elder saw his sons escape and his heart was filled with joy" is a metaphor for those of the various *hīnayāna* vehicles who, by hearing the Buddha's teaching, emerge from the triple world and realize the fruit of the Four Noble Truths.
There are no longer any obstructions of birth-and-death or afflictions; thus, it is like sitting in the open air.
Just as the sons’ minds are at peace, the father is likewise leaping with joy. It is just as when the son is ill, the father is also ill, and when the son is at ease, the father is also at ease.
Through the great compassion of shared essence (*samatā-karuṇā*), the Buddha gathers and transforms sentient beings; the meaning is seen herein. At that time...
The sons approaching their father and requesting vehicles is a metaphor for the śrāvakas who cling to provisional fruits as being real.
The elder giving each of them a single great vehicle and so forth is a metaphor for preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* now, bestowing upon each the prediction of attaining Buddhahood;
this is called "giving equally" to manifest the equality of Buddha-nature. That the vehicles are high and wide is a metaphor for the vastness of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

"Great indeed! As for the phrase "adorned with various jewels," it reveals that the elder’s wealth is immeasurable; it serves as a metaphor for the profundity of the One Vehicle and the two types of wisdom.
That is to say, he has fully perfected the *pāramitās* of skillful means (*upāya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and vision (*darśana*).

The flower garlands used for external adornment serve as a metaphor for the provisional wisdom of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya-jñāna*). The elegant mats and crimson pillows serve as [the adornment of]... [internal splendor].
The interior represents the Dharma-joy of true wisdom. Being drawn by white oxen represents the Great Dharma, which only sentient beings of great faculties are capable of bearing.
Their skin color and so forth represent the purity of those with great faculties. Their great strength represents their capacity to bear the burden.
Their gait being level and upright represents correct practice. Their speed being like the wind represents sharp faculties. Having many attendants represents manifold skillful means.
This is self-comforting. Why is this so? [The passage] below provides his own explanation for the meaning of "bestowing great chariots equally.

It means that since the elder’s wealth is immeasurable, he ought not to be lavish toward himself while being stingy toward his sons; this is precisely a metaphor for the Buddha dwelling in the Mahāyāna himself.
If he were to convert others using the Hīnayāna, it would constitute falling into avarice and greed. Now, from "this" below, is the conclusion: viewing all [beings] as one.
"Son" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s contemplation of sentient beings within the three realms as being like an only son; therefore, his love is without partiality.

As for the passage beginning "Why is this so?", it is a metaphor for the Buddha’s inexhaustible treasury: having already given to others, he possesses even more himself, and thus it is said that he is not depleted.
The phrase "the sons each riding great chariots" and so forth is a metaphor for the two vehicles now attaining Buddhahood, which truly exceeds all expectations.
[This is] external. Śāriputra, what do you think? ... "Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said. This Buddha truly [asked], Śāriputra:
"If a householder promises three and gives only one, would that be false? [He replied: "No, because of the three..."
The chariots originally do not exist; this is a metaphor for the provisional establishment of the Three Vehicles, whereas only the One Vehicle is real.

Regarding Śāriputra’s statement that his words were not false, his intention was to say that even one's own body and life are precious, let alone external objects. Having already preserved one’s entire person and secured one’s life is itself a great gain;
how much more so when one is spared from the calamity of the burning house? Thus, it would still be insufficient not to grant even the smallest single chariot.

It is not false. Since the elder’s original intention was merely to employ a provisional device as an inducement, how much more so now that he has bestowed upon them all equally a single great jeweled chariot, which exceeds their expectations;
how could this be false? Thus, Śāriputra has already come to believe that the three vehicles are provisional while the one vehicle is real;
in this way, the great disciples may attain awakening through this parable. Therefore, the Buddha—
He praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent! It is well that you have so perfectly accorded with the Buddha's mind.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also like this: [up to] "he distinguishes and speaks of three within the single Buddha-vehicle."
This applies the Dharma to the analogy. Because the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings with the mind of an only son, he is the Father of the World;

thus, he is likened to the elder who is the master of the house. His birth within the three realms below corresponds to the vastness of that house, as he has accomplished immeasurable knowledge and vision, just as the elder is of great wealth.
He inherently possesses the intent to rescue [beings] from the conflagration.
Because of the mind, one is born within the three realms. Sharing the sufferings of the people, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, leading them to the ground of peace and security;
thus, he desires to cause them to attain bodhi. When he sees all the sentient beings below, the fires have broken out on all four sides of the house.
The sons were so deeply immersed in their play that they did not consider it a cause for concern. Śāriputra [descends].
The elder, unable to devise a strategy to save them from the fire, reflects that this house has but a single door, which moreover is narrow and small; he contemplates a means to rescue them.
"If I were to rely solely on my supernatural powers and such, even though I reach the sentient beings, they would not be able to be delivered by this. Indeed.
This corresponds to the meaning of the narrowness of the single gate. As for the passage beginning "Why is this so?":
it corresponds to the father’s employment of skillful means and expedient devices to gather his children who were deluded and confused. As for the passage beginning "Just as that elder...":

it corresponds to the provisional assumption of the three vehicles to entice the children, while his original intention was to bestow a single great vehicle equally upon them all. As for the passage beginning "And he spoke these words...": it corresponds to the use of kind words.

This is an inducement and illustration for the sons. "Quickly exit the triple world below" corresponds to the elder’s permission for the three carts outside the gate, by which they may play and find joy.
"If there are sentient beings below" corresponds to the sons exiting the house and approaching their father to request the carts.
In the parable, the three were permitted though originally there were no three; in the Dharma, the three are permitted so that each may individually realize the fruit. The intent is to...

The followers of the three vehicles know that their former fruits were provisional. Although the phrasing of the dharma and the metaphor are not identical, the intent lies in opening up the provisional to reveal the real.
This section generally clarifies the provisionality of the three vehicles, corresponding to the sons hearing the promise of the three carts and vying to escape from the burning house.
From the passage "Just as that elder... onwards, it will reveal the present reality, corresponding to the elder [bestowing the carts].
"Each is bestowed with one great white ox-cart. This reiterates the parable to apply it to the Dharma.
The Tathāgata is likewise so; this truly reveals the present reality: that each and every person of the three vehicles is granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, it is said, "All are brought to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s extinction. The phrase "these various assemblies" below applies [the parable] to the bestowal of the carts upon all.
The "one great precious chariot" adorned with various treasures, lacking nothing, is a direct metaphor for the Dharma-realm’s adornment and the complete fulfillment of myriad virtues.
The "supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss" corresponds precisely to the "soft mat and crimson pillow," which refers to the true wisdom that personally experiences the bliss of the Dharma.
The passage beginning with "Just as that elder... further clarifies the initial granting of the three vehicles.
"False. This precisely accords with the present occasion of establishing the provisional to reveal the real. One should truly believe that this reality is not empty.

"The Tathāgata is also like this," and so forth, concludes the parable to clarify the intent of opening the provisional and revealing the real. The Dharma-treasury realized by all Buddhas is profoundly deep;

there is nothing they do not exhaustively bestow upon sentient beings. However, because the Dharma is great while the capacity of the faculties is small, [sentient beings] are unable to receive it in its entirety.
This is why the One Vehicle Dharma is explained by distinguishing it into three.
Desiring to reiterate this meaning, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Suppose there were an elder who had a large house (up to) where five hundred people resided within it."

This verse uses the metaphor of a householder to illustrate that the Buddha is the refuge for the three realms; thus, he is like the master of the house. The fact that the house is ancient refers to the twelve subsequent lines.
The "three realms" metaphorically represent the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment) produced by the common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*) of sentient beings.

The "hall and chambers" collectively represent the *mūla-vipāka* (primary retribution) produced by the individual karma (*asādhāraṇa-karma*) of sentient beings. "High and dangerous," etc., represents the state of impermanence and decay. "Ancient... [The text continues].
Therefore, it is said that this has been so from the beginning and is not merely the case now. Five hundred people dwell within it;
thus, sentient beings of the five realms of existence all cannot escape the suffering of impermanence—birth, old age, sickness, and death.
From the owls, hawks, eagles, vultures, crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons (up to) the various poisons, harms, fires, and disasters—these are not of one kind.
This is a detailed metaphor for the sentient beings of the three realms; it fully sets forth the circumstances of the causes and effects of their evil karma.

The previous statement that there were five hundred people within this dilapidated house, yet mentions only ten, twenty, or even thirty "sons," is intended to indicate that among the sentient beings of the five destinies, those capable of receiving transformation do not exceed one in ten.
This specifically refers to the virtuous classes of humans and devas; those who do not receive transformation and instead create evil are numerous. Now, [the text] speaks of evil in general.
Sentient beings driven by karma indulge in greed, anger, and ignorance;

due to the various impurities of afflictions and the manifold, diverse habitual tendencies of inversion, they experience the differing bitter fruits of the three miserable realms. This is truly terrifying.

The one hundred and thirty-two lines of this allegory collectively reveal that the causes and effects of the three miserable realms all arise from the evil habits, emotions, and perceptions within the human realm.
The manner of summoning them differs; this is likely because one cites the effect to verify the cause. Although these are spoken as metaphors, they are in fact actual phenomena.
This can be corroborated by the "habitual causes and reciprocal retributions" described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

The sixteen phrases beginning with "It is like an elder" generally metaphorize sentient beings within the triple world, while the twenty-four phrases beginning with "owls, crows, eagles, and vultures" specifically describe those in the realm of animals.
This is the law of cause and effect. Among the various creatures—whether flying, crawling, or wriggling—insects and soft-bodied beings—there are differences in the magnitude of their physical forms.
Some indulge in lust out of greed, while others unleash poison through the habit of anger; their wickedness is equal.

As the three poisons erupt unrestrainedly without inhibition, it is said that they "cross and run amok. The bodies of males and females consist of all manner of impurities, such as excrement and urine.
They overflow with such greed, attachment, and clinging that they do not relinquish them. Truly, it is like dung beetles gathering in manure or foxes and wolves gnawing at corpses;

their greed for acquisition knows no end. Like a pack of dogs in a state of panic seeking food, they struggle and compete without ceasing, tearing at one another and letting out the foul sounds of howling and barking. Such are the causes and effects of these animal-like beings. All...
This is the manifestation of the three poisons; therefore, it is said that "the house is terrifying and its transformations are such. This speaks generally of the conditions of the animal realm.
Regarding the phrase "in every place," etc., this specifically reveals the causes and effects of the hungry ghost realm.

To say that they exist "in every place" means that there is not a single sentient being who does not, through a mind of *chimei* (goblins) and *wangliang* (sprites), become part of the hungry ghost realm.
This is the cause. Regarding the yakṣas—translated as "suffering-living ghosts"—those said to eat human flesh do so because, in their former lives as humans, their evil karma was profound and heavy;
they damaged the Dharma-body, injured the life of wisdom, and severed their roots of goodness.

Consequently, they fell among the ghosts and must sustain themselves through suffering, taking human flesh as their food. These are those who, having been human, entered the realm of ghosts due to the three poisons.
They nourish one another; hence they are called "producers. They cling to them with stinginess and refuse to let go; hence they are called "guardians.

Because these beings, having been animals, enter again into the miserable fruit of the realm of ghosts, the yakṣas scramble for and devour them. This is how they pass from the animal realm into the realm of ghosts.
Since the animal species are already numerous, the realm of ghosts is likewise flourishing; thus, once they have eaten their fill, they become malicious.
The mind becomes increasingly inflamed; past habitual tendencies manifest and strike against one another. Therefore, the sounds of their fighting and quarreling are truly terrifying.
*Kumbhāṇḍas* are called "fearful ghosts" or "ghosts of impermanent death.

Regarding the phrase "at times leaving the ground," it means that sometimes a single thought of goodness may lead one to the realms of humans or devas, yet one immediately falls back down; hence it is said they "come and go" and wander about.
Regarding the term "playful sport": it refers to being in other evil realms as if in pleasure gardens or parks.
The hungry ghosts seize these animals; the animals fear death while the ghosts take delight in it. Thus it is said that they "frighten dogs for their own amusement.

Although there are many kinds of animals, the dog is singled out because dogs are habituated to associating with humans and their greed and anger are particularly intense. Furthermore, below this, there are various ghosts... [text ends].

Regarding the appearance of the hungry ghosts (*preta*): their bodies are massive and naked; their countenances are said to be hideous. They dwell therein eternally, meaning for a vast duration of time.
Once fallen into this state, they pass through five hundred *kalpas* without even hearing the names of water or drink;

hence it is said they "wail while seeking food. Their bellies are distended, their throats are like needles, and their heads are like those of oxen—thus their forms are described as hideous. They eat and devour human beings.
"Dogs": this means that both humans and animals alike fall into this category. "Their hair is disheveled" describes their hideous appearance. "Cruel and predatory" describes their evil nature;
all of these result from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from past lives. "They howl and run about" is caused by the pressure of suffering.
Below the term *yakṣa*, it generally concludes the section on ghosts and animals; all possess the desire to escape, yet there is no door through which they may exit.
Therefore, one merely peers through the window and concludes: "Such immeasurable hardships and terrors as these are all the actual retributions of the three poisons.
This is an instance of citing the effect to clarify the cause; the emphasis lies on the cause.
Since both categories exhibit the manner of mutually creating karma, the subsequent mention of the hells emphasizes their effects in general. This is [the meaning of] "朽" (xuǐ).
Below the section on the "Old House," [the text] generally reveals the causes and effects of the hells.

Since the two classes of beings [gods and humans] merely experience the torments of hell but cannot create them, the author, intending to clarify the nature of hell, again mentions the owner of the house.

This is metaphorically intended to show that this decaying house of the triple world can only be transformed by the Buddha; thus it is said to "belong to one person. Furthermore, the sentient beings of the triple world, by means of the three... [text fragment ends].
The poison is fierce and blazing; thus it is said that "suddenly fire breaks out. When the ruin of impermanence arrives, regardless of whether one is a ghost or a beast, all return to hell.
Therefore, when the house is consumed by flames, the ghosts cry out in great distress, and the insects are terrified, unable to escape on their own.
This is what is meant by: "If one does not cultivate merit while alive, one returns to a place of suffering upon death. Such are the evil beasts and venomous insects.
At first they spread their poison crosswise and horizontally; now they are fainted and unconscious.
Thus it is said that they "hide in holes and burrows," which describes the state of extreme suffering in hell. *Piśāca* means "tormenting and harming ghost.
It is said that even afflictions have no power to act here; thus it is said that they also "dwell therein. All of these are born without merit and virtue, and are therefore oppressed by fire.
They enter the hells, where enemies seek one another out; thus it is said they "mutually harm one another.
As for those such as the jackals, at first they indulged in greed and anger by gnawing on the corpses of others;
now they have died, and their own corpses are devoured by various great beasts of prey. Since the entire hell is ablaze with the fires of karma, it is foul-smelling.

Smoke fills the air, so dense that one can see nothing. Centipedes and venomous snakes, which initially displayed their venom to harm people, now scramble out as they are scorched by the fire, only to be devoured by malevolent ghosts; these are beings emerging from the hells.
They further fall among the animals. As for the hungry ghosts (preta), they are originally summoned by the habit of lust.
Taking birth as the fire of desire and death as the fire of karma, the fire burns upon their heads; having neither drink nor food, they wander about in agony from hunger and thirst.
Yet they are unable to escape this ultimate destination of the evil karma of the three poisons. Therefore, the summary concludes:
"That house is like this; it is truly terrifying, with manifold perils. How profound is the delusion and confusion of sentient beings!"
The three poisons burn fiercely; thus, they evoke the severe retributions of the three miserable realms. All of these result from being deluded regarding the One Mind.
Therefore, one should know that the evil matters of the three miserable realms are all merely objects manifested by the mind alone.

The Buddha first used the metaphor of a burning house to represent the triple world, speaking of its most prominent features. Within that house dwell various malevolent birds and beasts, as well as various malevolent spirits.
These are all actual realities within the three evil realms, as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding the internal differentiation of cause and effect.
Although these are spoken of as metaphors, they actually clarify the cause by means of the effect; they do not employ external objects unrelated to the realm as metaphors.
Thus, while the three poisons of sentient beings serve as the causes for the three miserable paths, although their physical forms have not yet transformed, their minds—

I have already discussed this together with them. Although the ancient commentaries on the integration of the exoteric and esoteric teachings are detailed, they are not as vital as focusing on the actual reality of cause and effect.
Therefore, I have not had the leisure to treat each point individually; here, I shall merely provide a general overview of the broad principles.
If you wish for a full and precise elucidation, please consult the separate commentary.
At that time, the owner of the house stood outside the gate... [until] he played and enjoyed himself with ease and without hindrance.
This verse describes the elder’s rescue from the fire. The owner of the house standing outside the gate is a metaphor for the Buddha alone emerging from the triple world.
Hearing someone speak is a metaphor for the three-week period of reflection [and] the invitation by the Brahma Kings of the heavens to turn the wheel of Dharma.
"First, regarding 'playing for sport': this refers to sentient beings within the three realms who, initially due to ignorance, allow their afflictions to run wild and thus fall into the three realms.
Since they did not originally have the intention to fall, it is called 'sporting.

The four lines following 'When the elder heard this' are a metaphor for the Buddha manifesting his body within the three realms to share the sufferings of the people. The sixteen lines beginning with 'He exhorted his children' [are as follows]."
This parable is intended to explain the Three Vehicles; it first demonstrates the characteristics of the suffering and afflictions of birth and death.

The four lines beginning with "The sons" eulogize how the sons have no intention at all to leave [the house], which is a metaphor for sentient beings who, though hearing the Buddha’s teaching, do not believe it.
The twenty-four lines beginning with "At that time, the elder" metaphorically represent the Buddha’s initial teaching of the Three Vehicles as provisional names used to guide them.
The sons hear the teaching of the six subsequent lines. The sons hear the teaching of the three vehicles and vie to exit the house;
this is a metaphor for sentient beings relying on the Buddha’s Dharma to emerge from the triple world. "The elder sees his sons" and so forth, comprising twenty lines;

this is a metaphor for the joy of the compassionate father when sentient beings are freed from suffering. "The labor of giving birth was exceedingly difficult" means that a human body is not easily obtained.
Thus it is. At that time, the twelve phrases beginning with "the sons" serve as a metaphor for the three vehicles adhering to provisional means while awaiting the ultimate reality.

The thirty phrases beginning with "the elder, who was immensely wealthy," serve as a metaphor for the present exclusive teaching of the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle. [This is] the adornment of precious objects.
This illustrates the fruit-dharma of the One Vehicle, in which all myriad virtues are fully present. The six lines following "At that time, the sons of the Buddha...
illustrate the joy felt upon hearing the Dharma now.
[The Buddha] says to Śāriputra: "I am also like this" (up to) "all shall surely attain the Way of the Buddha."
This verse uses the Dharma to correspond with the metaphor; each of the ten preceding sections may be understood accordingly.
In sum, all serve to abandon the provisional and resort to the real.
This vehicle is subtle, wondrous, pure, and supreme (up to the point where it is stated that) there is no other vehicle except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
This verse extensively praises the virtues of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It is that which the Buddha delights in; he says that the One Vehicle is what the Buddha joyfully expounds.

As for the Three Vehicles, they were originally not his fundamental intention. Regarding "days, nights, and kalpas," this means that once one enters the wondrous Dharma, all notions of duration—whether long or short—are forgotten.
One finds self-delight in the Dharma, regardless of whether it be great or small, until finally attaining Buddhahood.
It is non-retrogressive. Therefore, he concludes with these causes and conditions: there is no other vehicle.
He addresses Śāriputra and the rest of you: [you have appeared] for the sake of establishing sentient beings in peace and security, and thus manifest in the world.
This verse further clarifies that the Buddha appears in the world to save sentient beings and teaches the Dharma in accordance with their capacities;

it expresses the meaning of the statement, "I am the father of all the worlds," and so forth. The phrase "all are my children" indicates that the sentient beings of the three realms constitute the stage of being the Buddha’s only child.
There has never been a father who does not cherish his child; it is because he sees that sentient beings have been scorched by the fires of suffering for long kalpas that [he acts thus].
Giving rise to compassion, he appears in the world to deliver and rescue beings. Because the faculties of sentient beings are inferior, he first establishes the provisional vehicles (*upāya-yāna*).
Although these lead out of birth and death, they are in reality not true *nirvāṇa*. Now, he proclaims the Buddha-wisdom, which is solely the ultimate Dharma.
If among those previously transformed there are sentient beings who hear this and give rise to faith, they are all Bodhisattvas; they shall all together attain Buddhahood.
This is their distinction. If one possesses small wisdom and inferior insight, one must understand the reason why the former [teachings] were expedient means.

Regarding why the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path—is called an expedient means: it is because sentient beings of small wisdom are deeply attached to craving and desire;
therefore, the Truth of Suffering is taught first to alert them, causing them to recognize suffering and give rise to revulsion. As for "Truth" (*satya*), it is that which is real and without...
This is different. Sentient beings know suffering, yet they do not know the root of suffering;

therefore, I explain for them that craving is the root of suffering, so that they may know how to sever its accumulation and extinguish suffering. If craving is extinguished, then suffering has no basis to rely upon.
I cause them to know how to cultivate the path and realize cessation. To be free from suffering is what is called liberation. Regarding this person, in what [state] below...

There are twelve phrases. It is said that extinction is not true extinction. That which is called liberation merely refers to being free from false, segmented birth and death (*paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*);
this is termed liberation. In reality, one has not yet attained all-encompassing liberation, because the birth and death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarā-maraṇa*) still remains.
Therefore, it is said that such a person has not yet truly attained *nirvāṇa*, as they have not yet attained the unsurpassed Great *Nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, this is a skillful means (*upāya*). The Buddha’s fundamental intention was simply that all sentient beings should attain Buddhahood;
how could he consider this [the Lesser Vehicle] sufficient? However, the three vehicles—Great and Small—are all teachings that accord with the capacities of beings.

Now, although the Lesser Dharma is not ultimate, the Tathāgata nevertheless taught it because I am the Dharma King, possessing sovereign mastery over all dharmas. Whatever I have spoken, there is no... [contradiction].
"It is not merely for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings that I have appeared in the world.
You, Śāriputra, must not recklessly proclaim this Dharma-seal of mine wherever you travel."
This verse clarifies that what is being expounded here is the Great Dharma. It serves as a profound admonition for Śāriputra to discern the capacities of his audience before proclaiming it.
The warning against speaking recklessly is given because that which I have spoken today is called the "Seal of the Dharma" (*dharmamudrā*).

All teachings of the Buddha are sealed with the seal of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), thereby definitively establishing all phenomena so that Māras and non-Buddhists cannot confuse or alter them. This Dharma is intended exclusively for the benefit [of those who can receive it].
It is spoken for the benefit of the world; however, one must carefully select the recipient. If they are not the right person, do not transmit it recklessly under any circumstances.
If there are those who hear it, let them rejoice and receive it upon their heads (accept it with reverence). [This continues] until: "To follow this sutra is beyond the scope of one's own wisdom."

This verse precisely clarifies the discernment of the [suitable] recipient. If there are those who, upon hearing [this teaching], rejoice and receive it with reverence, such persons are non-retrogressive Mahābodhisattvas.
Even if one lacks the capacity of a great vehicle (mahāyāna), yet is able to believe upon hearing it, this too is difficult to find;
such a person may also be taught. The following twelve lines beginning with "If there is one who believes and accepts" describe the capacity for faith.
Those who are able to believe in this Dharma have already made offerings to Buddhas and heard the Dharma in the past; their merit and wisdom are profound and vast.
If they can believe you, it is as if they have seen me and the bhikṣus and bodhisattvas, just as we are gathered today at this single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Because he is capable of bearing this burden, it may indeed be taught to him. These eight lines beginning with "This Dharma" state that this Great Dharma is for those of profound wisdom and is not within the reach of those of shallow understanding.
Those eight lines beginning with "As for you, Śāriputra" explain the reason why [others] cannot reach it:
even you, whose wisdom is foremost, have entered by means of faith; how much more so the other śrāvakas who rely on the words of others?
This is because those who lack faith are not within the scope of their own wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, listen now once more to the karmic retribution for the sins of such a person, [arising from] arrogance and indolence.
This verse serves as a warning not to transmit [this teaching] to those who are unsuitable vessels. This Dharma is extremely profound, difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Even while the Buddha was still in the world and personally preaching it for the sake of the assembly, he waited forty years for the right opportunity before daring to speak of it in haste;

yet even then, there were those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*). How much more so after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa? Śāriputra belonged to the Hīnayāna; though he may be skilled in exposition, who would be able to believe him?
Indeed, among their peers there are many who are arrogant and self-exalting, as well as those who are indolent and of little learning.

There are also those who harbor views of self and consider themselves right. These three types of people are all beyond discourse; even if one were to speak to them, they would not believe, and instead would give rise to slander.
It is better not to speak at all, for that is what is gained. This is especially true for ordinary people who lack wisdom, let alone those who are deeply attached.
Regarding the five desires, even upon hearing them one does not understand; what benefit would there be in explaining them? Therefore, it is cautioned that they must not be propagated recklessly.
Those who lack the capacity will not believe, and this is not only useless but actually harmful. For this sutra is the seed of the Buddha-nature within every person.
All those who do not believe will surely give rise to slander; if one slanders this sutra, one severs all [roots of goodness].

This is the seed of the Buddha in the world. Even if one does not slander it, those who frown in distaste upon hearing it, harbor doubts without reaching a resolution, or belong to the ranks of the faithless—all such persons will suffer the retribution of the three miserable realms for their harmful speech.
Listen further now. I shall explain this to you one by one.
When that person’s life ends, they enter the Avīci Hell, and so it continues through successive rebirths for countless kalpas.
This verse enumerates the offenses of slandering the sutras in order to warn those who lack faith.
As for the offense of slandering the sutras, one will inevitably fall into hell. Once having entered hell, the duration is so long that escape is difficult;
this is because the seed of Buddha-nature is called the "eternally abiding true mind. Having turned one's back on this mind, one remains submerged in samsara for eternal kalpas. It is ever-present.
Hell is indeed their proper place.
Having emerged from hell, they shall fall among the animals (and so on), for it is because they slandered this sutra that they incur such retribution.
This verse clarifies the retribution of the animal realm. There are many kinds of animals; they receive their forms according to their karma. The nature of dogs is base...
Furthermore, because they have lost right faith, they fall as dogs; because they harbor much doubt, they fall as jackals.
Because they have impaired the Dharma-body, their forms are emaciated and afflicted with dark leprosy. Because they do not revere the Triple Gem, they are loathed and despised by humans.

Because they do not partake of the flavor of the Dharma, they suffer from hunger and thirst until their flesh withers away. Because they have forever destroyed their roots of goodness, they experience bitter agony upon birth.
Being struck by tiles and stones at death is the retribution for the sin of severing the Buddha-nature.
Those that were kept as small animals—such as camels and donkeys—are all creatures of great strength capable of bearing heavy loads.

Because their afflictions and ignorance are heavy, they constantly carry burdens while further receiving lashes and beatings; because their nature is stubborn and foolish, they think only of water and grass, having no other concerns.
All that you have known is the retribution induced by slandering this sutra. Alternatively, due to wrong views, he was reborn as a jackal;
furthermore, because he lacked one eye and did not know what to revere during his lifetime, he was beaten and thrown to death by a youth.
Having abandoned that body, he further received the body of a python, large in size but without feet—this is the severe retribution for the intensity of his anger and ignorance.
Furthermore, those who suffer the torment of being bitten and eaten by small insects do so because they slandered [others] with many mouths; thus their suffering does not cease.
All of these are the retributive consequences for slandering this sutra.
If one has obtained human form but possesses dull faculties (up to) being among those without wisdom, do not preach this sutra to such people.
This verse refers to the retribution experienced among humans. "If one has obtained human form" means that having fortunately emerged from the realms of hell and animals, one has become a human.
Because they are born without wisdom, their faculties are dull and dark; they do not revere the Triple Gem.

Therefore, because they were contemptuous and looked down upon others, they are born short and stunted; because they were blind to and deaf to what they heard and saw, they experience blindness and deafness;
because they were arrogant and self-exalting, they experience a hunched back; because they slandered the Dharma, people speak of them with lack of faith;
because foul words issued from their mouths, their breath is constantly foul-smelling; and because they were firmly obstructed by perverse thoughts, they are possessed by malevolent spirits.
Because they have not given rise to the Dharma-methods, they are poor, lowly, and driven by others.

Because they do not partake of the medicinal herbs of the Dharma, they suffer from many ailments and emaciation. Because they are far removed from their compassionate father, they have no one to rely upon or protect them, even though they are close to people.
People do not take heed of this. Because they lack right mindfulness, what they have attained is easily forgotten.

Because their nature and habits are inverted, when practicing medicine according to the prescriptions, they further increase the illnesses of others; when they themselves fall ill and encounter medicine, it conversely aggravates the severity of their condition.
Because they add slander through irrational means, others react with hostility and they suffer calamities unjustly. All of the above are retributions among human beings.
Because their roots of goodness have been forever destroyed, they shall never again see the Buddha or hear the Dharma. For long kalpas they will be deaf and mute, with their faculties incomplete.
Only after emerging from the three miserable realms to become human beings, they will immediately re-enter those three realms due to the karmic retribution of their human existence.
Thus, they dwell constantly in hell as if visiting a garden, and reside in the other evil destinies as if in their own homes—like camels, donkeys, and pigs.
The dog is its sphere of activity; all these are the karmic retributions summoned by the act of slandering the sutras.

The sixteen phrases beginning with "if one attains human birth" describe first emerging from the three miserable realms to become a human, then returning from that human state back into the three miserable realms, and now once again emerging from the three miserable realms to become a human—this is what is meant by being like wandering through gardens and pavilions. Having attained this human birth...

People are still thus unable to exhaust their past karma; they continue to be adorned with blindness, deafness, and the like, and wear the foul diseases of dropsy and so forth as their clothing—this shows that suffering never leaves the body.

The stench and impurity of the body are such as this, yet day after day, people persist in the view of self without repentance, harbor anger without ceasing, and indulge in lust without discrimination. How can one remain at peace in such a state?

They are able to escape the miserable realms. Why then would they linger within the swift wheel of such severe and grievous retribution? All of this is the karmic retribution for slandering the sutras.
[The Buddha] addressed Śāriputra, summarizing that those who are not suitable vessels suffer these many harms, which cannot be fully described.
For these reasons, I admonish you not to preach this sutra among those who lack wisdom.
However, if there are those with sharp faculties and clear intelligence, you should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to them.
This verse correctly describes those of superior faculties who are fit to be taught. As explained above, there are individuals of this kind;
they are true vessels of the Dharma and it is only for them that one may preach. Otherwise, one would fail such a person.
How could we allow the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) not to continue? To seek the relics of the Buddha is the height of sincere devotion. In the past, Kang Senghui...
From the Western Regions, they saw from afar that a five-colored light illuminated the heavens in Zhendan;

knowing it was the Buddha’s *śarīra*, they followed the light and arrived at Fotuo-li in Jiangdong. There they thatched a hut, set up an image, and practiced the Way. Some reported this to the Ruler of Wu, Sun Quan, as a marvel.
The Ruler issued an edict to inquire about them, and they replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. He asked, "Where is the Buddha? They said, "The Buddha has already..."
[He] passed away. There were śarīra relics available for verification. A question was asked: "Can they be seen? He replied: "If you seek them with sincerity, you shall obtain them.

Consequently, he ordered an altar to be established to seek them. When there was no response after the first seven-day period, the term was changed to another seven days, yet again there was no response.
After a third period had ended without response, he offered a prayer, saying: "I do not begrudge my own death; however..."
"The sentient beings of this land have utterly severed their karmic affinity with the Buddha-Dharma. Thereupon, his sincerity grew even more earnest.
At midnight, he called upon the name of the Buddha three times with all his might; blood and sweat poured from his entire body.

Suddenly, he heard a resonant *keng* sound within the vase, and its light illuminated heaven and earth. When he presented it to the Ruler of Wu, the latter was greatly delighted. He erected a stupa to enshrine it.
This Changgan Pagoda marks the beginning of Buddhist temples in Jiangnan. Since someone has come seeking the scriptures in this manner, how could I bear not to explain them to you?
I declare to you, Śāriputra: the faults of failing to meet the right capacity, though one were to speak of them for an entire kalpa, could never be fully exhausted;
yet the benefits of meeting the right capacity now are likewise inexhaustible, even if one were to speak of them for an entire kalpa.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Four: The Parable of the Faith and Understanding.
This chapter describes how those of middling faculties attain realization through the arising of faith and understanding based on parables. Regarding the purpose of this chapter’s inclusion:
the four great disciples, having heard the World-Honored One’s discourse on parables and having witnessed Śāriputra’s attainment of realization and his receiving of a prediction, [attained faith].
Only now do I truly believe that what was previously taught was provisional, and that the present One Vehicle is the ultimate reality.

Because I had previously harbored regret and were deluded by ignorance, [the Buddha] spoke the Parable of the Poor Son to recount his original intention, exhaustively depicting the state of paternal compassion contrasted with the son’s obstinacy, thereby serving as an analogy for the mind that fears the Great [Vehicle].
Now that I have heard this revelation, I finally gain self-confidence; thus I realize my former errors. This is why this chapter [is titled] "The Parable of the Poor Son."
It begins here with "The Entrustment. Its meaning extends all the way to the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) before the sense of entrustment is fully exhausted;
for it is through faith and understanding that the various sons become worthy of being entrusted.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti (up to: gave rise to a rare mind and leaped for joy with exultation.
This describes the four great disciples; having heard the exposition of the parables, they gave birth to faith and understanding, and thus they leaped for joy with exultation.
This is to recount former sentiments. In the preceding discourse on the Dharma, Śāriputra was the foremost in wisdom;

yet he alone attained realization. This present discourse through parables is likewise difficult to believe, for it has been discussed extensively through various causes, conditions, and similes from before.
Now, it is not comparable to the past; essentially, nothing can be understood without wisdom. Therefore, Subhūti is titled "Wisdom" (Prajñā).

"Life" (*jīvitendriya*) is that which occupies the foremost position. By means of the teaching of the emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), when the foremost among those such as Śūnyatāputra practices relinquishment, then the entire assembly is able to relinquish.
Because they have heard this unprecedented Dharma, they give rise to a mind of rare wonder;
this is why they leap for joy.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and [proceeded] to delightfully explain parables in order to clarify this meaning.

This section describes the circumstances of their gains and losses. Regarding the phrase "standing at the head of the Sangha," it first recounts why he formerly adhered to the belief that the Lesser Vehicle’s fruits were real:
because his years had advanced in age, he was fortunate enough to have attained the peace of *nirvāṇa*, and thus considered himself [to have reached his goal].
Being content with this, we no longer harbor the aspiration to further seek unsurpassed bodhi.

Therefore, while the World-Honored One has been teaching the Dharma exclusively, we have become weary and indolent, utterly lacking in vigor; we merely consider the realization of the dharma of emptiness for ourselves to be sufficient.
We lack entirely the resolve to deliver sentient beings. For this reason, regarding the great Dharma of the Bodhisattvas and the purification of Buddha-lands—
Regarding the task of teaching and transforming sentient beings, our hearts find no joy. The reason we do not rejoice is that the World-Honored One first caused us to emerge from the triple world;
we have already emerged and have realized the fruit of nirvana.

Moreover, as we are now advanced in years, we find peace only in being free from affairs. Therefore, [we have no interest] in the Bodhisattvas' work of benefiting sentient beings and attaining Buddhahood.

Regarding this matter, not a single thought of longing or delight arose within us. Moreover, whenever we heard the Buddha’s reproaches, we considered ourselves utterly devoid of the potential for Buddhahood.
How could we have known that his previous [teachings] were merely provisional devices? Now, below, we shall describe our current state of faith and understanding;
having heard the Buddha bestow upon us the prediction of attaining Buddhahood as Śrāvakas, our hearts are filled with great joy.

As for "joy": because one has suddenly heard this rare Dharma, the great treasure of the Dharma King, which was not sought but obtained all at once—how could one not feel profound personal celebration?
Since the heart of celebration cannot be seen by itself, an analogy shall be given to describe the meaning of this realization.
It is like a person who, being young in years, is serene and joyful, free from further anxiety or worry.

This is a metaphor for the state of faith and understanding; it first describes the condition of lack of faith in former times. It is because sentient beings, through ignorance (*avidyā*), are shrouded by darkness and their true nature is obscured.
Like a child lacking knowledge, they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust, long submerged in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

It is like a son who abandons his father and flees, dwelling for a long time in another land; having fallen into the five realms of existence, his cycle of birth and death is vast and distant, thus he is as if fifty years old.
As his years grow great, yet lacking roots of goodness, he is exhausted by passing through the four modes of birth, sustaining himself through suffering as if seeking food and clothing.
Because he possesses the perfuming of the true cause, he gradually reaches his native country through the Dharma-body of original enlightenment.
Transmigrating through the five realms is what is called a "sentient being.

This refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, which undergoes a transformation of the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings, yet remains shrouded like a garment covered in filth. Therefore, it is said that "the father had previously arrived.

Because they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects, it is said that "he sought his son but could not find him. Regarding the passage about "staying in a city where the household was immensely wealthy," and so forth:
It is like the Tathāgata Vairocana, who dwells in the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*) and manifests a majestic body whose adornments equal the Dharma-realm;
therefore, he is called "Greatly Wealthy. The phrase "immeasurable precious jewels" and so forth is a metaphor for the Buddha’s true wisdom.

Because the Buddha possesses the infinite *pāramitās* of knowledge and vision, all of which are already fully perfected, it is said that they "overflow completely. The "servants" and so forth are metaphors for the Buddha’s [disciples].
This is the activity of generating benefit through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Subjects and citizens can be employed for service, and elephants, horses, and so forth can be used for transport;
all of these are skillful means. Because the merit of this transformation is attributed to oneself, it is said that "income and expenditure yield profit.
The response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is immeasurable, pervading the worlds of the ten directions; therefore, it is said that "in other lands there are many merchants. As for these merchants:

The master’s original source from which he derives profit is a metaphor for the Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Having long been submerged in birth and death and having traversed all realms of existence, it is therefore likened to traveling through various kingdoms and towns.
Now, fortunately encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world, it is like gradually arriving at the father’s city.
As for the father constantly thinking of his son, the Sūtra says: "How marvelous! How marvelous! All sentient beings possess..."
The Tathāgata’s wisdom, virtues, and marks are not realized solely because of deluded thoughts and inversions.
This refers to being separated from his son for over fifty years; he knew in his heart that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet had not yet established the means to transform them.
Thus it is said: "I have never spoken of such a matter to others. From "But I have been reflecting to myself" onwards, this is a metaphor for the three weeks [of meditation].
Contemplate the methods for delivering sentient beings. Those who harbor regret should reflect that they ought not to abandon the seeds of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) already possessed in the past;

they should lament that these are easily lost and difficult to encounter again. "Decrepitude" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s causes being exhausted and his fruits perfected, as if the conditions for rebirth were coming to an end.
"Possessing much wealth" is a metaphor for the profound depth of the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*). "Lacking... [is a metaphor for...]
Having offspring is a metaphor for continuing the life of wisdom through those of supreme capacity. If the Buddha-dharma were not transmitted, it would be like the loss of a family inheritance.
Desiring someone to whom it might be entrusted, the Tathāgata first contemplated for seven days, thereby giving rise to great compassion that is without conditions.
Because he considered that the Dharma must have a recipient, the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of this great causal event. However, [the text continues:]

With the thought of protecting and entrusting [the teaching] as his primary concern, it is like a householder who, having found his son, can finally be free from anxiety once he has entrusted him with the family estate.
World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son wandered from place to place seeking wages, eventually arriving in a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing.

This parable illustrates the fear of the Great Vehicle experienced by those of the Two Vehicles during the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. When the *Avataṃsaka* was being taught, those of the Two Vehicles were also present;
however, they had not yet entered the gateway of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, it is likened to a destitute son who encounters his father’s house and stands by the side of the gate.
Seeing his father from afar seated upon a lion throne and so forth, is a metaphor for the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* on the stages (*bhūmi*).
The Bodhisattvas, surrounded by their retinues, and the various heavenly kings, like officials, subjects, and servants, truly represent those who are struck with terror.

Because they have eyes yet do not see the body of Śākyamuni, and have ears yet do not hear the Dharma of the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha), they are like those possessed of majesty and supreme dignity who, feeling fear, secretly consider [the Buddha] to be a king whom they cannot rival. For these two reasons...
Riding upon it, one perceives its narrowness and inferiority; thus, one reflects that this is not a place where things can be obtained through hired labor.

The *Avataṃsaka*—the vast, sovereign Dharma-gate that accords with the nature of reality—is not something the followers of the Two Vehicles can endure. The "poor village" is a metaphor for the realms of humans, devas, and the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

Because it is easy to practice and easy to attain, it is like having a place where one can exert effort and where food and clothing are easily obtained. Or, one may perceive oppression; this is a metaphor... [text ends]
Having no desire for it, he was forcibly converted by the Mahāyāna vision; fearing he would lose his own benefit, he fled in haste.
Upon seeing his son, he recognized him immediately—this is a metaphor for the universal perception that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

Since all who have a mind will certainly become Buddhas, it is thus compared to having something entrusted to one's thoughts. He yearned for this son but had no means to see him—this is a metaphor for the Buddha.

I observe sentient beings correctly and find no mark of a "sentient being. Because sentient beings arise spontaneously and naturally within my mind of impartial great compassion, they come of their own accord as if by chance;
this is most perfectly suited to my wishes. Yet, I am worn out by age and still harbor attachments.
The metaphors for the merits of the Dharma-body and Reward-body are protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness;

this immediately dispatches the "attendant," which is a metaphor for the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s sudden teaching—the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths expounded by Bodhisattvas through the Buddha’s empowerment, whereby one knows that all phenomena are the self-nature of the mind.
One accomplishes the body of wisdom, awakening not through another. This is what is meant by "urgently pursuing one back.
Generally, that which is not of one's own doing is termed an "enemy. Now, becoming a Buddha was originally not sought by those of the Two Vehicles;

therefore, it is likened to being caught despite having committed no offense. In the forty-two stages of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, each stage describes how the Bodhisattva seeks the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because he was engaged in the work of benefiting sentient beings in the ocean [of existence], the metaphor describes how he was seized with increasing urgency and forcibly dragged back.

The Bodhisattva’s coming and going through the three realms to benefit sentient beings is an activity of sporting in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). In contrast, those of the Two Vehicles view the three realms as a prison and loathe the four modes of birth as shackles;
therefore, the metaphor likens them to a destitute son who, though innocent, is mindful of being imprisoned and held captive—this is certain.
He dies and falls to the ground in a swoon; this precisely illustrates the state of having eyes yet not seeing, or having ears yet not hearing.
Because those of the Two Vehicles are very far from the ocean of fruition, they are likened to the father seeing them from afar.

However, since the sudden teaching of the One Vehicle does not extensively reach all capacities, [the father] wishes to open up the provisional means; thus, he lets them be without forcing them, admonishing that they not speak with him. Why is this so?
This concludes the explanation of why [the Buddha] allows [beings] to roam freely, intended to set forth the meaning of establishing skillful means (*upāya*).

The Buddha himself knew that the sudden teaching of the One Vehicle was not something inferior faculties could endure; thus, he used the analogy of an elder who knows that his own noble and wealthy status is difficult for his son to accept.
Regarding the phrase "thoroughly knowing" and so forth: it is a metaphor for the fact that if sentient beings were entirely devoid of Buddha-nature, that would be the end of it;
however, since they do possess Buddha-nature, there is no need to worry that they will not be transformed. For this reason, expedient means (*upāya*) must be employed to deliver them;

this precisely illustrates the intention to exercise skillful means. The statement, "I do not tell others that he is my son," is a metaphor for waiting for the proper time before allowing him to believe for himself.

As for "releasing him," it means simply leaving him to his own devices; it is a metaphor for not using forceful methods. His going to the poor quarter is a metaphor for his delighting in base activities.
That one knows he is one's own son yet allows him to act as he pleases is clearly intended to necessitate the use of skillful means (*upāya*);
it is evident that this provisional teaching of the Two Vehicles was specifically established for sentient beings of inferior faculties who lack faith.
At that time, the elder was about to entice his son [but] had not yet been able to abandon his inferior mind.
This is a metaphor for the employment of skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding the phrase "was about to," etc.: "about to" (*jiang*) is a term indicating a provisional state rather than a certainty;

it is a metaphor for the Buddha not yet manifesting his *nirmāṇakāya*, but first dispatching a bodhisattva who conceals within and manifests without, employing the means of "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*) to entice those of the two vehicles.

He acts as a guide. "Removing filth" is a metaphor for severing afflictions (*kleśa*). According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, ignorance and the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the Wisdom of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*).

How could this be something that those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) are capable of? Therefore, it is said that the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) severs only the views and discursive thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-vitarka*).

One quickly attains small fruits; their efficacy is easily seen. Therefore, it is said that one first takes the price [of the labor]. To long for the fruit while cultivating the cause is likened to seeking out and removing dung.
Seeing the seed and feeling pity and wonder is a metaphor for giving rise to *maitrī* and *karuṇā*. "Seeing from afar through the window," and so forth.

This is a metaphor for when the Buddha, before manifesting his physical body, surveyed the sentient beings of the six realms with his Buddha-eye and saw that they were impoverished, lacking both merit and wisdom.
Consequently, he contemplated for three weeks on how to deliver them through skillful means. Thus, he removed his jeweled necklaces and other ornaments;
this metaphor signifies the Buddha concealing his majestic *vairocana* body of a thousand feet and manifesting the form of an ordinary bhikṣu sixteen feet tall, holding a broom in his right hand.

The "feces vessel" and other such metaphors illustrate the process of conforming to inferior faculties and achieving Buddhahood through the severance of fetters by means of the thirty-four moments of mind.
Because one thereby attains the ability to interact with those of the Two Vehicles, it is metaphorically said that "by means of skillful means, one draws near to one's own son. The exclamation "Ho!
Man! and so forth rebukes [the listener] to settle his mind and cease further longing for other paths; this illustrates how those of the Lesser Vehicle initially followed non-Buddhist teachers.
Because they draw near to the Buddha, there may be a fear of falling back; therefore, he rebukes them to set their minds at ease.

"I shall increase your wages" means that for those beginning their study in the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), attaining the realization of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) is like receiving one day’s wage.

From this point, by progressing through the second, third, and fourth fruits, they gradually enter the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*); hence, it is metaphorically called an increase in wages. Whatever [there may be]...

"Those such as the attendants" is a metaphor for the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path. "The old and decrepit servant" is a metaphor for the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the Hīnayāna;
these are all discarded by the Buddha, and thus are like the old and decrepit.

"I am like your father" is a metaphor for Śākyamuni manifesting as the *phala-stha* (fruition-stage) Buddha of the Tripiṭaka; because this is not the true Buddha, it is said to be "like a father. "For what reason? and so forth below is a metaphor.
The phrase "as toward a father" refers to the gradual development of intimacy. "Hatred and various evils" is a metaphor for non-Buddhists slandering the Buddha.
"Furthermore, he gives him a name and calls him a son" is a metaphor for the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas entering the *dharmatā* together;

all should be called sons, yet because they are young and lack power, they are called "sons. The passage beginning with "At that time, the impoverished son" serves as a metaphor for passing through the [various stages].
This includes the Vaipulya [sūtras]. Because it severs the afflictions of views and thought, it is said that for twenty years he was constantly made to remove filth.
The passage "After this time... and below serves as a metaphor for the merit of passing through the Vaipulya and entering the Prajñāpāramitā, through the process of censure and refinement.

Those of the Two Vehicles gradually turn toward the Mahāyāna therein; hence it is said, "Their minds accord with one another and they trust each other's essence" at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha commanded Subhūti to further instruct the bodhisattvas. Although one of the Hīnayāna [vehicle], he was able to expound the Great Dharma;
thus it is said that "he enters and exits without difficulty. Yet, because he had not yet abandoned the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, it is said that "the place where he dwells remains as it was.

The passage concerning "the elder having an illness" and so forth is a metaphor for the concern that the life-force of the Dharma has not yet been sustained and that Nirvāṇa is imminent. This is because the Prajñāpāramitā has not yet fully exhausted the Dharma.
Because it defines the measure of the realms, it speaks of "taking and giving more or less. Because it causes those of the Two Vehicles to turn and teach, it says, "You all must know this.
Because it is about to establish the distinction between father and son, it first entrusts them, saying, "You should embody this meaning.

Since Prajñā is the impartial wisdom of the Buddha, it is likened to the non-difference between father and son. Because there is about to be an entrustment, it says, "You should apply your mind with diligence."
"Do not let it be lost or leaked. The above all serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s command to the followers of the Two Vehicles to turn the wheel of the Dharma.

"Thereupon they received the instruction" below serves as a metaphor for receiving the mandate to turn the teaching. The myriad practices of Prajñā are known by all three vehicles; therefore, this is metaphorically likened to taking charge of and knowing the various goods.
However, because these are not within the scope of their own wisdom, it is metaphorically likened to having no intention of seeking even a single meal. Because...
Because the followers of the Two Vehicles are unwilling to immediately relinquish their minor fruits, this is likened to the impoverished son whose inferior mind has likewise not yet been abandoned.

The above serves as a general metaphor for what was lost in the past—referring to events forty years ago. The following serves as a metaphor for what is now attained, specifically manifesting the present assembly.
"Again, after a short time, the father knew his son's intent... 'Now this treasure has arrived of its own accord.

This metaphor refers to what is attained now. "Again, after a short time," and so forth, is a metaphor for how, after the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the followers of the two vehicles have already come to possess a mind that delights in the Great [Vehicle].
"When he was about to pass away," and so forth, is a metaphor for when the time for *nirvāṇa* arrives, one immediately teaches this sutra.
This refers to the bestowing of the prediction of Buddhahood upon those of the two vehicles.

Being about to entrust [the teaching], he first causes the Buddha Prabhūtaratna to assemble the various emanated Buddhas from the ten directions to testify to this Dharma; hence it says, "and having gathered his kinsmen," and so forth.

The phrase "proclaiming" and so on serves as a metaphor for the matters concerning the causes and conditions of past teachings described within this sutra: that all wealth and possessions belong to the son.
This is a metaphor for the present bestowal of the prophecy concerning the adornments of the primary and secondary bodies, the kalpas, and the lands.
That the impoverished son, upon hearing these words from his father, immediately felt great joy is precisely a metaphor for what is attained now.
The World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder, is the Tathāgata; he has already attained all that ought to be attained. This is the application of the Dharma to the parable.
The Buddha regards sentient beings as his only son, whereas those of the two vehicles regard the Bodhisattva as their true son and view themselves merely as sons by adoption.
Because of the suffering of sentient beings, the Buddha... [specifically]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at the end. The translation reflects the available portion.)

He spoke the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle regarding suffering. The various śrāvakas, being deluded by the heat and affliction of all sufferings, sought liberation with such urgency that they took pleasure in and attached themselves to the lesser Dharma;
this is the disposition of those who delight in the small. Regarding the three types of suffering:

namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). From the words "Today, the World-Honored One" [downward], this accords with the lingering disposition of the provisional [teachings]. The World...

The passage beginning with "The World-Honored One, by means of his power of skillful means," describes how the Buddha caused those of the two vehicles to preach the *Prajñāpāramitā* so as to instruct the bodhisattvas.
Because they considered the attainment of the lesser fruits to be sufficient, they had no aspiration or pursuit regarding the Mahāyāna *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The section beginning with "Furthermore, because of us" describes how the World-Honored One, knowing that we delighted in the lesser [vehicle], did not immediately bestow upon us the prediction of enlightenment; therefore, we...
Not knowing this, one truly does not realize that one is a child of the Buddha; this refers generally to the failure to understand [the truth] in the past. "Now we...

and so forth refers to realizing today that there has been no loss; by observing the Buddha’s compassion today, one finally understands that from the very beginning there was never any secretiveness or parsimony.
Yet we ourselves have never lost it; it is simply that we did not delight in the Great [Vehicle]. In the passage below this, the realization of the Buddha-mind is described.
Observing that he now preaches the One Vehicle for us, we know that at the time of his former reproaches, he already intended to teach and transform us with the Mahāyāna.
This is what is meant by saying "it was our own fault. Therefore, the following section correctly corresponds to what we have now attained. Now...

Seeing the World-Honored One preach this Great Dharma and specifically bestow a prediction of Buddhahood upon Śāriputra, while also declaring that the twelve hundred disciples shall all likewise become Buddhas—
