this is truly the great treasure of the Dharma King arriving of its own accord without being sought; it is therefore a cause for supreme celebration and good fortune.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching (up to the point where it says) we are filled with great joy, having attained what we have never experienced before."
This verse generally describes the sentiments of faith and understanding. The section beginning with "For example" below illustrates the former loss.

The first eight lines illustrate the son’s flight and the father’s search. The thirty-four lines following "search" illustrate the contemplation at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) regarding the transformation of sentient beings with whom one has a karmic connection.
"The time of death is approaching" is a metaphor for the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) of untransformed sentient beings being on the verge of extinction.
This is the end [of the previous section]. At that time, the twelve phrases beginning with "the impoverished son" illustrate the matter of deluded wandering.

"Seeking food and clothing" illustrates having the mind to emerge from suffering while still within delusion. "Obtaining or not obtaining" illustrates practicing according to the Small Vehicle or external paths.
"Hunger and so forth" illustrates not yet attaining correct cultivation and, conversely, harming the essence of the Dharma. Thus...

"Arriving at his father's house" is a metaphor for reaching the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) yet not daring to enter. "At that time, the elder... and the following ten lines are a metaphor for the period when the *Avataṃsaka* was being taught.
"The impoverished son saw his father... and the following fourteen lines are a metaphor for the initial encounter with the reality of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"At that time, the elder... and the following twelve lines are a verse summarizing the teaching of the Great Dharma of the *Avataṃsaka*. However...
He universally observes that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet he does not immediately proclaim it; therefore, it is said that he "knows [it] in silence.

The terms "startled" and so forth are precisely metaphors for the fear of the Great [Vehicle] upon hearing the teaching of the sudden Dharma. The twelve phrases beginning with "The elder knew his sons... [are as follows].

The verse and the parable illustrate the disclosure of the provisional (*upāya*). "Sending a man" refers to being inwardly secret while outwardly manifesting, thereby demonstrating the gathering of others through *samānārthatā* (common purpose).

The four lines beginning with "the impoverished son" illustrate the delight in the small [vehicle]. The ten lines beginning with "the elder at the window" illustrate the concealing of the superior and the manifesting of the inferior.
The eight lines beginning with "I shall increase your wages" illustrate the teaching of the methods for practicing and progressing toward the small fruits. If you...
[It is] so. "Like my son" means he resembles a son but is not a true son. The twelve phrases beginning with "The elder possessed wisdom" eulogize the time of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Entering and exiting for twenty years" precisely symbolizes the matter of transmitting and teaching the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Because it was not within the scope of his own wisdom, he said, "I do not possess this thing," and thus did not hope to take it. The above [is the explanation].
The general verse illustrates the past loss; the twenty-one lines beginning with "The father knew" illustrate the circumstances of preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The six lines beginning with "Now" illustrate the present attainment. The preceding part is the illustration by means of a parable; the following part is the application to the Dharma.
The Buddha likewise knows that we delight in the Small [Vehicle] (up to: "universally worthy of receiving offerings therein").
These eight phrases below are likewise; because the verse combines them with "delighting in the Small," he therefore preaches the Dharma of the Small.
"The Buddha charged us" (the thirty-two phrases below) collectively summarize the lingering attachment to the provisional. From "The Buddha charged" down to "preaching the Unsurpassed."
The "Way" (Dharma) section corresponds to the teaching of *prajñā* regarding the affairs of bodhisattvas.
From "O sons of the Buddha" down to "shall attain Buddhahood," it corresponds to the fact that each bodhisattva who hears the *prajñā* receives a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood.

From "All" down to "expounding this essential truth," it corresponds to those who were themselves hindered by the provisional and small [vehicles], who doubted that the Buddha would preach the Great [Vehicle] for them. "As in that... and so forth is a repeated analogy.
Their faculties were stagnant; therefore it is said that they themselves lacked aspiration, and it was not that the Buddha was stingy and failed to teach them.

The twenty-one phrases following "Our internal extinction" (*asmākam antardhānam*) further clarify that from the beginning they delighted in the Lesser Vehicle. Thus, they were greedily attached to the Lesser Vehicle, considering a meager attainment sufficient.
Consequently, they did not give rise to joy. For this reason, they no longer had any aspiration for the *prajñā*—the Buddha-wisdom.
"Taking the Dharma we have personally attained as the ultimate. These sixteen subsequent phrases restate our inclination toward the Lesser Vehicle;
that is, regarding the small fruits we have obtained, we claim to have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
This is why we are self-satisfied and do not advance. Although these twenty-two subsequent phrases further clarify our stagnation in provisional means, the Buddha—
"Even if one sets it aside to await the proper time," this means waiting until the mind has been tamed; only then does one teach the Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*).
That the Buddha’s grace is difficult to repay lies precisely here. The twenty-eight phrases below, beginning with "We, on this day," correctly describe what has now been attained.
To speak of "attaining the Way" and "attaining the fruit" is to clarify that one has now realized the true wisdom of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This is because one has long maintained purity.
He observed the precepts and cultivated the holy life, and has now attained the unsurpassed great fruit.
Thus we know that the present reality indeed comes from the past expedient means. As it was said before, "If one does not believe this Dharma, one is not an Arhat";
today we finally know that he is a true Arhat, who should receive the offerings of devas and humans.
"The World-Honored One’s great kindness, through this rare occurrence... [teaching] the Single Vehicle path while provisionally speaking of three.

This clarifies that he deeply perceives the great kindness and reflects that it cannot be repaid. The twenty-six phrases following "The World-Honored One" further explain that the kindness is so great it is difficult to requite;
that is to say, the Buddha, through this rare occurrence, employs skillful means out of compassion to teach, transform, and benefit [beings].
We have been liberated from the suffering that is difficult to extricate over billions of kalpas and have realized the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi. What kindness could be greater than this?
Therefore, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, it can never be repaid. Regarding the phrase "beneath the hands and feet," it speaks of the difficulty of repaying such kindness;
since the measure of this grace is like space, how could it be requited with a physical body, a mind, or external possessions?
And how could it be possible to repay [the Buddha’s kindness]? Even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could not repay it.
The ten phrases beginning with "The Buddhas possess rare... restate the reasons why it is so difficult to repay.
Because the Buddhas, through their own realization of immeasurable, inconceivable, and vast supernormal powers, are able to endure this for the sake of us inferior sentient beings...
Furthermore, for our sake as ordinary beings who grasp at signs, he has skillfully applied expedient means and taught according to what was appropriate.
This great kindness and compassion of the World-Honored One is beyond comparison; how could it ever be repaid?

The sixteen lines beginning with "The Buddhas regarding the Dharma" describe and clarify how he taught according to what was appropriate, thereby expressing gratitude for the great kindness of his expedient means. This is why he was able to—

Regarding "teaching according to what is appropriate": because the Buddha has attained the dharma of supreme mastery—namely, that he is the Dharma King who possesses sovereignty over all dharmas—he is able to know the various inclinations and desires of sentient beings and what they can bear according to their capacities.
Therefore, he teaches the Dharma by means of immeasurable parables and expressions, bestowing the Dharma according to their faculties and making various assessments and distinctions.
Having distinguished them thus, the One Vehicle Dharma was taught as three according to what was appropriate. This summarizes the matters of the seven-times-seven contemplations;

it is here that one receives the grace of these skillful means so graciously bestowed. This is precisely that which is most difficult to repay. Since one cannot repay it, one can only feel it within the heart.
Among the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity, those who truly knew this debt of gratitude were rare. If one is indeed able to know this debt of gratitude, then—

This constitutes the very core of the matter. The parable of the impoverished son describes the circumstances of that son from beginning to end and reveals his fundamental state of mind at the critical moment;
nothing has been so detailed and exhaustive as this. Should one fail to recognize this grace...
How could this be possible?

*The Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty under Imperial Decree.
Expounded by the Chan Monk Deqing of Mount Nanyue.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Five: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.

The purpose of this chapter is as follows: Because the four great disciples above had attained realization and were granted the "one" after being permitted to receive the "three," they spoke a parable to express their own circumstances—how they had previously erred and now attained understanding—and the World-Honored One validated their minds.

Nevertheless, they had not yet fully comprehended the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; furthermore, there was concern that those who cling to signs would fail to understand that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with impartiality.
Regarding the principle of diverse understandings according to different types, it was thought that there were actually three vehicles of fruition to be realized.
Because the habitual tendencies toward *nirvāṇa* had not been forgotten, they were unable to penetrate to the very source of the Dharma;

therefore, the parable of the medicinal herbs was taught to reveal that the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is of a single, equal flavor, yet each receives it differently according to the size of their faculties—just as with a single rain.

I. The three types of grass and two types of trees receive the moisture according to their respective capacities; thus we know that the Dharma itself is not different, but that difference lies in the faculties of the beings.
This clarifies the principle that there is only the One Vehicle, with neither a second nor a third.
By causing those who hear it to suddenly eliminate habitual perceptions, they may enter the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharma-wisdom; the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is made manifest.
Following this, the prophecy is bestowed; therefore, this chapter follows.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa... [up to] ...revealing all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings.
This was the Tathāgata’s confirmation that although the four great disciples had attained realization, they had not yet reached the ultimate.

Having received the teaching through these parables, Kāśyapa and the others understood the Tathāgata’s compassionate intent to stoop down for the sake of those of the two vehicles—just as a wealthy elder, out of extreme compassion, employs skillful means to entice his impoverished son who fears him. This may truly be called...

You have well explained the true merits of the Tathāgata. However, what you understand seems to suggest that the Tathāgata acts with a deliberate mind, establishing the three vehicles merely for the sake of those of the two vehicles. You do not realize that the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is through impartial great compassion;
regardless of whether beings possess the Buddha-nature or not, he preaches with a single voice to universally cause them all [to attain awakening].
Upon hearing and knowing this, you shall all together attain the Buddha-way; from the beginning, there has never been a distinction between three or one.
This is the unconditioned, wondrous power of the Tathāgata—what is called the immeasurable and boundless merit that could not be fully exhausted even if explained for immeasurable billions of kalpas.
From the time he appeared in the world until now, what you have seen and heard is but a single drop in the ocean. This is not [the fault] of you.
This is what is to be known. Because the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas and has attained great mastery, whatever he speaks accords with the nature of the dharma-realm;
it is true and not false. Therefore, regarding all dharmas, he employs skillful means and provisional wisdom.
He teaches in accordance with the capacities of beings; thus, all that he speaks returns to the ground of ultimate, true wisdom, being devoid of empty talk.
By means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of reality, he realizes the principle and thereby perceives and knows that all phenomena ultimately converge in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
By means of his wisdom of skillful means, he examines their capacities and thereby knows the inclinations, desires, and conduct of all sentient beings.

There is nothing he does not thoroughly penetrate. Furthermore, he is skilled at discerning the characteristics of all phenomena—whether their nature or their marks, whether provisional or ultimate—understanding each one with perfect clarity.
Moreover, in his teachings, he is adept at revealing the primordial wisdom inherent in sentient beings.
This is but a brief outline of his immeasurable merits; how could you possibly know them all?

Kāśyapa, it is like this: for example, when the lands of the trichiliocosm [are flooded] (up to the point where they are) fully moistened and each attains growth—this is the analogy for the single principle that differentiates [beings].

The soil of the trichiliocosm generally represents the original ground of the mind of sentient beings within the one true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The grasses and trees produced by the mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys represent...
All sentient beings within the three realms differ in their species, names, and forms, just as the Three Vehicles and Five Natures are distinct.

Among trees there are both the fragrant *zheng* and the worthless *chū*; among grasses there are both the beneficial and the toxic. Now, we select those sentient beings who are capable of receiving transformation.
Just as grass can serve as medicine and wood can become fine timber, those that cannot be transformed are merely rotten, poisonous, or worthless *chū* trees;
thus they are called "medicinal herbs. The faculties and natures of sentient beings are manifold and not uniform, differing according to the three vehicles and five natures;
therefore it is said that their species are numerous and their names and forms are each distinct. This is the metaphor for those who are reached by the teaching.
This is the pivotal mechanism. The Buddha, through clouds of bodies of the Dharma-realm, pervades the ten directions; thus, he is like dense clouds spreading everywhere.

When his perfect voice is uttered once, it instantly reaches throughout the ten lands; thus, he is like a single rain universally moistening all. Those sentient beings who hear it each understand according to their own kind;
thus, they are like the three types of grass and two types of trees, each receiving what it can. According to their respective natures and dispositions, each attains [enlightenment].
It is indeed so. That is to say, when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind.
From those of the human and heavenly realms and the Small Vehicle, up to the Bodhisattvas, there are none who do not achieve success; all are able to benefit themselves and others.
It cures the disease of birth and death and secures the peace of nirvāṇa; therefore, it uses only medicinal herbs as a metaphor.
As for icchantikas, non-Buddhists, and sentient beings who commit the ten evils and lack faith—though they are like wolf-poison and rank weeds—they too are not excluded from receiving its moisture.
However, because they are unable to believe and accept it, they are simply not the proper recipients (*yogya*). This is illustrated by the analogy: "Though grown from the same ground," and so forth.
Sentient beings equally receive the one true dharma-nature, yet they differ according to the ripening of their respective seeds. That is to say, the Dharma is fundamentally without differentiation;
the difference lies in the capacity of the recipient. Viewed from this perspective, the teachings of the Three Vehicles are not the result of the Buddha’s intentional discrimination;

rather, he universally expounds them through the wisdom of the ocean of the dharma-realm with impartiality. It is only because the hearing and seeing of those with different capacities vary that they distinguish [the teachings] for themselves.
Regarding the distinction between the great and the small: these were all provisional teachings from the past that expounded the Buddha’s wisdom.
It was only because those of small intelligence were self-centered that they did not accept it; it is not that the Buddha definitively possessed three vehicles to be grasped.

Although Kāśyapa and the others have awakened to the former provisional teachings, they do not yet know that, fundamentally, there is no division into three or one. This is the Tathāgata’s impartial great wisdom.
That the measure of his merit cannot be fully described is certainly beyond the comprehension of those of the Two Vehicles.

"The Tathāgata is likewise so" and below—this may be understood by applying it to the Dharma. From "proclaiming these words amidst the great assembly" down to "for the sake of hearing the Dharma," this refers to when the Buddha first attained Perfect Enlightenment;
the Dharma King appeared in accordance with the times and issued a proclamation to the Three Realms.
This is a verse. Since there was no Buddha during the kalpa of emptiness, sentient beings within the triple world had not yet seen a Buddha.
Now that the Dharma King has emerged from the realm of reality, they do not know who this Buddha is, why he has come, or what dharma he knows.
Fearing they might be terrified, he therefore declares, "I am the Tathāgata," and so forth, so that all may know him to be the Buddha, for the sake of their deliverance.

"Those who have crossed over," and so forth, means that he causes them to know that the Buddha has come for the sake of delivering sentient beings, enabling them to emerge from suffering and attain happiness.

"Knowing it as it truly is," and so forth, refers to his proclamation of the Dharma he has realized; being able to open and expound it, he ensures that all sentient beings within the triple world should come here to hear the Dharma.
This is precisely why he has appeared in the world for this one great cause and condition.

This is the fundamental intention [of the Tathāgata], just like a great cloud raining down. At that time, as indicated by the phrase "countless [beings]" and below, sentient beings of the three realms come because they have heard the proclamation and summons.
At that moment, the Tathāgata observes their faculties and preaches the Dharma accordingly;

just as the three types of grass and two types of trees receive moisture according to their respective capacities, humans, devas, and those of the three vehicles each attain maturity. Therefore, it is said: "He causes them all to..."
Rejoicing, each attains wholesome benefit. This Dharma that accords with their faculties appears as if preceded by intentional discrimination;

yet in reality, the Buddha, through his impartial great wisdom, observes that sentient beings are each distinct. Therefore, the Dharma manifested in a single voice is complete in both the Great and Small Vehicles.
Although it is simply the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, the three vehicles each understand it differently. This is the True Dharma.

The single principle is different; it is not that there is a distinction in the mind [of the Buddha]. Therefore, when Tiantai judges the teachings, he establishes the categories of the "secret" and the "indeterminate," which refers precisely to this.
As for what was said previously—that the Tathāgata does not preach the Great—this does not mean that he is now separately preaching one "Great" [teaching].

I merely explain that what was taught in the past was entirely the Great Dharma. Because Kāśyapa had only realized today’s teaching to be "great," he presumed that what was taught in the past was "small.
Therefore, the Tathāgata spoke this parable again to wash away his narrow habitual tendencies regarding the past and lead him to fully awaken to the equality of the Buddha-wisdom;
only then is he worthy of receiving the prediction [of enlightenment]. These sentient beings... [narrate].
By hearing the Dharma, they gain benefit and each attains accomplishment, gradually entering the Way.

This is just like a single cloud raining everywhere, where the three types of grass and two types of trees all receive nourishment and grow accordingly. What is called "gradually entering the Way" does not mean that the Buddha possesses a gradual teaching;
one must know that the Dharma is fundamentally sudden. It is simply that those who hear it ripen gradually, just as rain [falls upon various plants].

This is universal. Just as grasses and trees each receive its full measure of moisture according to its roots and grow accordingly, so it is with the Bodhisattvas on the stages of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, who progress through the cultivation of the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the Four Noble Truths, and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

Is it not the case that even the minor virtues of humans and devas are the Great Dharma of the Dharmadhātu? How much more so, then, are the Truths and the Links of Causality? If one were to divide them...
To differentiate between dharmas is what is known by those of the Two Vehicles. If it is non-discriminative discrimination, then it is not known by those of the Two Vehicles.

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is of a single characteristic and a single flavor (up to: he teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, which is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
This describes the Buddha’s teaching of the single, uniform flavor of the Dharma. The Dharma taught by the Buddha is fundamentally the one true reality (*dharmatā*);
from the beginning, it has no differentiated characteristics. It is purely ambrosial *amṛta* and *sarpis*, never possessing any other flavor.

One who attains liberation, though preaching all dharmas, remains detached from all dharmas; one who is detached from characteristics, though preaching all characteristics, remains detached from all characteristics. Extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
As for the "characteristics": although it speaks of arising and ceasing, it reveals quiescent extinction and non-arising. This explains the Dharma of the single characteristic and single flavor.
For this reason, every teaching spoken is ultimately consummate, reaching all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
How could there be a Dharma of three vehicles? It is only that sentient beings who hear it, according to their faculties and natures, either uphold or cultivate it.
Each receives according to their own attainment yet remains unaware of it; this Dharma is one, but the capacities [of beings] differ naturally.
Why is this so? It is to explain why sentient beings do not know [the truth].

Now, although the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is equal and of a single sound, the faculties, dispositions, natures, inclinations, thoughts, and practices of sentient beings vary, and thus they attain [it] differently.
They are not the same. One must first observe and fully comprehend [the capacities of beings], and only then preach universally according to their individual dispositions.
Thus, while the Buddha knows the inclinations and natures of sentient beings exactly as they are, sentient beings themselves do not realize the magnitude of their own fundamental capacities.
Therefore, the Dharma they hear is like a mosquito drinking from the ocean; each is satisfied according to its own measure, and they imagine that the Buddha-dharma ends there.

This is all there is. How could one know the Dharma of equality and the single flavor? From the passage "The Tathāgata knows this" onwards, [the text] explains why the Great [Vehicle] was not taught immediately above.
For the Buddha has already universally bestowed the great Dharma of equality upon all sentient beings.
The capacities of sentient beings vary in degree; the Buddha did not preach the refutation of them prematurely, but remained silent regarding this essential point for a long time.
This was because every word and every phrase of the Buddha’s teaching ultimately and completely returns to the true emptiness of the *dharmadhātu*.
However, because the inclinations and desires of sentient beings differ, he preserved [the truth] to await the proper time. Therefore...
I did not immediately explain the matters of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), fearing that they might be startled or filled with doubt; thus, I specifically remained patient and waited.
It was not that I would ultimately not speak of it. Now, as the faculties of the assembly have matured and the time for *nirvāṇa* has arrived, I cannot help but speak.
It is truly rare that Kāśyapa is able to know that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate (*yathāyogam*). Yet, within this teaching according to what is appropriate—
Equanimity—this is what is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world... (omitted)... by means of various conditions, he causes them to attain right view."
This verse reiterates the preceding meaning. The four lines beginning with "destroying existence" (*bhava*) summarize Kāśyapa’s intent in praising the Buddha.
Sentient beings of the nine realms all fall into existence: ordinary worldlings have birth and death; those of the two vehicles have nirvāṇa;
bodhisattvas have sentient beings to deliver; and there is a fruit of buddhahood to be sought. Because only the Buddha can destroy these, it is called "destroying existence."

Because he possesses mastery over all phenomena, he is called the Dharma King. The following twelve lines, beginning with "The Tathāgata holds [the Dharma] in high esteem," are verses praising the Buddha’s intention in waiting for the proper time to preach the Mahāyāna.
The reason the Tathāgata remained silent for so long without speaking was his fear that those of inferior intelligence might give rise to doubt.
Therefore, I teach according to their capacities, gradually leading them to attain right view; this is something Kāśyapa did not yet know.
Kāśyapa, you should understand that it is like a great cloud (until) what is moistened by it is one and the same, yet each [plant] flourishes accordingly.
This metaphor illustrates the meaning of impartial great compassion. The Buddha’s body is like a cloud; his preaching of the Dharma is like rain—thus, his impartiality may be known.

Yet, by describing them as "dense clouds" and "vast clouds" that descend until they can be grasped, it serves as a metaphor for the Dharmakāya’s universal pervasiveness and its inclination to accommodate the dispositions of all beings.
The thunder and lightning that precede the rain serve as a metaphor for when one first preaches the Dharma.
It must first emit light, manifest auspicious omens, and cause the earth to tremble as preliminary signs.

The initial mention of "three types of grass and two types of trees" and the subsequent verse regarding "the hundred grains" and so forth serve as metaphors for how the three vehicles and five natures are all equally moistened and benefited; yet even parched ground is thoroughly saturated.
Thus, it is that those icchantikas who lack the [Buddha-]nature have never failed to flourish.

The phrase "the clouds from which they issue forth" and so on serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s single body and single wisdom, which are equal and of one flavor; yet the capacities of those reached by this teaching receive benefits differently, each flourishing and maturing according to their own respective capacity.
The Buddha is likewise thus manifested in the world (up to) "equally raining down the rain of Dharma without weariness.

This "the Buddha is likewise thus" below corresponds to the Dharma [teaching]. The first four lines correspond to the basis of the analogy. The subsequent four lines following "already manifested" eulogize the original intent of his appearance in the world.
The fourteen lines beginning with "The Great Sage" eulogize the words of his proclamation. The various devas...
The following ten lines of verse praise the gathering of devas and humans to proclaim the Dharma of equality.
The final six lines of that section praise the Dharma of equality characterized by a single mark and a single flavor. Whatever is taught should be made the causal basis for the Mahāyāna.
What is meant is that, ultimately, all shall attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
I observe the following twenty-four lines, which correctly praise the impartial preaching of the Dharma to the noble and the lowly alike. This explains the meaning of equality:

regardless of whether one is noble or lowly, upholds or violates the precepts, follows the heterodox or the orthodox, or possesses sharp or dull faculties, all are universally covered by the single Great Wisdom of Equality. From this, it is clear that the three vehicles and the five [vehicles]...
Their nature does not depend upon receiving a prediction of enlightenment today.
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma (up to) gradually practicing it will all attain the fruit of the Way.
The following section below summarizes how sentient beings receive different benefits according to their faculties, each attaining the realization of the fruit.
The first four lines provide a general summary of all the stages (*bhūmi*), ranging from the nine stages of the three realms up to the ten stages of the Bodhisattva.
The subsequent explanation of the various stages (*bhūmi*) is as follows: the first four lines clarify humans and devas who know the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*);

the next eight lines clarify the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and the final four lines clarify the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka teachings who practice according to the provisional teachings, and are thus termed "small herbs.
As the verse says, "I shall become a Buddha," yet that which is aimed for by the Tripiṭaka teachings is the Three Piṭakas themselves.

This refers to the Buddha at the culmination of the fruit (*phala-koṭi-buddha*). Furthermore, the six lines beginning with "And all the sons of the Buddha" clarify the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

The six lines beginning with "Abiding securely in supernormal powers" clarify the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*). The six lines beginning with "The Buddha’s equality" praise the fact that while the Dharma is one, the capacities of sentient beings differ.
The six lines beginning with "The Buddha uses this parable" conclude by stating that the Buddha’s merits cannot be fully described through words.
Venerable, because Kāśyapa was unable to fully comprehend the merits of the Tathāgata, this parable was spoken to elucidate it.
Nevertheless, a single cloud and a single rain moisten all equally and universally, so that the three types of grass and two types of trees all reach full maturity.
Although this metaphor illustrates that the Buddha’s merit is vast and inconceivable, in reality it is but a single drop within the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom;
how could it fully illustrate the Buddha’s merit? This is why Kāśyapa was unable to know it exhaustively.
The eight lines beginning with "I rain down the rain of Dharma" collectively clarify the benefit of bringing beings to maturity. All Buddhas...

The six lines following this verse collectively clarify the capacities of those to be matured. The subsequent section specifically clarifies how they attain their respective fruits according to their individual dispositions.
From "The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas dwelling in mountain forests" up to "moistening human flowers so that each attains its fruit," [the text explains this].
The section beginning with "This [refers to] the śrāvakas" praises the respective growth attained by them. The first six lines praise the growth attained by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The subsequent six lines, beginning with "If there are bodhisattvas," refer to the growth attained by bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching (*upāya-śāsana*).
Furthermore, there are eight phrases concerning abiding in dhyāna, which state that the Bodhisattvas of the definitive teaching attain increase;
that is to say, being fully moistened, each attains growth. Thus, Kāśyapa, the following six phrases summarize the *Saṃdhinirmocana* (the Realization of the Ultimate).
"Kāśyapa, you should know that through various causes and conditions (up to) gradually practicing and training, all shall attain Buddhahood.

From "This, Kāśyapa," onwards, the verse reveals the provisional to manifest the real, showing that the path of all Buddhas is the same. The first six lines clarify that by revealing the real within the provisional, the paths of all Buddhas are identical.
The subsequent eight lines from "Now, for your sakes" summarize the present reality, thereby encompassing [the entire teaching].
This is a passage that discards the provisional [teachings] of the past and opens up the text of the future prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

Although they have already received the prediction, the statement that they "should gradually practice and study until all become Buddhas" precisely reveals that their former practice was not the true cultivation. From now on, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) is the true cause for becoming a Buddha;
this is what is meant by taking the "unborn and undying mind" as the fundamental cause of cultivation. As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says:
Principle must be realized suddenly, while phenomena are eliminated gradually; therefore, it is said "gradually.
Regarding the intent of the arrival of this sixth chapter, "The Chapter on Prophecies," in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
it follows from the fact that the four great disciples have already understood the principle of the single flavor of equality.
Originally, there was no reality of the three vehicles. Now that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision have been revealed, the true cause for attaining Buddhahood is already complete.

It is for this reason that he bestows predictions of enlightenment upon the four types of people, specifically designating them by their names and categories; it is for this purpose that he has come here.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses (up to the point where it says), "Even though there are Māras and their followers,
they all protect the Buddha-dharma," the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
He addressed the bhikṣus: "With my Buddha-eye... [omitted] ...the World-Honored One’s radiance is thus.
This was the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) upon Kāśyapa. Regarding the matter of the predictions bestowed upon the disciples, there are causes and there are fruits;
yet among the fruits obtained, some are identical and some are not. This is because each is induced according to its own original cause. All of them—
Today, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened for the first time to inspire the initial resolve for enlightenment.

From this point forward, the practices one cultivates constitute the true cause for attaining Buddhahood, for it is through the perfection of the cause that the fruit is subsequently attained. Furthermore, within the causal stage, one must necessarily serve and make offerings to the Buddhas:
by making offerings to the Buddhas, one cultivates merit; by proclaiming the Dharma, one cultivates wisdom. Thus, the two adornments are complete.

It is sufficient. One attains the fruit only after the conditions are fulfilled; therefore, it is only in one's final body that one achieves Buddhahood. Regarding this "final body," the Treatise states:
"When the stages of the Bodhisattva are exhausted, awakening-mind first arises. Yet the mind has no initial characteristic, for it is far removed from even subtle thoughts.
Thus one perceives the nature of the mind. This is the moment when ignorance is utterly purified and the two types of death are forever extinguished."
They are called those in their final bodies (*caramabhavika*). However, the variation in the number of Buddhas they serve is due to the inequality in the thickness of their ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, there are those who build stupas and those who do not, because the depth of the merit they have accumulated differs.
Although their names are distinct, each follows its own original cause; yet, the adornment of their lands is identical.
Purity is the true recompense evoked by the purification of the single mind alone. That the sentient beings to be transformed are free from the three evil realms is summoned by one's original vow.
As for the magnitude of one’s retinue and the length of one’s lifespan, [these likewise arise from that same purity].
The duration for which the Dharma remains is entirely determined by the power of one's vows; this is the case for all such examples.

Kāśyapa, whose name means "Drinker of Light," served the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa during his causal stage, lighting lamps to continue the illumination and anointing the Buddha’s images with purple-gold light.
Consequently, he attained the fruit of being named "Radiance. His land was called "Virtue of Light" (Prabhāśrī), and his kalpa was named "Great Adornment" (Mahāvyūha).
This is indeed fitting. Their lifespan and the duration of the Dharma’s abiding are both twenty minor kalpas; thus they differ from Śāriputra, yet this too is sustained by their original vows.
Their land is pure because they share a single pure mind. Their retinue of followers of the Three Vehicles is likewise due to past affinities.
Since it is not an age of evil, the Māras all protect the Dharma.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and the others [up to] spoke these verses with one voice:
"O Great Hero, O Fierce World-Honored One, Dharma-King of all the Śākyas... [up to] ...like one who is hungry, he requires instruction on food."
These individuals, such as Maudgalyāyana and others, because they had received their predictions from Kāśyapa, requested them now out of a desire for such confirmation.

However, since the previous Buddha had already stated in general that all twelve hundred śrāvakas would likewise become Buddhas, it was clear that each person possessed the distinct certainty of attaining Buddhahood.
Yet, these three sons wished to have their names specifically mentioned so that the actual facts could be declared; this was likely because they feared that...
"I may not [accept]. To tremble with awe and thus request [permission] is precisely because those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) have long harbored the habit of clinging to signs;
their narrow and inferior minds have not yet been suddenly cast aside. Although they have now received the Buddha’s permission, they do not yet dare to accept it themselves.
Thus, it is like a hungry person encountering a king’s banquet who does not dare to eat immediately, but must wait until he receives the command before he dares to eat. Therefore...
Although they had heard that he would become a Buddha, their hearts still harbored anxiety; they could find peace only by hoping for the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the great disciples [and so forth], had delivered and liberated immeasurable bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, I now tell you... (until) the Semblance Dharma shall also abide for twenty minor kalpas."
This refers to the attainment of the prediction of enlightenment by Śūnyatā-utpāda (Empty-Born). Regarding his future practice as a Buddha, he will be like Kāśyapa and the others;

as for the names and characteristics of their resultant titles, each follows its own original cause. Since Subhūti is foremost in understanding emptiness (*śūnyatā*), yet that which is empty consists of nothing other than names and characteristics, when he attains Buddhahood in the future, the names and characteristics of his resultant title will precisely manifest emptiness itself.

The Dharma is realized. When the Venerable One was born, the treasuries were all empty; thus, the kalpa of the fruition stage is named "Possessing Jewels" (Saratna), and the land is named "Jewel-Born" (Ratnasambhava).
This is likely because emptiness is used to manifest the meaning of non-emptiness; it is also the fundamental cause.
Since that land is pure, it shares in the same purity of mind, and the people all dwell upon jeweled terraces; this corresponds to the meaning of "possessing jewels. [His] retinue...

The duration of the Dharma’s abiding depends upon the length of the Buddha's lifespan. As for [the Buddhas] such as Kāśyapa and others, that Buddha constantly dwells in space while preaching the Dharma;
because he has realized the reality of the Dharma through space, his fruit is likewise so.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus (up to: "The semblance Dharma shall also remain for twenty minor kalpas.
Then, wishing to reiterate this meaning, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
All the assembly of bhikṣus listened with one mind (until) his land was adorned with immeasurable and innumerable [treasures].
This was the prophecy for Candra. Following that prophecy, Candra first served eight thousand koṭis of buddhas.

After those buddhas had passed into extinction, he constructed stūpas and temples of the seven treasures to enshrine the buddha-relics. He continued this through twenty-two thousand koṭis of buddhas; in total, it was but a small portion [of his practice].
As for Kāśyapa, who attained Buddhahood swiftly after his birth in the void, it was because he had previously excelled in debate and his realization of the *dharmatā* was brilliant and refined;
thus, his resultant name was Nadi-Kanaka, signifying the ultimate degree of clarity and purity, which arose from the nature of his causal practices.

His lifespan of twelve kalpas corresponds to the karmic conditions of those he influenced; as for the duration of his stay in the world and the longevity of the Dharma’s endurance, these were sustained by the power of his vows.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly... [up to] "the Semblance Dharma shall also remain for forty minor kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"This disciple of mine, Mahāmaudgalyāyana—[up to: 'I shall now cause you all to listen well. This Maudgalyāyana has received his prediction.
Regarding the record of Maudgalyāyana’s attainment of this prediction: he was slightly junior to Kātyāyana.

Yet, after the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, he constructed stupas to make offerings to the Buddha, numbering two hundred million *koṭis* and even more; this was likewise due to his meritorious practice."

The progression of their cultivation is not uniform. Maudgalyāyana, having cultivated supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) as his primary practice in past lives, was thus named Candanagandha (Sandalwood Fragrance) as a result.
This fragrance, being pure, far-reaching, and subtly pervasive, is the very image of supernatural power.

His retinue is likewise equal [to that of Śākyamuni], though his lifespan is somewhat shorter, which also depends on the karmic conditions of those he encounters. His Dharma will abide for forty minor kalpas—an exceedingly long duration—sustained by the power of his vows.
However, as for those śrāvakas who are consistently terrified by the long duration of the Buddha-way, it is because they have not yet seen the actual fruit that can be expected;
having no destination in sight, they give rise to fear.

Now, those who receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood—even though it still requires many kalpas—do not fear, because the actual fruit lies before them and the time to realize it is certain. Thus, their [fear] is...

Habitual tendencies are easily abandoned. Because those who rely on the verbal designations and habitual tendencies esteemed by the Hīnayāna do not recognize them as the Buddha’s words, their minds remain unsettled.
Thus, we know that the matter of bestowing predictions (vyākaraṇa) is used precisely to encourage them through such verbal designations. It is like using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying;
it is simply the principle of using one wedge to extract another. It is like a person who has long taken dream-events to be signs of good or bad fortune.
The omens of these matters must be judged by the standards of dream interpretation (*yuanmeng*). Yet, are dreams truly auspicious or inauspicious?

During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty, there was a man skilled in interpreting dreams. The Emperor tested him with a fabricated dream, saying: "In my dream, two tiles from the palace roof fell."
He transformed himself into a pair of mandarin ducks and flew away. The man said, "There must be someone who has killed another within the palace.
Shortly thereafter, it was reported that a palace woman had indeed been killed and died. The Emperor said, "I was merely joking; it was not a dream. How could this have been a response?
The man replied, "A dream is where the spirit reaches. When the spirit moves, good or ill fortune follows."
Therefore, it is believed that when the Buddhas preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, they do so like describing the events of a dream.
The ten phrases beginning with "My disciples" and following introduce the discourse on subsequent causes and conditions.
The Seventh Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "The Parable of the Phantom City.

Regarding the purpose of this chapter: although the five individuals previously mentioned have all received their predictions of enlightenment, there remains among those in the assembly a class of śrāvakas with dull faculties.
Because they previously regarded the fruit of Buddhahood and bodhi as beyond the scope of their own wisdom, their narrow and inferior habitual tendencies have not yet been forgotten.

One might have thought that those who serve as leaders of the assembly would naturally receive a prediction of enlightenment; yet these individuals still harbor thoughts of being beyond such a destiny.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has distantly cited the past causes from eons ago, during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, when sixteen princes were taught and converted.
They had once planted the seeds for the conditions of the One Vehicle, and from that time until now, they have received [the fruits] in every successive birth.
Transformation. Now that the conditions have ripened, this is the time for formal authorization.

To shatter the doubts and attachments of the great assembly, to cause them to leap forth with a yearning for the Great [Vehicle], and to eliminate their long-standing habitual tendencies, he extensively cites the past events of Mahābhijñājñāna and the causes and conditions of the sixteen princes preaching the Dharma, thereby manifesting the Buddha-nature as the condition-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Thus he says:
The parable of the conjured city was originally established as a fiction to clarify that the three vehicles are ultimately provisional.

It was intended to provide temporary rest for those weary from traveling a long distance and fearful of the journey, so that they might proceed toward the place of treasure. By means of this, the dull-witted were inspired and urged forward;
thus, upon hearing this teaching, the great assembly suddenly awakened to their past causes, gained self-confidence in their future buddhahood, and each received their prediction.
Commentary: This chapter follows for this reason.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In the distant past... [up to] observing that long ago as if it were today.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

I recall that in the past, throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas—up until the point of penetrating immeasurable kalpas—this Tathāgata traced back to the original cause of his Great Universal Wisdom-Victory (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*). This serves as proof for the causal seeds of the present Dharma assembly.
The Buddha named Great Universal Wisdom-Victory is the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas, endowed with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

It is the essence of the fruit, the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings. Only this essence of wisdom transcends the dimensions of the *dharmadhātu*, and is therefore called "Great" (*mahā*).
It penetrates the realms of both the holy and the ordinary, and is therefore called "Pervasive" (*viśva*). It is eternally present and never obscured, and is therefore called "Wisdom" (*jñāna*).
It is the true ultimate nature within the ultimate truth, and is therefore called "Supreme" (*parama*). Because this wisdom is most supreme, its function is not separate from its essence.

Therefore, he is endowed with the ten titles and eternally dwells in the Land of Quiescent Light; thus, the land is named "Good City. Since this existed prior to the kalpa of emptiness, the kalpa is named "Great Mark.
Sentient beings have turned their backs on this essence of wisdom since time immemorial; hence it is said that they have passed through inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
As for Jiyin, he [interprets this] through the *Huayan* contemplation of the Dharma-realm as "True Emptiness Beyond All Marks."
The non-obstruction between principle and phenomena is all-pervasive and inclusive. The three types of contemplative gates explain the three characters "Great Penetration Wisdom" (*Mahābhijñājñāna*).

It is most excellent that these three meanings are fully present; this is most consistent with the ultimate principle. However, while the term "inherent" refers to the fundamental endowment and the term "contemplation" refers to cultivation and manifestation, they appear to have a sequence of priority.
This wisdom is also called "teacherless wisdom" (*asaṃśikṣita-jñāna*) and "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*); all Buddhas realize this wisdom.
Its essence is named "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "How marvelous, how marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, because of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachments, they do not realize it.
If one is free from deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachments, then all-knowledge, teacherless knowledge, and spontaneous knowledge are attained in this very moment."
Manifest before us. Know that this wisdom is the essential body of the fruit of all Buddhas and the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings.
Because those of the Two Vehicles are deluded regarding this fundamental wisdom, they all say it was lost in the past, claiming that there is no possibility of attaining Buddhahood.
Although the five people were previously granted predictions of enlightenment, they were those who truly believed in the Buddha-mind without doubt.

There still remain those of inferior understanding and low faculties who cling to the habitual tendencies of the names and phrases of the Two Vehicles. Their doubts regarding what was previously lost have not been forgotten;
thus, even though they have now heard this prediction, their state of doubt is not yet exhausted, and they do not realize the reason why [the Buddha-nature] is not lost.

Therefore, the Buddha specifically explains the causes and conditions to trace back to the origin of the Buddha-nature: that it has never been lost since beginningless time. Thus, he points directly to it.
Since the past events of the Greatly Enlightened One are clearly seen as if they were now, the future matter of receiving predictions and attaining fruition is likewise not false.
This is what is meant by using causes and conditions to shatter the attachments of those with inferior faculties.

Although it was previously stated repeatedly that the Buddha’s wisdom is not something known by the followers of the Two Vehicles, the ocean of merit and virtue of the Buddha-fruit is inconceivable; this too is one thing that cannot be known.

This is the essential point. As for the statement that "it has been an exceedingly long time since that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa," this precisely reveals that the Dharmakāya has remained hidden and unmanifest;
sentient beings have been deluded by it for a very long time. Therefore, it speaks of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust and grains of ink to illustrate this.
Suppose one were to take the entire trichiliocosm and grind it into ink to serve as the medium for writing. Within the ten directions, let us consider the eastern direction alone:
having passed through a thousand lands, one places a single drop of ink, as large as a minute mote of dust. Thus, after traversing a thousand lands, there is but a single dot.
Continuing in this manner, traveling further east, one proceeds to place dots in succession across as many lands as in the first instance.
Those that have black dots upon them can no longer be discerned; this is beyond the reach of even the most skilled mathematician. How much more so those with dots and those without?
If one were to wipe them all away until they become dust, the number of these particles would be exceedingly vast. Let each single particle represent one kalpa.
If one were to measure the kalpas [since his passing], they would be immeasurable; this implies that tracing back to their origin, there is no beginning.

Since the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, more than these numbers of kalpas have elapsed. This sufficiently proves that sentient beings have been deluded regarding this Buddha-nature for a very long time;

how could it be known by those of the Two Vehicles? Nevertheless, when previously addressing those of superior faculties, I spoke only of the time since he attained Buddhahood, without specifying its duration.
Regarding those of middling capacity, the matter of teaching was addressed by mentioning only twenty trillion Buddhas; this is what is meant by "citing one corner.
Now, as for those of inferior capacity, their duration extends to the full measure of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.

This is because those of the Two Vehicles, possessing inferior understanding, still maintain views of annihilation and permanence regarding the beginning and end [of existence], and their debased habits are difficult to eradicate; it is not possible to shatter these through any means other than this. This...
This is the expedient means by which the Tathāgata draws beings toward him. Moreover, with his knowledge and vision, the Tathāgata perceives that which is remote as if it were today;
how much more so for me, the Tathāgata, who has appeared in the world for forty years and have not been apart from the *kṣaṇa-limits* samādhi.
How could these words be false? Therefore, what the Tathāgata speaks is true and not in vain. When those of inferior capacity hear this, although...
To the utmost degree of ignorance and delusion, one cannot help but believe the Buddha’s words of truth.

When the Buddha exerts himself for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles, how could the householder in the burning house or the father of the impoverished son fully exhaust the Buddha’s true compassion?
As a verse says: "The Buddha's wisdom is pure and subtle; it is untainted and unimpeded; it penetrates throughout immeasurable kalpas. Thus we know the Buddha...

When wisdom first contemplates the beginninglessness [of saṃsāra], it subsequently contemplates its endlessness; this is precisely what is meant by bestowing the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that a disciple shall attain Buddhahood.
Even the most distant point does not exceed three million billion kalpas, yet when observed with the Buddha-eye, it is as if before one's very eyes—how could one not believe this?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus (up to) "attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
These words indicate that the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū manifested the traces of his responsive incarnation from the Dharma. His lifespan was five million *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas;
this specifically cites the traces of his responsive conditions. When it says he originally sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it refers to his emergence [from that state].

The "true omen" (*shinjō*) marks the beginning of the manifestation of the sacred response. It is called "about to attain enlightenment" (*chitoku bodai*) because whenever a Buddha appears, he must demonstrate his initial attainment of perfect awakening;
hence the term "about to. "About to" (*chi*) means "imminent. Question: Since the Buddha is already manifesting himself, there is no need for him to further attain anything;
why then do you say he is "about to attain enlightenment," as if the Buddha-dharma were not yet present? Answer: This is a matter of waiting.
This is the pivot. It is said that the Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things like the moon reflected in water.
When the water of sentient beings’ minds is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears therein. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Vairocana..."
Within the bodies of all sentient beings, he attains equal and perfect enlightenment. This is to know that the Buddha is fundamentally not a body, but takes sentient beings as his body.
Now, because the Great Penetrating Wisdom Buddha has no response despite having manifested, although he has attained bodhi, the Buddha-dharma does not appear before him.
This is precisely because the mental vessels of sentient beings have not yet been purified; therefore, he waits for ten minor kalpas.

"At that time, sitting cross-legged with body and mind unmoving" refers to entering the Samādhi of the Momentary Limit (*kṣaṇāntara-samādhi*), which is what was initially called the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meaning (*ananta-artha-sthāna-samādhi*).
Now, for the Nirmāṇakāya of the World-Honored One to wait for forty years—how could this be considered a long duration?
The devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven had already preceded him to beneath the Bodhi tree to spread out seats and await his arrival.
This clearly demonstrates that without departing from beneath the Bodhi tree, he universally responds to beings.

That as soon as he sat upon this seat, the devas rained down flowers and played music, up until his final parinirvāṇa, demonstrates that from the Buddha’s appearance in the world until his passing, he never for a single moment arose from the Samādhi of the Limit of Moments (*kṣaṇānta-samādhi*).
In the light of the Introduction Chapter, the beginnings and ends of all Buddhas are perfectly manifested; one might think that within the light—

This is merely the realm of the provisional teaching. Now, it is directly revealed that this sutra explains the actual reality within the light. As for the statement that one attains bodhi after ten minor kalpas once the Buddha-dharma has appeared before one:
this is the moment when the resonance between the capacity of the practitioner and the response of the Buddha coincides, and when the mind and its objects are beyond all dependence.
As the ancients said, "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season. Thus, we know that now...

He spoke of the causes and conditions for the Buddha’s wisdom; however, this must await the convergence of the appropriate opportunity and conditions, for he did not dare to preach forcefully at an improper time.
Before the Buddha had left the household life, he had sixteen sons... (until) they bowed their heads at his feet, circumambulated him, and finished their prostrations.
This is the fundamental cause of the original Śākyamuni. "Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū" (Greatly Pervasive Wisdom-Victor) clarifies the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
That it is now said this Buddha had sixteen sons before he left home clarifies that the wisdom of all modes is formed through the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*).
Because one is deluded regarding this wisdom, the *ālayavijñāna* is formed; thus, it arises while still bound within the defilements.
This is the name for death. As for the substance of this consciousness (*vijñāna*), its functions are eightfold.
What was previously called the "Sun, Moon, Lamp, and Light" having eight sons referred solely to consciousness; therefore, it was named "Possessing Mind" (*yì*).

Now, what is called the sixteen [sons] and named "Accumulated Wisdom" (*Zhìjī*) refers to the source of consciousness being rooted in wisdom. Through delusion, wisdom is transformed into consciousness; thus, its functions are eightfold.

Upon awakening, the consciousnesses are transformed into wisdoms. Their functions number four; however, as for the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), its functions are five, and thus there are eight in total.
Now, by taking the true and the delusive as a single essence, they are said to be sixteen, whereby the four wisdoms are perfected.

It is collectively termed "Omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*); thus, his son is named Jñānakūṭa (Wisdom-Peak). This refers merely to the designation used while he was still bound by worldly entangments prior to his renunciation.
If one penetrates the essence of the fruition, however, truth and delusion are non-dual, and the sentiments of father and son vanish.
Since Śākyamuni’s original cause was as the sixteenth son, the provisional and the real can be understood. Each of the sons has their respective equals.
This means that as long as the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has not been transformed, all the various consciousnesses are characterized by defilement, ignorance, craving, and attachment.

Once the fundamental consciousness is transformed, all the various consciousnesses are transformed simultaneously, suddenly shattering the two types of ignorance: that which initiates karma and that which nourishes rebirth.

Therefore, it is said that upon hearing their fathers had left the household life, they all abandoned what was most precious to them. As initial awakening merges with the fundamental nature, it is said that they went to the place where the Buddha was.

A sutra states: "Ignorance is taken as the father, and craving is taken as the mother. Now, since consciousness has been transformed into wisdom, craving and afflictions instead nourish the functioning of wisdom;
thus, it is said that the various mothers wept and followed him as he departed. This is because...
Attachment is difficult to relinquish; one must relinquish it even against one's will.

As for his ancestors, such as the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings (*cakravartin*), they established nine consciousnesses in addition to the *ālaya-vijñāna* mentioned in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, naming them the "Pure White Consciousness," which is also *tathatā*.

Now, when the *ālaya* undergoes this single transformation, the hundred mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and all subtle afflictions (*kleśa*) are simultaneously and collectively transformed, all becoming [one with] *tathatā*.
Just as for the sake of employing great wisdom, his ancestor, the Wheel-Turning Sage King,
was followed to the site of enlightenment by one hundred ministers and the rest of the populace, all surrounding him.
With single-minded devotion, he joined his palms, gazed up at the World-Honored One, and spoke in verse:
"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings... [I] take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One."
At that time, after the sixteen princes had praised the Buddha with verses, the devas and the people spoke further in verse:
"O Hero of the World, peerless and unequaled, adorned by a hundred merits... [until] you shall turn the unsurpassed wheel."
This prince praises how the Buddha’s appearance in the world is solely for the benefit of devas and humans.

The six lines beginning with "Of great majestic power" praise the Buddha’s perfection of merit and attainment of the fruit. The eight lines beginning with "The World-Honored One is most rare" praise the Buddha entering meditative concentration to await the proper opportunity.
The four lines beginning with "Now" express his own joy at this auspicious benefit. The eight lines beginning with "Sentient beings are constantly afflicted by suffering" [express their plight].
The phrase "should transform them" refers to the opportune moment for conversion. The six lines following "Now the Buddha" celebrate the mutual benefit of both self and others.

Having offered praise, he requests the turning of the wheel of Dharma, manifesting that the Buddha’s appearance in the world is fundamentally for the sake of bringing peace and security and out of compassion for sentient beings; it is not in vain.
Therefore, he requests the teaching of the Dharma with the four lines beginning "O Hero of the World, peerless one," which is a request for the teaching of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
With the six lines beginning "Deliver us," he requests that the Buddha teach expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
With the eight lines beginning "World-Honored One, you know my mind," he requests that the Buddha certainly employ the opening of the expedient, in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "From the time the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū [attained enlightenment] until his light filled the world, surpassing the radiance of all devas—this Tathāgata specifically opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for those of inferior faculties.
In the Sanskrit language, *Vairocana* means "Universal Radiance," which is precisely the Great Pervasive Wisdom (*Mahābhijñājñāna*).
To speak of him as "attaining Buddhahood" refers to the attainment of the All-Encompassing Wisdom (*Sarvākārajñatā*).
This wisdom is the Buddha-knowledge and vision inherently possessed by all sentient beings. It is for this purpose that the Buddha appears in the world;
it is called the "One Great Matter" (ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya). Because sentient beings are singularly deluded regarding this wisdom, they become bound fast by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Consequently, their physical bodies, faculties, and the objective world become obstructed and disconnected, resulting only in false conceptualizations and afflictions (*kleśa*).
They are agitated and disturbed by it, yet they live their daily lives unaware of it; thus they create deluded karma and undergo manifold sufferings.

Therefore, the Buddha appears in the world through his great compassion of same essence (*sahaja-karuṇā*) to reveal this to them, enabling them to awaken and enter [the truth] so as to transcend birth and death.
This is the fundamental intention for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world. As soon as sentient beings clarify this wisdom, they immediately—
To be a Buddha in this very moment—this meaning is startling and is not something that those of inferior faculties can endure; therefore, it was taught only after waiting for their capacity to ripen.
This single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* universally reveals that for forty years, everything has been the fundamental intention of this matter.
Yet, it is not something that can be easily or hastily proclaimed. As for what is called "opening" and "showing": it is to enlighten through words and to point toward the truth through facts.

Therefore, at the beginning of the Dharma assembly, he first emitted a single ray of light that illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, perfectly manifesting the phenomena of the dharma-realm and the beginning and end of the arising of Buddhas.
This was to present a single corner of this wisdom’s entire substance as a precursor for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
It was intended that once the faculties and capacities of the disciples had matured, it would not be necessary to speak further.
This is already evident. Furthermore, regarding this realm of wisdom, even Maitreya, who stands as the successor to the position of Buddhahood, still harbors doubts.

Therefore, Mañjuśrī—the teacher of the seven Buddhas—is invoked to explain it away on his behalf. By tracing back to the origins of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he validates the auspicious signs of the present Buddha.
This is the first instance of revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As the assembly remained bewildered and unenlightened, [the teaching] was further supplemented by...
The World-Honored One emerged from meditative concentration and earnestly praised skillful means (*upāya*), revealing them until the end of the "Chapter on Skillful Means.
The World-Honored One had already proclaimed this with all his might, yet only Śāriputra alone attained realization; thus we know that the delusion of sentient beings is indeed profound.
Furthermore, he spoke the parable of the burning house to illustrate the nature of the manifold sufferings within the triple world. This can be...
This means that [the Buddha] has explained it in full detail, as clearly as showing the palms of one's hands. Furthermore, only four people have attained realization;
yet the assembly of twelve hundred followers remains as if in a state of sleep or a dream. What can be done?
It is truly because the gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Therefore, the Buddha spoke of his past causes and conditions to clarify and inform them. Far...

He cites the original beginning of the Great Universal Wisdom Victor (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) as the causal condition for the present day, specifically providing a great illumination for those of inferior faculties.
Initially, the light from his brow awaited its release before it shone, and at first, it was seen only in the eastern direction.

Now, this light of primordial wisdom, which is inherently present, does not depend on being gathered or released, yet it is ever-luminous; thus, even in places of profound darkness, it shines with great brilliance.
This is the essence of wisdom, naturally and unclouded, which sentient beings use in their daily lives without realizing it.
Now that the essence of wisdom suddenly manifests before them, each and every sentient being suddenly realizes what has been inherently present. Therefore...
Everyone said, "How is it that sentient beings have suddenly arisen here? How marvelous, how marvelous!
This great light fills everywhere, universally illuminating the ten directions. This was specifically for those of inferior faculties, the second time the Buddha revealed his knowledge and vision.
This is still a remote reference to the Buddhas of antiquity. However, if one looks down to the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Jeweled Stūpa," it points directly before the great assembly;
this is the third instance of revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The ten directions' heavenly kings seeking the light and requesting the Buddha all fulfill the remaining intent of the various Brahma heavenly kings and others at the end of the "Chapter on Extensive Means."
At that time, from within five hundred million worlds in the eastern direction... [up to] he spoke these verses:
"The radiance of our various palaces is such as has never existed before... illuminating the ten directions everywhere."
At that time, the Brahma Kings from five million billion lands (up to) with one mind and in a single voice, spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter... (up to) we only pray that you will compassionately accept us."
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they spoke these verses with one mind and a single voice:
"O Hero among Men, Honored One among the Two-legged, we pray that you will expound the Dharma; through the power of great compassion, deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction."
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently gave his consent.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus from five million billion lands in the southeast [arrived] and spoke these verses:
For what cause and condition does this phenomenon appear in such a manner... [to] deliver sentient beings from suffering?
At that time, five hundred trillion Brahma kings... with one mind and a single voice, spoke in verse:
“O Holy Lord, King of Devas, with a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird... [until] now we have encountered the World-Honored One.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha in verse, they spoke these verses with one mind and in unison:
"The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma to reveal the characteristics of all phenomena... (until) those who are well-established in patience shall increase.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus in five million billion lands to the south [proceeded] and spoke these verses:
"The radiance of our various palaces is most majestic and brilliant... [it is] because a Buddha has appeared in the world."
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings (up to) with one mind and in unison praised him in verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One is most difficult to behold, he who has shattered all afflictions... (up to) we only pray that you will graciously accept [our offerings]."
At that time, having praised the Buddha with verses, the Brahma Kings, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke these verses:
"We pray that the Honored One of Gods and Humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma... [and] shall now proclaim the profound and far-reaching sound."
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent; the same occurred for the regions from the southwest down to the nadir.
At that time, [the Buddha] proceeded through five million billion lands in the zenith and spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās:
"Now, by what causes and conditions have all our palaces [become thus] until the Buddha has appeared in the world?
At that time, five hundred trillion Brahma Kings [and others] with one mind and in a single voice spoke in verse:
"Excellent! To behold all the Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world... (until)... may they all together attain the Buddha-way.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings... (until)... then those Brahma Kings spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One turns the Wheel of Dharma and beats the drum of the nectar-like Dharma" (up to) "practicing the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas.
These words indicate that the Victor of Wisdom first sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). It refers to the request by the devas and Brahmā kings to turn the Wheel of Dharma.

At the end of the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*, the Śākya-muni himself recounts how he first sat at the site of enlightenment, gazing at the tree and walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), contemplating for three weeks. His intention was...

Desiring to distinguish and explain the Single Vehicle Dharma as three, he was undecided whether to proceed or retreat. At that time, the Brahma Kings among the various devas requested that the Buddha open the way for gradual teaching.
Consequently, he proceeded to teach the Three Vehicles. Reflecting upon the skillful means employed by past Buddhas, he realized that he too should teach the Three Vehicles.
Now, at this moment, the Brahma Kings of the ten directions all simultaneously [made their request to] the Greatly Enlightened and Victorious Buddha.
The general labor service (*pǔqǐng*) and the teachings spoken upon emerging from meditative concentration (*chūding*) concern the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

Thus, it is known that the previous reference to the Buddha of the Past is none other than the present Jñānavijaya. This establishes that Śākyamuni was the son of Jñānavijaya and that his preaching of the Dharma followed the example of his own Teacher;
this is the ancestral tradition of filial succession. Previously, I had merely provided a general and brief account; now—

This, in fact, indicates the underlying reason for establishing [the teaching] for those of inferior faculties. Whenever Buddhas appear in the world, they invariably take Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas as their petitioners;
this is surely the standard pattern. As for the phrase "The light of supreme wisdom pervades the ten directions," the various devas each follow the direction of that light and come toward it.
This is as stated in the previous *Bhaiṣajyavastu* (Medicine Herb) Parable: "I am the Tathāgata," and so forth.
They are summoned by speech; this is summoned by light. Yet, when they preach the Dharma, it is all of one and the same standard.

This is sufficient evidence that the various skillful means of the Buddhas are all for the sake of the One Vehicle; of this there is certainly no doubt. Nevertheless, while the celestial beings who attend upon the Buddha and present offerings are always the same, their words of praise differ.
It is simply that when no Buddha appears in the world, the kalpas are different, according to the dialects of the southeast.
