One hundred and eighty kalpas; in the south, it is said to be one hundred and thirty kalpas; in the zenith, it is said that for immeasurable kalpas in the past, time passed in emptiness without a Buddha.
These are all differences according to the varying capacities and responses of sentient beings, and they reflect the far-reaching and vast illumination of the supreme wisdom.
With the Great Brahmā King as the lord of the Sahā world, it is now stated that in each of the ten directions...
The great Brahma kings of five million billion lands, illuminated by the Buddha’s light, have their entire realm—extending to the limits of the Dharma-realm—unified into a single land;
this is vastly different from the illumination of the eastern eighteen thousand lands by the light from between his eyebrows.
The wisdom of the Buddha is difficult to understand and difficult to know; it may be illustrated by a single corner for those of superior faculties, but as for those of inferior [faculties]...
As for their faculties, they do not fall within the scope of my own wisdom; therefore, I cannot but disclose everything to them with full sincerity, so that they may clearly attain self-confidence.
Thus we know that these individuals possess dull faculties, and it is through this very means that faith and understanding can be produced in them.
This is the skillful expedient employed by the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū [up to] "this is the cessation of suffering, this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This refers to Jñānābhibhū’s acceptance of the invitation to preach the Dharma. The wheel of the Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects is the teaching of the Four Noble Truths.
As for the "three turnings," they are: indicating the characteristics, exhorting to practice, and realizing through witness. The first turning indicates the characteristics, meaning: "This is..."
The "characteristics of suffering, oppression, and so forth" demonstrate the marks of the Four Noble Truths. Next is the "turning toward exhortation to practice," which means:

"This is suffering; you should know it," and so on. This exhorts one to now loathe suffering, abandon its origin, aspire to its cessation, and cultivate the path. As for the "turning toward realization":

This refers to "I have known," and so forth, by which one realizes for oneself what has been realized by another. When those of the Two Vehicles hear this, they attain awakening in accordance with the sound;

hence they are called *śrāvakas* (Hearers). Regarding the traditional interpretation that the three turnings cause one to enter the three stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, as well as the statement regarding the twelve aspects, Jiyin (Jiguang) comments that these cause those who hear the Dharma to give rise to the untainted, true, noble eye of wisdom.

Within each Truth (satya), observing the three periods of time constitutes the general [contemplation]. Furthermore, within each Truth, observing the past is "knowledge" (jñāna), observing the future is "clarity" (vidyā), and observing the present is "awakening" (buddhi).
These constitute the specific [contemplations] of the Four Truths. Thus, there are four modes of practice consisting of these general and specific aspects for each turning;
therefore, they are called the "three turnings and twelve modes. "Truth" (satya) means to be examined and verified, as well as being real and authentic.
Indeed, ordinary beings dwell in suffering yet do not discern its reality; those of the Two Vehicles discern this as real, yet do not know the ultimate truth.
Bodhisattvas penetrate the emptiness of the nature of suffering, whereby the names of the Four Truths become one. This reality permeates both the Great and Small Vehicles;

thus, Tiantai explains that there are four aspects of the Four Truths—namely, the Arising and Ceasing, the Non-arising, the Immeasurable, and the Unconditioned—according to the differences among the four teachings.
The Hinayana teachings of the Tripitaka know only arising and ceasing, but do not know non-arising.

Although the Shared Teaching knows non-arising, it does not know the immeasurable and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*). The Distinct Teaching is immeasurable, while the Perfect Teaching is unconditioned.
It is simply the Four Noble Truths, each differing according to what is perceived. In the "Expedient Means" chapter, when Śākyamuni accepts the invitation, he says:

The One Vehicle Dharma was previously explained by distinguishing it into three. Now, when Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepts the invitation, he speaks directly of the Small Vehicle Dharma without further mentioning its distinctions;
this is precisely to resolve the doubts of those with inferior faculties regarding how their former provisional teachings are in fact the ultimate reality.

Because those who adhere solely to the Small Vehicle do not realize that these teachings are provisional, the "Expedient Means" chapter specifically reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate. And...
Those of superior faculties have already understood; however, those of middling faculties have not yet realized the meaning of the three provisional designations and one reality.

Therefore, the parable of the burning house is taught, using the metaphors of the three carts and the single cart, to cause them to attain realization. Yet, although those of the Lesser Vehicle understand that the former was a skillful means, they do not know that this skillful means is itself the reality.

Therefore, the parable of the medicinal herbs is taught, showing how the single rain is impartial, while the three types of grasses and two types of trees grow according to their respective capacities.
The faculties receive moisture, thereby revealing that the Dharma is fundamentally one; it is only that the capacities [of beings] differ.
Although those of middle capacity have attained awakening, those of inferior capacity still harbor doubts, failing to comprehend the principle that the Dharma is one while capacities differ.

Therefore, [the Buddha] cites at length the causal conditions for the Great Penetrating One’s preaching of the Dharma to reveal the oneness of the Dharma, which precisely accords with the intent of the "single rain" upon the medicinal herbs. Thus, the wisdom now excels.
When requested to preach the Dharma, he did not speak of it by distinguishing three vehicles; rather, he spoke directly of the Four Noble Truths.

According to their faculties, there were differences in how they were understood—whether as Great or Small—but the Four Truths are but a single teaching. When those of the Hīnayāna heard them, they realized only arising and ceasing;

when those of the Shared Teaching heard them, they realized non-arising; when those of the Distinct Teaching heard them, they realized the immeasurable; and [when those of the Perfect Teaching heard them, they realized the unobstructed].
If one hears the teaching, one awakens to non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Is this not because the Dharma is one while the capacities of beings differ?

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* names the Four Noble Truths; these are the truths practiced by those on the stages (*bhūmi*), let alone those of the Hīnayāna. Thus, when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma...
"This is what is meant by the gateway of wisdom that is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
Furthermore, he extensively expounded the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, up to its being immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.

This extensive exposition of the Four Noble Truths is the teaching on the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*). The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination constitute the vehicle of the Middle Way (*madhyamāyāna*) and possesses two gates:

that of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) and that of cessation (*nivṛtti*). From "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) up to "birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair," this constitutes the gate of transmigration;
it extensively explains the two truths of Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), which are the causes and effects of the mundane world. From ignorance... [text continues].

Cessation, up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, constitutes the gate of reversal (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). This extensively explains the two truths of Cessation and the Path, which are the supramundane cause and effect.
In the Hīnayāna, the Truth of Origination is regarded as the root of suffering; "origination" refers to the various afflictions such as the three poisons.
In the Madhyamaka-yāna, it is stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of the Truth of Origination—the afflictions of the three poisons—and thus it proceeds even deeper.
This is the origin of delusion; therefore, it is taught for those of sharp faculties. As for "ignorance" (avidyā):

it means that the wondrous nature is fundamentally luminous, yet due to a single thought of forgetfulness and movement, it suddenly becomes dark and obscured. Because one is deluded regarding the original perfect luminosity, it is termed "ignorance.

Since the fundamental substance is tranquil, yet is stirred by ignorance, there arises transmigration and flux; thus it is called "formations" (saṃskāra). Once its substance has been displaced, then...
Wisdom transforms into consciousness; thus, volitional formations condition consciousness. These three links constitute the original causes from the past.
However, a cause must necessarily have a result; therefore, consciousness serves as the root that binds one to birth and death.

Since wisdom is fundamentally without name or form, whereas consciousness now grasps the four great elements and the union of matter and mind, it possesses both name and form; thus, it is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). This...
At the very beginning of conception, the source of receiving a physical form, there is the state of the embryo as it coagulates within the womb.

Once it has entered the womb, after five times seven, or thirty-five days, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are fully developed; hence they are called the "six entrances. Once the six sense faculties are complete...

The formation [of the body] issues from the womb; when the sense faculties meet with their objects, there is contact (*sparśa*). Because one experiences the agreeable or disagreeable objects thus contacted, there is sensation (*vedanā*).
These five links constitute the present fruit. Sensation inevitably gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and craving inevitably leads to grasping (*upādāna*).
Grasping arises. Grasping necessarily leads to the formation of karma. Once that karma has been formed, its subsequent fruit does not perish;
therefore, it constitutes "existence" (*bhava*). These are the three links of the present cause. Since the causal karma exists, the subsequent fruit follows it;

therefore, it constitutes "birth" (*jāti*). Birth conditions aging, death, and so forth; these are the two links of the future fruit. Thus, the three periods of time circulate, and birth and death continue in succession throughout kalpas.

Because it is uninterrupted, it serves as the causal condition for the manifold sufferings of birth and death; thus, it constitutes both the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

For those of the Middle Vehicle who practice through abandonment, they contemplate that with the extinction of ignorance alone, the remaining eleven links are simultaneously extinguished—just as when the root of a tree is uprooted, the branches and leaves all fall at once.
This is the practice of abandonment for those of sharp faculties; this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
This concerns the two truths; hence it is said that he extensively taught the twelve links of dependent origination and so forth.
"The Buddha among devas and humans" refers to the assembly that heard the Dharma and obtained benefit at the first assembly. "Not receiving any dharmas" means realizing the principle of emptiness.

Regarding the mention of "all outflows" (*āsrava*), there are three types: the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Now it is said that "the mind attains liberation."
This means that when the peripheral conditions are severed, the fundamental ignorance is suppressed and does not arise; this is liberation.

It is not the severance of ignorance itself that constitutes Great Liberation. As for dhyāna-concentration, the three insights (*vidyā*), and so forth, these are all fruits realized by the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding the second, third, and subsequent assemblies, it is said that they likewise taught the Dharma of the Truths and Dependent Origination, yet [these were] minor...
Those who attained deliverance by means of this vehicle were so numerous that they could not be counted.
At that time, when the sixteen princes requested to leave the household life, the king immediately granted them permission.

This prince requested that the Dharma of the Mahāyāna be preached. When the sixteen princes first renounced their cherished possessions, they approached Jñānavijaya and requested him to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
Their request merely stated, "May gods and humans be brought to peace and security.

Although the word "Hīnayāna" was not explicitly mentioned, the underlying intent was directed toward it. Therefore, Jñānavijaya first taught the Dharma of the Truths and the Conditions (the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination). Thus it is said:
Now, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni first taught the gradual instruction of the Āgamas.

Since those of the various Hīnayāna schools had already attained deliverance, all the princes left home as youths and specifically requested the Buddha to expound the Great Dharma for attaining Unsurpassed Bodhi.
They personally declared their profound inner vows, resolving to achieve Buddhahood—a goal beyond the comprehension of those of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, the prince makes this request. The prince’s renunciation is a symbol of all consciousnesses emerging from their entanglements.
Once these consciousnesses have been transformed, then all fundamental and derivative afflictions are simultaneously and entirely transformed into the wondrous function of True Suchness (Tathatā).
This is why the wheel-turning monarch leads his eighty trillion subjects to renounce the world as well. By means of this—
The simultaneous transformation of all consciousnesses into the function of wisdom is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood; this is why he requested that the Great Dharma be taught.
At that time, that Buddha accepted the śrāmaṇera’s request... [up to] "...the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are inexhaustible even now."

This wisdom excels in accepting invitations to preach the Great Dharma. Yet, although he had already accepted the invitation, it was only after twenty thousand kalpas that he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This was because he waited for the time to ripen before speaking, just as he does today.
Since his lifespan was so long, the waiting period was likewise prolonged; this is only natural. When he finally preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were only sixteen [bodhisattvas] present.
The Prince was the primary recipient; therefore, he was able to receive, uphold, and fully believe and accept [the teaching].
Among the other śrāvakas, there were also those with faith and understanding, yet they were unable to uphold it.

As for the other sentient beings who all gave rise to doubt and confusion, these were precisely the "remaining dust" of that time, who have become the primary recipients of today. Because those with doubts and confusion were numerous, [the Buddha] taught at that time.

It has also been long—eight thousand kalpas have passed. Yet, since the preaching of this sutra, not even several years have elapsed, and those for whom the teaching was intended have already reached their end.
This limit is specifically set because those whose conditions were ripe have now ceased; as for those whose conditions are not yet ripe, they shall serve as seeds for future opportunities.
As for why the World-Honored One entered nirvana shortly after preaching this sutra, it was because his work of transformation had been completed.

As for Jñānavijaya entering the meditation chamber to practice dhyāna-samādhi, it was to await the maturation of the sixteen princes, desiring to transmit the wondrous Dharma so that it might continue without end—namely, the teaching on the methods for instructing bodhisattvas through protective mindfulness and entrustment.
At that time, the princes preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; thus, these princes were the original progenitors of the wondrous Dharma, and [the lineage] was established.
The Buddha has been delivering sentient beings, yet to this day has not emerged from the Great Universal Samādhi.

As for Jñānottara entering meditative absorption for eighty-four thousand kalpas, this symbolizes that the eighty-four thousand afflictions of sentient beings serve as the gateway to the dhyāna-concentration of all Buddhas.
Through the wisdom and function of the Bodhisattva’s sublime conduct, he is able to deliver six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
This manifests the turning away of the subtle afflictions of the six consciousnesses, all of which constitute the sublime conduct for attaining Buddhahood;
thus, it causes them all to resolve upon Bodhicitta. Therefore, one knows that for sentient beings who harbor doubts, there is no need for further instruction.
How could the long-term power of the perfuming of consciousness have given rise to right faith? Truly, it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand;

yet even in this assembly, there are those who withdraw from their seats. When Jñānavijaya emerged from samādhi, he certified that the sixteen śrāmaṇeras had well expounded the essential points of the Dharma, and he earnestly exhorted the great multitude that they should all repeatedly draw near to them, make offerings, and [uphold] the Right [Dharma].
This serves as the causal seed for the present occasion. Why is this so? [The passage] from "Below" explains the meaning of drawing near to the Buddha's teaching.
It indicates that those of the Three Vehicles who can simply believe these words of the sixteen śrāmaṇeras will all obtain the great benefit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
therefore, he instructs them to draw near. From "The Buddha told the bhikṣus" onwards, he provides the formal demonstration.
The past serves as the causal seed for the present. The sixteen bodhisattvas constantly preach the sublime Dharma; the sentient beings they transform do not part from them life after life.

After a long time, these beings gain self-assurance, which clearly demonstrates the efficacy of hearing and permeation (*śruta-vāsanā*). Thus, having encountered many Buddhas in succession, this influence remains inexhaustible even to this day.
This reveals that the source of the sublime Dharma flows directly down to the present—how could it be anything less than profound?
How wonderful!

O bhikṣus, I now tell you: from this point until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these sixteen princes shall each achieve Buddhahood through the merit of preaching the wondrous Dharma, manifesting themselves throughout the eight directions.
Their names and titles differ, for they are designated according to their respective virtues. The ancient commentaries explain this by means of the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*);

while this certainly possesses its own logic, scholars have not been without instances of forced interpretation. Śākyamuni appeared in Sahā, which is named the "Endurance Land" (*saha-loka-dhātu*), specifically in accordance with his original vow;
thus, he teaches and transforms sentient beings within this world that is difficult to endure. This is not merely due to profound compassion or great... [text fragmentary].
Aspiration: Who is capable of this? The *Juryō-hon* (Chapter on the Lifespan) states: "Since I truly attained Buddhahood, it has been an exceedingly long time.
This refers to having already attained Buddhahood and appeared in the Sahā world. However, the present Śākyamuni is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Vairocana;
thus, one knows that the three bodies are of one essence. When the distinctions of duration and proximity are forgotten, this is the inconceivable power of the Buddha.
"O bhikṣus, those of us who were śrāmaṇeras at that time [are] these very śrāvaka disciples in future ages.
This account by Śākyamuni Buddha of his past acts of teaching is precisely the causal seed for the present occasion.
Initially, Śākyamuni used only the seed of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) of the wondrous Dharma to teach and transform immeasurable beings.
All these sentient beings have already resolved their minds toward Bodhi under the Buddha. Yet, there are now those who abide in the stage of the Śrāvakas;

this refers to those who have subsequently fallen back from their former resolve. This is what was meant when it was said previously: "In the past, I taught you to set your aspirations on the Buddha-way, yet you have now completely forgotten it.
For this reason, I originally taught you the Great Dharma with the desire to cause you all to attain Buddhahood, but you have forgotten it.
Therefore, on this day, I ought to cause you to gradually attain the Buddha-way by means of these three vehicles.
These past causes and conditions are perfectly clear; yet you merely cling to the former expedient means and do not comprehend the Tathāgata’s true meaning.
This is why the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. At that time, the assembly who were transformed—immediately...
"You disciples who are here before me receiving my instruction, today is the time when your conditions have ripened and you may attain the Way.
As for those who are unable to attain realization now, their past causes still remain;
furthermore, they serve as conditions for the future—namely, the śrāvaka disciples of the future world after my parinirvāṇa. How could they ever be oblivious to their original cause?"
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples [up to] those who remove the various skillful means of the Tathāgatas’ preaching of the Dharma.
These words are spoken extensively to serve as the causes and conditions for those to be delivered in the future.

However, among the disciples I have transformed, there are those in this life who cannot fully receive the Buddha’s teaching. If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who do not believe in this sutra and are greedily attached to the Lesser Vehicle...

As for "the vehicle," it means that when I become a Buddha in other lands under a different name, and for the sake of the causes and conditions of liberating beings, those who receive transformation in those other lands will likewise necessarily enter through this sutra; there is no other vehicle, except for the teachings of various skillful means.
Thus, one knows that whenever every Buddha brings sentient beings to maturity and attains Buddhahood, they all preach this sutra as the ultimate.
It concludes thus. In other lands he acts as a Buddha, as described in the "Chapter on Names" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where the Buddha has four hundred billion ten-thousand names.
These are titles manifested in response to the capacities of sentient beings; yet, though the names differ, the reality does not.
Thus, all of them use the wondrous Dharma to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha-wisdom.
"O bhikṣus, if the Tathāgata knows [for himself]—up to—the point that only by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle can one attain extinction;

this concluding statement reveals the ultimate reality. Although the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is for the sake of the single Great Matter, they invariably first teach the Three Vehicles as a means of guidance.
Only when the time has come for the capacities of beings to ripen, and when their transformative conditions are about to end, do they finally speak [of the One Vehicle]."
This sutra completely abolishes former provisional teachings and uniquely reveals the single reality; this is the method by which all Buddhas benefit sentient beings.
Furthermore, the assembly is pure, and it is said that those whose faculties are matured and capable of receiving the teaching have gathered.

Thus, for the sake of the various Bodhisattvas, he preaches this sutra and bestows upon each of them a prediction of Buddhahood, thereby finally exhausting the fundamental purpose of his appearance in the world.
"Monks, you should know that this city created by the Tathāgata through his skillful means is not real; it is merely my transformation.
This is the parable of leading people forward by opening a provisional city. First, establishing the lingering provisional [teachings] serves as the basis for the parable.
The reason the Tathāgata first establishes the gradual teachings is that, through the provisional wisdom of skillful means, he observes the inclinations of the deep minds of sentient beings."
Because their desires differ, knowing that those who delight in the small are difficult to speak to regarding the Great, he taught the nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna as a mere temporary rest.
To illustrate this, he established a gradual intention through the following parable: the five hundred *yojanas* represent the transmigration of sentient beings through the five realms;
being filled with the three poisons, it is likened to the evil paths; and being desolate and devoid of people, it represents the delusion of sentient beings.
Having lost their original truth, they indulge only in greed and anger; therefore, it is called "a place of fear.

The "place of precious jewels" is a metaphor for the sea of wondrous adornments—the fruition-recompense land of awakened enlightenment. The "many people" are a metaphor for those of the three vehicles who, wishing to transcend birth and death, seek to become Buddhas.
When merchants from the Western Regions seek jewels, there must be one who acts as a guide to lead the multitude.

This parable illustrates how the World-Honored One appeared in the world as a guide for the multitude to lead them out of the five realms of existence; hence it says, "desiring to cross over these difficulties.

That the people he leads become exhausted and wish to retreat is a metaphor for the narrowness and inferiority of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), who all harbor thoughts of ceasing their progress due to their fear that the Buddha-way is too long and arduous.
"The guide’s skillful means," and so forth, is a metaphor for the World-Honored One’s application of expedient means.
This is a skillful means (*upāya*). Beyond three hundred *yojanas*, he magically manifests a city; this is a metaphor for that which lies outside the triple world (*tridhātu*).
He establishes the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle as a place of rest along the way. The joy of the weary multitude is a metaphor for satisfying the minds of those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
The multitude entering the city conceives the thought of peace and security; this is a metaphor for those of the Lesser Vehicle who become attached to *nirvāṇa* and no longer press forward.

When the Guide knows that the multitude is no longer weary, he immediately causes the conjured city to vanish; this is a metaphor for when the faculties [of beings] have now matured, the provisional is discarded, and the real is established.
That the place of jewels is near is a metaphor for the fruit of Buddhahood not being remote. Since one can attain it simply by being willing to advance, the number of *li* is not mentioned.

This parable clarifies that for those of inferior capacity, the provisional is opened up to reveal the ultimate. From "The bhikṣus... onwards, the Dharma corresponds to the basis of the parable. From "Knowing all births and deaths...
onwards, it corresponds to knowing the passages and obstructions. From "If the assembly... onwards, it corresponds to fearing [the journey] and becoming weary and exhausted.
If one were to preach only the Buddha-vehicle without opening the gradual stages, then sentient beings would fear that the path of the Buddha is long and distant; this is therefore...
It was unavoidable that expedient means had to be established. From the passage "The Buddha, knowing this" onwards, it corresponds precisely to the "City of Transformation" (nirvāṇa).

The two types of nirvāṇa refer to the two fruits of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha. From the passage "If the assembly... onwards, it corresponds to the "resting of the multitude," which is the extinguishing of the City of Transformation and the urging forward toward the Place of Jewels.
The One Vehicle of Buddha-wisdom is precisely the Place of Jewels. The Two Vehicles have already departed from the three [realms].
Because the realms are perilous paths, it is said that one is "near to the Buddha-wisdom. Since the provisional is abandoned for the sake of the real, attaining Buddhahood is not difficult.
This is the meaning of "opening up the provisional to reveal the real."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas... (until: do not harbor fear or alarm."
This verse concerns the causal circumstances. The sixteen lines beginning with "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū" eulogize the attainment of Buddhahood by Jñānābhibhū.

The four lines beginning with "The sixteen sons of that Buddha" eulogize the princes beholding the Buddha. The lines beginning with "Bowing his head to the Buddha’s feet" eulogize the princes requesting the Dharma.
The twenty lines beginning with "In the various worlds of the eastern direction" eulogize the ten directions.

"Brahmā King requests the turning of the Wheel of Dharma" refers to the eight lines beginning with "The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom," which praise the acceptance of the request and the opening of the gradual teaching.
"Six hundred trillion *nayuta*s" refers to the four lines following, which praise the preaching of the Dharma at the first assembly and the benefits obtained by those of the Two Vehicles.

"At the time of the second preaching of the Dharma" refers to the eight lines following, which praise the third, fourth, and fifth assemblies where vast multitudes obtained benefits. "At that time, the sixteen kings... [and so forth].

The eight lines following the "son" verse praise the prince’s request to preach the Great Dharma. The ten lines following "the Buddha knew the child’s mind" praise his acceptance of the request to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that there are verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this means that because the capacity of the audience is vast and the duration of time is long, the words and phrases of the sūtra spoken therein are likewise many.
This discourse, which accords with the nature of reality and responds to the capacities of beings, is fundamental.
There is no fixed number of dharmas; therefore, this present sutra consists of only twenty-eight chapters.

Yet, Dīpaṃkara preached for sixty kalpas, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū preached for eight thousand kalpas, Sadāparibhūta heard two hundred trillion verses at the place of Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, and Priyadarśana heard eight million [verses] at the place of Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī.

There are a hundred million *acchobhya* verses. These are discourses that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); therefore, they differ in being either extensive or concise, which is what is meant by "teachings that apply universally.

The sixteen lines following the phrase "After that Buddha had finished preaching the sutra" eulogize the Great Penetration Entering Samādhi (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*), during which the Prince preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and saved a multitude of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The four lines beginning with "After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" [refer to the subsequent events].
The verse describes the assembly of those to be converted, serving as the causal conditions for their deliverage throughout successive lifetimes.
While the prose lacks mention of *nirvāṇa*, it is brought forth within the verses. The final four lines of these sixteen novice monks praise the princes attaining Buddhahood.
The eight lines beginning with "At that time, those who heard the Dharma" praise the sixteen Buddhas all preaching the wondrous Dharma and leading others into the Buddha-wisdom.

Thus we know that the conditions for those to be transformed have existed for a long time. By means of these four lines below, which explain the fundamental causes and conditions, it is shown that all those currently being transformed were originally conditioned by past causes.
Tracing back to the seeds for attaining Buddhahood, one should not harbor any doubts regarding the present attainment of Buddhahood.
When such distinct past conditions are considered—even those involving dull and inferior faculties—how could one fail to believe?
For example, it is like a perilous and evil road, remote and desolate, abounding in venomous beasts... [and so on] until "introducing them into the Buddha-wisdom.
This analogy corresponds to the following forty-six lines, which generally provide metaphors as can be understood from the text.

However, while the prose section speaks only of the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*), the verse refers to "cities, walls, houses, gardens, groves, bathing ponds, towers, pavilions, men," and so forth.
The matters such as "the daughter filling [the world]" and so forth extensively illustrate the provisional fruits and the functional merits of the Three Vehicles;

these are similar in their relative scale and are not all actual realizations. Therefore, it is generally said that they are merely "transformed manifestations" for the sake of cessation. "We too are likewise" and below apply the Dharma to the analogy.
The first ten phrases correspond to the "opening of the provisional," while the subsequent sixteen phrases correspond to the "abolishing of the provisional to establish the true."
"Indeed. The four lines following "All Buddhas" summarize both the Dharma and the parable, concluding the meaning of this chapter.
*The Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Three.
*The Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Four.

The Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecies upon the Five Hundred Disciples, the Eighth, from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty under imperial decree, expounded by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of the Southern Peak.

The purpose of this chapter is as follows: Having heard the two cycles of the preceding teachings and parables, and having seen five people receive their predictions, and further having heard the account of past-life causes and conditions, the five hundred disciples came to realize that the Buddha employs immeasurable supernatural powers and skillful means to guide sentient beings and originally plant the seeds of the One Vehicle.
Thereupon, they came to believe in the Buddha’s mind and also believed in their own minds.

Having attained certainty of attaining Buddhahood, all doubts and hesitations are suddenly exhausted; hence it is said that "the mind is pure. As his aspiration yearns for the bestowal of the prophecy, he leaps with joy;

hence it is said that "his profound mind and original vow" can only be known by the Buddha. He is now capable of shouldering the family legacy, and thus the paternal affection is forgotten. Hence it is said that "only the Buddha can know [it]."
Therefore, the World-Honored One bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon each of the twelve hundred followers alike, thereby fulfilling his original aspiration for transcending the world.

Consequently, the compilers of this collection designated this section as the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*), signifying that having now given rise to great faith, they are capable of receiving and upholding [the Dharma];
thus, this chapter follows. As for why the Sūtra mentions twelve hundred people while the chapter title specifies five hundred, it is because the five hundred were [the primary recipients].
Because he was the foremost among the twelve hundred [monks].
At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance, his eyes never wavering for a moment.
This compiler [of the sūtra] describes the state of realization attained by Pūrṇa. Regarding the phrase "having heard these things from the Buddha": it refers to what he heard from the Buddha.
That is to say, he has heard the teaching on the profound nature of the two kinds of wisdom; the parable of the three carts and the single cart as skillful means according to suitability;
and how five companions of equal standing each received their prediction of enlightenment.

Now, hearing these past causes and conditions of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and the supernatural power of the Teacher’s "city of transformation"—all these matters above which he had never before heard—this is why he [has attained this realization].
"It is truly unprecedented! Previously, having never heard this Dharma, I still harbored doubts and clung stingily to the lesser fruits.
Now that I have heard this revelation, my doubts and delusions have been eliminated; thus it is said that 'the mind is pure.
Having gained self-confidence that Buddhahood may be attained, I leap for joy and exult. Therefore, I rectify the three karmas and stand back gazing up, hoping for the Buddha’s prediction."
And he formed this thought: "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary (up to: able to know our profound inner resolve and original vows.

This describes the words of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. Regarding his praise that the Buddha is most extraordinary and rare: it is because, upon hearing the three successive turnings of the Dharma wheel, he attained realization in accord with the Buddha’s mind, and thus he uttered this praise.
[The passage] "in accordance with the world, pulling out [beings from] greed and attachment," and so forth, follows.

This is a formal expression of praise for a most extraordinary and rare occurrence. Śāriputra, while at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, suddenly perceived the World-Honored One’s heart of protective mindfulness and entrustment; thus he marveled at its rarity, which was understood without words.

Now, Pūrṇa, having heard the teachings of the three turnings, fully perceives the Tathāgata’s great kindness and great compassion, all of which are nothing other than protective mindfulness and entrustment.
He entrusted this to their hearts, so that those of the five natures and the three vehicles might be led far away from attachment; this is an exceedingly marvelous and rare occurrence.

It is because one awakens through words that the World-Honored One previously stated that Kāśyapa and others could not fully know the Tathāgata’s true merits, and that Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra himself said, "As for us regarding the Buddha's merits, in truth our words do not [suffice]."
"You are able to proclaim it. Yet we, with our profound resolve, assist in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma and protect its vow for universal circulation.

We desire to receive a prediction [of our future enlightenment], yet this intention cannot even be expressed in words. Only the World-Honored One, the Buddha, bears witness to our hearts; it truly requires no further explanation.
Previously, when Kāśyapa and the others described their own realizations, they still harbored many lingering doubts and hesitations. Now, [Kātyāyanīputra] is full..."

In the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā*, it is simply stated that the profound mind and original vow are known only through the Buddha’s own realization; thus, one has never harbored doubt regarding the Buddha from the outset.
This is intended to reveal the inner secret essence in order to inspire faith in those of inferior faculties and weak understanding.
It is precisely for this purpose of aiding the proclamation [of the Dharma] that this sutra is placed at the beginning of the twelve hundred [sutras], for there is indeed a profound reason for this.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus... [up to] "...none can exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.

From here below, the World-Honored One recounts Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra’s inner secrets and outer manifestations as he assists in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma, thereby describing how his profound mind and original vows are thus fulfilled.
"You all see this... from here below describes the manifestation of Pūrṇa.
Among those who previously assisted in proclaiming the Dharma of Śākyamuni, there was one such as this: Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was most skilled in preaching the Dharma;
therefore, the World-Honored One designated him as the foremost in preaching. Even the Tathāgata could not exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
This describes the pinnacle of skillful exposition.
"You all must not think [that Pūrṇa]—up until—"constantly performs the work of a Buddha to transform sentient beings.
This describes how Pūrṇa (Māmatīputra) protected, upheld, and assisted in proclaiming the Dharma at the abodes of past Buddhas; it also reveals his profound mind and original vow.

He has attained thorough penetration of the dharma of emptiness. "Attained" means he directly realizes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of emptiness. He possesses the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). He preaches...

Regarding the eloquence of the Dharma, only a Buddha can fully possess it; Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra also possesses it. Being constantly able to examine with discernment, he contemplates the faculties to suit the capacities of beings.
Teaching the Dharma with purity, he does not cling to the characteristics of phenomena. Being free from doubt, he teaches with certainty.

Being fully endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva, he conceals his inner state while manifesting outwardly; thus people do not know his secret conduct and all assume he is truly a śrāvaka, knowing only his external traces.
Yet the many beings he transforms and establishes in bodhi indicate that what he teaches is not a minor dharma.
His birth through transformation in a pure land indicates that his practice is not a minor one. All of this arises from his profound mind and original vow.
Regarding these matters:
the bhikṣu Pūrṇa likewise, from the time of the seven Buddhas until now, has gradually fulfilled the path of a bodhisattva.
The above recounted distant events concerning many past Buddhas; this recounts proximate events, namely the seven Buddhas of the past. The past...

Although there are many Buddhas, those belonging to the final period of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*—namely the three Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū—as well as the four Buddhas from the beginning of the *Bhadrakalpa*, namely Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and myself, Śākyamuni, together constitute the seven Buddhas.
These are the Buddhas who transmitted the seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*) during this proximate eon. From...

From this present Bhadrakalpa into the future, until the time of the Buddhas of the Tārakakalpa, they shall be able to protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma at the abode of each and every Buddha.

They shall take the exclusive practice of preaching the Dharma as their vocation, be born through transformation in pure lands, and fulfill the bodhisattva path as the foundation for attaining Buddhahood.
The World-Honored One has merely spoken of these five individuals receiving the causal prediction (*hetu-vyākaraṇa*).

It is merely the practice of drawing near to and making offerings to all Buddhas. Now, in the *Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra-parivarta*, the matters of assisting in and protecting the Dharma are described in full detail.
Such thoroughness exists because the World-Honored One’s secret intent places exclusive emphasis on upholding the True Dharma;
to extensively establish the conditions for attaining Buddhahood is considered the Great Practice. Therefore, there is no need to cultivate further practices during the causal stage.
Regarding other practices, the foremost and most sublime practice is solely that which assists in proclaiming and upholding the Buddha-dharma;
the subsequent detailed exhortations to uphold this sutra and the extensive praise of the merits of the Dharma-master are all intended to convey this very meaning.
After immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—up until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—he shall erect stūpas made of the seven treasures that fill his land.

This is the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) received by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. Because he propagated the Dharma during the causal stage and transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal, he realized *bodhi* without leaving his current location;
therefore, the fruit of this prediction is that he shall attain *bodhi* in this very land. Behold this Sahā world!
The original state of Vipaśyin was defiled, yet the land of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is purely and solely pure;
this clearly demonstrates that defilement and purity are identical, secretly revealing the true land of the *dharmatā*. This can be understood through the transformation according to the mind.

Because one has attained clear and thorough penetration into all empty phenomena during the causal stage, the fruit is named "Dharma-Illumination" (*dharmāvabhāsa*); it is because it accords with the pure land of the *dharmatā*.
Because his benefit for sentient beings is vast and immeasurable, his resultant environment is manifested as a single land encompassing the Sahā worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Because he preaches the Dharma with pure, impartial great compassion, the ground of this resultant land is as level as the palm of a hand.
There are no mountains or hills, for all phenomena are established in accordance with the Dharma-nature; thus, towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures fill its interior.
Because the Dharma is being preached, the distinction between purity and defilement has vanished, and good and evil are equalized; therefore, humans and devas interact and can see one another.
There are no evil realms, as they have constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) during their causal stages and extensively transformed sentient beings. Thus...
In that land of fruition, there are no women and no sexual desire; all sentient beings are born by transformation. This is the retribution for preaching the Dharma with purity.
Since sentient beings are not born from sexual desire, their bodies emit radiance, and they are forever liberated from the bonds of craving.
Therefore, they possess mastery over flight. All sentient beings are born through transformation from the Dharma;

thus, their resolve and mindfulness are firm, and they possess diligence and wisdom, free from all confusion and delusive thoughts. Their bodies are all golden in color, which is the retribution for being free from desire.
Sentient beings take food as their life. Since the people of this land are all born by transformation, they do not partake of physical sustenance;
therefore, they subsist solely on the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna. Hitherto, it has been taught only the Dharma for bodhisattvas;

thus, the retinue consists entirely of great bodhisattvas. As for the fact that there are also many śrāvakas, it is because they are gradually becoming fully endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva.
The Way—this is also a multitude gathered through the power of vows. The above are all adornments of the *niṣyanda* (dependent retribution).

The eon is named Treasure Radiance (*Ratnaprabhā*), because the Dharma-treasure is perfectly luminous. Since it is not a time of the five turbidities, the land is named Good Purity (*Suvimala*), which also accords with the cause of preaching the pure Dharma.
As for the lifespan, it is simply said to be "immeasurable" without specifying a number; such is the duration of the Dharma.
It does not speak of the *saddharma* (True Dharma) or *pratirūpadharma* (Semblance Dharma), but merely says "a very long time" without fixing its duration.

This is because he preached the Dharma in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); since the nature of phenomena is fundamentally without beginning or end, his life of wisdom remains eternally present and the True Dharma perpetually abides.

After his passing, stupas were erected and filled the entire land; this is the cause and effect of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s preaching of the Dharma, recorded uniquely in this manner. From this, it is sufficient to know [the depth of his realization].
The Tathāgata’s secret intention is solely to manifest the superiority of the merit of upholding this sutra. Furthermore, the Sahā world is the transformation land of Śākyamuni;
it is called the "World of the Five Turbidities and Evil," where all manner of sufferings are gathered, and thus it is named "Endurance.
In that land, mountains, hills, ravines, and valleys are uneven in their heights and depths; it is filled with filth and impurities, such as excrement and urine, and its sentient beings are lustful.

Desire is a place of sinking and wandering within birth and death; it is that which those of the Lesser Vehicle loathe and fear, like a prison or shackles, from which they bid a long farewell and dare not enter again.
Yet now, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra has received his prediction, attaining Bodhi without leaving this land.
The ground is as level as the palm of a hand, and the purity of the land is such that there are absolutely no women among its sentient beings.
They are born by transformation. The radiance of their physical forms is such as that; furthermore, immeasurable Sahā worlds are unified into a single land, and its vastness is likewise so great.

This is precisely to demonstrate to those of the Two Vehicles the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, whereby their narrowness and meanness are eliminated, their sentiments of acceptance and rejection perish, and their minds of longing and aversion cease. Thus, all that is encountered before one's eyes is purely the Lotus Land.
The treasury of adornments—the pure land of true retribution—is not to be sought elsewhere;

by directly ceasing doubt, one suddenly ascends to the stage of Buddhahood. This is where the power of the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) is fully manifested, even for those of inferior faculties and weak understanding.
How can you not have self-confidence, yet willingly place yourself outside the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?

That the purity or defilement of a land transforms according to one's mind—is this not truly beyond belief? By observing this, one can fully perceive the Tathāgata’s skillful means in manifesting through transformation;
it is truly said that the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable. If one were to view this prediction alongside other such records and treat it with negligence...
This does not reach the subtle and profound meaning of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Bhikṣus, listen attentively to the path practiced by the Son of the Buddha... (up to)... I shall now briefly explain it."
This verse generally describes the inner secrecy and outward manifestation of the disciples. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Śāriputra, and the other ten great disciples all shared identical virtues;
yet he alone manifested the traces of provisional response, standing at the head of the twelve hundred followers.
This was precisely to demonstrate a special expedient means for leading in those of dull faculties, intending to cause them to recognize their debt of gratitude and attain faith and understanding.
However, among the śrāvakas there are both those who are provisional manifestations and those who possess actual fruits.

If the twelve hundred were all of dull faculties with actual fruits, they would surely abandon the small [vehicle] and believe in the Great [Vehicle] once they understood the traces of the provisional responses of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and others.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has revealed his secret here. Now, these following thirty phrases generally praise the protection of provisional manifestations.
This is proclaimed for practice. The subsequent twenty-two lines separately eulogize the matter of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra’s prophecy.
The final six lines of the section on Pūrṇa constitute the concluding eulogy, which is clear. It is said that if one were to explain it only briefly, his merit would be inconceivable.
At that time, the twelve hundred arhats [received] the prediction of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

These twelve hundred requested the prediction. Because the Tathāgata praised Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra for the profound depth of his past causes and conditions, this was not something the twelve hundred had dared to hope for.
Now, having heard the Buddha’s revelation, they realize it was originally intended to guide those of dull faculties; thus, each of them [also received the prediction].
They were confident that they possessed the potential for Buddhahood; thus, they requested [the teaching] with joy. The Buddha, knowing the minds of the assembly, addressed Kāśyapa.
This was because he had already fulfilled his original intention and felt a sense of inner satisfaction; therefore, he specifically addressed the foremost disciple.
It was just like colleagues who, having accomplished their shared task together, congratulate one another.
"Among this assembly, my great disciples (up to) all share the same name, called Samantaprabhāsa.

This was the bestowal of the prediction upon the five hundred disciples. When the World-Honored One first turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths three times at the Deer Park, he delivered the five who had attended him;
however, Kauṇḍinya attained awakening first, and because he was the very first to receive deliverance, he became the foremost among the Saṃgha.

Śāriputra was the leader among the Arhats who had truly realized the fruit; therefore, he was singled out from among the five hundred and specifically granted a prediction (vyākaraṇa) to distinguish him from the others.
Although the prediction does not explicitly mention his causal practices, the intention is that the six individuals previously mentioned serve as models for emulation.
His name as a realized fruit is Samantaprabha (Universal Radiance), signifying that he has opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, entered the Buddha’s wisdom, and is no longer subject to delusion.
"Darkness. The verse says: "Constantly emitting great radiance, constantly preaching the unsurpassed Way. For this reason, he received this title.
His five hundred arhats all share the same title because their virtues are identical. Matters such as kalpas and lands are not mentioned here, as they are fully contained within the verses.
The sūtra follows the convention of alternating between long verses and concise summaries.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya shall see immeasurable Buddhas... you should proclaim it for them."
This verse records the prophecy of Dharmapāla to designate the assembly. The ten lines beginning with "Kauṇḍinya" eulogize the name of the primary retribution fruit (*vipākaphala*).

The lines beginning with "His land is pure" eulogize the environment and retinue (*upabhogaphala*). The three lines beginning with "The Buddha’s lifespan" eulogize the duration of his life and the persistence of the Dharma.
The eight lines beginning with "The extinction of the Dharma" eulogize the sequential attainment of Buddhahood by five hundred [disciples], as well as those whom he transforms.
The world is likewise; as it is for me today, those beings to be transformed all first receive the provisional and later the ultimate.
The six lines beginning with "The land is adorned and pure" eulogize the environment and retinue. Each of the Dharma and lifespan is like that of Kauṇḍinya.
The six lines beginning with "Kāśyapa, you already know" cite the five hundred to exemplify the remaining seven hundred. All...
The attainment of the fruit and the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) are identical.

Regarding these passages concerning the predictions for the twelve hundred [disciples], the causes and practices are not detailed because they were intended merely to inspire faith in Arhats of dull faculties. As for the meritorious practices of serving the Buddha, these must await each individual’s own resolve;
one dares not hastily impose upon them tasks that might be feared as difficult to perform. This is the Tathāgata’s...
This is the intention of providing protection.
At that time, the five hundred arhats— up to the point where they considered their own limited wisdom sufficient—
these five hundred described their state of realization, saying, "We should attain [this]," meaning exclusively for themselves.
"Because we had lost the wisdom of the Tathāgata, it was only today that we realized we had never actually lost it;
it was merely that we ourselves were satisfied with our own limited wisdom. This is the realization.
“World-Honored One, it is as if there were someone who went to the house of a close friend and experienced great joy at having attained what he had never before encountered.
This statement regarding the causes and conditions serves as a metaphor for his own situation.
The sixteen princes of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, along with the countless people, are like those close friends; the princes’ preaching of the Lotus Sūtra is comparable to [the friend] doing so for us.
The following illustrates the causal seeds for the One Vehicle, like the fastening of a jewel. At that time, one does not awaken, like being drunk and lying down.

From this point on, one wanders lost in birth and death, like traveling through foreign lands; one retreats and dwells in the stage of a śrāvaka, thus considering oneself sufficient upon attaining even a slight measure of realization.
Later, one encounters a close friend, just as one now encounters the World-Honored One Śākyamuni. Alas!

The phrase "the one who" is a metaphor for the rebuke [of the poor man] in the past. "Pointing out the jewel in the garment" is a metaphor for the present opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), causing [beings] to awaken to their inherently existing Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
This metaphor illustrates what was lost in the past and obtained in the present. "The Buddha is also like this" and following [the passage] corresponds to the causes of the past.
"Now, the World-Honored One" and following corresponds to the conditions of the present. "I now finally know," and so forth, corresponds to the attainment of the present.
Therefore, they were filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having heard the voice of the unsurpassed, peaceful prophecy, our bodies and minds are filled with universal joy."

These verses beginning with "This Kauṇḍinya" describe how he now attains repentance for his past failings. The four lines beginning with "We have heard the unsurpassed three phrases" celebrate his present attainment.
The seven lines beginning with "I pay homage to the Immeasurable One" express regret for his past failings.

The sixteen lines beginning with "For example, like a poor man" illustrate the analogies for his past conditions. The eight lines beginning with "The close friend who gave him the jewel" illustrate the present.
The [first] eight lines beginning with "Because of this" (*pratyaya*) correspond to the causes of the past. The four lines beginning with "Now the Buddha" correspond to the conditions of the present.
The four lines beginning with "I now" are a general verse expressing self-congratulation because he has received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Nine: The Bestowal of Predictions upon Those Who Have Completed Their Training and Those Who Are Still in Training.

Regarding the intent of this chapter’s inclusion: following the three previous cycles of revelation, those present who were suited to receive the teaching heard it and each came to believe their own minds, no longer doubting the Buddha’s words.
Consequently, the foremost disciples—including those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the five hundred, and the twelve hundred—were all...
Having long been taught and transformed, each has received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Their minds have already been comforted.

Yet there remain newly trained *śrāvakas*, such as Ānanda, Rāhula, and others, who each wish to receive a prediction in order to fulfill the hopes of the assembly and to perceive the Buddha’s impartial compassion;
therefore, he grants them predictions individually. Because of this, the chapter is titled accordingly, and thus this chapter follows. However—

The Buddha-nature has three kinds of causes: namely, the direct cause (*zhengyin*), the conditional cause (*yuan-yin*), and the revealing cause (*liaoyin*). If these three causes are manifested, one will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.

It is inherently possessed by every person; therefore, it is the direct cause. It must rely on the assistance of the teachings and wisdom to be brought forth and revealed; therefore, it is the conditional cause.
Because one personally realizes and awakens to it with confidence, it is the revealing cause. If Śāriputra and the other five— [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated.*

That a person’s realization is swift indicates that their primary cause (*nidāna-hetu*) is profound. As for the five hundred disciples, the extensive citation of past conditions demonstrates that they have long been subject to transformation;
this indicates that their secondary causes (*pratyaya-hetu*) were matured. Within these secondary causes, there are both those who are "intimate" and those who are "causal.

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Sometimes he manifests as a relative or friend. This refers to the ranks of those currently training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), such as the [five hundred] disciples.
If these sons are the most intimate among the causes and conditions for enlightenment, there is no reason why they should not attain deliverance;
therefore, they are all granted predictions of future Buddhahood. Only then is the Tathāgata’s intention of impartial compassion fully revealed. Hence, this follows the preceding chapter.
At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula [stood] to one side, as they had wished.

This record refers to the assembly of those still in training (*śaikṣa*). They are called "those in training" because they are still learning in contrast to those who have completed their training (*aśaikṣa*); they are merely newly initiated *śrāvakas*.
Ānanda was the younger brother of the Buddha, and Rāhula was his son; these are what are known as the "intimate retinue."

Because he saw that the twelve hundred who were beyond training (aśaikṣa) had all received their predictions, Ānanda—leaving aside those still in training (śaikṣa)—deliberately reflected and made his request.
For while Ānanda was preeminent in learning and Rāhula in secret practice, both were among the inner circle; yet now they were listed among those still in training.

Because those in training did not dare to hope for a prediction, and because previously [Ānanda] had thought that attaining Buddhahood was not within the scope of his own wisdom, he did not know what to do.
Please understand this: had I not been granted great authority to guide others, I would not have received the Buddha’s direct designation to resolve the doubts of the assembly;

thus, I merely manifested my residence here. With these two venerable elders serving as the spiritual guides for the community, and with the students now listed before you, if you receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), then all shall attain it.
Therefore, I say: "My own vows are fulfilled, and the expectations of the assembly are likewise satisfied."
At that time, two thousand learners and non-learners, having seen Ānanda make his request, joined him with one mind in a collective petition.
Then the Buddha said to Ānanda: "In a future age... [you shall be] praised together by all for your meritorious virtues."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I now declare within the Saṃgha that Ānanda is the upholder of the Dharma... [until] planting the causes and conditions for the Buddha-way."
This Ānanda was of vast learning; he upheld the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma, his wisdom was lofty and profound, and he attained mastery and freedom.

Thus, his fruition was named accordingly. He taught and transformed twenty quadrillion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* bodhisattvas, doing so solely by means of the Great Dharma to gather and transform them, being pure and without admixture.
His land was named Constantly Established Victory (*Nityasthita-vijaya*), and its banners were used to strike down the heterodox with the True Dharma.
The Honored One is supreme like a banner. The eon is named "Pervasive Wondrous Sound," which is evoked by the sound of the Dharma.
His lifespan is beyond calculation, and the duration of the Dharma is twice that; this is the manifestation of the eternal abiding of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because he upholds the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, all Buddhas praise his merit. The verses may be understood according to the text.
At that time, among those in the assembly, from the newly resolved bodhisattvas down to the śrāvakas who had received such predictions—
those newly resolved bodhisattvas who heard Ānanda’s prediction and gave rise to doubt were intended to have their past causes revealed.
That which they doubted was the fact that the lifespan and the duration of the Dharma would be far-reaching and infinite.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the various bodhisattvas [had made such vows]—because their original vows were thus, they obtained this prediction.
This was the World-Honored One’s elucidation of Ānanda’s distant causes in order to resolve the doubts of the great assembly.

Since Ānanda and the Buddha had simultaneously resolved their minds toward enlightenment, yet the Buddha’s vow was to deliver sentient beings, he applied himself with diligent vigor; whereas Ānanda delighted in much learning.
Because he heard [the Dharma], he vowed to uphold the treasury of the Dharma. Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is immeasurable, his lifespan is infinite.
Because he purely teaches bodhisattvas, there are no followers of the two vehicles in his land. Since his original vow was such, its fruition is likewise so.
Among all the disciples, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and Ānanda alone are particularly distinguished from the rest; this is surely due to their great merit in upholding the Dharma.
Ānanda heard his own prediction of enlightenment directly before the Buddha (up to the point where he realized that what he has now heard was also known by him through his original vow).
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One is truly marvelous! He has caused me to remember the past [up to] the protection and upholding of the Buddhas' Dharma.

Having heard the Buddha’s prediction and recounted his own past causes, Ānanda was immediately able to recollect the Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable past Buddhas and also recognized his original vows—just as Sudhana, before Maitreya’s pavilion, heard the lute being played.
At the sound of his finger snapping, he suddenly beheld the infinite realms of the Buddhas within the pavilion.

Thus one knows that the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas is, in fact, nothing other than the property within Ānanda’s inner chambers. The verse says: "Acting as an attendant through skillful means is precisely the recognition of one's own original vow.
This cannot be discussed on the same level as those who lament losses or rejoice in gains. This record is uniquely extraordinary.
This is entirely appropriate. Such was Ānanda’s past karma. How could the events concerning the *Laṅkāvatāra* and Mādrī have been mere inverted dreams?
At that time, the Buddha told Rāhula... [until] ...he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son... (omitted) ...in order to seek the unsurpassed Way."
This is the prediction of Rāhula. Rāhula was foremost in secret practice (*guhyacaryā*).

That he now attains the fruit and receives the name "Treading upon Seven-Jeweled Flowers" is the result of the subtle and profound practices he has cultivated. As the Buddha’s eldest son, it is said that he is capable of upholding the family lineage;
this signifies that in attaining Buddhahood, practice is paramount. His land, lifespan, and retinue...

The statement that those who belong to the persistence of the Dharma are all equal to Ānanda and others reveals that there is no difference in the root of their practice—namely, hearing, contemplation, and cultivation—and that their life of wisdom is uniform;
therefore, it is logical that their karmic fruits are also equal. This is indeed how it ought to be.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that two thousand individuals, both those in training and those beyond training, were entirely equal in their realization of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma.
Then, wishing to reiterate this meaning, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"These two thousand śrāvakas now stand before me... gradually entering into nirvāṇa.

At that time, the two thousand [monks], both those still in training and those beyond training, having heard the Buddha’s prediction of their enlightenment, were filled with joy and exultation, and spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One, lamp of wisdom, Having heard the sound of this prediction, My heart is filled with joy, As if drenched by the nectar of immortality."
This is the bestowing of predictions upon the assembly of those still in training (*śaikṣa*). This assembly of those in training consists entirely of newly initiated *śrāvakas*;

they all know their own limitations and lack the status of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). To avoid causing doubt among the assembly by granting them such a uniform prediction, the World-Honored One first stated their intention:
that they were gentle, serene, and pure, and that through hearing the sublime Dharma, they would subsequently realize the state of being beyond training.
This is a realm wherein they are worthy of receiving a prediction (vyākaraṇa). What the assembly does not yet know is that the Buddha asked Ānanda, "Do you see these two thousand people?
This was intended to reveal the minds of those present who had attained realization;

by showing this, he subtly dispelled the doubts of the assembly and thus conferred the prediction upon them. Because they had protected and upheld the Dharma-treasury during their causal stage, they were granted this prophecy.
Their fruit is called "Jewel-Phase" (*ratnākāra*), meaning they take the jewel-treasury of the Buddha-dharma as their own adornment.
As for the fact that their lifespans, lands, and so forth are all identical, this is because their causes are identical. These two thousand people had not yet witnessed the practice of the Dharma;
therefore, the predictions are also given in broad outline rather than individually. The verses are self-evident. It says, "gradually entering into..."
Nirvana is likewise brought about through the guidance of the three vehicles. Having heard this prediction, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
therefore, they spoke verses of praise and gratitude.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Ten: "The Dharma-Preacher."

The purpose of this chapter is as follows: Previously, the World-Honored One extensively praised the profound and subtle One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), stating that those who can believe and accept it will immediately attain Buddhahood;
consequently, each of the great disciples received their respective predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).

Yet, this One Vehicle is the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) that serves as the fundamental correct cause (*samyag-hetu*) inherent within all sentient beings. Now, by means of the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*), it is revealed and explained.
This sublime Dharma serves as the auxiliary condition and causal factor for its manifestation; there is nothing that will not be awakened to, and thus one becomes capable of bearing this burden.

By using the present to verify the past, and having known the fundamental cause of the Great Pervasion, and because these conditions have continued until now without being lost, one knows that the Dharma-conditions of this single assembly today shall again become inexhaustible seeds for the future. This is what is meant by "all... [ordinary beings].
Among those who hear the Dharma, there is not one who does not attain Buddhahood; even one who rejoices for a single thought-moment immediately attains Bodhi.
Therefore, the chapter is titled "The Dharma-Master. One who takes the mind as a teacher is called a Dharma-Master.
The intent here is that the correct cause of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* must rely upon a Dharma-Master to be revealed and manifested, so that it may endure through kalpas to come.
This refers to the superior conditions. For the seed of the Buddha-nature must rely on the熏 (xūn, perfuming) of conditions; this perfuming is of two kinds: old and new.

The Great Pervasive [Perfuming] is old perfuming, whereas the present case is new perfuming. There are five types of Dharma-preachers: namely, those who rejoice in [the teaching], those who read and recite it, those who receive and uphold it, those who transcribe it, and those who explain it.
Even if one can perform only one of these, one is called a Dharma-preacher. This is because this sutra already contains the entirety of the Tathāgata’s [teaching].

Therefore, one who is able to uphold [this teaching] is indeed one who bears the burden for the Tathāgata; thus, they should be revered and attended to as if they were the Buddha himself, so as to manifest the supreme and wondrous Dharma.
Since the Dharma must rely upon persons to propagate it, this ensures that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.

Consequently, the offense of those who slander it is exceedingly grave, for they sever the seed-nature of the Buddhas. It is by means of this that one perceives the original purpose of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
The [previous] exposition is complete; therefore, this chapter on the bestowal of the prediction follows next.
At that time, the World-Honored One, because of [the merit of] Bhaiṣajyarāja... shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
From here below, the eight classes [of beings] are recorded in detail to demonstrate that great universal compassion is impartial and to most clearly manifest the benefits of upholding this sutra.
As previously seen within the light of the white tuft between the Buddha’s brows: if various sons of the Buddha seek the path of the Buddha through manifold causes and conditions...
These, then, are the previous predictions of enlightenment for those of the three vehicles who seek the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.
Furthermore, it is said that if any among those seeking the three vehicles have doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them for them.
From this, we know that the eight classes of beings present here are all persons seeking the three vehicles. Tracing back their past causes, how could these people—?
Is this not the legacy of the Greatly Penetrating and Victorious Wisdom? Indeed, for such as these, every Buddha appearing in the world acts to protect the Dharma;
thus, their karmic conditions for hearing the Dharma have already matured.

How much more so for those who now hear even a single verse or a single phrase of this wondrous Dharma, or even those who rejoice in it for a single moment—they are all granted the prediction that they shall attain Bodhi, so it is shown.
Because the Buddha-wisdom is impartial, he bestows individual predictions of enlightenment upon each person present to manifest the supreme benefits of the wondrous Dharma.
This specific address to Bhaiṣajyarāja indicates that one who forgets the self and relinquishes attachments, thereby wondrously accords with this Dharma and is able to uphold it,
serves as the exemplar for all who uphold the sutra.
The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja (up to): "I also grant them the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This is a prophetic declaration concerning those who will uphold the Dharma in the future. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when this Dharma remains in the world, it is the eternal abiding of the Dharmakāya.
Therefore, if anyone hears even a single verse or a single phrase, or even for a single moment rejoices with sympathetic joy, they have already [attained this].
There exists the true seed for attaining Buddhahood. Just as when a person consumes a small amount of diamond, it will eventually pass through the skin and emerge;

there is no principle by which they would fail to attain Buddhahood. Therefore, they are also granted a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). This passage merely mentions those who rejoice in merit (*anumodana*);
below, the text properly demonstrates the six kinds of Dharma-preachers.
If there are further persons who receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra], they will certainly attain Buddhahood in a future age.
This demonstrates that these six kinds of Dharma-preachers are precisely those who uphold the sutra.
That is to say, if these six kinds of people who uphold the sutra can revere this sutra as they would the Buddha and make offerings to it with respect, such persons have already [in the past]...
Having made offerings to many Buddhas, those whose past merit is profound and who have come having fulfilled their great vows—
if someone asks which sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood in the future, I should show such people that these individuals will certainly become Buddhas.
Tiantai judges that the six kinds of Dharma-preachers correspond to the five grades of the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), namely, the grade of "following" (*suixing*).
Rejoicing in the sublime Dharma constitutes the true seed for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, one will certainly become a Buddha without doubt.
Jiyin (Jixian) maintained that the *sūtras* contain two gates—contemplation and illumination—which are sublime skillful means.
