Thus, all who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or expound this sūtra do so through the power of the skillful means of contemplation and illumination. This refers to the five grades of contemplative practice.

These are: first, sympathetic joy (*anumodana*); second, reading and reciting; third, preaching the Dharma; fourth, practicing the six perfections concurrently; and fifth, practicing the six perfections correctly.
Regarding "sympathetic joy": what dharma does one hear and rejoice in? Answer: the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*). The Sublime Dharma is precisely this mind.
The essence of the sublime mind is fully endowed like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without difference.
It is distinct. This mind is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle. The constant object is signless; the constant wisdom is objectless.

To take an object while being objectless—there is nothing that is not the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). To manifest signs while being signless—the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāni*) are perfectly present.

Therefore, the reason those of the five kinds of Dharma-masters must necessarily attain Buddhahood is the power of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). Thus, the King of East India invited two...

During the seventeenth patriarch’s vegetarian feast, the King asked the Venerable, “Why do you not read the scriptures? The Master replied, “In my humble way, when I breathe out, my breath does not involve external conditions;
when I breathe in, it does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates. I am constantly turning such a scripture as this, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of scrolls.”
Thus we know that what is emphasized in upholding this sutra is the contemplative observation and the maintenance of the mind;
it is not the counting of characters or the grasping of paper, ink, and written words that serves as the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Why is this? [If a good man... (up to) "how much more so when he extensively explains it for others in a great assembly."
This interrogative explanation clarifies the reason why the conditions for upholding this sutra are superior.
It was stated above that one who can uphold even a single phrase possesses the merit of the six kinds of Dharma-preachers; how much more so for one who can uphold the entire sutra.
Furthermore, those who expound this sutra in an evil age are certainly beings who have attained the fruit of the Pure Land and manifest birth in an evil age. If it were otherwise, the Tathāgata...

If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be one who can secretly recite even a single verse of this sutra for another person, that person is one sent by the Tathāgata and is one who performs the work of the Tathāgata;
how much more so those who extensively expound it for the assembly?
For they thereby sustain the life-force of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there should be an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, [acts against this teaching], their transgression is exceedingly grave.
Do not lightly disparage or revile those who uphold this sutra. The body of the Buddha is like space; to revile him is merely like spitting upon space.
Those who uphold this sutra are the very foundation of the life of wisdom. To revile them is to sever the lineage of the Buddhas; therefore, their transgression cannot be pardoned.
Repentance.

O Bhaiṣajyarāja, those who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra [up to] for the sake of *samyaksaṃbodhi*—this is an exhortation to honor those who uphold the sūtra as one would honor the Buddha. By being able to maintain this mind, one is complete.
One whose essence is that of a Buddha is carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata; indeed, one carries not only the Tathāgata.

Formerly, when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Udayana and his disciples, longing for the World-Honored One, dispatched thirty-two people including Maudgalyāyana to the celestial palace. There, they fashioned an image of the Buddha out of sandalwood incense.

The image arrived. When those who had requested its return asked the fourfold assembly to pay their respects, and when the World-Honored One himself returned from the celestial palace, he saw the image, prostrated before it, and praised it, saying:
"After my parinirvāṇa, you shall rely upon this to deliver immeasurable people in the land of China (Zhendan).
If even a single incense image can thus sustain the Buddha’s life of wisdom, how much more so for one who upholds this sutra? Thus, the Tathāgata..."
It is fitting that one should honor and make offerings to those who bear this burden upon their shoulders, wherever they may go.
Such persons as these deserve respect because, by speaking with joy, even a moment’s hearing of them leads one to attain Bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way and achieve spontaneous wisdom... [performing] the deeds of a Tathāgata."
This is a general verse on the supreme benefits of upholding this sutra. The Buddha-way is lofty and remote, not easily dwelt upon;
natural wisdom is subtle and transcends the mundane, not easily accomplished. However, if one simply makes offerings to those who uphold this sutra, all things will become easy.
The "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit; it is only after accumulating causes over many kalpas that one finally attains it.

Now, if one merely upholds this sutra and makes offerings to those who uphold it, one will attain it swiftly. Thus we know that the entire essence of the wondrous Dharma resides in the sutra and in the person [who upholds it].
Therefore, as for the person who upholds the sutra, they are not merely those dispatched by the Tathāgata—whom else could they be? All those who...
The first eight lines [of the verse] are capable of receiving and upholding; they correspond to the passage on "renouncing pure karmic retribution" and so forth.

The following four lines should correspond to the statement that since this person is one who has already attained the fruit, they ought to be honored with offerings. The twelve lines beginning with "After my parinirvāṇa... state that in an evil age it is difficult to uphold [the Dharma], yet one can uphold it;
it is difficult to hear [it], yet one has fortunately heard it. Therefore, one should pay homage and offer support, hoping to obtain what is required.
This is merely a brief mention. As for those who can uphold [the Dharma] in an evil age, none can do so unless they are sent by the Tathāgata.
If, throughout an entire eon, one constantly harbors unwholesome thoughts—[until finally reaching the point where] the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is supreme and foremost.
This verse compares the demerit of disparaging with the merit of praising; it may be understood as explained in the prose section.
Such is the sin of the one who disparages, and such is the merit obtained by the one who praises. What is most valued is that the life of wisdom (*prajñājīva*) is not severed.
Regarding the eight lines following "for eighty billion kalpas," the verse celebrates the momentary attainment of hearing [the teaching] as being superior to long-term offerings.
Making offerings is a minor merit for humans and devas, whereas hearing [this sutra] directly attains bodhi; therefore, it is said to yield great benefit.
The four lines beginning with "Yao Wang" (Bhaiṣajyarāja) eulogize the conclusion of the supreme benefits, because among all sutras, this Lotus Sutra is the foremost.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja... [up to] "...there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa.
From here below, the profound and subtle nature of the Dharma is revealed. This follows upon the first admonition not to bestow [the teaching] lightly.

Among the immeasurable tens of billions of sūtras spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time—that is, even among the immeasurable tens of billions of sūtras spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha himself—[this is the most profound].
This Lotus Sūtra alone is difficult to believe and difficult to understand because it is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas;
it is the treasure of all Buddhas, and thus must not be rashly bestowed upon those who are unworthy.

It has been guarded with single-minded devotion and remained hidden for a long time without being revealed, because even while the Tathāgata was in the world, there were many who were envious and hostile, such as those who withdrew from their seats; how much more so now?
After my parinirvāṇa, you must be extremely careful not to bestow this lightly.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa... [up to] ...then the Tathāgata will stroke their head with his own hand.
This statement—that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, one is able to uphold [the Dharma] in an evil age where it is difficult to do so—arises from two causes:
first, by relying on the Buddha’s protection; second, by possessing three kinds of great power oneself.

The Buddha takes patience as his robe, meaning that the essence of the mind is the wondrous Dharma, abiding in the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*). This is the Tathāgata covering one with his robe. Because one accords with the nature of awakening, it is therefore...
They are those whom all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Thoroughly believing in one’s own mind constitutes the power of great faith.

Resolving to universally bestow this Dharma upon all sentient beings constitutes the power of great resolve. Serving all Buddhas with a mind free from weariness constitutes the power of roots of goodness.

Because they wondrously accord with the Dharmakāya, they dwell together with the Tathāgata. Because they practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they should be patient; therefore, they are like [the Tathāgata].
Come, Maudgalyāyana, and listen with earnest attention. If one does not possess these qualities, it will be difficult to uphold this sutra in this evil age.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever [this is practiced], they shall all draw near to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This statement means that the sūtra is the entire body of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya; therefore, stūpas should be erected everywhere.
Since the Dharmakāya has no support, it takes the stūpa as its support. Thus, this stūpa should be honored with various kinds of offerings.
By seeing the stūpa and prostrating, one draws near to the Dharmakāya, and thereby draws near to Bodhi.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, whether lay or ordained, who—up to and including those who have attained proximity to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—[do so because of this].
This statement indicates that the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*) is the foundation for Bodhisattvas to practice and seek Buddhahood.
If any monastics or laypeople wish to practice the Bodhisattva path but do not hear this sutra, such persons have not yet skillfully practiced the Bodhisattva path."
This is because one has not realized the fundamental source. The Great Sūtra states: "To cultivate various roots of goodness while having forgotten the bodhicitta is the work of Māra.

This is because one grasps at phenomena as being external to the mind. What is meant by "realizing the source, the emotional attachments vanish" is that one knows the essence of the mind and merges with it.
This is why one performs good deeds; thus, only upon hearing this sutra can one truly practice wholesome conduct. This, then, is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If one hears this sutra and believes, understands, accepts, and upholds it, then one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby drawing near to Bodhi.
Below, a metaphor is provided to clarify this wholesome conduct.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, being thirsty and needing water, becomes determined in his mind that water must be near.
This parable illustrates the essential method for seeking the Dharma as an analogy for virtuous practice. Water symbolizes the true cause of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
The high plateau symbolizes the profound depth of afflictions (*kleśa*). Digging represents contemplative observation and exhaustive investigation. Dry soil symbolizes not yet having seen the Buddha.
Because its nature [is such], it is said that "the water is still far away. The continuous application of effort is a metaphor for the gradual progress of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

The moist soil is a metaphor for partially perceiving the True Reality (*tattva*). Reaching the mud is a metaphor for the stream of the Dharma being near; thus, it is said that "one knows the water must be close.
In this way, the moist soil is like hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā*, while the mud is like hearing this sutra. Furthermore, upon hearing this sutra, one must...
By relying on the power of provisional contemplation and skillful means to enter into awakening, one then beholds the true source of the Buddha-nature;

this is what is meant by "connecting with the flowing stream of the Tathāgata’s Dharma. Viewed from this perspective, if one were to consider that [the truth] can be attained through written words and spoken language, [it would be a grave error].

This refers precisely to relying on others to form interpretations, which blocks the gate of self-awakening. For one who hopes to attain the coolness of liberation by quenching their thirst, this will be difficult.
Thus, the Sūtra says, "one merely approaches it. The previous passage stated that the place of treasure is near; this passage states that knowing the water, one must be near it.
It further says, "attaining proximity to Bodhi. It does not say "reaching" but "approaching. This is what is meant in the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) by the term "words."
Is it not because they fear those who have reached completion?
The Bodhisattva is also like this; even now, the Buddha teaches and transforms them, bringing them to fulfillment and providing them with instruction.
This is the application of the Dharma. This sutra is the very life-force of the wisdom of all Buddhas. If a Bodhisattva’s practice has not yet—
Those who have heard this sutra but do not yet understand it or practice it remain far from Bodhi;

they are like dry soil, being covered by the afflictions of ignorance. If, however, one hears, understands, contemplates, and practices it through the skillful means of contemplative observation, one draws near to Bodhi, like seeing mud while digging a well. Nevertheless, a Bodhisattva’s cultivation must necessarily rely upon...
As for this sutra, it is because all bodhi belongs to this sutra; it is because this Lotus Sutra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the mark of reality.
This treasury of the Lotus Sutra is the *tathāgatagarbha* of sentient beings.

If it has not yet been opened and revealed, it remains latent within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Because of this storehouse consciousness, even when the stages of a bodhisattva are exhausted, one cannot fully know it.
Only a Buddha can know it; therefore, it is said to be profound, firm, deep, and remote, such that no one can reach it. Those without great faculties cannot even believe in it.
Thus, the Buddha now reveals it for the sake of the Bodhisattvas; it does not fall into the hands of other sentient beings.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, [become startled or afraid], you should know that they are persons of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

This statement means that [such people] are not suitable vessels and are difficult to bring to faith. If a bodhisattva hears it and is startled or afraid, they are one who has newly resolved their mind;
if a śrāvaka hears it and is startled or afraid, they are all persons of overweening pride. None of them are suitable vessels.

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are good men (up to) and the fourfold assembly who extensively expound this Lotus Sūtra"—this demonstrates the method for preaching the sūtra, namely, the teaching of the Dharma for bodhisattvas.

By stating at length that those who reverently expound the sūtra should be honored as Buddhas, it is shown that one who reverently expounds it does not merely engage in verbal recitation; they must necessarily possess the very embodiment of a Buddha.
What is taught accords with the Buddha-mind; it is to embody the Buddha-mind.

Therefore, it is said that one must enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat before one may preach the Dharma. To settle the body is to take it as the chamber.
Now, the Dharma-body is not a body; it takes sentient beings as its body. Thus it is said that compassion is its object of focus. By focusing on suffering sentient beings, the Buddha—
Compassion is his dwelling; the covering of his body is his robe. The Buddha is fundamentally without self. Being without self, there is nothing with which he can be confronted.
When there is nothing with which he can be confronted, no thing can cause him harm. To conceal himself within patience is the ultimate state of non-self.
Therefore, patience is taken as his robe. A detached mind is his seat. When the mind is empty, it is quiescent;

when it is quiescent, its sounds are like echoes in a valley. He speaks without anything being spoken; thus, the emptiness of phenomena is taken as his seat. Such are the body, mind, and speech of the Tathāgata.
If a Bodhisattva can possess this essence and dwell securely within it, only then, by means of non-...
With a mind free from indolence, one should preach to the fourfold assembly; only in this way can one be called a preacher of the sutras.
Otherwise, it will be difficult for them to revere and serve you as they would the Buddha.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I shall dispatch emanated persons to other lands; when I return, I will explain [the Dharma] for them so that they may attain full perfection.
These words describe the essence of the Buddha’s practice, which moves the Buddha to provide protection and assistance for its wide propagation. As previously stated:
"If among my disciples there are those who have not yet been transformed, after my parinirvāṇa I shall become a Buddha in other lands. Furthermore, there are others... [text ends].
I shall deliver them by means of their names. Now, it is said that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there may be those who preach this sutra in accordance with the Dharma;

for such people, I will surely dispatch emanated beings from other worlds to serve as members of the assembly listening to the Dharma, so that they may first have faith in this teaching and cause others who do not yet believe to do so.
If the preacher of the Dharma is in a secluded place, I will certainly dispatch the eight classes of supernatural beings in great numbers to protect him.
I shall protect the Dharma so that no demonic disturbances occur. I will not merely dispatch others; I shall personally manifest my own body before those individuals.
Should they forget any phrases or sections, I will certainly explain them for them, ensuring they master the text thoroughly without any loss.
Because after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, in this age of defilement and evil, it is difficult for those who uphold this sutra to do so;
were it not for relying upon the Tathāgata’s empowerment and protection, how could the Dharma be made to abide long?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra... until they attain the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
These first four lines of the verse collectively demonstrate that it is not easy for those who have faith in the excellence of the Dharma to accept it;
they abandon indolence, their minds do not harmonize with worldly sentiments, and this is true diligence. To bring the mind into accord with the sublime Dharma is called the practice of diligence.
Therefore, those who wish to abandon indolence should listen to this sutra. The lines beginning with "Just as a person" (six lines) provide a simile.
The lines beginning with "Medicine King" (ten lines) apply the Dharma to the analogy. The lines beginning with "If a person" (fourteen lines) describe the essence of the Buddha’s practice.

The lines beginning with "In my thousands of millions of lands" (thirty-six lines) describe how the Buddha assists in the propagation and proclamation [of the teaching] by manifesting the body of light and so forth; thus, he manifests his physical form.

This refers to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of verbal expression. "The Buddhas protectively mindfully attend" precisely means that they protectively mindfully attend to the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas.
The four lines beginning with "If one draws near" constitute the concluding exhortation.

As for the statement "one shall see Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," it means that the nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges reside collectively within the source of the mind; by following the Teacher of the Mind, these nature-virtues will become manifest.
The nine grades prior to this are judged to be those for whom the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened. There are two meanings to "opening":
from the perspective of the Buddha, it means to reveal, manifest, and develop [the truth] for the sake of the assembly, so as to cause listeners to gain self-confidence in their own minds;

from the perspective of the receptive capacity [of sentient beings], it means to bring about awakening, because sentient beings have long been deluded and did not believe in their own minds, and now, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, they rejoice.
The calamities are fully understood. That is to say, the practitioner who has awakened to the mind is like a lotus flower in full bloom.

Although the sutra generally speaks of four kinds of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), in terms of its underlying meaning, these first ten chapters of the sutra collectively reveal the Tathāgata’s original intent in appearing in the world.

Because the great disciples had consistently failed to understand the Buddha’s mind, they frequently harbored doubts regarding the Buddha’s teachings; at times, they even regarded the Buddha as a demon.
Now, one’s faith is resolved and free from doubt; this is precisely the manifestation of the awakening of this mind. As the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) says:
"To believe that one's own mind is Buddha" is to reach the stage of non-doubt; therefore, it is classified under the character "open" (kāi).

Ancient worthies generally held that the preceding sections describe the three cycles of the Dharma and the bestowing of predictions upon the three capacities, while the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" (Fashier pin) constitutes the bestowing of the extensive prediction.

This encompasses the preceding record in its entirety. Contemplating the meaning of the sutra, it is clear that the text places singular emphasis on the person who upholds the sutra and speaks most highly of the benefits of the *Saddharma*.
This is because sentient beings previously did not know [the existence of this teaching], but now that they do know it, they must revere it;

it must not be rashly bestowed upon those who are unworthy. As it is said: "That which is not a fit vessel shall not be transmitted. This fully elucidates the principle of opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
[End of Volume] The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa. Regarding the intent of this chapter’s inclusion:
it is judged to be for the purpose of revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as it demonstrates the eternally abiding Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The "Body" directly points to the true realm of the Pure Land’s actual recompense (*vipākaphala*). It is intended to cause sentient beings to know and perceive this realm of the *dharmakāya*;
this constitutes the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). While previously it was merely explained through verbal discourse, here it is specifically indicated by means of actual facts;
therefore, this chapter focuses solely on the character "to show" (*shi*). This is the true realm of the *dharmakāya*.

At the beginning of the sutra, a single ray of light shines eastward, perfectly manifesting the phenomena and signs of the Dharma-realm and revealing the beginning and end of the Buddha’s manifestation;

this serves as a general demonstration of the wondrous nature of the mind and objects for all sentient beings. Because the audience has not yet awakened to this wondrous mind, they instead employ the conceptualizations of their conscious intellects to deliberate upon it.

This is what is meant by "sentiment arises and wisdom is obstructed. It is simply that one does not realize what is right before one's eyes. One assumes it is not within the scope of one's own wisdom;

yet now, having received the Tathāgata’s various instructions, those present have already believed the Buddha’s words and know for themselves they shall become Buddhas, each receiving their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Thus, although they believe in their own minds, they still do not yet believe in the true realm of *dharmatā*. This is [the stage of] *utpāda* (arising).
The view of extinction has not yet been forgotten, and the attachment to purity and impurity has not yet subsided.

Therefore, as the World-Honored One reaches this point, intending to reveal that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, a magnificent stupa made of the seven treasures emerges from the earth, and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna appears in his entire body, in order to eliminate the view of arising and ceasing.
Thus, this Sahā world is transformed into a pure land three times, in order to dispel the notions of purity and impurity.

Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions fill its interior, manifesting that throughout every atom and every land of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), whatever meets the eye is the true realm of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
This is the true knowledge and vision of the Buddha. Therefore, this chapter is presented to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
it follows immediately after the bestowal of the prophecy has been completed. Moreover, the stupa is five [yojanas] high.

That the entire body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna remains undispersed within the stupa extending for a hundred *yojanas* is shown to sentient beings as this very arising-and-ceasing body and mind of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*),
which is itself the dwelling place of the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*.

That this Sahā world undergoes three transformations to become a pure land is shown to be the true realm of the *sambhogakāya*, adorned like the Flower Treasury (*Puṣpaka-ratnavyūha*), which does not depart from the five [aggregates].

This refers to the function of turbid karma. This specifically demonstrates a mere glimpse of the adornment of the true retribution of the *dharmakāya* (Vairocana) and its environment, with the intent that sentient beings may know the wondrous nature of this mind and its objects, such that they can realize them directly before their eyes and not give rise to fear regarding the long duration of the Buddha-way.
The view that "the provisional leads to the real" is found herein. How is this clarified?
This sutra elucidates the opening of the gate of expedient means and the manifestation of the true aspect. What is meant by the "true aspect"?
It refers to the Dharma-body of the true Buddha realized through my cultivation of causes over vast kalpas as Vairocana, and the True Land of Quiescent Light where he dwells;
from this Dharma-body, the retributive body descends, namely the Pure Land of Adorned Real Retribution where the thousand-fathom Rucaka Buddha resides.

However, this body and its land are both real; therefore, they constitute the aspect of ultimate reality. Śākyamuni, moreover, is a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) manifested from his reward body (saṃbhogakāya).
The land in which he dwells shares the same afflictions as the people—it is the defiled land of the five turbidities (pañcakaṣāya) in Sahā.
Since this body and land are both provisional, all his arrangements and his initial teachings were conducted with this in mind.
This refers to the provisional, namely the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*).

When Vairocana first attained perfect enlightenment, he manifested a body one thousand *zhang* in height and sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to preach the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Yet, while the followers of the two vehicles were seated there, they were as if blind and deaf.
Thus, although both his body and land were truly real, and the teachings were entirely authentic, how could they alone reach those of great capacity, while the small [vehicle] remained excluded?
In order to sever the roots [of affliction], he enters the Samādhi of the Limit of the Instant (*kṣaṇakoṭi*). He manifests two simultaneous aspects; these two beginnings occur at once.

While correctly preaching the *Avataṃsaka*, he does not hinder the manifestation of the eight phases of enlightenment through the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and transformation-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

At the Deer Park, he provisionally distinguishes the One Vehicle Dharma into three to accommodate those of lesser capacity. That is to say, by the power of skillful means, he speaks of the Four [Truths].

The Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and so forth, are all subsumed within the three roots. Although there are teachings on the Bodhisattva Dharma, these belong collectively to the provisional teachings.
This is just as a wealthy elder entices his children by promising them three chariots; they do not actually exist.
Therefore, the original intent for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world has not yet been fully realized, because his disciples have not yet perceived the true realm of the Dharmakāya.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "I originally established my vow, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.
His intention was to lead sentient beings directly to personally realize the realm of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, thereby proceeding toward the Adornment of the Flower Treasury (Huazang).

Only when this fruit of the essence is realized will one’s original aspiration be fulfilled. Alas, those of inferior capacity cling exclusively to the provisional as if it were the ultimate, refusing to advance further;
they harbor doubts and lack faith in what the Buddha has taught.
Thus, the World-Honored One’s forty years of effort in employing various skillful means to refine and purify them have now reached full maturity, and his work of transformation is drawing to a close.

Therefore, in this assembly, he directly expresses his original intent: to open up and eliminate the provisional teachings of the three vehicles of the past, thereby revealing the reality of the One Vehicle.
The wealth of the elder’s household described in the sutra is precisely a metaphor for the perfectly wondrous Dharma of the Huayan One Vehicle.
This is because the śrāvakas merely recognize the Śākyamuni of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) as the true Buddha, and do not...
They know that the true Buddha still exists, yet they see only the defiled land of Sahā as something loathsome; they fail to realize the true realm of the real mark (dharmatā).
Consequently, their views of arising and ceasing and their sentiments regarding purity and impurity remain fixed in attachment, which they refuse to relinquish.
Because they have not realized that all manifestations are but the mind itself, before preaching this sutra, [the Buddha] first emitted a single ray of light from his white tuft of hair,
which universally illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, clearly revealing the true realm of the Dharma-dhatu as it exists within the daily activities of sentient beings.
Since this cannot be reached through the conceptualization and discrimination of the mind and consciousness, he again resorts to skillful means.

He gave various expositions, and the great assembly each came to believe that their own minds were [the source]. Consequently, he bestowed the prediction of Buddhahood upon each one. This is precisely as stated in the *Avataṃsaka*:
"At the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one knows that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind;

one accomplishes the body of wisdom without depending on another for awakening. This merely realizes the truth of the mind but does not yet penetrate the reality of objects; thus, mind and object have not yet been integrated. Not yet...
This is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood; yet it still belongs to the knowledge and vision of sentient beings and is not yet the knowledge and vision of a Buddha.

Therefore, while the previous bestowal of the prediction already revealed the truth of the mind, the present exposition of this chapter reveals the subtlety of the objective realm (*viṣaya*). It points directly to what is manifest before one’s eyes for realization;
thus, it is specifically designated as "revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Hence it is said: "By pointing with concrete matters, one washes away the small [vehicle]."

Riding upon the knowledge and vision cultivated through past habituation, one easily achieves realization; only then does one fulfill the fundamental intention of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
The underlying meaning of this chapter is profound and far-reaching; unless one examines it with a meticulous mind, it is extremely difficult to comprehend.
However, by harmonizing the contemplation with the *Avataṃsaka*, one will naturally understand the ultimate destination within it.
At that time, before the Buddha, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures... (up to) making offerings to the stupa with reverence, respect, and praise.
This is a direct indication of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). The Buddha’s knowledge and vision are what is known and seen by the noble wisdom of self-awakening;
they are the true realm of the single, true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Only this Dharma-realm is the abiding place of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Dwelling: It is upon this that the Reward and Transformation bodies arise. Thus, the Buddhas realize it as the All-Seed Wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*);
the Reward Body occupies it as the Flower Treasury Adornment (*puṣpakūṭa-garbha-vyūha*); and the Transformation Body employs it as its wondrous functions of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

Sentient beings, being deluded by it, take it to be the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of body and mind, the eighty-four thousand afflictions, defilements, and labors. For those who cultivate the mind...
If one does not penetrate and perceive the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*), one remains entirely outside the gate, dwelling merely in a thatched hut; this is not a true realization.

Therefore, these three cycles of teaching are expounded to bring about perfection. The appearance of the jeweled stupa before the Buddha serves as a sign to demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Now, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) has no dependence; it takes the Dharma-realm as its support. As for the Dharma-realm, it is quiescent extinction (*śānti*).

This is the mind. The jeweled stupa is the realm of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). The five hundred *yojanas* is a metaphor for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the sentient beings' body and mind;

it is precisely the true realm of quiescent extinction. The two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth is a metaphor for being deluded regarding this Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), such that this very body and mind do not transcend the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). From the ground...
"Surging forth" is a metaphor for when the ground of the mind of ignorance is broken, the realm of quiescent extinction manifests before one.
That is to say, once birth and cessation have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests; then these five aggregates—the body and mind—have fundamentally never existed.

Therefore, it is said that "one dwells in the midst of space. That various precious objects serve as adornments is a metaphor for this *dharmadhātu*, which is fundamentally not a state of annihilation.
It is extinguished. It possesses merits that accord with the nature of reality, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with the wondrous functions of supernormal powers.
To rise high above the four heavens means it cannot be constrained by the four great elements.

That the various devas scatter flowers and the eight classes of beings present offerings is a metaphor for how this *dharmadhātu* is fundamentally revered by the devas and protected by the eight classes of beings; it is originally not a state of mere silence or emptiness.
This is the ground of humanity.
At that time, a great sound issued forth from within the jeweled stūpa... [up to] "...all that has been spoken is true reality.

This statement regarding the sound issuing from the stūpa is intended to demonstrate that while quiescent, it is capable of speaking; it is not a state of total annihilation. He praised it, saying, "Excellent!"

"Excellent! Excellent! and so forth. This praises Śākyamuni for being able to accord with the essence of the *dharmadhātu* by preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* through his impartial great wisdom (*samatā-mahājñāna*).
"Thus it is, thus it is" serves as a seal of authentication, confirming that all that has been taught is ultimately identical to the *dharmadhātu*.
It confirms that all that has been taught is true and that what was spoken is not false. Thus, before the World-Honored One...

Throughout his life, the Master addressed his disciples, declaring that his words were not false. Now, the manifestation of the sound from the stupa serves as direct evidence that Śākyamuni preached the Dharma of quiescence.
His intention was that those of the three vehicles would surely believe; by this, he seals the capacities of all sentient beings.
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the great jeweled stūpa [up to] reverently joining their palms and withdrawing to stand to one side.

This fourfold assembly was both joyful and astonished upon seeing the stūpa. As for their joy: it was truly marvelous that a wondrous stūpa made of the seven treasures suddenly surged forth and remained suspended in mid-air;
this was certainly a cause for joy. Yet, the fact that a voice issued from within the stūpa was truly astonishing.
Furthermore, if one awakens to the fact that the sounds emerging from within the stupa are themselves quiescent, then all sounds are utterly extinguished.
The great assembly, unaware of why this was so, stood with palms joined, hoping for the Buddha’s instruction.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva (up to) who also uttered these sounds therein.

This refers to the occasion when the assembly, seeing the stūpa, raised doubts and made a request. The Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna made this request because the Dharma of quiescent extinction is a path beyond words;
were it not for eloquence (*pratibhāna*), it would ultimately be cut off from speech. — *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*
He said: "Although it does not rely on the path of language, nor does it cling to wordlessness—this is the meaning of delighting in discourse.
A stūpa does not manifest without cause; therefore, I request that you explain its causal conditions."
At that time, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāratnakūṭa (up to the point where those who had emerged from the earth praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!").
This explains the cause for the manifestation of the stupa. Regarding the fact that there is the complete body of the Tathāgata within the stupa:

the stupa is a metaphor for the five-aggregate body of sentient beings, within which resides the complete body of the Tathāgata. That which is called the illusory, transformed, empty body is precisely the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature;

it manifests the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings, like a precious jewel of great value wrapped in soiled garments. Now, the name of this land is "Treasure-Purity" (*Ratnaviśuddhi*), which is a symbol of the Tathāgatagarbha emerging from its wrappings and being free from defilement.
The Buddha’s name is "Dharmakāya of Many Treasures" (*Prabhūtaratna*), which refers to the Tathāgata...
Because he possesses merits that accord with the nature of reality, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he is named Prabhūtaratna (Many Treasures).

When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made a vow that after his parinirvāṇa, wherever in the ten directions the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached, his stupa would appear to serve as a witness.
Because Prabhūtaratna attained realization of the Dharma-body through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, whenever a sutra is preached, the Dharma-body immediately manifests.

Within the assembly, upon hearing the preaching of the wondrous Dharma, if one can open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, then this five-aggregate body and mind will suddenly reveal the entire substance of the Dharma-body;
this is the sign of such realization. After that Buddha had attained enlightenment...

The entrustment of his entire body for a great stūpa upon the point of death truly reveals the Dharma of ultimate nirvāṇa—the mark of eternal quiescence that is free from both marks and the mark of extinction.
That Buddha, descending into the stūpa by means of his supernormal powers, praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent," and so forth;
this refers to the fact that while remaining in stillness, he can manifest throughout the ten directions, as this very sūtra is precisely...
The entire body of the Dharma-body, once the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, immediately manifests as realization.
The preceding section recounted the causes and conditions of Prabhūtaratna; this concludes with the present circumstances as shown by Mahāpratibhāna.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsāhasrapramardana [and others] said, "We wish to behold this Buddha-body;

we wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna within the stupa during this Dharma assembly. Although the Dharma-body is manifest, even by means of one's own power of wisdom, it must rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power;
therefore, they invoked it by borrowing the Buddha’s supernatural power.
The Buddha addressed Mahāpratibhāna (up to): "I also wish to see the Buddhas who are emanations of the World-Honored One, to pay homage to and make offerings to them.

This was the World-Honored One’s permission for them to see [the emanations]. Furthermore, he recounted the original vow of Prabhūtaratna to assemble the emanated bodies, thereby manifesting that the three bodies are one essence.
This serves to directly refute the attachment of the two vehicles who mistakenly identify [the Buddha] as merely the nirmāṇakāya. From "Mahāpratibhāna" onwards, the World-Honored One...
The assembly of emanated Buddhas was gathered; the great multitude, because of the presence of Prabhūtaratna, also desired to see those emanated Buddhas.
At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows (until: wherever it shone, it was likewise so).

This light summons the various emanations of the Buddhas. When the Buddha was about to preach this sutra, he entered the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meanings and emitted a single ray of light from his white tuft of hair, which illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, perfectly manifesting the phenomena and signs of the Dharma-realm and the beginning and end of the Buddhas' appearance in the world.
This is intended to reveal the entire essence of the wondrous Dharma by citing a single corner of the Dharma-realm.
This reveals that from beginning to end, the appearance of all Buddhas in the world does not transcend the samādhi of the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
All the teachings they proclaim are matters within the light. Mañjuśrī leads back to the origin and beginning of Dīpaṃkara; this is the manifestation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
It was intended to bring enlightenment to the great assembly.

Because the great assembly did not awaken, the Tathāgata emerged from samādhi and skillfully expounded the Dharma—namely, opening the gate of expedient means—up to the account of the Great Universal Wisdom-Victorious One attaining Buddhahood.
When he first entered samādhi, the worlds of the ten directions were all brilliantly illuminated; this was the revealing and manifesting of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. And...
Sentient beings of inferior capacity, although they have awakened to the causes and conditions of the past, have not yet personally realized the true realm of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, the teachings given during the three turnings of the wheel still contained verbal expressions.

Now, since it is extensively recorded that all who hear this Dharma—whether in the present or the future—will without exception attain Buddhahood, [the Buddha] further fears that followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) who cling to signs might [misunderstand] names and words.
Because habitual tendencies have not yet been forgotten, and the mind still harbors views of birth-and-death and purity-and-impurity, it is difficult to enter the realm of the single truth.

Therefore, a jeweled stupa emerges as a provisional means, and the Many Treasures Buddha manifests his body; he summons the Buddhas of the ten directions with light and transforms the pure lands in three ways.
This is precisely to perceive the Dharmakāya within the five aggregates and to realize the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) before one's very eyes;

it is the direct pointing-out of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, when a single ray of light was emitted from the white tuft between his brows, and [the Bodhisattva] immediately beheld the Buddhas in five hundred trillion Ganges-sand worlds in the eastern direction, it was to demonstrate that sentient beings in the five realms of existence all abide in the One True [Dharma] of the Buddhas.

This is the ground [of realization]. When one sees various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes, it is shown that the deluded thoughts and distractions of sentient beings are themselves the constant manifestation of the Dharma-sound by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The fact that within this light the affairs of sentient beings’ birth and death, or the pursuit of the Way through the Three Vehicles, do not appear, is because one now directly realizes the Dharmakāya; thus, it is named the teaching of the Bodhisattva-dharma.
Therefore, the various other [buddhas] are not mentioned. As for the current statement that the buddhas of the ten directions are all emanations (*vibhāga*) of Śākyamuni:

there are three bodies (*trikāya*) of a buddha—namely, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which descends from it to the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and from the Reward-body to the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Now, by manifesting these three bodies as one essence, the intent is to reveal that Śākyamuni is identical to Prabhūtaratna, and that the emanated bodies are none other than Śākyamuni; thus, the Dharma-body and the Transformation-bodies are mysteriously one.
It is like an elephant. As it is said: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm and manifests universally before all sentient beings;
responding to conditions and meeting with those who seek him, there is nowhere he does not reach, yet he ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi.

Now, his emanations have gathered together to collectively realize the wondrous Dharma, thereby manifesting that the Way of the Buddhas of the ten directions is identical and that past and present are one and the same limit—this is what Śākyamuni has taught.

This is true and not false. It signifies that the realms of infinite lands are not separated by so much as a hair’s breadth between self and other, and that the ten periods of past and present do not depart from the present moment of thought.
As for the three transformations of the pure land, it signifies that the defiled is itself the pure, and that Sahā is itself the Flower Treasury (Huazang).
All that appears before one's eyes is entirely the true realm of *dharmatā*. Therefore, within the light...
All the lands are adorned with the seven treasures. The first light reveals them; the next three cycles elucidate them;
and now, at this assembly, they are pointed out—this is the full extent of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is precisely the ultimate manifestation of the spiritual power of all Buddhas.
To propagate this matter: it is what is called the Elder’s assemblying of the king, his kinsmen, and the entrustment of the family inheritance.
The great causal condition for the one great matter is fully realized herein; it is not merely that.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions (up to) together with the stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna were being offered worship.
These Buddhas of the ten directions, having been summoned by the light, were about to assemble.
At that time, the Sahā world immediately transformed into purity (extending until) all devas and humans were moved to other lands.
This transformation of the land was to accommodate the various emanation bodies of the Buddhas; it is what is called "manifesting the true aspect.

Within the one true Dharma-realm, there is fundamentally neither purity nor defilement; it merely undergoes transformation according to the mind. Thus, the defiled land of Sahā is originally the Flower Treasury World (*Kusuma-garbha-loka-dhātu*).
It is solely because it is accumulated by sentient beings who are defiled by evil that it is filled with filth and impurity; the mountains of earth and stone are uneven in their heights and depths.
Those of the Two Vehicles do not realize that all is but mind, and thus they falsely give rise to longing and aversion, acceptance and rejection.
Because they perceive phenomena as existing outside the mind, they cling exclusively to nirvana and fail to give rise to even a single thought of delivering sentient beings; therefore, they fear it.
It is like a prison; one fears it as if shackled by fetters. This is because they have not yet seen that the defiled land is fundamentally pure and that sentient beings are fundamentally empty.

Now, in this assembly, the Tathāgata specifically points out the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, desiring only that they fully comprehend the single, true, and equal Dharma-realm, clearly awaken to the fact that both mind and objects are truly real, and thoroughly perceive the true mark of all phenomena. This is...

The threefold exposition has opened the gate of skillful means; now the appearance of Prabhūtaratna and the three transformations of the pure land reveal what is called the manifestation of the true aspect.
Yet, although the Sahā world is fundamentally pure, sentient beings have their minds shrouded by ignorance, and because the light of wisdom has not yet dawned, they falsely perceive it as defiled.
Now the Buddha emits light from the tuft of white hair between his brows, illuminating the ten directions and manifesting [the truth].
To reveal the realm of Mind-only and open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, every thought-moment within the atoms of all lands becomes the emergence of a Buddha;
thus, this defiled land is transformed into a pure land. Therefore, the Sūtra says that it "accommodates the manifested bodies of all Buddhas," which is why the land is purified three times.
Purity and defilement are solely a matter of the mind and do not depend on external force; they are transformed immediately simply through the radiance of light.
This Sahā world is revealed as being identical to the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha). Therefore, its ground is made of lapis lazuli and adorned with jeweled trees;
because it is the equality of the single reality, there are no villages, mountains, rivers, or the like. It entirely enters the Great Radiant Treasury of Spiritual Powers (Abhijñāmaha-ābhāsagarbha).
Therefore, great precious incense is burned; this constitutes the ground for sentient beings to attain Buddhahood. Therefore, flowers are strewn upon the ground;
the myriad practices are all-pervasive, and all are the sounds of the Dharma. Therefore, precious nets cover and suspend various jeweled bells. Sentient beings are fundamentally empty;
therefore, the devas and humans are moved and placed in other lands. If one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, then one shall immediately cast down worldly emotions.

Upon forgetting [all conceptualizations], one suddenly beholds the true realm of the real mark (*dharmatā*). In the past, at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, those of the two vehicles were like the blind;
now, it is clearly and distinctly manifest before one's eyes. This is what is called "revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
At that time, each of the Buddhas brought along a great Bodhisattva; even after these emanated bodies had arrived, they were still not exhausted.
This was the gathering of the emanated Buddhas from the eastern direction.
Each Buddha took a great Bodhisattva as an attendant, intending to manifest the unity of fruit and cause. The jeweled trees were five hundred *yojanas* high, and there were jeweled thrones.
It is five *yojanas* high. To clarify the Buddha’s knowledge and vision means that the Buddha appears in every thought-moment, never departing from the body and mind of the five aggregates.
As for the Buddhas each sitting cross-legged upon these seats, it refers to not departing from their current location.
They fill the trichiliocosm; even the emanated bodies distributed in a single direction have not yet been fully accounted for.
"Exhaustion" (jìn) signifies that there is an infinite succession of layers without end.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha desired to accommodate [the assembly], and divine jeweled flowers were spread everywhere across the ground.
These two transformations purify the Buddha-land thrice, intending to expand it into the true realm of the Dharma-dhātu.
Regarding the first transformation mentioned previously, the Sahā world has already been universally transformed into a single pure land;

yet, even after the Buddhas who have manifested their bodies from the eastern direction have been accommodated within it, it appears there is not so much as a needle’s point of space remaining, and even this is still insufficient. This is the first [point].
If compared with the Buddha, there is still a surplus; yet the entire realm of this land is insufficient. From this, one can know the great number of his emanated bodies.
Now, outside of this Sahā world, in each of the eight directions, he further transforms two hundred trillion nayutas of lands.
All are made pure. Thus, the realm is not limited to this single Sahā world alone. A question is asked:
Within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbhadhātu), it is only the single Sahā world that constitutes a defiled land, because it is filled with the impurities of the three evil paths;
all other Buddha-lands are entirely pure. Now, regarding those lands transformed beyond the Sahā world, they all likewise possess [the three evil paths].
The path of humans and devas: for now, the evil realms are concealed and beings are shifted to the realms of humans and devas; this is as if the Sahā world were a single land.

Furthermore, since the previous transformation has already been universalized and the Buddhas of the eastern quarters have already filled it, what kind of land would these three further transformations result in?
The answer is: This meaning is extremely profound. It reveals that the Dharma-realm is boundless, thereby clarifying [the nature of] sentient beings.
Delusive conditions are inexhaustible. Yet, regarding this single land of Sahā, the realm of Śākyamuni’s transformation, it is commonly said to be merely a trichiliocosm.
However, if one observes closely, one sees that Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was able to take as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and designate them as a single buddha-field.
Thus, we know that the Sahā world does not consist of only one trichiliocosm.
Thus it is. Because sentient beings are deluded regarding the true mind of the fundamental Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), their entire being transforms into ignorance and false conceptualization.
This delusion is universal; it is the total transformation of the Dharma-realm into the realm of sentient beings.
In this way, sentient beings fill the entire Dharma-realm—how could a single Sahā world-system possibly contain them? This is what is meant by "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

It is this that constitutes a single world-system of three thousandfold great thousand worlds. Nevertheless, each person perceives it according to their own vision, restricting it to being a single world.
Thus, the Flower Treasury World (Huazang) encompasses many pure lands because it is perceived according to the pure minds of the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Because delusion itself is awakening, that which is defiled is itself pure. Because it is seen according to the deluded minds of sentient beings, that which is pure is itself defiled.
Now, by causing sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, this is the turning back from delusion toward awakening;
thus, the delusive thoughts of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas are now, in a single thought-moment, entirely transformed into the wisdom-function of all Buddhas.
This is the manifestation of Śākyamuni’s emanations from the ten directions gathering together. Because deluded thoughts are inexhaustible, the Buddhas are likewise boundless.
However, as objects transform according to the mind, now that the true mind has been transformed, the true realm transforms accordingly;
thus, beyond this Sahā world, each of the eight directions further transforms two hundred trillion nayutas of lands.
This is intended to expand to the full extent of the Dharma-realm; yet for now, it is still only a partial transformation, not a complete one.

If it were a complete transformation, how could there be directions, names, or numbers? If these infinite deluded thoughts were transformed into Buddha-wisdom, it would be fitting that Buddhas would be numerous and their realms crowded;
how could a single Saha world possibly contain them? Nevertheless, [the Buddha] performed the three transformations.
The text states: "In order for all Buddhas to sit here in the future, [the land] is further transformed in each of the eight directions, each by two hundred million *koṭis* and so forth.
This shows that since sentient beings have now opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), delusive thoughts are forever severed.
From this moment on, in every thought-moment, all Buddhas appear before them; this is what is meant by "all Buddhas sitting here in the future. Question: Regarding what was said about "entirely..."?
The Dharma-realm was previously obscured by delusion; now that awakening has been opened, it should be fully transformed all at once.

Why, then, rely on three successive transformations of the pure land to bring this about? The answer is: This precisely reveals the Tathāgata’s great skillful means (*upāya*) for attracting and guiding sentient beings.
Because the defilements of sentient beings are heavy, they cannot suddenly perceive the entire body of the Dharma-realm; therefore, [the Buddha] provisionally established...
The provisional means of the Three Vehicles are employed to lead them forward step by step. However, those who cling to these provisional means possess narrow and inferior knowledge and vision;
therefore, the Tathāgata does not dare to suddenly reveal his entire essence to them. As it is said: "If this matter were explained, they would all be struck with alarm and doubt.
Fearing that they might be terrified and fail to believe, he employs immeasurable and various skillful means to guide them. Nevertheless...
Although they now have faith in the Buddha’s mind, they have not yet perceived the true realm of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, he provisionally employs the three transformations of the Pure Land to demonstrate it to them. Now, as for the initial transformation of the Sahā world:

because those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) exclusively perceive the cycle of birth and death within the triple world as utterly terrifying, they give rise to weary detachment and seek *nirvāṇa*, not daring to enter it again. This is precisely [the state of] sentient beings.

This is knowledge and vision. Now, he shows that this Sahā world is itself the Pure Land, in order to shatter the two-vehicle practitioners' mind of longing for the pleasant and loathing the unpleasant, or grasping and rejecting.
Next, as for the further transformations in each of the eight directions:

this is to lead the two-vehicle practitioners toward the Dharma-realm, desiring to cause them to abandon the provisional and follow the real, so that they do not give rise to a heart of retreat or cowardice upon reaching the treasure-place. Next, for...

Because all Buddhas shall come to sit [upon these thrones], the statement that each of the eight directions further transforms into two hundred *koṭis* of worlds and so forth serves to lead the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings (*upāya-śāsana*) into the ultimate wisdom of the Buddha.

While intending to exhaustively reach the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is for now merely a temporary accommodation for those of inferior understanding within the Three Vehicles, providing only a brief indication of a small portion; how could it possibly manifest the entirety of its whole?
How great is this function! Thus we know that the pure lands beyond transformation are inconceivable;
they are precisely the immeasurable and boundless merits of all Buddhas, and it is for this reason that the wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.

This is what was meant previously when it was said that the gateway of their wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; were it not for the Tathāgata’s skillful means of revelation and his vast, divine power...
By briefly illustrating this through the matter of Prabhūtaratna, it is clear that the gate of wisdom is ultimately difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
Furthermore, regarding the present transformation of the land and the gathering of the Buddhas, how could those of the Two Vehicles possibly know or comprehend it?
This is clearly what is meant by "manifesting the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Yet, as for the transformed lands, it is said that they are all covered with precious flowers.
He spread it upon the ground and clearly revealed this Buddha-knowledge and vision as the true cause for attaining Buddhahood.
At that time, from the east, Śākyamuni [and the other Buddhas] likewise dispatched messengers; the same was done by all the Buddhas.
This statement that the emanated Buddhas of the eastern direction have already assembled implies that they are assembling sequentially from all ten directions.
Beyond the Sahā world-system, two or three [emanations] each transform two hundred *koṭis* of Buddha-lands; thus, the eight directions together total four hundred *koṭis*.
Now that these are completely filled, the intention is to manifest that the Buddha-body pervades every atom and every land, being inexhaustible and boundless.
It is exhausted. As for the Buddhas, each sitting upon a lion throne beneath a jeweled tree, this refers to their constant dwelling upon this very Bodhisattva seat.
Each has dispatched an attendant to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha; those Buddhas have not yet seen him in person.
This is because the so-called Dharmakāya has no distinction of self and other, nor do they see one another.
As for each carrying a handful of precious flowers to offer to the Buddha, it reveals that this wondrous Dharma is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood.
The words of inquiry [regarding his health] demonstrate Śākyamuni’s intention to manifest in accordance with the common ailments of the people.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [proceeded] up to the stupa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha and Śākyamuni Buddha.
This Śākyamuni opened the stupa of Prabhūtaratna to manifest the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). The Buddha’s body is like space, having no basis;
because the stupa is in the void, and since the World-Honored One Śākyamuni wished to open the precious stupa, he likewise abided in the void.

This demonstrates the image of the Dharma-body being identical [to all]. By opening the door of the seven-jeweled stupa with his right finger, he shows that the self-nature unfolds without the exertion of external effort;
it is like removing the bolt and opening the gate of a great city.
The ignorance and deluded thoughts, solidified over kalpas, suddenly burst asunder, and the Dharma-body manifests instantaneously—what the Zen school calls "breaking through the ground."
With a single sound, the entire assembly beheld the whole body of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, undivided, as if he had entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

This demonstrates that when the self-nature of sentient beings is developed, the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the present body and mind suddenly reveal the entire reality of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
It is the manifestation of the state where the mind and its objects are realized as quiescent in their very place; it is for this reason that [the Buddha] has come to hear this sutra.
"Those who have arrived here" refers to those whose exposition of the wondrous Dharma profoundly accords with the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the Dharmakāya.
"The assembly rejoices and scatters flowers" signifies that each displays the image of the true cause.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, from within the jeweled stupa, [reached out] until all the great assembly was received into the void.

This act of Prabhūtaratna offering half his seat so that Śākyamuni might enter the stupa and sit together with him demonstrates that the Buddha is one who arises through the conditions of the five aggregates.
They are of the same substance as the Dharma-body; this is the manifestation of the non-duality of the True and the Responsive.

When the great assembly saw two Tathāgatas and wished for their Buddha-seats to be high and distant, all vowing to dwell in the void, it precisely revealed that the followers of the Two Vehicles had previously feared the long and distant nature of the Buddha-way.
Now that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision have been opened, they truly see that what was distant is not distant, and thus they all vow to draw near.

"Near" signifies the omen that the stage of Buddhahood is now foreseeable. As for the Buddha using his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to receive the assembly into the air, he manifests that those of the Two Vehicles could not have approached the Buddha’s wisdom without being guided by the skillful means of the Buddha’s supernatural power.
The merit of forty years of guidance has finally borne fruit this day; how could this be a minor circumstance?
With a great voice, he universally addressed the fourfold assembly (up to the point where it says): "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is entrusted to those who shall uphold it.
These words concern the matter of protection and entrustment. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the Dharma by which the Tathāgata protects and maintains beings.
One who is able to uphold this sūtra is a person who is protected and maintained by him. If there is anyone who upholds it, then this Dharma...
The entrustment has its locus. The original intent for which the Tathāgata appeared in the world was solely this one great matter;
thus, if the Dharma is entrusted, the great matter is complete. What is called "this one matter alone" means there is no other matter.
Therefore, it is said that he shall soon enter nirvana. It is just as when an elder, on the verge of death, finds his son.

"The family business has been entrusted; my aspirations are now fulfilled. Viewed from this perspective, the Buddhas and Patriarchs in their reception of people can lead one directly to the very side of the Dharma-body.
As for matters that transcend the Dharma-body, one should realize them before the Buddha appeared in the world or before the Patriarch came from the West;
one need not wait for the present.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Although the Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, has long since entered parinirvāṇa... [he now] speaks this vow before the Buddha himself."

These ten lines beginning with "This Holy Lord" eulogize the cause [of the assembly's gathering] through the encouragement of Prabhūtaratna; the intent is to find someone to whom the entrustment may be given.
The four lines beginning with "That Buddha" eulogize the original vow of Prabhūtaratna.

Furthermore, the twelve lines beginning with "And I" eulogize the arrival of the manifested Buddhas to bear witness to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, desiring that it endure for a long time. The four lines beginning with "To sit" eulogize the three transformations of the earth.
The Pure Land. Each of the Buddhas has eighteen lines [of verse] below, which complete the eulogy of their universal assembly and praise their beautiful appearance and pure, wondrous demeanor.
They are like lotuses in a clear pond; their radiance shines forth like torches at night; and their sublime fragrance perfumes everywhere.
When sentient beings come into contact with them, their hearts rejoice and their spirits are gladdened. It is like a great wind blowing against the branches of small trees;
they bend, sway, and prostrate themselves, unable to contain their joy. The majestic arrival of the Buddhas is thus, for the sake of causing the sublime Dharma to abide for a long time.
The fourteen phrases following "Addressing the great assembly" seek out those who can uphold the Dharma;
those capable of protecting and maintaining it should themselves make a vow that Many Treasures, myself, and all the manifested Buddhas shall act as witnesses.
The twenty phrases following "O sons of the Buddha" again seek those who can uphold and expound it; such persons shall be as if seeing me and making offerings to Many Treasures and all the others.

This is an emanation Buddha. The reason for requesting that one uphold the sutra again and again is that, since the Buddha’s knowledge and vision have already been revealed, the priority lies in being able to uphold it so as to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed.

If one regards this as ordinary, one will fail the great causal conditions of the Tathāgata on this day. Upholding the sutra necessarily requires making a vow, because the evil age is difficult to endure.

"Hold [this]. Desiring that the power of faith be made firm and solid, so that one does not encounter conditions that give rise to retreat or cowardice, the subsequent text enumerates its difficulties.
The eight phrases beginning with 'Good sons' cause one to reflect deeply that this sutra is difficult to uphold, unlike the ease of other sutras;
be careful not to treat it lightly. Therefore, it causes one to make a vow before upholding it. If [the text] continues...

The sixteen phrases beginning with "Mount Sumeru" describe the difficulty of expounding this sutra. If one were to grasp Mount Sumeru with the hand and move the great trichiliocosm with a finger, that would indeed be difficult;
yet those possessing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can achieve it. However, as for the various devas of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), their wisdom is difficult to surpass.
Even those whose wisdom and eloquence are superior can transcend them;
yet this sutra alone is the most difficult to preach in this degenerate age, for people are mostly corrupt, full of resentment, and difficult to inspire with faith. Suppose there were a person who...
It is said that writing it is difficult. Space is difficult to grasp.
Once Ānanda attained awakening in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, he perceived the space of the ten directions as if holding a leaf in his hand; in that case, even space could be grasped.
But as for this sutra—the path of quiescent extinction beyond words—how could it ever be written down? This is why writing it is so difficult. If one were to...
The first eight lines, beginning with "The great earth," are difficult to read. The great earth is most heavy; the Brahma Heaven is most high; a toenail is most minute.
To place the great earth upon a toenail and ascend to the Brahma Heaven is not difficult for one of vast supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Yet, it is not as difficult as reading this sutra in an evil age. The second eight lines, beginning with "Even if," concern the difficulty of upholding [the teaching]. Carrying dry grass... [into the fire].

To remain unburnt by the fires at the end of an eon is not yet considered difficult. To be able to uphold this sutra amidst the violent afflictions of sentient beings in a degenerate age—this is what is truly difficult.
If one can uphold the eighty thousand [dharmas] below, then listen to the difficulty:

the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma are merely elaborated through words and phrases; how could these be considered difficult? It is only the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of this single sutra that is immeasurable.
To be able to hear its meaning and intent is difficult. As for the twelve phrases beginning with "If a person preaches the Dharma," they present a challenge.
If someone skillfully preaches the Dharma such that all who hear it attain the six supernormal powers of an Arhat, this is not yet difficult.
To be able to uphold this sutra and thereby attain Bodhi—this alone is truly difficult. The eight phrases beginning with "I [have practiced] for the sake of the Buddha-way" [follow].

[This] phrase clarifies the reason for its difficulty. It states: "Since my own attainment of Buddhahood, from beginning to present, the various sūtras I have preached across immeasurable lands are indeed infinite in number.
Yet all were spoken according to the capacities of beings; only this sūtra explicitly reveals the One Vehicle and Buddha-nature.
Anyone who upholds it shall swiftly attain Bodhi; therefore, it is the foremost. If one can..."
To uphold this sutra is to fully uphold the body of the Buddha, ensuring that the life of wisdom is never severed;

yet, without great faculties and the power of firm endurance, it is truly difficult to uphold. The six lines beginning with "O sons of good family" cause the upholder to make a vow, solely to strengthen their power of aspiration.
The preceding section generally praises its difficulty to uphold.
This sutra is difficult to uphold; yet if one upholds it even for a moment, all devas and humans should make offerings to them.
This verse is difficult to uphold, but because one can uphold it, I and all the Buddhas rejoice and praise them.

However, upholding this sutra does not refer to paper, ink, or written characters. It requires that one transcend words to grasp the essential meaning, suddenly attaining accord with the Buddha-mind. This is...
To practice with courageous diligence is to encompass all myriad practices and to suddenly sever the afflictions;

therefore, through the observance of precepts and the dhūta austerities, one may suddenly attain the stage of Buddhahood without passing through many kalpas. This is why maintaining [the precepts] for even a brief moment yields such great benefit.
The eight lines beginning with "In future ages" follow upon the aforementioned great benefits; thus, it is because one can maintain them in this evil age that [this is so].
True sons of the Buddha who are able to understand its meaning shall become the eyes of the world, for they open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The four lines following "in times of fear" conclude that those who can preach this should be honored as if they were the Buddha himself. A question is asked:

Since the Many-Treasures Buddha has testified to the Dharma and the manifested Buddhas have all assembled, and the World-Honored One has no other teaching to give, why does he alone, through the hardship of his own mouth, urge [the assembly] to uphold the sutra?
"Why is it that you exhort them three, four, or even five times? He replied, "Because the delusion of sentient beings has been firmly established for a very long time.
Tracing back from this present age to the kalpa of the dust-motes of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, they have consistently remained deluded without awakening.
My Buddha-nature has already expended its efforts in teaching and transforming them through birth after birth over immeasurable and inconceivable kalpas."
It has been so for many ages, yet even until this day, it still requires forty years of skillful means and instruction.
How few are those who possess faith and understanding in its presence? Such is the rarity of encountering the Buddha-dharma.
Now that it has been revealed, if one does not maintain it with firm resolve, I fear that once lost, one will not know how many more kalpas will pass before it is encountered again.
In this kalpa of extinction, it is uncertain whether one can hear [this teaching] as one does today. If this Dharma is lost and no longer upheld, the lineage of the Buddhas will be severed;

how could this be a trivial matter? It is just like a wealthy elder who founded his enterprise with great difficulty, toiling through successive generations until he achieved wealth and established a family estate.
If there were no filial heir to maintain and preserve it, [the legacy would surely perish].
Once these are lost, they will be difficult to recover as they were before.

This is precisely the meaning behind the World-Honored One’s repeated and earnest exhortations to uphold [this teaching]. The preceding ten chapters collectively reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

thus, they are generally termed "Faith and Understanding" (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). Consequently, the subsequent chapters frequently speak of the merit of upholding the sutra, thereby manifesting awakening.
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision—once awakened, it is difficult to maintain them.

Regarding the twelfth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "Devadatta," the purpose of this chapter, together with the ten subsequent chapters, is collectively to realize the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is because of the three previous cycles [of teaching].
