"Revealing" means to open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Those of the two vehicles merely believe in this mind;

although their faith in the mind is true, they have not yet reached the subtlety of the objective realm. Therefore, the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa" directly reveals the subtlety of the realm, which is called "revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
What follows is called "awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," because although the śrāvakas believe in themselves—

Even if one visualizes the mind as the Buddha, there may still remain the ignorance accumulated over kalpas that has not yet been exhausted; the habitual tendencies of narrow and inferior views and knowledge from the past have not yet been forgotten.
Although this is called "faith and understanding," it still belongs to the realm of intellectual comprehension.

Therefore, one must employ various skillful practices to cultivate and transform the mind before the Dharma-body can attain purity. Furthermore, fearing that such individuals, when engaging with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, might not be adept in expedient means, [the teaching] is provided in advance.
Various methods of protection are demonstrated; through sublime conduct, one attains entry [into realization].

This ensures that one does not fall into ordinary worldly sentiments nor give rise to fear. This is precisely the vast compassion of the Tathāgata, which is what is meant by "providing medical prescriptions in advance.
Below, the practice and realization are universally revealed; each section corresponds to its respective passage. This constitutes the judgment of realization.
The reason he was designated by the name Devadatta at the beginning was to demonstrate that there are difficulties and ease in awakening, and that practice is fundamental.
Because the various śrāvakas had long harbored fear regarding the long duration of the Buddha-way, they did not give rise to even a single thought of joyful aspiration.
Although they have now received their predictions of enlightenment, it will still require the passage of many kalpas before they attain it.
Regarding the realization of the fruit: fearing that [beings] might be led by their past habitual tendencies to refuse diligent seeking, the World-Honored One himself cited his own former lives.
Although he was a king, he did not spare his own body or life in his quest for the sublime Dharma;

through such ascetic practices, he finally attained the realization of Bodhi on this day. This difficulty of awakening is thus an instance of gradual awakening. Furthermore, fearing those of inferior capacity...

Those of their class feared the difficulty and did not advance; therefore, [the Buddha] further recounted the matter of the seven-year-old dragon girl transformed by Mañjuśrī attaining Buddhahood, so as to demonstrate how easy it was.
Furthermore, the ocean is a place of drowning in birth and death; the dragon is the foremost of the three poisons;
and the woman is a vessel of female, perverse, and defiled impurity—these are the most difficult to transform. Yet, [she] offered the pearl...
"One will soon attain Buddhahood; how easy this is! This is sudden enlightenment. It is truly because one takes great wisdom as one's refuge.
The intention is that those who are ready for the teaching, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, should personally rely upon the most excellent spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)."

One can thereby preserve the ultimate state of wondrous awakening and never again fall into the stage of the two vehicles. Therefore, at the beginning of this awakening, the gradual and the sudden are established;
it is for this reason that this chapter follows.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas... [and so forth] ...to serve him with diligence so that he lacked for nothing.
This was the Buddha’s own account of the hardships of his diligent quest for the sublime Dharma in the past, intended to warn the practitioners of the two vehicles against their indolence.
To say that he sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* through immeasurable kalpas without weariness or fatigue refers to the quest for the Dharma.
His resolve was not formed in a single kalpa; how much less so when he constantly served as a king throughout many kalpas, diligently seeking [the Dharma].

Furthermore, he was no ordinary person. Moreover, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, he practiced external giving by offering elephants, horses, and the like, and internal giving by offering his head, eyes, and so forth.
To renounce his royal throne constitutes the giving of all things. Yet, there were those who preached the wondrous Dharma.
"I vow to serve as your messenger for the rest of my life. I shall humbly endure toil and suffering, reaching the height of self-forgetfulness.
At that time, there was a rishi who, responding to his request, spoke for him; this was the result of the power of his sincere devotion. Upon hearing this, the king immediately rejoiced.

He attended upon [the rishi], undertaking all manual labor without weariness, even using his own body as a bed and seat without ever growing weary, continuing thus for a long period of a thousand years.
Yet he did not decline; his provisions were always sufficient. How diligent, arduous, and long-lasting was this mind of his in seeking the Dharma!
Furthermore, let those of the two vehicles present here who have received predictions of their own enlightenment each reflect upon their own minds in seeking the Dharma.
"Has there ever been such sincerity as this? It is for this reason that I now bestow upon you the great treasure of the Dharma King;
it has come to you spontaneously without being sought. How could it be regarded with ordinary indifference?
This means that in the future, as you serve many Buddhas, you must surely embody such a spirit of mine; only then can you be called a person who upholds the Dharma. As it was said of old:
Having realized that maintaining [this realization] is difficult, if one does not practice with austerity and fortitude, how can the fruit of sainthood be attained?
Therefore, he first informed the awakened mind of this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I recall that in past kalpas, for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma... (up to) "therefore I now speak it for you.
The twenty-two lines beginning with "I recall in the past" collectively praise the World-Honored One’s diligent pursuit of the Dharma in former times.
Asita—translated here as "Incomparable"—was the Buddha’s original teacher in the past. If there were any [other] Dharma...
By comparison, [the Buddha] could not have caused seekers to forget their own bodies to reach this point.
The eight lines following "universally for all sentient beings" praise the difficulty of seeking the Dharma in the past and the ease of preaching it for the sake of the multitude now,
so as to cause the great assembly to know what is truly precious.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "At that time, the king... [and so on] ...all because of the good friend Devadatta.
This passage recounts how the Buddha’s former teacher, the rishi, was the present-day Devadatta; it clearly demonstrates that his ascetic hardships were the cause for his attainment of Buddhahood.
Devadatta means "Heavenly Heat" (Divyadatta); at the time of his birth, the hearts of both humans and devas were filled with heat.
Therefore, he was given this name. Furthermore, because his mother prayed to Heaven before giving birth to him, he is also called "Heaven-Conferred" (Devadatta).

He was the son of King Droṇodana and the younger cousin of the Buddha. However, his conduct has been contrary to the norm; for generations he has focused solely on harming the Buddha, and now it has become even more extreme.
He constantly concealed poison under his ten fingernails; when he prostrated himself to touch the Buddha’s feet, his feet were not harmed, yet his fingers fell off on their own.
Furthermore, he conspired with King Ajātaśatru, intending to kill the Buddha and become a new Buddha himself.

When the king unleashed five hundred intoxicated elephants to trample the Buddha, the Buddha pointed his finger and manifested a lion; the elephants were all struck with terror and submission. He also pushed down a massive boulder.

He attempted to crush the Buddha, but the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī-devatā) obstructed him. Fragments of the stone shattered and splintered; one small piece struck the Buddha’s foot, drawing blood. Because of this, he fell into hell.
The Buddha sent a messenger to inquire after his well-being. He replied, "While I am here, it is like the bliss of the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven.
The Buddha asked again, "When will you emerge from hell? He answered, "I shall wait until the World-Honored One himself enters hell."
Thus he finally brought them forth. Such are the types of those who commit the five heinous crimes; their harm has persisted for more than a single lifetime.
Now, you say that Devadatta was the very seer who formerly preached the wondrous Dharma, yet you also claim it was because of Devadatta as a "good friend" [that the Buddha attained enlightenment].
It was because of Devadatta as a spiritual friend that I have been able to fulfill the six pāramitās, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
That I have attained perfect enlightenment and am now able to extensively deliver sentient beings is entirely due to Devadatta.
Thus, the present fruit of Buddhahood of the Tathāgata today was accomplished through Devadatta; his kindness is so profound that it is beyond words. In truth, this is so.
All were harmed by resentment. That the World-Honored One esteemed them so highly allows us to know that the fruit of Buddhahood is difficult to achieve.
It is said that he sometimes manifested as an enemy, using the torment of resentment to strengthen their power of patience and ensure they did not retreat from their diligent practice;
were it not for this, how could they have reached this day? It is said that those icchantikas are not truly icchantikas. The world...
Regarding the question of who turns [the wheel] through intermittent liberation, the World-Honored One explained this as follows:

Because the preceding chapter spoke extensively of the difficulty of upholding the Dharma—due to the many enmities in an evil age—he wished for those of the Two Vehicles who have received their predictions to uphold this sutra in the future during such an evil age.
They should contemplate how the Tathāgata attained Bodhi despite the enmity and harm of Devadatta; only then...

If one can remain free from a heart of retreat or cowardice, then attaining the fruit of Buddhahood will be without difficulty. Therefore, one should first realize the importance of maintaining the initial resolve.
Only by taking the Buddha’s service of Deva as an exemplary model can the Dharma be made to endure for a long time.
The Buddha addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta has [attained] the arousal of the bodhicitta up to the stage of non-retrogression.
This was a prediction (vyākaraṇa) bestowed upon Devadatta; yet he is not listed among the [other] disciples because he was the World-Honored One’s original teacher.
Furthermore, he served as a whetstone to polish his practice, thereby strengthening the Tathāgata’s power of patience.
He attained Bodhi; thus he stands at the head of those who abide in awakening and serves as a model for upholding the sutras in this degenerate age.

As for the Buddha being named "Heavenly King" (Tianwang), it means that through the infliction of enmity and harm, he compelled the Buddha to exercise great forbearance until he reached the natural state, thereby attaining Great Sovereignty (Mahāvaśitā);
hence his resultant fruit is accordingly named. As for the land being named "Way of Heaven" (Tiandao), it means that since the time of the Buddhas, there has never been...

It is not achieved through the endurance of suffering; this is the natural law. He constantly preached the wondrous Dharma because, during his causal stage, he first taught the World-Honored One using the wondrous Dharma; therefore, in the state of fruition, he constantly preached it.

That sentient beings who hear the wondrous Dharma all attain the fruits of the Three Vehicles precisely demonstrates that while the Dharma is one, the capacities [of the recipients] differ. After the passing of the Tathāgata Deva-rāja Buddha...
That those who make offerings to the stūpas all attain the fruits of the Three Vehicles is likewise the result of what has been induced by their causal practices.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: ... (up to) ... if they are before the Buddha, they will be born through transformation upon a lotus flower.
This statement refers to those in the future who, upon hearing this chapter, will have faith and reverence without doubt; they shall never fall into the three miserable realms.

Even if they are born by transformation upon a lotus flower in the presence of a Buddha, it is because they have witnessed the difficulty of the World-Honored One’s quest for the Dharma and the power achieved through overcoming many enmities, thereby gaining the benefit of upholding the wondrous Dharma with diligence, firmness, and patience without retreating.
Therefore, they obtained such a supreme reward.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas who had followed the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna from the lower regions [were told] that they could return to their own lands.
This request by the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa for the Buddha Prabhūtaratna to return to his own land was made because the Dharma-assembly had been concluded.

It is not appropriate to remain for long. This indicates that although realization has been attained, the attachment to dharmas (dharmagrāha) has not yet been forgotten and still persists. You must surely return and cut off all traces;
only when both subject and object are forgotten will there be wondrous enlightenment. Even the word "enlightenment" (*wu*) spoken of in the Chan school must be spat out;
this is the sign of returning to the root and restoring the source. That Śākyamuni left it behind to await Mañjuśrī signifies this.

By taking the wondrous Dharma one has realized and fusing it into contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*), one dissolves attachment to phenomena; only then does one fully perfect the subtlety of upholding the Dharma.
Therefore, one must wait for Mañjuśrī before being able to meet him and discuss the wondrous Dharma.
At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower (until) they had exchanged greetings and withdrew to sit on one side.
This statement—that Mañjuśrī sat upon a precious lotus flower and emerged from the ocean—symbolizes that for one who has awakened the mind, it is like a lotus flower opening;
wondrous wisdom manifests before them, standing forth alone and prominent within the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*. Upon arriving at the place where the Buddha was...
The act of paying homage to the two honored feet symbolizes the convergence of initial awakening (shijue) with the wisdom of original awakening (benjue).
The mutual exchange of greetings at the abode of Zhiji represents the profound union of these two wisdoms. Without this, it would be impossible to speak of wondrous enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakoṭi asked Mañjuśrī: [up to] "the manner in which he taught and transformed beings in the ocean was such as this.

This question concerns the assembly transformed by Mañjuśrī. As for the statement that their number is immeasurable and incalculable, it refers to the great ocean of birth and death, the dwelling place of the three poisons;
one cannot enter it deeply without great wisdom, nor can one do so without the wondrous Dharma.
One is able to transform afflictions (*kleśa*) into sublime conduct. When delusion is forgotten through wisdom, then countless afflictions are pure in their very essence.
Therefore, countless bodhisattvas sit upon precious lotus flowers and proceed to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, dwelling in mid-air.
Once afflictions are transformed, all practices are the practice of a Buddha; thus, they all cultivate these practices.
This is the meaning of emptiness in the Mahāyāna. Therefore, Mañjuśrī said: "My work of teaching and transforming beings in the ocean was such as this.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa praised him with a verse:
"By means of great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, he transforms and delivers immeasurable multitudes (up to: causing them to quickly achieve Bodhi).
These verses of praise by Jñānākara for Mañjuśrī consist of eight lines. The first four lines mean that one who lacks great wisdom and heroic vigor cannot transform such a vast multitude.
The subsequent four lines mean that without the sublime Dharma, such rapid transformation would not be possible.
Mañjuśrī said: "In the midst of the ocean, I have always preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is Mañjuśrī’s repeated response to the preceding verse, stating that he has always preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and no other dharma.
The intent is to manifest the swiftness with which the *Saddharma* brings accomplishment; therefore, the following question concerns whether one can swiftly attain Buddhahood."
The person Zhijī asked Mañjuśrī, saying: "By practicing this sutra, will one quickly attain Buddhahood?
Zhijī asked Mañjuśrī again, saying: "The Sublime Dharma is extremely profound; can there be sentient beings who rely upon it to practice?"
"Will she quickly attain Buddhahood? This question is asked specifically to reveal that the efficacy of the Sublime Dharma is exceedingly swift.
Mañjuśrī replied: "...[until] one would not believe that this woman could attain perfect enlightenment in a mere moment."
This passage is a profound praise of the eight-year-old dragon girl’s sharp faculties. It shows that by practicing according to this sublime Dharma, she was able to attain Bodhi immediately;

such is her nature. That one born of a different species within the ocean, defiled by the three poisons, and possessing a soft and weak female body, could yet possess such supreme and wondrous virtues, truly reveals the impurity of the afflictions of birth and death.
This essence is fundamentally the wisdom-function of attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that one can reach Bodhi.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that one attains non-retrogression upon the initial aspiration in a single *kṣaṇa*, this refers to the power of a single thought-moment’s transformative capacity.
This is indeed difficult for ordinary minds to believe, which is why Prajñākūṭa gave rise to doubt: Śākyamuni attained Bodhi only after cultivating causes over many kalpas.
Why did the dragon girl attain perfect enlightenment in an instant?
It is because those who grasp the essential meaning are equal to all Buddhas in a single kṣaṇa, whereas those who lose the gateway labor in vain through cultivation over kalpas of vast duration.
This clearly demonstrates that the supreme power of the wondrous Dharma cannot be measured by feelings of temporal brevity or length, nor by distinctions between purity and defilement.
Before his speech had concluded, the Dragon King’s Daughter suddenly appeared before him and praised him with these verses:
"Thoroughly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit... [I] propagate the Mahāyāna teaching to deliver suffering sentient beings."
This dragon girl’s manifest realization serves to eliminate the attachment to narrow, inferior, and stagnant characteristics.
To cling to Śākyamuni’s long period of cultivation while viewing the dragon girl as stained by sin is to fail to reach the emptiness of the nature of both sin and merit.

Only when the great wisdom of Mañjuśrī shines universally does one realize that there are no differing characteristics, that all is of a single limit and equality—how, then, could there be any question of slowness or speed? I...
He expounds the Mahāyāna teachings to deliver suffering sentient beings; his intention lies solely in upholding the wondrous Dharma to save all beings.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the dragon girl: “...how can a female body so swiftly attain Buddhahood?”
This passage shows that Śāriputra has given rise to doubt; it precisely demonstrates the view of those of the Two Vehicles who cling to signs.
As Śāriputra perceives it, the female body is subject to the five obstacles and is utterly devoid of the potential for attaining Buddhahood.

This is a notion commonly held by ordinary people because they fail to realize that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty, and thus entirely devoid of the characteristics of male or female, pure or impure. One who understands this can enter into equality.
This is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
At that time, the dragon girl possessed a precious jewel [and] preached the sublime Dharma to all sentient beings.
This dragon girl personally demonstrates the swiftness of her attainment of Buddhahood. That which dragons hold most dear is the jewel; now this dragon...

The fact that the maiden attains Buddhahood in the very moment she offers the pearl signifies that when one can suddenly sever attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), the Buddha-nature manifests before one.

This means that clarity is received within the mind itself, without depending on external factors. The sudden transformation of the dragon girl into a male signifies that the Buddha-nature is not subject to the impermanence of gender;
it is understood to be devoid of the characteristics of male or female. This precisely refutes the attachment to signs held by those of the Two Vehicles.

Regarding this adherence: one immediately proceeds to the South. "South" signifies clarity and correctness; it represents the departure from the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), whereby the nature of the treasury suddenly manifests and the Buddha-body appears before one.
One thus proceeds to the Immaculate World (*Vimala-loka*) in the South, where, seated upon a precious lotus flower, one attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because awakening was attained through the Wondrous Dharma, one universally expounds the Wondrous [Dharma] for the sake of all sentient beings.
Because the Dharma caused Śāriputra to give rise to doubt, the Dragon Girl immediately transformed herself into a man and attained Buddhahood on the spot.
This was intended to stimulate the Two Vehicles; it truly means that each and every "great man" is not equal to a single weak woman.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the entire assembly of the Sahā world accepted this with silent faith;
thus did this dharma assembly receive its benefit. As for the sixfold earthquake of the Vimala world, it signifies the transformation of defilement into purity.

This is the sudden realization of the manifestation of Mind-Only. That the sentient beings of this Sahā world dwell in the stage of non-retrogression and receive their prediction of enlightenment is due to the inspiration provided by the Dragon Girl, whereby they obtain supreme benefit. The doubts of Prajñākūṭa, Śāriputra, and the great assembly are suddenly dispelled;
thus, they accept it in silent faith. By means of this chapter, it is shown that one’s resolve should be as firm as that of Śākyamuni.

Through such diligent application, he naturally feels no weariness or fatigue; knowing that the dragon girl can swiftly realize Bodhi, he naturally feels no fear that the path to Buddhahood is long and distant.
This is how the World-Honored One uses these skillful means to instruct bodhisattvas.
The Thirteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Chapter on Upholding.

Regarding the purpose of this chapter's inclusion: although those who were the primary recipients of the teaching have attained understanding and received their predictions of future Buddhahood after passing through many kalpas, the World-Honored One fears that the narrow and inferior habitual tendencies of the Śrāvaka vehicle have not yet been eliminated, and that they might again give rise to thoughts that the path to Buddhahood is too long.
To dispel their fear, he then recounted the hardships of his own past quest for the Dharma to alleviate their weariness;
furthermore, he related the story of the dragon girl’s imminent attainment of Buddhahood to inspire in them a vow of joyful aspiration. Therefore, the "Chapter on Encouragement" follows next;
for this sutra is the life-intelligence of all Buddhas and the Buddha-nature that serves as the direct cause for sentient beings.

"If, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, people become increasingly depraved and evil, it will be most difficult to uphold [this teaching]. Should its upholding be lost, the lineage of the Buddha would be severed;
this is the Lord's hidden anxiety. Therefore, the various bodhisattvas silently grasped the Buddha's intention and comforted the World-Honored One, saying, "Please do not have such concerns.
We each vow to uphold it and shall extensively expound this sutra, not sparing even our bodies or lives."
Furthermore, the five hundred disciples, both those still in training and those beyond training, also grasped the Buddha’s intention;

each of them likewise vowed to propagate this sutra extensively in other lands, because they judged themselves incapable of transforming and delivering the people of the Sahā world due to their prevalence of arrogance.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt and the other bhikṣuṇīs, having previously observed for themselves—

"The female body is beset by many obstacles; one dares not hope for the fruit of Buddhahood. Now, seeing how easily this dragon girl has attained Buddhahood, I also have confidence that I too am destined for Buddhahood.
Therefore, I request the World-Honored One to grant me a special prediction of enlightenment.
Consequently, I vow to propagate this sutra widely in other lands, thereby manifesting my resolve for non-retrogression. At that time, the World-Honored One then looked upon the eight [bodhisattvas].
As for the ten billion nayutas of bodhisattvas who remained silent, their intention was this:
although the śrāvakas wished to uphold the sutra, they had not yet practiced the conduct of benefiting sentient beings within the secular world, nor did they know the methods for avoiding harm.

Their power of the Dharma was insufficient, and they feared encountering obstacles that would prevent the conditions for the Dharma from becoming widespread; thus, they desired for the bodhisattvas to provide them with protection and care.
Therefore, all the bodhisattvas silently understood the Buddha’s intention and together made this vow:

"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, we shall travel back and forth throughout the worlds of the ten directions, upholding this sutra solely through the practice of patience. Yet this shall not be by our own power;
it shall be through the Tathāgata’s spiritual power that we are protected. This was intended to guide those of initial resolve and thus to comfort them.

The Tathāgata’s vow is that you need have no such concern. However, regarding this chapter on "Holding the Name," "holding" (chí) carries the sense of guarding what one possesses so as not to lose it—much like the worldly saying that "guarding one's ancestral occupation is difficult.
It is, for example, like a wealthy elder who entrusts his entire household estate to his son; should he fail to guard it even once, the ancestral lineage will be severed.
How could this be a trivial matter? Therefore, the text of this chapter speaks solely of the practice of upholding the sutra in order to clarify the difficulty of awakening to and maintaining it;
hence, this chapter follows.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja (up to the point where he speaks of those with minds clouded by anger, crookedness, and insincerity).

Because the World-Honored One had previously spoken most emphatically of how difficult it is to uphold this sutra, and had repeatedly and earnestly exhorted him, asking, "Who can protect and uphold this sutra?", Bhaiṣajyarāja himself declared his vow;
thus, out of a joyful desire to speak, he made a vow to receive and uphold it.
This is because Bhaiṣajyarāja had forgotten his own body and relinquished all attachments, possessing the joy of eloquence and the analytical power of speech;
that is to say, it is only through an untiring mind that one can uphold [this sutra]. Therefore, at the head of the assembly, he made this vow.

As for what the World-Honored One feared regarding those in the末法 (mofa) age who would find it difficult to uphold this sutra—namely, that many people would be corrupt and evil—Bhaiṣajyarāja vowed to uphold it. First, he describes these corrupt and evil people:

Because their roots of goodness have become so diminished, they are difficult to transform and teach. If one wishes to uphold this sutra, one must arouse the power of great forbearance and not begrudge even body or life.

This correctly summarizes the preceding instructions of the Tathāgata regarding entering the Tathāgata’s chamber and so forth, as well as the diligent hardships endured by the rishis who served him in seeking the Dharma.
Only through such means can it be upheld. Thus, the two Great Beings [exerted themselves] to inspire others.
To encourage those of the two vehicles, he inspired them to make vows to uphold this sutra; thus, five hundred arhats simultaneously resolved to uphold it.
Yet, they ultimately did not dare to travel through the Sahā world, intending instead to widely proclaim this sutra in other lands.
This clearly shows that the narrow and inferior minds of the Hīnayāna could not be abandoned all at once.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt... [up to] ...spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One, Guide who brings peace to devas and humans; having heard this prediction, our minds are fully satisfied."
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, [they] widely proclaimed this sutra in other lands.
This aunt of the Buddha made a rare prediction; she, too, joined the assembly in generating the resolve to uphold this sutra.
The Buddha was constantly followed by six thousand women, all of whom were beginners. The Buddha’s aunt was their leader. Previously, because of these women...
Her body was heavily obstructed and she lacked entirely the potential to attain Buddhahood.
Now, seeing that the Dragon Girl had attained Buddhahood, she too gained self-confidence in her own ability to become a Buddha and thus hoped for a prediction of her enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

Yet, not daring to request it directly, she gazed at the Tathāgata with a sorrowful expression; her heart of longing and thirst was indeed most acute. Therefore, the Tathāgata called her by name and addressed her, saying:
"The reason you look upon the Tathāgata with such a sorrowful countenance is surely because you think that I have not mentioned your name when bestowing the prediction of enlightenment.
However, I have already previously declared in general that all twelve hundred śrāvakas shall likewise become buddhas.
If you now wish to know your specific prediction, you and six thousand bhikṣuṇīs shall serve sixty thousand [buddhas]."

Two thousand billion Buddhas all acted as Dharma masters for him. Through these causes and conditions of preaching the Dharma, he gradually fulfilled the path of a Bodhisattva and was destined to become a Buddha named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (All Living Beings Who Delight to Behold).

Because he delighted each and every being by opening his mind through the preaching of the Dharma, he attained a fruit that accorded with this quality, and thus received such a name. These six thousand people, in succession, were entrusted [with the teaching].
[The Buddha] gave a prediction. Now, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, also longed for a prediction;
therefore, the World-Honored One also specially granted her a prediction, saying to her: "In a future age, you shall also serve many Buddhas and become a great Dharma-preacher.
Gradually perfecting the path to Buddhahood, you will in the future attain enlightenment under the name *Kāñcanaprabhāsottama* (Thousand Million Radiant Marks). This was due to [her past] causes.
In her previous life as the wife of a Buddha, she was able to remain unattached to deluded love and assisted in perfecting the ten thousand virtues of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, she preached the Dharma, being able to open the fundamental nature of sentient beings; thus, it is fitting that her resultant name be "Ten Million Radiant Marks.
Having both received their predictions, they also vowed to uphold this sutra; however, while they would widely proclaim it in other lands, they ultimately felt apprehensive about the Sahā world.
This is because the power of the Dharma of those who have newly begun their practice has not yet been fully realized.
At that time, the World-Honored One looked upon eight hundred trillion [beings] (up to... and saw from afar, in other directions, those who were providing protection.
When the World-Honored One gazed upon these eighty trillion nayutas of bodhisattvas, although he did not speak with his mouth, his intention was this:
that the followers of the two vehicles are weak and inferior, and thus unable to widely proclaim this sutra in this world;
he desired that these bodhisattvas protect and uphold it during the final age. This is what is meant by "the entrustment has a specific recipient. For all these bodhisattvas...
Abiding in non-retrogression, they have attained the gate of *dhāraṇī*. It is because these multitudes gathered from the ten directions are capable of bearing this burden.

These bodhisattvas have already realized the Buddha-mind; therefore, out of reverent compliance with the Buddha’s intention and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, they uttered the lion’s roar before the Buddha, making a vow in unison, each aspiring toward the Tathāgata.
After my parinirvāṇa, you shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions to protect and uphold this sutra;
it shall not be limited to this single land of Sahā alone. Previously, when the World-Honored One asked, "Who can protect and uphold this sutra? [the Bodhisattva] made a vow of his own accord.

Therefore, these bodhisattvas profoundly grasp the Buddha’s intention. Furthermore, they pray that the World-Honored One may behold and protect them from afar in other lands, for in this degenerate age the Dharma is difficult to uphold and must rely upon the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power.
Immediately, all the bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison and spoke these verses:
"We pray that you do not harbor concerns regarding the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa... (until) the Buddha himself knows our hearts."

At this assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa today, that which is most pleasing to the World-Honored One is that all those of the three vehicles have accorded with the Buddha’s mind and each has been granted a prediction of enlightenment.
What He concerns Himself with, however, is that in an evil age this sutra will be difficult to uphold;
and most difficult of all to find is a person of firm endurance and great power who can maintain it. This is the World-Honored One’s hidden anxiety, for He fears—
This is because the lineage of that Buddha has been severed. None of those śrāvakas who have received their predictions can stop it;

therefore, they gaze silently at the bodhisattvas who have gathered like clouds. Thus, these bodhisattvas, out of reverence and compliance with the Buddha’s intention, vow to uphold [the Dharma] extensively.
Therefore, the first four lines of the verse express this reverence and compliance with the Buddha’s intention, vowing to uphold it in the evil age. Below this...

The preceding passage speaks of enduring various hardships to demonstrate the reasons why [the precepts] are difficult to maintain. The four lines beginning with "There are those who lack wisdom" refer generally to base and evil persons;

these are all later classes of demons among those who have left the household life. The single verse concerning bhikṣus in an evil age refers generally to the false pride of those who have left the household life.
The eight lines beginning with "Or there may be forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka)" speak of those who merely bear the name [of practitioners].

Regarding the demonic class among practitioners: those in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages), which are called "places of tranquility," falsely claim to be practitioners while taking the false as true, becoming arrogantly self-important as if they were Arhats possessing the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

The twelve lines beginning with "this person harbors an evil mind" are verses praising the endurance of an evil mind; they describe the state of one who destroys the Dharma, fabricates sutras, and greedily seeks profit.

To nurture [such views] and to slander the virtuous and good is the true lineage of Māra. The fourteen phrases beginning with "Constantly amidst the great assembly" eulogize the practice of enduring slander and the destruction of the Dharma.
These various forms of false pride are the most difficult to endure; one must endure them all.
The twelve lines from "In the turbid kalpa of the evil world" onwards praise the endurance of evil matters.

It states that because of being possessed by evil spirits who harass and harm them, or because of being subjected to insults and humiliation, they endure these various hardships out of reverent faith in the Buddha;
they do not even cherish their own bodies or lives, much less tolerate injury or invasion. It says that they value only the unsurpassed path.
That which is most valued is the Buddha-lineage and the life of wisdom; all else is not worth considering, for it is the upholding of the Dharma entrusted by the Buddha that is paramount.

The World-Honored One himself should know the following ten phrases, which praise the matter of enduring being expelled from the assembly—namely, that the monks of the degenerate age do not understand that the sūtras thus proclaimed were taught by the Buddha according to his expedient means.
"Thinking that what has been taught was created by us ourselves, they revile us with harsh words or frown in hatred;
they even go so far as to expel us and refuse to allow us to dwell in the stūpas and monasteries. The World-Honored One himself should know such people."
Reflecting upon the Buddha’s instructions and entrustment to us, we must all endure these various evils.
How difficult it is to propagate the Buddha-dharma! If laypeople were to give rise to slander, there might still be grounds for excusing them;
yet now, those who are themselves disciples of the Buddha are destroying it. If the disciples do not believe, who else will? It is, for example, like this:
The worm within the lion’s body devours the flesh of the lion’s own body; even the Buddha can do nothing about it.
The World-Honored One’s concern is precisely as it is today. Were it not for the firm maintenance of the power of patience (*kṣānti-bala*), how could one endure such resentment and harm?
The eight lines beginning with "In various villages and cities" are verses praising the propagation [of the Dharma] everywhere wherever there are [beings]. All that...
"Regarding those who seek [the Dharma], I shall go to each of their places in person and expound the teachings entrusted by the Buddha.
Because I am sent by the World-Honored One and rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I do not fear hardships; I shall explain them well one by one.
May the Buddha remain at peace and not worry. As for the seed of the Buddha-nature of the One Vehicle, its revelation lies with the Buddha, while its realization and entry..."

It depends upon conditions. Therefore, for a practitioner, if one does not possess a will that is firm and unyielding, by what means could one attain thorough awakening and reach the stage of personally realizing the ultimate reality?
Thus, one must rely on the guidance and protection of a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) to enable gradual progress toward profound realization.
This is why the World-Honored One today entrusts the protection and maintenance of this sutra; it concerns the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu).

Furthermore, if one merely recites the words and phrases, what difficulty could there be? In the four lines following "I [shall do so] before the World-Honored One," I compose this verse to summarize the essential meaning.
As the previous passage on the jeweled stupa stated: "After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to protect, uphold, read, and recite this sutra?

Now, in the presence of the Buddha, I personally utter this vow; therefore, this is the summary of the essential meaning. For this reason, I request the World-Honored One to summon the Many-Treasures [Buddha].
And the Buddhas who have manifested their own bodies act as witnesses together.
*The Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Four;
*The Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Five.
The Chapter on the Peaceful Practices, the Fourteenth, from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva under imperial decree during the Yao Qin dynasty;
expounded by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Nanyue.
The purpose of this chapter is as follows: In the "Treasure Stūpa" chapter, the Tathāgata specifically sought those who would uphold this sutra.
Although the assembly who had initially received their predictions followed the Buddha’s command, they feared that the people of this Sahā world were mostly corrupt and evil;

thus, none dared to cast themselves into it, preferring instead to travel to other lands to propagate the teaching. However, Bhaiṣajyarāja, delighting in eloquence and wishing to respect the Buddha’s intent, vowed—

One sustains this through the power of patience. Although one may be able to practice this, enduring insults with great forceful patience is not something achievable by those at the beginning of their path, nor is it a sustainable long-term strategy.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī specifically requested the method for upholding this sutra during the final age.
Because one must awaken to and maintain the Dharma through instruction, the Buddha taught the four modes of peaceful practice (*catur-āśvāsa-carita*).

The underlying intent is that the various hardships of this degenerate age are summoned by oneself; if one knows how to dwell within them, then naturally all hardships will be distanced and will no longer be regarded as afflictions.
Only when these four practices are fully perfected does one attain the power of awakening and maintenance, whereby one can finally fulfill the upholding of the sutra.
It is marvelous. Therefore, the simile of the crest-jewel is taught to manifest the foremost merit; thus this chapter follows.

These four lines alone were previously explained through the four dharmas of the sphere of practice (*caryā-viṣaya*), the sphere of proximity (*upaniṣad*), the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), and the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*).
Although the meaning was applicable, it was not convenient to reconcile them directly with the text. The ancient commentary [interprets] right body, right speech, and right...
The four dharmas of the mind of great compassion have very clear textual divisions; therefore, I now follow them.
However, these four dharmas take the precepts of nature (*prakṛti-śīla*) as primary, much like the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which enters [the path] by taking the restraint of the mind as the precept.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, [from "how can one preach this sutra in the evil world of the future"]— this passage describes how Mañjuśrī,
following the lead of the aforementioned Bodhisattvas such as Bhaiṣajyarāja and Rativarṇa,

who out of reverence for the Buddha’s intent had made vows to uphold the sutra in future ages, specifically inquired on behalf of newly initiated Bodhisattvas regarding the method for upholding the sutra, desiring [to hear it].
He causes these [beings] each to possess methods for warding off harm, so that they do not fear calamitous or difficult matters.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “[Up to: When one wishes to expound this sutra, one should abide securely in four dharmas.”
In response to Mañjuśrī’s request, the World-Honored One subsequently taught the four modes of peaceful conduct (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*).

By practicing these to propagate the sutra, one may remain far removed from all calamities and hardships. These four modes of conduct are: rectitude of body, rectitude of speech, rectitude of mind, and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Now, when a bodhisattva engages with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, there is nothing that exceeds the two practices of benefiting oneself and benefiting others; thus, the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] must be upright. Self-...
The essence of benefit is the single practice of great compassion; this is the merit of benefiting others. If the three karmas are not upright, it becomes the source of future calamities;
if there is no heart of mercy, it becomes the cause of inflicting harm. How, then, can one engage with the secular world?
This is the sublime model for the Tathāgata’s instruction on safeguarding the household legacy. Of the two practices, wisdom is the foundation.
As the precursor, Mañjuśrī specifically requested [this teaching]:
"First, abiding in the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva... this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

This is a specific explanation of the four dharmas, beginning with the correct practice of the body. In the preceding "Chapter on the Dharma Master," regarding the method for upholding this sutra, it says:
"Enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat. The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion;
the Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of patience; and the Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all phenomena.
This refers to the ultimate degree of intimacy and compliance. Now, these four dharmas provide a detailed explanation of the preceding meaning.

However, regarding the "place of practice" (*caryā*) and the "place of proximity" (*upaniṣad*), there are two types of practice: those pertaining to phenomena (*dharma*) and those pertaining to principle (*artha*).

Yet, patience (*kṣānti*) must be regarded as primary; this is what is meant by "donning the robe of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the opening statement of the "place of practice"—that one "dwells on the ground of patience"—refers to ultimate quiescence.
This is the ground [of patience]. Patience consists of the patience toward arising, the patience toward non-arising, and the patience toward cessation.

Regarding the patience toward arising: it refers to enduring abuse through sheer force while one has not yet forgotten the self. If I do not forget myself, how can I possibly dispel their violence? Regarding the patience toward non-arising:
it refers to when adversities and injustices come, observing that the mind is fundamentally unarisen. Thus, even though they may inflict evil upon me, [I remain unmoved].
Yet one’s own mind does not arise and is not moved by anything. Although this state of non-movement is peaceful, one has not yet forgotten external objects;
therefore, it is advised that one should not associate with them, in order to prevent unwholesome thoughts and habitual tendencies, thereby entering well into the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

As for "patience regarding cessation" (*śānti-kṣānti*), it means observing that the bodies and minds of oneself and others are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning. When there is quiescence, both mind and object are forgotten.
Being entirely free from opposition, one perceives no signs of insult or humiliation whatsoever. Thus, one is able to be gentle, harmonious, and compliant rather than impulsive or violent;
the mind remains undisturbed. This is what is called the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), and it is entering the chamber of the Tathāgata.
Because that has already been stilled and extinguished, there is no one who destroys, nor is there anyone who receives; even the characteristic of patience does not exist. Therefore it is said:
"Furthermore, one does not engage in any activity regarding dharmas. If there were engagement, then self and other would not have been forgotten, and it would not be the stage of stillness.
Thus, one does not see any engagement because one contemplates dharmas according to their true mark—that is, by taking their very substance as the object.
Quiescent extinction is originally suchness; therefore, one does not perceive any patience that can be practiced, nor does one discriminate the insults that are endured.
This is equality and non-duality, wherein both subject and object are forgotten. The sphere of mental activity ceases;
this is what is called "taking the emptiness of dharmas as one's seat. It is the subtle perfection of principle and practice. This is the place of practice.
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s place of association? This refers to the first place of association.

This statement that the first place of association takes precepts and meditative concentration as its foundation means that one must exclusively observe the precepts and not associate with those who are unfit for association, fearing that they might lead one into evil habits and greatly obstruct right practice.
This is precisely what is meant by the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding entering the state of non-outflow through the three gradual stages.

This is the intent of patience toward living beings (*satva-kṣānti*). One does not associate with kings and the like to prevent the habit of being defiled by wealth, honor, and arrogance, which obstructs right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
One does not associate with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to prevent the habit of wrong views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), which obstructs right view (*samyak-dṛṣṭi*).
O Brahmin, the *pravrajita* (renunciant) who holds wrong views refers to such people; the *nirgrantha-putra* (Jain) who holds wrong views refers to those who remain at home. Thus it is said.
One does not associate with worldly literary compositions, for they consist of false speech, frivolous talk, and miscellaneous discourses that obstruct right reflection (*samyak-cintā*).
Regarding *lōkāyata*: it refers to the teacher refuting the evil arguments of the disciple, and the disciple refuting the evil arguments of the teacher;
one does not associate with such, as it is said to obstruct right knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*). One does not associate with those who are violent and dangerous.
"Boxing, wrestling, and the like" refers to the habit of preventing inverted distraction. "Nārāyaṇa" means "Power.
"Caṇḍāla" means "Fierce Banner"; this refers to adorning oneself with evil as if it were a banner, which obstructs the practice of tranquility.
"Rearing pigs, sheep, and so forth" refers to the unwholesome vows (*akuśala-saṃvara*), which prevent the habits of killing and stealing. As for "those who come":
Then he preaches the Dharma for them to eliminate evil thoughts; this is what is called the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
As for not associating with those who seek the state of a *śrāvaka* and so forth, it is to prevent the habit of the narrow and inferior vehicle of the *Hīnayāna*. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"One should abandon the heterodox views and discursive arguments of the *Hīnayāna*, and instead draw near to the most excellent spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). This refers to not even inquiring after their well-being, up to and including [avoiding]...
Dwelling together serves to prevent the habit of gradual defilement. When others arrive, one preaches the Dharma for them, transforming their narrow habits so that they may enter the Great Way;
this is what is meant by "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber. Not associating with women and the like is to prevent the habit of lust.
Not approaching those who are neither male nor female is because such persons are said not to be vessels for the Dharma; it is to prevent vulgar, lewd, and deviant conduct.
This is a matter of training. One should not enter the homes of others alone, for one must guard against the suspicion of improper intimacy and the fear of losing right mindfulness.

When preaching the Dharma to women, one should not smile with bared teeth; even for the sake of the Dharma, one should not become overly familiar, guarding against the arousal of lustful impulses that would destroy the mind of precepts.
Regarding not keeping young disciples and the like, it is because one fears they might obstruct the practice of the "Dharmas of Peaceful and Joyful Conduct."

Observe this proximate stage: it is precisely the category of the fundamental precepts. That is to say, to restrain the body so as not to act, and to restrain the mind so that [afflictions] do not arise.
The three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices are all contained within these.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "From the precepts arises concentration; from concentration, wisdom is developed. To constantly delight in sitting meditation means that concentration is established upon the precepts. This is called the first [stage].
The first locus of intimacy still pertains to the practice of deeds.
Furthermore, from "the bodhisattva mahāsattva" up to [the end], this is called the second locus of intimacy of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
This is the second stage of close proximity (*upaniṣad*). It takes contemplative observation as its essence.

Previously, by not associating with those of evil discipline (*duḥśīla*) and deeply guarding against defiled habits, one maintains a mind that does not give rise [to afflictions]; this is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This contemplation that all phenomena are empty is the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*). This is precisely what is meant by "taking the emptiness of all phenomena as one's seat. That is to say, one should contemplate all phenomena as follows:

The essence is empty and quiescent; it is called the mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). One thoroughly realizes that not a single dharma can be apprehended, nor does one perceive any marks of inversion, movement, arising and ceasing, or agitation.
Because one contemplates that all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning, they are neither born nor extinguished.
Since they are thoroughly devoid of movement and their very substance is suchness (*tathatā*), the mind and its objects are like space, fundamentally non-existent.
If the mind and its objects are quiescent, then all things are quiescent. Therefore, the path of language is cut off.

In this state, there is no one who destroys the self, nor is there any recipient. Because it is absolute and without counterpart, it lacks the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;
thus it is said to be "nameless and signless. Since everything is non-existent, the pathways of mind and speech are severed; therefore, it is immeasurable and boundless.

The "boundaries" are without obstruction or hindrance. By contemplating that although all phenomena are quiescent, they are not annihilated, one sees that they exist merely through the provisional conjunction of causes and conditions.
All things arise from inverted deluded thoughts; thus, there are only words and speech.
This is the state of settling the mind in quiescence—what is called abiding on the ground of patience. Therefore, it is said: "Constantly."

To contemplate the characteristics of dharmas in this manner is called the second station of intimacy. In this degenerate age, upholding this sutra and practicing its sublime conduct cannot transcend this.
Although it speaks of "rectifying the body," in reality, it means the three karmas are tranquil;
encompassing all myriad practices and engaging with the secular world to benefit sentient beings, nothing surpasses this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If there are bodhisattvas in the evil world of the future... (up to)... by means of these two bases, they will be able to preach with peace and joy."
If there is a bodhisattva who is able to comfortably explain even as few as sixty lines, this encompasses both the *caryā-viṣaya* (sphere of conduct) and the *upaniṣad* (proximate cause).

The first six lines provide a general heading. The subsequent six lines, beginning with "Always avoid kings," eulogize the four matters of not associating with kings, violent games, evil disciplines, or non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, the twenty lines beginning with "Nor should one associate closely" eulogize [the avoidance of further improper associations].
"Seeking the Lesser Vehicle," etc., refers to the four lines beginning with "widow. These verses praise not associating with women or eunuchs.

Furthermore, "Nor should one draw near," etc., consists of twelve lines; these verses praise abstaining from the three matters of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. "Do not [be] alone," etc., consists of eight lines.
The verse states that one should not preach the Dharma to women; when going for alms, one should be accompanied by another bhikṣu—namely, a senior ācārya—to prevent errors and omissions.
Ānanda lacked this safeguard, and thus he fell into error. "Single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha" refers to the purity of mind.
These four lines below summarize the practices and conduct of these two instances.
Furthermore, one does not practice the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas (up to the point where) one is able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in future lives.
Furthermore, one does not practice the following thirty-two phrases. These collectively praise the practice of the two points.

The first ten phrases praise the state of having no practice regarding dharmas and so forth; that is to say, the mind is stilled and quiescent, and no conceptual discrimination arises. It is said that [these] cannot be attained.

Regarding "all phenomena" (*dharmas*): it means that there is not a single phenomenon that can be grasped by the mind. Therefore, if one does not know or see them, this verse describes the practice of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The twenty-two lines following "all phenomena" describe the practice of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The lines beginning with "empty and non-existent," etc., describe the contemplation of all phenomena as empty, non-existent, and possessing their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), expressed through the mind and speech.
The path is cut off; therefore, his mind dwells securely and is unmoving. "Observing all [dharmas]" and below is a verse praising the meaning of observing that all dharmas are like empty space.
Because all dharmas are like space, they eternally abide in a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

The six lines beginning with "If there is a bhikṣu" and below conclude the verse on these two points, explaining the aforementioned ability to teach with ease and security, because the mind is free from cowardice.
It is pleasing to the ear. The twelve phrases following "At times, the Bodhisattva" eulogize the reason why there is no timidity or weakness.

That is to say, when the Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and contemplates phenomena according to their meaning, it is called "investigating according to principle" (*yoniśaḥ-pravicaya*); thus he attains the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Because he preaches the sutras after arising from meditative concentration, his mind is at ease and free from fear.
The five lines following "Mañjuśrī" conclude the verse on the practice of maintaining a correct physical posture.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, from the time after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa until he provides explanations so that [beings] may attain all-knowledge—this is the practice of right speech.
As for abiding in the practice of peace and bliss, it consists of the two aforementioned states, observing them according to reality.
With a mind free from conceptual discrimination, one then speaks in accordance with the truth; thus, there is no fault of speech.

One does not speak of the faults of the sūtras, for having realized the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmas*), one knows them to be what the Buddha taught according to the needs of beings; therefore, one does not say that those teachings have any fault.
"Faults" refers to such things as biased emptiness or the wisdom of a lame donkey. One does not disparage other teachers, for there is no person...
Because they possess the mark of selfhood (*ātman*), they do not speak of others' faults. Regarding śrāvakas, they do not mention names when speaking of their errors;
observing according to reality (*yathābhūta*), they do not perceive any faults in others. They do not praise by mentioning names, fearing that those who are not praised might harbor resentment.
They give rise to no thoughts of enmity or aversion, for they do not see anyone who would disparage them.
Furthermore, whenever anyone asks questions, one answers solely with the Mahāyāna Dharma so that they may attain the knowledge of all modes;
this is the mind of great compassion. In this way, one may be said to be well-cultivating the practice of peaceful conduct.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma for peace and security... (up to) it cannot be fully exhausted even by means of calculation or parables."
This verse concerns the practice of right speech (*samyag-vāc*). The thirty-six lines beginning with "The Bodhisattva always delights in...

collectively describe the practice of right speech. The first ten lines concern teaching the Dharma with composure; they state that both the internal and external are pure. "Composure" refers to purifying the internal mind.
"Purifying the ground," "anointing with oil," "bathing," and "clean clothing" refer to external purity. Anointing the body with fragrant oils, as well as [using] ghee...
[He] blends oils; the Western Regions use these to anoint the body, taking [their] fragrance and purity. He takes his place upon the Dharma-seat;

that which is called the "Dharma-seat" is the seat of the emptiness of dharmas, whereby both the internal and external are empty. He expounds according to the questions, so that his words do not contradict their intent.
The twenty-six phrases beginning with "If there are bhikṣus... are verses on the ritual for preaching the Dharma. (4)

The various kings and others are seekers of the Dharma. By means of subtle and profound meanings—that is, by teaching only the Dharma of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna—they speak with a serene countenance.
They delight in preaching, answering in accordance with the meaning and teaching in response to the capacities of beings.
They cause all to resolve their minds toward awakening, which refers to great compassion. By eliminating laziness and indolence, they become courageous and diligent.

One finds delight in the Dharma; thus, one is free from all sorrow and affliction. To speak constantly day and night is the height of diligence, causing all to rejoice—this is what is meant by "instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening.
The ten lines beginning with "robes and bedding" praise the pure preaching of the Dharma without seeking material gain.
To aspire to the Buddha-way is to offer the Dharma as an offering—this is what is meant by...
Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme. This means that by taking the Dharma as one’s joy, one personally receives the offering of peace and happiness;
thus, there is no longing for external things. The twelve lines following "After my parinirvāṇa" are a verse that expands upon the practice of patience (*kṣānti*) from the preceding chapter.
Because the mind is governed by patience, there are no verbal transgressions, and thus one is able to distance oneself from all harms. This is because...
Regarding the statement on "all hardships": these all arise from one's own mind’s inability to endure.
By abiding in patience (*kṣānti*), as it is said, "the blade of the soldier has no place to enter," because there is no ground for death, therefore all such things cease to exist.

The eight lines below this, beginning with "The wise person is thus," are the concluding verses that summarize the practice of right speech. This means that when a bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the mind, they are able to abide in peace.
If one finds joy [in this], then naturally all hardships will cease; the benefit of the Dharma will be vast, and those who receive its transformative influence will be many.
Thus, its merit is inexhaustible and cannot be fully described.
Furthermore, from Mañjuśrī [up to] the *Sūtra on Offerings*, one should revere, respect, and praise [the Buddha].

This is the practice of right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). Among the various evils and afflictions of the faculty of mind (*manas*), the three poisons are foremost; envy and malice are [the primary among them].
To flatter those above and deceive the masses is the result of greed and delusion.
To revile and insult those who study the Buddha-way, seeking out their faults and fearing they may surpass oneself, is the manifestation of the three poisons.

In this degenerate age of the Dharma-ending period, when the three poisons are rampant, those who uphold this sutra do so fundamentally to transform such violent and oppressive people; yet instead, they themselves [succumb to] the three...
This poisons and opposes [the Dharma]; it is like adding fire to fire, which is called "overflowing excess. How can this be considered good?
Therefore, one should observe the precepts, uphold the sutras, purify one's own mind, and accord with the Dharma.
If there are bhikṣus or others among the fourfold assembly who seek the path of the Three Vehicles, do not boast of yourself as a practitioner of the Mahāyāna and thereby disturb or trouble them.
If one causes another to fall into doubt and regret, they will lose their fundamental practice. One should instead use compassion to tame, gather, and transform them, proceeding gradually.
To speak such words to that person is to cause them further distress and agitation.

Since one is unable to tame or guide them, yet adds harsh and contrary speech, mocking what they have studied, they remain far removed from the Way and fail to attain the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvajñajñāna). Furthermore, one should reprove them...
Such negligence means that while one’s words are correct, one’s mind is not; thus, by provoking their minds, one frequently incurs slander, which is brought about by oneself.
To engage in frivolous discourse regarding all phenomena refers to the discrimination between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, or between emptiness and existence, the partial and the perfect.

This leads to the arising of strife and contention; all such things originate from the three poisons. Because the faculty of the mind (*manas*) is not yet purified, one is unable to abide in the practice of peaceful bliss.
Regarding all sentient beings, one should first establish the method for upholding the sutra through correct teaching, taking compassion as the foremost principle.
Sentient beings are deluded and inverted; therefore, one should conceive a heart of pity and mercy, regarding them as if they were one's only child. One should contemplate thus:
The Tathāgata’s compassion is like a father’s equal love for an only son; thus, there is no heart of weariness or fatigue.

A Bodhisattva is one who has skillfully studied the Buddha’s conduct and is dedicated solely to benefiting sentient beings; they should be regarded as a teacher or guardian, and one should model one's own actions after theirs.
Therefore, one should always, with a profound mind, pay homage and prostrate to Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions. Regarding this—
"Regarding 'all sentient beings' below: it means teaching them the practice of upholding the sutra and self-regulation.
To preach the Dharma with equanimity means not to allow one's mind to fluctuate based on whether others are noble or base, wise or foolish; this refers to preaching with impartial great compassion."

"Conforming to the Dharma" means being free from the four types of false attribution (*apavāda*): to say "it exists" is the false attribution of superimposition (*samāropa*); to say "it does not exist" is the false attribution of denial (*apavāda*);
to say "it both exists and does not exist" is the contradictory false attribution; and to say "it neither exists nor does not exist" is the false attribution of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Because one speaks in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one is free from these faults; thus it is said to be "neither too much nor too little. One who deeply loves the Dharma does not speak excessively, as [stated in the following verse]:

Just as a compassionate mother nourishing an infant does not give him much ghee, fearing that he might not digest it and it would instead produce poison, so too, if one who upholds this sutra in the final age can abide in this practice, no one will be able to disturb or confuse them; this is what is meant by "skillfully cultivating the mind.
By doing so, one will find enlightened companions and attract a multitude to listen, causing the benefits of the Dharma to gradually spread.
These six kinds of merits are naturally complete within oneself; this is truly the wondrous practice of upholding the sutra.

If there is someone like this, who would not joyfully follow their transformation? How could there be any cause for resentment or harm? This is what is called the "True Practice of Peaceful and Joyful Conduct."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, one should abandon jealousy, anger, and pride... [until] being honored by immeasurable multitudes."
The first four lines of this verse [correspond to] the initial section of the stanza.

"Upright conduct" means that because one’s mind is upright and correctly mindful of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, the afflictions such as the three poisons within the faculty of the mind naturally abandon themselves. The following four lines concern not disparaging others.

The second verse section concerns the meaning of contemptuous neglect. The prose commentary directly criticizes this as being extremely remote from the Way, stating that it refers to treating [the Dharma] with disdain and negligence.
The twelve lines beginning with "These sons of the Buddha... constitute the third verse section.
However, patience (*kṣānti*) is the primary theme throughout; therefore, it says: "Always gentle and able to endure," and "Regard the Buddha as a father, and respect the Bodhisattvas as..."
The Master [said]: "It is for the purpose of shattering one's own mind of arrogance that he preaches the Dharma without any obstruction.
Below the third dharma, there is a concluding verse:
Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī" up until "when this Dharma was preached," there is no fault.
This is the practice of great compassion. The first three practices constitute donning the Tathāgata’s robe and sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat;

this one practice is what is called entering the Tathāgata’s chamber. While the preceding "Chapter on the Dharma-Master" merely taught the methods for bodhisattvas by briefly citing essential practices, this present chapter provides a detailed explanation of those previous meanings.
Furthermore, while kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness, compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to...

To extract them from suffering: when there are those, whether lay or ordained, who are able to believe and accept this Dharma, one generates the mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) because it increases their joy in the Dharma.

As for those who are not Bodhisattvas—namely, those of no faith and the icchantikas—one should generate the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) out of pity for their ignorance and delusion, seeking to discipline and guide them so that they may give rise to right faith and thereby extract them from their suffering.
"Below, one should form this thought," it says, which expresses the intent of his compassion. Toward those who lack faith, he feels pity for their great loss.
The reason for this loss is that they have never heard the wondrous Dharma taught by the Tathāgata according to his expedient means.
Therefore, they do not know and do not perceive; moreover, they cling to their own ignorance as being correct, and thus do not inquire.
Because they have not heard it, they do not believe or understand. Since they are so utterly ignorant and deluded, I shall never abandon them.
When I attain Buddhahood, wherever they may be, I will surely employ my supernatural powers and wisdom to lead them and cause them to dwell within this Dharma, making them upright.
If the causes are not lost, one will ultimately possess the destiny to attain Buddhahood; this is the height of great compassion.
In the final age, those who uphold this sutra and preach the Dharma with these four practices will be able to remain free from all faults and will perfectly accord with the Buddha’s mind.
This is what is called performing the deeds of a Tathāgata.
It is always [the case for] bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs (and so forth)—how much more so for those who obtain a vision of it, receive it, uphold it, read it, and recite it.
This concludes the summary of the supreme benefits of these four practices. It means that a person who upholds this sutra possesses these four practices. Thus:
He is honored, respected, and praised by the fourfold assembly, kings, and others; how much less could there be the disgrace of slander?
The devas of the void constantly follow and protect him; how could there be any interference from Māra?
Even if he dwells in a desolate place where no one else is present, should someone arise with the intent to challenge or question him, the divine power of the protecting devas shall ensure that—

Those who hear it will rejoice; how could there be any affliction or harm inflicted upon them? It was previously stated that I have dispatched devas, nāgas, and spirits to constantly provide protection.

Since this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, we know that those devas who guard [the practitioners] day and night are precisely those dispatched by the Tathāgata. This is because their practice accords with the practice of the Buddha. Therefore...
The protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas is just like this.
Because of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, even its name cannot be heard in immeasurable lands, let alone being seen, received, upheld, read, or recited.

Since the Dharma is so difficult to encounter, those who uphold this sūtra must certainly be solemn and careful. It is the wisdom-life of all Buddhas and the eyes of devas and humans; therefore, it is not...
They fail to receive protection and mindfulness. If they do not hear or believe [this], is this not a great loss?
Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful Wheel-turning Sage King (cakravartin) [who, upon seeing this, would] surely be greatly astonished and amazed.
This establishes the metaphor of the wheel-turning king’s crest-jewel to illustrate that this sutra is not given to those who are unworthy.

The Buddha is the King of the Three Realms and is titled the Great Hero because he is able to shatter all states of existence (*bhava*). A powerful wheel-turning king subjugates all nations by his majesty;
this is analogous to the power that shatters all states of existence. Lesser kings who do not obey his commands are analogous to the five aggregates, the afflictions, and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
All māras turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust; they do not accord with the nature of awakening.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of the one great matter, he specifically manifests his body and preaches the Dharma to subdue all māras.

Beginning at the Deer Park, he taught existence to shatter the ordinary person’s attachment to the suffering of birth and death; next, he taught Prajñāpāramitā and spoke of emptiness to shatter the two vehicles’ view of revulsion toward existence.
Next, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* was taught to harmonize emptiness and existence, thereby shattering the biased attachments of the two vehicles.

Next, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was taught to point directly to the ālayavijñāna, which is the tathāgatagarbha, so that one may suddenly perceive the Buddha-nature and shatter the provisional practices of the two vehicles.
Thus, throughout forty years, various sūtras were taught using immeasurable and innumerable diverse skillful means to dismantle [these attachments].
Because of the attachments of those who follow the three vehicles, it is said that "various armies are raised to go forth and subjugate them.

"Subjugation" (*dao*) means proclaiming their crimes; "subjugation" (*fa*) means destroying their kingdoms. This refers to the censure of the two vehicles and the destruction of the city of *nirvāṇa*.

However, when those of the three vehicles hear the Dharma, each attains a realization of their own; thus, they are likened to soldiers who have performed meritorious service, for whom rewards are granted according to their merits. [The text continues with] "fields and lands."
Even down to the slaves and common people, all these matters concern the merits and practical applications of the stages of fruition of the Three Vehicles;
yet the bright jewel within the King’s topknot alone was not given. This is analogous to not immediately preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The reason it was not preached was that he feared the assembly would be startled or doubtful; therefore, he did not speak of it lightly, just as one dares not rashly bestow the topknot jewel.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this (up to) "he shall expound it for you and others. This is the correspondence of the Dharma.
The Tathāgata is also like this. [The section on] "joining the heads" corresponds to the passage beginning with "those who have merit. The following corresponds to...
The next section, beginning with "Just as the Wheel-Turning King," reiterates the preceding metaphor to clarify that the single crest-jewel was not given [to the other princes].

The subsequent section, beginning with "The Tathāgata is likewise," reiterates the previous point to clarify that while all other sūtras were preached, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone was not, because it is difficult to believe.
That which was previously unspoken is now spoken; this is what is meant by being rare and difficult to believe.
This Dharma is like the wheel-turning king who unties the jewel from his topknot to bestow it; one who has not performed supreme merit cannot abide in it.
