Therefore, it is said that this sutra is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas, and thus it is granted only at the very end, just as the topknot jewel is reserved for a great achievement.
This Lotus Sutra is the secret treasury of all Buddha-Tathāgatas. [It concludes...]
This reveals that the Buddha has guarded [beings] throughout the long night of birth and death for over forty years, awaiting the proper opportunity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Constantly practicing patience and compassion for all [up to] the light of wisdom shining like the sun.

These four lines beginning with "constantly practicing patience" generally praise the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as the foundation. The twelve lines beginning with "in the future age" praise the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*).
"Causing them to abide therein" means causing them to dwell securely within the dharma of quiescent extinction (*śānta-dharma*).

The sixteen lines beginning with "For example, like one of great strength" illustrate the parable. The twenty lines beginning with "The Tathāgata is likewise" illustrate the application of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃkrama*).
Since the Dharma King preaches the Dharma by means of the great power of patience (*kṣānti*), the wondrous practice of upholding this sutra must take patience as its supreme excellence.
The six lines beginning with "This sutra is honored" illustrate the exalted status of this sutra.
The six lines following "After my parinirvāṇa" are a verse summarizing the intent of the response to the question.

The fourteen lines following "Those who read this sutra" are a verse on how those who uphold the sutra can leave behind obstacles and distance themselves from harm. The four lines beginning with "Wandering without fear" are a verse on the fearlessness of those who uphold the sutra.
As for "radiant light," it is because the mind and the Dharma are one; thus, they possess great, upright fearlessness.
It is just like this.
If, within a dream, one sees only wondrous things—up to and including entering deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions;
seeing that the bodies of those Buddhas are golden in color—up to and including their eventual entry into *nirvāṇa*, like smoke vanishing or a lamp going out.
This verse describes the supreme benefits of upholding this sutra. As for "if one constantly sees wondrous things even in dreams":

because the mind of one who upholds the sutra is in profound accord with the principle (*dharma*), habitual tendencies are eliminated and defilements are purified; thus, as the moon appears in clear water, wondrous realms manifest before them.
This is the manifestation of such supreme benefits. The sixteen lines beginning with "seeing all Tathāgatas" describe these [benefits] within dreams.
It was a wondrous thing. He saw the Buddha preaching the Dharma for the assembly; he also saw the nāgas and devas listening to his own preaching of the Dharma;
and he saw the Buddha emitting light while preaching the Dharma. Regarding the Buddha’s teaching for the fourfold assembly, there are twelve phrases.

Furthermore, he saw the Buddha preaching the Dharma, and himself sitting within the assembly hearing the Dharma, attaining *dhāraṇī*, realizing non-retrogression, and perfecting the causal practices. Because the Buddha knew his mind, [he acted accordingly].
He bestows a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). The eight phrases beginning with "You, son of good family" describe the matter of the prediction.
Furthermore, the ten phrases beginning with "Again seeing oneself" describe what occurs after receiving the prediction:

seeing oneself practicing austerities on a mountain, realizing the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), attaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and within that concentration, further seeing the Buddha’s body adorned with a golden hue; having seen this, one hears the Dharma from the Buddha.
He then related this to others. Furthermore, regarding the sixteen phrases beginning with "dreaming of becoming a king":

it means that in his dream he became a king, relinquished his royal throne, and proceeded to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). There he sought the Way for seven days, whereupon he finally attained the wisdom of a Buddha and realized the Unsurpassed Path.
He continued to preach the Dharma for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, delivering all sentient beings. Once his work of transformation was complete, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Within this single dream, from beginning to end, he saw the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and awakened to the Way;

he received the Buddha’s prophecy of future enlightenment, and after receiving that prophecy, he again dreamed of renouncing his royal throne to seek bodhi, until finally attaining buddhahood in a single lifetime. Thus it ended.

Until they enter into *nirvāṇa*, even after the passage of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, these successive events are all exactly as manifested within the white tuft of light (*ūrṇā-kośa*) previously described.
That the beginning and end of all Buddhas constitute the single great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa-pratyaya*) is because,

prior to opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*), the Buddha uses his radiant marks to demonstrate the beginning and end of his attainment of Buddhahood, never departing from what is manifest.

The preceding thought-moment causes one to see clearly and with perfect clarity. Now, having heard the wondrous Dharma and already opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), one perceives through the benefit of upholding this sutra the beginning and end of attaining Buddhahood for oneself. Thus, eons of vast duration reside solely within a single thought-moment of the person;
they do not depart from the limit of a single *kṣaṇa*. This is intended to cause them to have self-confidence and be free from doubt. However, this is [explained] in terms of...
Regarding the discourse on dreams: it is said that birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday. The intent is to cause those who uphold this sutra to achieve the four practices.
They should contemplate all phenomena as being like events in a dream—empty and non-existent, ultimately unobtainable.
This is the supreme benefit for one who has deeply realized the samādhi of the true mark (*dharmatā*). How marvelous, how marvelous!

To see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and awaken to the Way within a dream; furthermore, to dream of entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), preaching the Dharma to benefit others within that absorption, and even relinquishing one’s throne to seek the Way, proceeding until attaining Buddhahood, delivering sentient beings, and entering *nirvāṇa*, enduring for the duration of immeasurable kalpas—although this is...

The matter of dreams—how could it ever be fathomed by ordinary understanding? Herein is fully revealed that the *Avataṃsaka* is where past and present are one and the same, and where extension and brevity are simultaneous.
To describe such inexhaustible matters in only three hundred words—if this were not the Buddha’s wondrous eloquence, how could it be so?
If, in the evil ages of the future, one speaks of this foremost Dharma, that person will obtain great benefit, including all the aforementioned merits.
This verse concludes the superior benefits of the four practices.
The Fifteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "The Emergence from the Earth.
The purpose of this chapter is to reveal that when one’s own mind awakens, the ocean-like inherent virtues manifest before one;
this constitutes the ultimate wondrous practice of upholding the sutra. Although the śrāvakas who previously received their predictions vowed to uphold the sutra, their own power was insufficient.
It is difficult to enter the perilous path of birth and death; one must rely upon the power of others. For this reason, the Buddha has commanded Bodhisattvas to provide guidance and protection.

Since there are now Bodhisattvas from other directions, numbering as many as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, each vowing to protect those who uphold this sutra—why does the World-Honored One stop them and not grant permission? It is because they come from without...
Therefore, what the Chan school calls "entering through the gate" is not one's own family treasure.
Only when it flows forth from within one's own breast does it truly encompass heaven and earth. Thus it is said: "I myself have sixty thousand Ganges-sands of assemblies surging forth from the earth.
When essence and function are both manifested, the retinue is equal [to the master]. It is by means of these inherent virtues that one upholds the sutra.
Only then can one wondrously accord with the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Therefore, they proceed into the void and approach the two World-Honored Ones.
Upon reaching this point, the views of arising and ceasing subside, and extension and contraction become simultaneous; thus, fifty minor kalpas are said to be like half a day.

Because this constitutes practice in accordance with the nature (dharmatā), the four leaders are all designated by names derived from their practice. This is intended to reveal that only by upholding the sutra in this manner does one truly accord with the Tathāgata.
This fulfills his original aspiration; it is brought about by the accomplishment of the four practices for peace and bliss.
Because the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) have manifested before him, this is by no means something that can be known through the discrimination of the mind or consciousness.

Therefore, Maitreya and the assembly of eight thousand Ganges-sands all gave rise to doubt, saying they did not recognize a single person; thus, they simultaneously questioned along with the attendants of the Buddhas.
This is no small matter. Therefore, you must first exert yourselves by donning the armor of diligence and generating a firm resolve;

only then can you believe and accept this. For the Tathāgata himself has declared that he now wishes to reveal and proclaim the power of the wisdom, sovereign spiritual penetrations, the power of the lion’s leap, and the power of fierce majesty of all Buddhas—the original [nature] of all Buddhas.
The entirety of his intention lies herein; how could this be a minor matter?

Nevertheless, because the World-Honored One declared that this great assembly consists entirely of those whom he first inspired to resolve for enlightenment since his own attainment of Buddhahood, Maitreya and the rest of the multitude all gave rise to doubt, as they had seen with their own eyes that these were those whom the World-Honored One had been teaching for forty years since his realization of the Way.
They are all present here at this single assembly on Vulture Peak, yet the multitude who have emerged from the earth has never been seen before.

Furthermore, while we, having previously received the Buddha’s teaching, still possess such inferior understanding, this great assembly consists entirely of those who have long planted the roots of virtue and deeply sown the seeds of goodness.
How could he have converted such a vast multitude in so short a time? Therefore, it is said that his father was young.
The parable of the son and the old man describes the state of doubt; this [chapter] emerges from that ground to manifest the subtlety of the traces.

The Tathāgata’s lifespan specifically reveals the subtlety of the fundamental reality in order to dispel the views of the two vehicles that cling to the traces, and to clarify that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and does not belong to the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, this chapter follows the chapter on the Lifespan in its sequential order.
At that time, as for the bodhisattvas who have come from other lands (up to) to protect, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound this sutra—
if these bodhisattvas from other lands wish to remain in this Sahā world to uphold this scripture, and the Buddha restrains them and does not grant permission— then [this is so].
The Buddha’s intention in upholding this sutra is that one must be self-sufficient in inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) without depending on external factors.

This is intended to reveal the subtle mystery of the original and the manifested (*honji-suijaku*), thereby demonstrating that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding and does not belong to the realm of birth, death, coming, or going. Therefore, he said:
"There is no need for you; I myself have sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges] attendants who shall protect and uphold it," and so forth, as explained at length.

This is a sutra. The reason the number of bodhisattvas is always stated as sixty thousand is intended to signify that when the six consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom, the ocean-like inherent virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) manifest immediately.
This is what is called the "patriarchal penetration of self-nature" (*svabhāva-yukti*), wherein wondrous function is infinite.
If one relies on the other six consciousnesses, one falls into the discrimination of names and phrases; this is not the subtle essence of upholding the sutra. Therefore, the "other" is insufficient.
[This is] reliance.
When the Buddha spoke these words, sounds from what was said in the Sahā world [arose]; from below they issued forth.
Here, there were sixty thousand assemblies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who, in response to the Buddha’s speech, simultaneously surged forth from the earth.

Regarding the preceding passage: as for the statement that the lands of the three thousandfold world system all quaked, split open, and gushed forth, it means that the earth is fundamentally the one true *dharmadhātu*.
Previously, because it was conditioned by the fetters of ignorance (*avidyā*), its inherent virtues were obscured and did not manifest.
Now, with the arrival of the Buddha’s voice of Dharma, ignorance is suddenly shattered and the self-nature is fully revealed; thus, one attains wondrous awakening to one's own mind. Therefore...
The nature-virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all fundamentally present within the source of the mind; their wondrous functions are boundless. Being thus, one may uphold this sutra;
it is not comparable to those who engage in the conceptual discrimination of names and phrases. Therefore, there is no need for anything from another direction—this is what is meant.

That Bodhisattvas all possess the marks of a Buddha is because virtue and function are non-dual. Because this is the essence of the mind, which is the wondrously luminous original enlightenment, the body...
All are golden and possess immeasurable radiance. Because the world conforms to the emptiness of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*), it abides in the void beneath this world.
Since the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is manifested through the efficacy of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), the sound of the Buddha is heard as it issues forth from below;
this signifies that the hearing of the sound constitutes the essence of the teaching.
Each and every bodhisattva was a leader at the head of a great assembly (up to the point where they were beyond what can be known).
This statement refers to the fact that the number of retinues brought by each of the arriving bodhisattvas was not uniform.

That is to say, among those who had come, some led followers numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, gradually decreasing down to tens of billions (*koṭi*); others led followers numbering in the tens of billions, gradually decreasing down to being alone. And...
Those who are solitary and without retinue are also more numerous than the sands of the Ganges; this is intended to manifest that their number is infinite.
Furthermore, it serves to distinguish between the companion and the leader, as well as the inequality of their respective functions.
These bodhisattvas, having emerged from the earth, [filled] the space of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lands.
This describes the manner in which the multitude that surged forth beheld the Buddha.

The statement that they each proceeded through the void toward the Two World-Honored Ones means that they entered the emptiness of the Dharma-realm and wondrously accorded with the Dharmakāya. They praised him with various eulogies of the Dharma.
The Buddha [taught] that while fifty minor kalpas passed in this manner, the great assembly perceived it as being like half a day.

To speak of deeply realizing the true mark (*dharmatā*) and entering the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is to realize that extension and brevity are simultaneous. As the Great Sutra says: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas;
there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. This is what is meant by the ten periods of time throughout antiquity and the present, where beginning and end are not distinct.
One should remain mindful of detachment; there is no characteristic of extension or contraction to be found.

As for the fourfold assembly seeing the bodhisattvas filling the void through the Buddha’s spiritual power—this refers to the realm of boundless lands, wherein self and other are not separated by even the tip of a hair.

By means of the wondrous power of the dharmadhātu—which is empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of volitional action—it is not something that can be seen by those of the three vehicles; therefore, it is only through the supernatural power of the Buddha that it is seen.
Among this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four leaders who [asked]: "Will this not cause the World-Honored One to become weary?"
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"World-Honored One, are you at ease, with little illness and little affliction... (up to)... do you not cause the World-Honored One to experience fatigue?"

Regarding the statement that the leaders of the assembled multitude inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being: this refers to those who draw near to and accord with the nature of awakening (bodhi).
Because they uphold the sutras and prioritize wondrous conduct, they are all termed "practitioners" (*xing*).

The words of inquiry concerning illness, affliction, and fatigue are spoken because they perceive that Śākyamuni Buddha manifests suffering in common with the people, and furthermore, because they witness the corruption and evil of the Sahā world.
They are difficult to transform and teach.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas... [until] they may hear this sutra and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
This is the Tathāgata’s response to the greetings of the assembly, which precisely reveals the excellence of the fundamental source. He says of these sentient beings:

Having received transformation through successive lifetimes, their affinity for the Dharma has already matured; having made offerings to many Buddhas, their accumulation of merit has already become profound.

This proves that they possess the causal conditions from the distant past for attaining great penetration; therefore, upon seeing a Buddha and hearing the Dharma even once, they immediately enter the Buddha-wisdom.

This refers to Bodhisattvas of superior faculties and sharp wisdom. With the exception of those who previously practiced the Hīnayāna, even they are now led to enter the Buddha’s wisdom upon hearing this sutra.
Thus we know that the Buddha’s transformation of sentient beings depends entirely upon the presence of a karmic affinity.
As for those currently faithless and depraved individuals who have not yet planted the seeds of affinity, the present emphasis on upholding the sutra serves as a means to establish such a connection.
Regarding the conditions for the future, this is why the Tathāgata has been so earnestly seeking such people.

However, those sought must perfectly accord with the Buddha’s mind and deeply embody the Buddha’s practice; only then can they accept and endure the conditions of the world. This is why such individuals are so difficult to find.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"Excellent, excellent, Great Hero, World-Honored One! Having heard [this], we shall practice with faith; we rejoice in accordance [with it]."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the leaders [up to] those who were able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata.
Because the assembly present there heard it said that the transformed assembly was easy to deliver, they also each resolved their minds; thus it is said, "We rejoice.
The World-Honored One praised the assembly for having a mind of sympathetic joy, commending them for having a dharma upon which to rely.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva (up to) joined his palms toward the Buddha and questioned him with a verse.
This was because Maitreya, prompted by the doubts raised by the assembly, came to inquire about the causes and conditions of the gathered multitude.

As for the statement that "eight thousand developed doubts," this reveals the condition in which the eight consciousnesses have not yet been shattered. It means that this wondrous function of the inherent nature is fundamentally not a consciousness.
The mind’s conceptual discriminations can be known; therefore, everyone gives rise to doubt. Thus it is said that [the Buddha] neither saw nor heard.

Maitreya, being a master of the Vijñaptimātra (Consciousness-Only) school, knew the thoughts in the minds of the assembly and therefore requested a resolution of their doubts on their behalf by means of verses.
"Immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of the great assembly of bodhisattvas (up to) by what causes and conditions have they gathered?
This question concerns the causes and conditions for the assembly's gathering.
These beings of massive bodies and great supernormal powers possess wisdom that is inconceivable... (up to) "from where have they come?
This assembly of those who have arrived appears extraordinary in both appearance and conduct; one does not know from where they have come.
The number of retinues brought by each of these bodhisattvas exceeds the former even further.
This question concerns the varying numbers of the leaders and their attendants among those who have come.
From sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* down to one ten-millionth part, he describes the attendants they bring; yet those who bring fewer actually exceed those who bring more.
First, he asked by way of the number of *śata* (hundreds). Then he asked by way of the number of *koṭi*, *nayuta*, and *bimbara*.

By taking the number *bimbara* down to the single unit (*eka*), those that gradually decrease become more numerous than those that were previously many. This is most skillfully expressed in the translation;
consider it carefully. Simply observe the concluding phrase: where the number exceeds what precedes it, it proceeds in descending order, gradually increasing.
This is regarding the aforementioned.

Thus, among this great assembly, if one were to count by means of tally sticks as to which Buddha-way each person has practiced, it would be a detailed inquiry into who among those gathered has been taught.
Since they have emerged from the earth, they are not of the ordinary world.
He saw them dwelling in the space below, yet they were not visible; thus, doubt arose.
Observing this great multitude, each with distinct and preeminent deportment and wisdom, he realized that they could not have been converted by a single Buddha at one time.
Therefore, he inquired in detail: "Who was it that preached the Dharma and transformed him? From whom did he resolve his mind [on enlightenment]? What Dharma did he extol? What sutra did he uphold?
And what Buddha-way did he practice, such that he could become so exceptionally distinguished? It was precisely through these questions that the discourse on the length of his lifespan was initiated.
Thus, regarding these bodhisattvas’ supernormal powers and great power of wisdom (up to the point where it says): "I only pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly.
Although they were seen emerging from the earth, it was ultimately unknown from where they had come—from beneath the ground.
Therefore, he asked for the name of the land from which they had come. An ancient master said: "They have no land; how [could there be one]?"
"Meeting him while passing through a place," it is therefore said: "In all the lands I have traveled, I have never seen such a multitude.
Now this great assembly wishes to know the causes and conditions of this multitude; thus they pray that the World-Honored One will resolve their doubts.
At that time, the various Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha [up to] "you yourselves shall hear it through this" [each spoke].
These disciples of the respective emanation Buddhas each addressed their own original Buddha, also questioning him out of doubt.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha—[extending from "to" the power of the majestic might of all Buddhas]—this Honored One Śākyamuni granted the answer.
First, he exhorted those among the assembly who were diligent, because the matter was difficult to believe.
Maitreya is named Ajita, meaning "Unconquerable. The "Great Matter" refers to the wisdom and supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of all Buddhas.
The display of fierce and majestic power, as well as the causes and conditions for the manifestation of the multitude emerging from the earth, are all matters of great significance.
I shall now proclaim and reveal them; those who lack diligence will be unable to comprehend them, and thus I urge you to persevere.

Regarding the wisdom of the Buddhas, it was previously described as profoundly deep and immeasurable; I have merely briefly pointed it out here. Having provided this initial exposition, I shall now proceed to the ultimate point.

The fact that [the Buddha] attained Buddhahood long ago, his teaching and transformation of vast multitudes, and matters such as his limited lifespan all extensively reveal the profound and immeasurable nature of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Regarding the power of the Buddhas’ sovereign supernormal abilities:

it is like the three previous transformations of the pure land, receiving the assembly into the air, opening the stupa with a finger, and later saying that the tongue reaches the Brahma-heaven, or the clearing of the throat and the snapping of the fingers.
The sound of his finger shaking the great trichiliocosm and so forth are all the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*).
Regarding "the lion-like vigorous display of power of all Buddhas": whenever a lion makes a vigorous display or performs a dance, it exerts its full strength without reserve.

Likewise, when [the Buddha] universally preaches with a single voice, or when his emanated bodies assemble simultaneously to preach upon the basis of the lifespan, these all directly reveal the entire substance of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); there is nothing that is not so.
This is the *śeṣa-dharma*. Thus, it is like the lion’s vigorous springing. Regarding "the power of the Buddhas’ fierce and great majesty":

this refers to the transformation of the vast multitude who emerge from the earth, the uprooting of the dense layers of the three vehicles, and the subduing of the host of Māras—the afflictions of the five aggregates—all of which are the power of fierce and great majesty.
These four phrases are the Buddha’s own description of his inherently possessed capabilities.

Examining this matter across all Buddhas, it is evident that their realization of the Way is identical. The entire essence and great function of the Buddha have been kept secret until now and have not yet been revealed.
It is only now, through the assembly emerging from the earth, that matters such as the Buddha’s lifespan and his merits are being discussed;
these are all difficult to believe. Therefore, he exhorts them to don the armor of diligence so that they may accept this with faith and without alarm or doubt. [The Buddha] addressed Maitreya:
The "Successor" (upapadya-parivartin) acts thus because he intends to establish a model for the future.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"You should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter... you all should listen with one mind."

This verse permits the exhortation to listen attentively. These matters—namely, the four things consisting of wisdom, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth—are difficult to believe and easily met with doubt because they are not of the ordinary kind.
Since these four things collectively belong to the Buddha’s wisdom, it is said that "the Buddha's wisdom is inconceivable.
If one lacks the power of faith, then one will not be able to believe. Regarding patience within the wholesome: this refers to abiding in non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Within this patience, one may indeed believe without doubt. What is now being taught is the Buddha’s wisdom—an inconceivable, foremost, most profound, and indistinguishable Dharma.
Since it is now being proclaimed, he repeatedly offers consolation so that you will not doubt;
he encourages the power of your faith and exhorts you to listen well.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses— up to the point where it says, "With single-minded diligence, seek supreme wisdom"—
this was the Buddha’s answer to Maitreya’s question. As for the statement,

"The multitude who have emerged from the earth are all those whom I have taught since my attainment of Buddhahood in this Sahā world," this was the answer to the question, "Who is it that preaches the Dharma and teaches them?"
From whom did this accomplishment arise? It abides in the empty space of this realm; the statement "not departing from the present moment" answers the question of the land from which it came.
Regarding the one who has read, recited, mastered, and correctly recollected the various sūtras—this answers the question of whose sūtras were upheld and practiced.
The statement that "all sūtras are mastered" does not refer to only a single sūtra, but means that all dharmas are [mastered].
This is the Buddha-dharma. Regarding the phrase "not delighting in being among the multitude," the answer is: what path of the Buddha does one cultivate?
It is said that all enter the Buddha-wisdom through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). One constantly delights in quiet places and does not dwell in reliance upon humans or devas;
this is the cultivation of *śamatha*. As the ancient masters said, "I do not come from among humans or devas. The *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* states: "One who cultivates *śamatha*..."

This is because all things—such as form, body, mind, and the world—are entirely detached [from inherent existence]. "Constantly delighting in profound wisdom" and so forth refers to the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
When contemplative observation is clear and distinct, then the true reality (*dharmatā*) of every phenomenon is revealed.

This means that among all Bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha-way, there are none who do not enter it by means of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Below, in the space of the lower direction, this is precisely demonstrated.

This is the manifestation of the principles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. It is revealed that without *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is impossible to destroy the afflictions (*kleśas*) dwelling in the earth-like stages, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges.
Those who emerged from the earth at that time are precisely these.
Then, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Ajita, you should know" (up to) "I have been teaching these multitudes for a long time.
This verse answers the underlying meaning [of the question]. The first six lines answer who it was that taught them and from whom they resolved their minds.
The following eight lines, beginning with "These are my sons," answer whose sutras they uphold and what path they practice. This says:
This is the section on "Cessation. The six lines beginning with "Day and night always diligent" eulogize the answer to the question of the land from which he comes;
they also signify "contemplation. Because he seeks the Buddha-way, he dwells in the midst of space. Because he diligently seeks wisdom, he preaches various sublime dharmas.
The phrase "having already entered the Buddha-wisdom" means his mind is free from fear. The phrase "the two adornments are already complete" refers to these two lines of the eulogy.
Regarding his virtue: in the eight lines below the city of Gayā, the sūtra describes the causal conditions for the beginning and end of the teaching.
Although the words concern the immediate traces of attaining enlightenment at Gayā, the intent of the teaching regarding the realization of the Way points toward distant causes.

Therefore, Maitreya gives rise to doubt from this point, employing the analogy of the father being young while the son is old to initiate the discourse on the lifespan, thereby revealing the fundamental origin.
I now speak these four lines of true words to conclude and answer the intent of the question.

Since it is said that they cause those who have first resolved their minds [to attain Buddhahood], yet also speaks of long-term transformation, and since the matter of attaining Buddhahood is described as both near and far—a point difficult to believe—I therefore emphasize this with true words.
The intention is that you must not doubt but must certainly believe; there must surely be a reason for this. Thus, the Great Assembly...
Doubt arises.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [says], "Such matters as these are difficult for the world to believe.

This refers to the doubt of sentient beings. The meaning is: since it has not been long since the World-Honored One attained the Way, how could he have taught and transformed [beings] in such a manner?
This great assembly has each been established in bodhi. This mark is near while the finger points to what is far; therefore, it may be doubted.
However, the assembly reflects thus, and Maitreya speaks in response to their request:
"When we saw the Tathāgata as a prince, leaving home and attaining the Way, only forty-odd years have passed until now. That time is very short. This is the adherence to the near mark. It says:
"How could they transform so many beings in such a short time and attain enlightenment? Their aim is exceedingly remote and is certainly suspicious.
Moreover, these bodhisattvas have all long planted the roots of virtue; they cannot achieve success in a short time.
This matter is difficult for the world to believe."
For example, suppose there were a person with a handsome appearance, black hair, and twenty-five years of age—[to say that he could do such a thing] would be difficult to believe.
This analogy is established to address the doubt regarding how one so young could teach and transform such a vast multitude.

"Twenty-five years of age" signifies extreme youth; "one hundred years old" signifies extreme old age. "Youth" represents Śākyamuni Buddha, while "the old man" represents the multitude of beings who emerged from the earth.
The contradiction is extreme; therefore, it is what the whole world doubts:
how is it that since the Buddha attained the Way, he has been able to perform such great meritorious deeds?
This dharma is appropriate. It has not been long since he attained the Way; it is fitting that his father be young, yet this great assembly is exceedingly rare, which is fitting that his son be old.
Today the World-Honored One performs this deed of great merit, which seems contradictory.
To say that this Bodhisattva skillfully enters, emerges from, and dwells in immeasurable samādhis, while this great assembly has not yet witnessed such an act—[is this not strange?]
Maitreya then stated that each had attained samādhi; such mastery over wondrous functions was not something he did not know.
Therefore, he later said of himself, "I believe what the Buddha has taught."
"Although we have already had faith in the Buddha’s teachings according to his adaptive means (yathā-yathā-vaineyika), upon hearing this matter, we likewise do not give rise to doubt.

This is a request for a definitive resolution of doubts for future generations. Maitreya personally declares that he has followed the Buddha for a long time and has faith in what the Buddha has taught;
yet, since the Buddha knows all things and has attained complete penetration, there is nothing he does not know, and thus [Maitreya] believes and understands this.

The matter is certainly beyond doubt. However, I fear that bodhisattvas who are newly trained, possessing shallow wisdom and coarse minds, might hear this after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and fail to believe it;
they would thereby incur the sin of destroying the Dharma. Therefore, I pray that the Buddha will explain its refutation, which is why I make this earnest request.
If the Tathāgata had not answered with the measure of his lifespan, the doubts of the long night would have remained unresolved.
Therefore, the assembly emerging from the earth truly served as the foundation for the revelation of the lifespan.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
In the past, the Buddha [from among the Śākya clan]... [taught and transformed them], causing them to resolve their minds and abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
This verse expresses doubt. In the past, the Buddha went from among the Śākyas and, according to the *Tattvaviniścaya-sūtra*, spoke twenty phrases.

Because he described those who cling to what is near while doubting what is distant, this question arises. "Like a lotus flower in the water" praises the virtues of those who have emerged from the earth.
"Just as a young man," and so forth for the following eight lines, sets forth a simile. "The World-Honored One is also like this," and so forth for the following ten [lines].

The six lines praise the virtues of the assembly’s elders and accomplished ones. The twelve lines beginning with "We have heard from the Buddha" praise the request for clarification and the resolution of doubts for the sake of future generations.
The Sixteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "The Lifespan of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the intent of this chapter: because the assembly emerging from the earth had raised doubts through Maitreya, the World-Honored One spoke of his own lifespan to reveal the excellence of his original and manifested traces, thereby exhausting his fundamental intention and shattering the notions of arising and ceasing held by those of the two vehicles.
This is seen as a manifestation of the eternal Dharma-body, which universally responds according to conditions, with its concealment and appearance being unimpeded.

It clarifies that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is profoundly deep and immeasurable, employing skillful means to benefit sentient beings; it conveys the sense that the gateway to this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
Nevertheless, for all practitioners, unless they penetrate the Dharma-body, there can be no true awakening. Even the slightest trace of emotional conceptualization—
It has not yet been forgotten; it all belongs to the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, not to the knowledge and vision of the Buddha.
In the preceding "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," [the Buddha] distantly relied upon the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna to open up the realm of the Dharma-body.

Although the great assembly believed in Prabhūtaratna, they did not believe that Śākyamuni was of one and the same body and one and the same power of wisdom as him, because of what the śrāvakas had previously seen.
They know only the Buddha who preached the Dharma at the Deer Park as the true Buddha, yet they remain unaware that there is a matter beyond this.

Furthermore, hearing that he is about to enter parinirvāṇa, they again give rise to views of arising and ceasing. Although they have received predictions of enlightenment, they merely trust the Buddha’s words without having seen the Buddha’s mind;
thus, they will ultimately find it difficult to attain the fruit of Bodhi, for their awakening is not true awakening.
Thus, even such cultivation is not yet true cultivation. Yet the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world remains ultimately unfulfilled;

therefore, his previous manifold teachings and revelations still belonged to the realm of the dependent nature (*paratantra*). Reaching this point, the Tathāgata exhausts his supernatural powers to disclose his original intent and clearly manifest the entire body of the Dharmakāya.
Thus he speaks of the infinity of his own lifespan, clarifying this through the analogy of a physician.
It is extinguished yet not extinguished. All śrāvakas must directly awaken to this fact that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding;
only then can it serve as the true cause. Therefore, this chapter follows the response to the emergence [of the question].
Since the revelation of the principle is now complete, what follows merely distinguishes the merits, with the intent that one may attain awakening by following along with them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas (up to the point where they said): "We pray only that you will speak it; we shall faithfully accept the words of the Buddha.
Because the assembly had previously emerged from the earth and Maitreya had raised doubts and made this request, the Buddha spoke this chapter to answer them.
Before speaking it, he repeatedly and earnestly exhorted them to believe the Tathāgata’s truthful words.
This is because the matter of the lifespan is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. That is to say, the wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
were it to be spoken now, I fear that hearers would regard it as a tale of absurdity and unreality.
Should they give rise to doubt and fail to believe, they would instead incur transgression. Therefore, I have admonished them with earnest words before speaking. Maitreya and the great assembly—
"O Three Whites, you should believe and accept the Buddha’s words; we only pray that you will explain them. Such was the utmost sincerity of their request for the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the Bodhisattvas would not cease their triple entreaty, [revealed] the power of his secret spiritual penetrations.

This is the direct response to the various questions. Regarding the statement that "the three requests did not cease," this precisely elucidates the two phrases from the beginning of the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means):

the Tathāgata’s own words upon emerging from meditative concentration, stating that "the wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable, and its gateway is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
Previously, the Buddha had praised it himself but did not explain it; it was only due to Śāriputra’s three successive requests that [he spoke].
Regarding the statement "having first brought them to stillness, he then preached": previously, by means of the Two Vehicles, he led them gradually into the Buddha-wisdom;

as he was about to open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), Śāriputra served as the primary recipient of the teaching. Now, in preaching the Lifespan, he extensively clarifies that previous intent.

As for the reason he employs Maitreya to request the teaching: it is because through the three previous weeks, he had already used skillful means (*upāya*) to reveal and instruct them, and had already explained the gateway to his wisdom.

Therefore, he bestowed predictions upon those of the Two Vehicles. However, as for those who have received such predictions, they have in reality not yet awakened to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Consequently, the Buddha manifested from the earth to proclaim his lifespan, intending that the newly predicted Bodhisattvas would awaken to this Dharma-body as the true cause and thereby certainly attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
For this reason, he requested [this teaching] through the Great Being Maitreya, who is currently in his final birth before succession to the position of Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

Furthermore, by observing the subsequent analysis of the merits, one will know that awakening to this fundamental Dharma alone constitutes true awakening, whereby one may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Yet, the Buddha appears in the world for a great causal purpose:
solely to reveal and instruct sentient beings in the Buddha’s wisdom, which is the true essence of the Dharmakāya, so that they may awaken to and enter it. For this reason, he first appeared...

In the *Samādhi* chapter, he specifically addressed [the matter], yet merely indicated it; though there were various explanations, it was not until the *Baiṭakaprabhāsa* (Jeweled Stūpa) chapter that the Buddha’s wisdom was clearly revealed.
Even there, it was only through the mediation of Prabhūtaratna that his shared essence was shown;
he had not yet personally expounded upon his own fundamental matter. Now, however, he directly reveals his originally inherent lifespan, as it is said:
Unfurling the eight characters, revealing them throughout the entire body, only then can one be said to have exhausted one's original intent.
Regarding this matter, for forty years I have long kept this essential point in silence, not seeking to speak of it hastily. Even now, as I reveal it, I do not dare to speak precipitously;
it has required three weeks of various skillful means before I finally speak. All of these are the Tathāgata’s secret and divine [powers].

This is due to the power of the *pratisaṃvid*. Thus we know that from the Tathāgata’s single appearance in the world until this entire *Lotus Sūtra*, he has spoken solely to reveal and shatter [the veil] regarding the Buddhas’ wisdom, which is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
it is comprised of nothing more than these two phrases: "this gate of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
How could those who observe it easily perceive it?

For all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, this single response destroys all doubts regarding the three vehicles of humans and devas. This is because they perceive the traces but do not perceive the source. As it is said:
"When one reaches the source, emotional attachments vanish; when one knows the mind-body, they merge with the essence. To know the source is what constitutes true knowledge and vision.
It is power.
For example, [it lasts] for five hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* (up to) *nayuta-asamkhyeya* kalpas.
This describes a lifespan so long and inconceivable that one must take the dust and ink of the earth-element to measure the atoms of the world-systems.

This is the number of dust motes. In the preceding section on causes and conditions, it was explained that when the World-Honored One was a prince before the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and established the conditions for the One Vehicle.
To clarify this distant cause, [it is said that] one trichiliocosm was used as the ground and ground into ink; now, five hundred ten-million...
Suppose that *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* trichiliocosms were made into the element of earth, all of which were reduced to dust, each particle finer than a dot of ink.
Even when all these minute particles have been exhausted, the element of earth would still not be surpassed in its abundance.
Previously it was said that one dot is dropped after passing a thousand lands to the east; now, however, [it is said] after passing to the east...

If one were to drop a single mote of dust every five hundred thousand million *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, the number of worlds that remain untouched by dust would be even more numerous than those touched.
This number of motes is beyond what can be known through calculation or reached by the power of the mind;
thus, both the practitioners of the Three Vehicles and the non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas [are unable to fathom it].

This is already beyond comprehension; how much more so when all worlds—whether those attached to defilement or those unattached—are collectively regarded as a single speck of dust, and each speck of dust represents one kalpa?
How could this possibly be conceived by thought? Thus, we know that "Great Penetration" (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) was spoken merely in reference to many traces.
Therefore, in the "Expedient Means" chapter, it speaks extensively of Śāriputra’s three vehicles, as well as the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who have fulfilled [their practice].
In the three thousandfold world system, there are as many people as there are grains of rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds;
yet even if they were to combine their intellectual powers, they would not know the wisdom of the Buddhas—the meaning of this is seen here.
"From that time forth, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world... leading and benefiting sentient beings.
These words refer to the lifespan of his attainment of Buddhahood; it is as vast and numerous as the aforementioned kalpas of dust.
Furthermore, it states that from that time forth he has always been in the Sahā world preaching the Dharma and teaching, while also leading and benefiting sentient beings in other directions.

This is why it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. Thus, when those of the Two Vehicles and the devas and humans hear this, it is no wonder that they are all struck with alarm and doubt.

This directly reveals that the eternally abiding Dharma-body is fundamentally without birth or extinction, and that the environment of dependent retribution is identical to the single realm of tranquil light (*śānta-prabhāsvara*).
As it is said: "Whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature and characteristics [of reality] are eternally abiding. Therefore, one should know that all Buddhas are fundamentally...
There is no nirvana. Sentient beings fundamentally have neither birth nor death; herein, the wondrous Dharma of the true mark of the equal dharma-realm is fully revealed.
How could those of the inferior understanding of the Three Vehicles possibly believe or comprehend this?

Therefore, one must open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to know and see exhaustively. It is precisely said that only Buddhas and Buddhas can thoroughly investigate and exhaustively realize all things.
This is the true reality of the Dharma. It is precisely so that practitioners of the three vehicles may know this and see this that it is called awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
O sons of good family, all that has been explained in the interim [up to this point] was done through skillful means and distinctions.

This is the passage that addresses and subdues potential objections. Above, it was stated that the attainment of Buddhahood occurred long ago, and that the wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.

This present statement—that the conferring of predictions and the teaching of *nirvāṇa* are all skillful means—is intended to reveal the reality by means of the gateway of wisdom through the provisional power of expedient means; this is why it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.

"Good sons, if there are sentient beings [up to] who can cause those beings to give rise to a heart of joy—this refers to the Dharma-body, which is profound, tranquil, and eternally abiding. Yet it manifests bodies to benefit and transform sentient beings;

these traces of response and transformation merely differ in name according to the capacity of beings, whether sharp or dull. Thus, as in the 'Chapter on Names' of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, its lifespan is long."
The brief [sections] are like those in the "Asaṃkhyeya" chapter. The Dharma has both sudden and gradual aspects, as in the "Four Noble Truths" chapter;
these are all functions according to conditions, not the fundamental Dharma itself.
"Sons of good family, when the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings [up to] causing them to enter the Buddha-way, he speaks thus.
These words are proximate in their traces while their root is remote; all that he has established is merely a skillful means."
"Good sons, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata, and everything that has been spoken, are entirely true and not false.
Regarding the Dharma spoken therein—whether concerning oneself or others—it is like the events of the Lamp-Light Great Pervasive One, Prabhūtaratna, and so forth."
All of these are matters manifested by a single body and a single wisdom; they are all actual realities and what is spoken is not false.
It is because the wisdom of sentient beings is shallow that they give rise to doubt and fail to believe, thereby engendering divergent views.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives things as they truly are (up to the point where) the Buddha-works he performs have never for a moment ceased.
This explanation clarifies that all meanings are real and not false, thereby manifesting that the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is eternally abiding.
Regarding "knowing and perceiving the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are," it refers to the fact that all phenomena possess such characteristics, nature, power, and essence.

This refers to the ultimate equality. Because the Tathāgata clearly perceives that the characteristics of the triple world are fundamentally devoid of birth and death, emergence and disappearance, arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence, reality and unreality, or distinctions such as similarity and difference—namely, the Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor—it is the state free from characteristics, the extinction of characteristics, the ultimate, eternally quiescent characteristic of cessation.
It is because the sentient beings of the triple world are deluded regarding this fundamental Dharma that [this teaching is given].

Deluded views perceive such distinctions as arising and ceasing; however, the Tathāgata clearly perceives the single limit of equality, free from all error—this is what is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Therefore, it is said that he does not view the triple world as the triple world does.
Now, for the sake of sentient beings, I shall open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It is simply that they desire to know this vision and these characteristics of the triple world;
it is nothing more than this. Therefore, what was previously called "such a wondrous Dharma" refers to this very thing.

This is what is meant by the wisdom of all Buddhas being profoundly deep and immeasurable. It is only because the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ that there are various inclinations, desires, and memories.

Because they conceptualize and discriminate, [the Buddhas] provisionally establish teachings according to the capacities of beings. Through various causes, conditions, and parables, they preach the Dharma in manifold ways;
all that they do is the work of a Buddha. This is what is meant by saying that the gateway to their wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
"In this way, since my attainment of Buddhahood has been for a very long time... [until] it abides eternally and is never extinguished.
This passage concludes by demonstrating that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) abides eternally and is never extinguished.
"O sons of good family, from when I first practiced the bodhisattva path (up until now), I have used these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings.

These words regarding the proclamation of extinction clarify the provisional nature [of the teaching]. Previously, the lifespan illustrated through the analogy of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust clarified that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and indestructible over a vast duration.
These words clarify what was accomplished during the time one originally practiced the bodhisattva path.
"To live for twice the duration of one's entire lifespan" refers to the matters pertaining to the Dharmakāya.
To manifest passing into extinction in such a manner is merely a provisional trace adapted to the capacities of sentient beings.
Why is this so? If the Buddha were to remain for a long time, [people] would not conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter, nor would they give rise to a heart of reverence.
It is for the sake of such people that the Tathāgata speaks through skillful means; this explains the reason for proclaiming his parinirvāṇa.

If the Buddha were to remain long in the world, those of meager virtue would not perceive him as rare to meet and would fail to develop a mind of respect. It is for these reasons that he proclaims it.
He has entered extinction. He manifested through expedient traces; though he is actually present, he speaks of extinction. This is why it is difficult to believe.
Monks, you should know that from the appearance of all Buddhas in the world [until their passing], they act for the sake of delivering sentient beings—all is real and not false.

This statement—that the Tathāgata is truly imperishable yet speaks of extinction—is intended to cause sentient beings to conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter, to harbor a heart of longing and devotion, and to plant roots of goodness; thus, though he does not truly perish, he speaks of extinction.

This is a provisional manifestation of extinction. Such is the method by which all Buddhas benefit sentient beings; it is entirely for the sake of delivering sentient beings that this provisional [expedient] is shown.
This is precisely the reality; therefore, it is said that "all is real and not false.
It is, for example, like a skilled physician whose wisdom is sharp and penetrating—[whether there be] ten, twenty, or even a hundred [patients].
This establishes the analogy of the physician to illustrate that although the Tathāgata truly speaks of extinction, it is intended for the purpose of liberating sentient beings.
The physician is a metaphor for the Buddha; the medical formula is a metaphor for the teaching; and the excellent medicine is a metaphor for the principle.

The various medicinal properties of the many diseases serve as a metaphor for the treatment of the diverse afflictions of the dispositions and desires of sentient beings—namely, all that the Buddha has taught.
The Dharma is for the purpose of treating all minds; if there were no such minds, what use would there be for all dharmas?
"From ten to a hundred sons" refers to the sentient beings of the triple world. "Ten or twenty" indicates the progression from humans and devas through the ten classes of beings.
Due to certain affairs, he traveled far to another country; when his medicine took effect, he became dazed and rolled upon the ground.
This is a metaphor for the Buddha, who, having completed his transformative work, conceals his body and does not appear. Furthermore, appearing in other regions is like being an old physician.
Since the previous Buddha had already entered parinirvāṇa, the sentient beings of the three realms became intimately accustomed to external paths and the Hīnayāna;

thus, they were like those who have drunk another's toxic medicine and wallow upon the ground—this is a metaphor for abandoning suffering through further suffering as they transmigrate through the six destinies of saṃsāra.
At that time, his father returned home, swiftly eliminating suffering and affliction so that there were no longer any ailments.

This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who perceives that the multitudes in the three realms are oppressed by manifold sufferings, and therefore manifests in the world. This refers to the "new physician.
Yet, when it says "his father returned," it means there is no second father. Sentient beings are lost in delusion; their distance from the Buddha is immense.
Because it is distant, it is said that they see it from afar. Because they know the names and recognize the characters, it is said that they all rejoice greatly.

Because they resolve their minds to practice cultivation, it is said that they prostrate, kneel, and inquire after one's well-being. Having already understood that afflictions are the root of suffering and that birth and death are the calamities of misery, they wish to seek liberation;
thus it is said: "We, being ignorant and deluded, have mistakenly taken poison; we pray for you to save and treat us. This refers to returning the false to the true.

Therefore, it is said that he was granted a further extension of his life-span. The Buddha, in accordance with the formalities of all Buddhas, teaches in response to the capacities of sentient beings;

thus, he differentiates the teaching of the One Vehicle and speaks of three vehicles. Hence, it is said that one seeks fine medicinal herbs and the like according to the prescriptions of various scriptures.

Because the myriad practices are fully perfected, it is said that they possess color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor. All the teachings he expounds are dharmas of a single characteristic and a single flavor.
Therefore, it is said that they are "fully ground, sifted, and blended. By means of these skillful expedients (*upāya-kauśalya*), they are delivered;

hence it is said, "You may take this medicine. Through the severing of delusions and the realization of the Truth, it is said, "Quickly eliminate suffering and affliction, and never again experience manifold calamities."

Among those sons, those who have not lost their minds—even upon encountering these fine colors, fragrances, and medicines—claim they are not pleasing. This is a metaphor for the ease or difficulty of being transformed by the teaching. Those who see the medicine and immediately take it are what are called those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom; they encounter [the teaching] and immediately believe and accept it, making them easy to transform. As for those who say that although they rejoice at seeing their father, they still seek to cure their illness yet are unwilling [to take the medicine], this refers to those of middling faculties. They do not reject the medicine, but because they are not yet certain of its efficacy, they wait for further instruction before they will take it. This is the meaning of "difficult to transform. Those who see the medicine and immediately take it are like the great ocean that receives all rivers; they are like a diamond that cannot be broken; they are like a lotus flower that is not defiled by water; they are like the moon reflected in water, which is not stained by the water. Such people are called those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom. Those who see the medicine and do not take it are like a person with a cataract who sees things inverted; they are like a person with a fever who perceives fire in cold water; they are like a person with jaundice who sees white conch shells as yellow; they are like a person with a wind disorder who hears sounds as if they were voices. Such people are called those of inferior faculties and dull wisdom. Those who see the medicine and claim it is not pleasing are like a person who has never seen the sun or moon and, upon seeing them for the first time, says they are not bright; or like a person who has never smelled sandalwood or aloeswood and, upon smelling them for the first time, says they are not fragrant. Such people are called those of inferior faculties and dull wisdom. Those who see the medicine and immediately take it are like a person who has long been ill and, upon meeting a skilled physician, immediately takes the medicine and recovers. Such people are called those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom. Those who see the medicine and do not take it are like a person who meets a skilled physician but refuses the medicine, saying, "I am not ill," and thus perishes. Such people are called those of inferior faculties and dull wisdom. Those who see the medicine and claim it is not pleasing are like a person who meets a skilled physician and says, "I am not ill, so there is no need to take medicine," and thus perishes. Such people are called those of middling faculties. Therefore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great physician; sentient beings are like the sons. The medicine is the various teachings; taking the medicine is practicing according to the teaching. Recovering from the illness is attaining liberation. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a skilled physician who knows the nature of the illness and prescribes medicine accordingly; it is like a great rain that falls equally upon all, yet each plant receives it according to its own capacity. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like a great rain; it benefits all sentient beings according to their respective capacities. This is the meaning of the parable of the physician. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great treasure house; sentient beings are like those entering the house. The treasure is the various teachings; obtaining the treasure is attaining realization. Leaving the house is transcending the world. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great treasure house where all who enter find what they need; it is like a great mirror that reflects all forms without discrimination. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like a great mirror; it reflects the capacities of all sentient beings without exception. This is the meaning of the parable of the treasure house. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great bridge; sentient beings are like travelers crossing the river. The bridge is the various teachings; crossing the river is attaining liberation. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great bridge that allows all travelers to cross safely; it is like a great boat that carries all passengers across the sea. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like a great boat; it carries all sentient beings across the sea of suffering. This is the meaning of the parable of the bridge. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great lamp; sentient beings are like those in darkness. The lamp is the various teachings; dispelling the darkness is attaining wisdom. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great lamp that illuminates all things clearly; it is like the light of the sun that shines equally upon all. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like the light of the sun; it illuminates the minds of all sentient beings without distinction. This is the meaning of the parable of the lamp. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great drum; sentient beings are like those listening to the sound. The drum is the various teachings; hearing the sound is attaining awakening. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great drum that resounds throughout the land; it is like the sound of thunder that awakens all living things. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like the sound of thunder; it awakens the slumbering minds of all sentient beings. This is the meaning of the parable of the drum. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great cloud; sentient beings are like the thirsty. The cloud is the various teachings; the rain is the nectar of immortality. Quenching the thirst is attaining liberation. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great cloud that covers all lands; it is like a great rain that satisfies all creatures. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like a great rain; it satisfies the thirst of all sentient beings. This is the meaning of the parable of the cloud. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great king; sentient beings are like the subjects. The king is the various teachings; the subjects are those who practice. Governing the realm is attaining the fruit of the path. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great king who governs the realm with justice; it is like a great minister who assists the ruler in bringing peace to the land. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like a great king; it brings peace to the minds of all sentient beings. This is the meaning of the parable of the king. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great physician; sentient beings are like the patients. The physician is the various teachings; the medicine is the various practices. Curing the illness is attaining nirvana. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great physician who knows the nature of the disease and prescribes the correct remedy; it is like a great herb that heals all ailments. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like a great herb; it heals the illnesses of all sentient beings. This is the meaning of the parable of the physician. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great road; sentient beings are like travelers on the journey. The road is the various teachings; the journey is the path to liberation. Reaching the destination is attaining the ultimate goal. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great road that leads to the capital city; it is like a straight path that avoids all dangers. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like a great road; it leads all sentient beings to the city of Nirvana. This is the meaning of the parable of the road. Furthermore, the Buddha says: "The Dharma I preach is like a great mountain; sentient beings are like those dwelling in the valley. The mountain is the various teachings; the valley is the mind of birth and death. Ascending the mountain is attaining the summit of enlightenment. Thus, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is always appropriate to the capacity of the recipient; it is neither too much nor too little. It is like a great mountain that towers over the world; it is like a high peak that is not shaken by the winds. Therefore, the Buddha says: "My preaching of the Dharma is like a great mountain; it is unshakable by the winds of affliction. This is the meaning of the
"Those who take the medicine" is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles who, though they are close to the Buddha-dharma, are unwilling to attain Bodhi.
Because their habitual obstructions are profound and heavy, it is said that "the poisonous vapor has penetrated deeply."
The father thinks to himself, "This son is to be pitied," and so forth, until he dispatches a messenger to return and announce, "Your father has already died.

This parable refers to the teaching that the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa and preach this sutra. The phrase "this son is to be pitied" and so forth is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles who cling to provisional means, neither relinquishing them nor seeking the Mahāyāna;
thus it is said they are "unwilling to take [the medicine]. That the "excellent medicine remains" is a metaphor for preaching this [sutra].
The Sūtra states that the father has died; this is a metaphor for proclaiming entry into *nirvāṇa*. It is like actually going to another country while saying one has died;
it is a metaphor for the fact that while he does not truly perish, he manifests the passing into extinction.
At that time, when the sons heard of their father’s passing, they immediately returned and were all allowed to see him.
This is a metaphor for how those who receive and uphold this sutra immediately attain awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, it says:
"They immediately returned and were all allowed to see him. This refers to my dwelling on Vulture Peak, ever-present and never extinguished. This...
This demonstrates that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding; it merely appears or disappears according to the capacities of sentient beings.
"What do you think, sons of good family? [The assembly replied: "No, World-Honored One.
This confirms that [the previous account] was empty and false, thereby manifesting the truth of the Buddha’s words. This concludes the preceding analogy.
The Buddha said: "I am also like this; since my attainment of Buddhahood (up to) those who speak of me as having committed the fault of falsehood according to the Dharma.

This statement means that the Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding and imperishable; it is only in accordance with the capacities and responses of sentient beings that he provisionally manifests *parinirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is said: "By the power of skillful means," and so forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"From the time I attained Buddhahood until now, throughout the number of kalpas that have passed—countless kalpas."
This verse generally praises the fact that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, appearing or disappearing according to the capacities of sentient beings.
The eight lines beginning with "Since I attained Buddhahood" praise the long duration since his attainment of Buddhahood and his eternal, non-extinguishing presence.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests nirvana through skillful means, yet in reality he does not pass into extinction; he eternally abides preaching this Dharma.
This verse concerns extinction that is not extinction. Because it is an extinction manifested as a provisional appearance, it is not a real extinction.
"I always abide here through these various supernormal powers (up to) manifesting both extinction and non-extinction.
This verse explains the meaning of being extinguished yet not extinguished. In reality, the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding;
however, that which is called "extinction" refers to using supernormal powers to cause deluded sentient beings to fail to see [the Buddha] even though he is near, leading them to think: "I..."
"I shall enter parinirvāṇa. [The passage] from "The assembly sees my parinirvāṇa" (the fourteen phrases following) explains the reason why I do not truly perish.

If the assembly, upon seeing my extinction, were all to offer to my relics and give rise to a heart of longing, yearning, and veneration, desiring to see the Buddha even to the point of not sparing their own bodies or lives, then their seeking would reach its ultimate limit. At that time, I and the community of monks—
They appear simultaneously on Vulture Peak and say to sentient beings, "I am always here. This is called skillful means (upāya).
Therefore it is said that by the power of expedient means, they manifest extinction yet do not truly cease; it is not a real extinction.
"In other lands there are sentient beings who revere, believe in, and delight [in the Dharma]... (up to) they merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa.
This verse describes how the Dharmakāya universally responds according to capacities, appearing or disappearing as appropriate—what is called "the moon appearing when the water is clear.
It is a matter of the mutual resonance between the stimulus and the response; fundamentally, there is no intentional mind of "this" or "that" involved.
"I see sentient beings submerged in suffering (up to: 'I then emerge to preach the Dharma for them')":

this verse expresses the principle of appearing or remaining hidden according to the capacity of beings. When their capacity is indolent, he remains hidden; when they respond with resonance, he emerges.
Thus, one knows that appearing or remaining hidden depends on the capacity of beings, not on the Buddha.
With such supernormal powers, he remains constantly on Vulture Peak and in other various abodes throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
This verse reveals that the Dharma-body is eternally present; it signifies the sense that, whether in this world or other realms, it is ever-present and never extinguished.
"When sentient beings see the world at the end of the kalpa being consumed by the great fire" (up to) "scattering the Buddha and the great assembly.

This verse describes the destruction of the kalpa by the three calamities, yet this land remains peaceful and secure. It is the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhā*), the fundamental nature-realm (*dharmatā-dhātu*) where the Dharma-body dwells, as well as the Land of Adornment through True Reward (*samyag-vipāka-alaṃkāra*).
To say that the Buddha constantly resides on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and does not pass away refers to this Sahā world.
Although this land passes through the three calamities, it is destroyed yet not truly destroyed. Thus we know that this defiled land is itself the adornment of true retribution;
it does not require three transformations to become a pure land. Because sentient beings possess heavy defilements and perceive through ignorance, it is filled with filth and evil.
Yet when viewed with the Buddha-eye, it is the profound stillness of true emptiness, a subtle and wondrous adornment. Therefore, [the previous...]
The three transformations of the pure land are specifically shown to sentient beings as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Gardens, groves, and so forth are all matters of the adornment of true retribution; this very Sahā world is itself the realm of true retribution—how could it be what ordinary perception sees?
"My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as utterly consumed by fire, filled with all manner of grief, fear, and suffering.

This verse indicates that although the pure land is in reality not destroyed, the fact that sentient beings see it as being consumed by fire is merely due to their deluded perceptions arising from their individual karma and the summons of their own evil deeds.

These sentient beings with various offenses, due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma—[up to] "the Buddha is difficult to encounter"—these twelve phrases praise purity and defilement according to the capacities of beings.
Their concealment or manifestation does not belong to the Buddha; he responds according to what is invoked, and thus there is no fixed characteristic.
"Such is the power of my wisdom; the light of my insight shines immeasurably. (Up to: "The words of the Buddha are true and not false.
