This verse summarizes that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding and fundamentally neither hidden nor manifest, exhorting the assembly to have faith.
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *Vairocana*; here it is translated as "Universal Illumination," for the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* illuminates the immeasurable with its light.
Therefore, his lifespan is likewise immeasurable.
It is like a physician who, through skillful means, tells a mad son that he is dead in order to cure him; though he is actually alive, no one can say he is speaking a falsehood.
This verse is an analogy.
"I am also the Father of the World who rescues those suffering from all afflictions... [down to] those fallen into the evil realms.
This verse accords with the Dharma. Because ordinary beings are subject to inversion, that which truly exists is said to have ceased. For this reason, I manifest cessation.
I feared that if they were to see me constantly, they might give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence; it was for the sake of such people that I manifested my passing into extinction.
Thus we know that whether the Buddha remains hidden or appears, he acts every single day without fail to deliver sentient beings.
"I always know whether sentient beings practice the Way or do not practice the Way" (up to) "quickly accomplishing the Buddha-body.
This verse explains the reason for employing provisional means (*upāya*). That is to say, he preaches the Dharma through skillful means according to the varying capacities of beings;
in short, it is nothing other than to cause sentient beings to quickly achieve the wisdom of a Buddha.
The Seventeenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "Distinguishing Merit.
Regarding the purpose of this chapter’s inclusion: having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the long duration of his lifespan, they have already realized that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding;

furthermore, having witnessed the realms of the threefold transformation of the pure land, they have understood that the triple world is nothing but mind. This constitutes a profound and wondrous realization.
Faith and understanding serve as the true cause, capable of attaining the Tathāgata’s eternal and true fruit. To uphold this sutra in this manner constitutes a sublime practice.
Because the Dharmakāya is eternally abiding, the pure land of the world is not separate from one's own current location;

therefore, those who can diligently cultivate such contemplation possess the marks of profound faith and understanding. Thus, the distinctions regarding these merits are not [exhaustively] detailed here.
It is inconceivable. Upon reaching this point, the emotions of arising and ceasing vanish, and the dualistic views of purity and impurity are extinguished.

Only when wondrous realization has reached its ultimate limit does one truly become a practitioner who upholds the sutra; it is for this reason that this chapter follows. Tiantai Tathāgata classifies five types of Dharma-preachers, assigning this to the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*).
Thus we know that the intent of upholding the sutra lies in wondrous realization, not in mere words and letters. Therefore, one is able to transcend all things.
Regarding conditioned merit:
at that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha’s discourse on the vast number of kalpas of his lifespan (up to the point where they attained great benefit).
This is the sūtra-master’s narrative account; that is, the great multitude in the Dharma assembly heard the exposition of the measure of the lifespan and attained great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya... [until] "...shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the Tathāgata’s correct demonstration of those who, upon hearing this discourse on the lifespan, shall obtain great benefit.

Regarding these individuals described as obtaining benefit, there are gradations of depth and shallowness in their realization; thus, they are distinguished according to the depth of their awakening and the fruits they attain.

It is merely due to the sequence of cause and effect. As for the "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): it arises because one previously cultivated the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-caryā*) and attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) during the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).
Now, hearing that the lifespan and the Dharma-body are eternally abiding, one realizes there is no arising or ceasing; thus, the practice of patience is perfected.
Because one accepts the dharma of non-arising within the mind, as many sentient beings as the sands of the Ganges attain this non-arising.
It is patience (*kṣānti*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Through three gradual stages, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This signifies the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), whereby one suddenly awakens to non-arising and enters the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

In the present sutra, because the four practices of peaceful bliss (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*) are cultivated with patience as the primary focus, one initially proceeds from the patience of arising to the patience of non-arising—just as in the case of Avalokiteśvara’s faculty of hearing, where movement and stillness do not [disturb him].
"Birth arises; what is heard is exhausted. This, too, is the realization of non-arising through contemplative observation; its meaning corresponds to the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
Since faith pertains to the outer ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), the term "sentient beings" is employed here. Regarding the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining:
*dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention," meaning it summarizes all phenomena and maintains immeasurable meanings. The present term "hearing and retaining" refers to the cause.
Hearing the life-span, one realizes the Dharma-body and dwells securely in the true mark (*dharmatā*), upholding it without loss. In meaning, this corresponds to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*);
dwelling in and maintaining the ultimate truth through perfect realization and perfect upholding, one does not pass through successive stages, and is therefore called *saṃdhāraṇī*.
This means that the perfect realization of the Dharma-body universally encompasses all ten stages, perfectly accomplishing the single mind; hence it is termed the *Śrutadhāraṇī*. One attains it.
Regarding the unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): its meaning corresponds to the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).

Because the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) involve the perfect realization of the true mark of reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) and ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one merely dwells in the principle of emptiness. Now, emerging from emptiness into the provisional (*upāya*), one engages with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings; therefore, this constitutes the Ten Practices.
Furthermore, the unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition is precisely the practice of preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, wherein a single practice perfectly accomplishes all practices.

Therefore, one who attains the *amita-āvarta-dhāraṇī*—wherein "āvarta" (旋) refers to a whirlpool or the swirling eddy of a rapid current—this meaning corresponds to the tenth stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Because the preceding two practices of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*) are subsumed and returned to the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), they are dedicated toward the three spheres, thereby perfecting the single mind.
Since every thought-moment is both empty and provisional, it is itself the Middle Way within each thought-moment; it is like water—[which flows yet remains still].
The "rapids with whirlpools" refers to the mind and mental factors being gathered into the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

"Able to turn the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma" corresponds in meaning to the first stage (*bhūmi*); this means that upon first ascending to the stage, one attains great joy (*pramuditā*) and never again regresses.
"Able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma" corresponds in meaning to the second stage, because one has abandoned a portion of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because it is free from the defilement of breaking the precepts, it is called "pure. All [who attain this] are said to be able to turn the wheel of Dharma because they accord with awakening and accord with practice;

thus, in the meaning of this sutra, awakening is itself practice. Therefore, regarding those who, after eight births or fewer, pass through successive stages until attaining bodhi in a single lifetime:
this refers to one who proceeds from the third stage through the successive stages up to the tenth stage, becoming a candidate for Buddhahood in their next life (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

This refers to the stage of attaining Buddhahood. Regarding the classification of these stages from shallow to deep, sentient beings are extremely numerous, while Bodhisattvas gradually decrease in number as they progress.
Starting from a number equal to the atoms of a world-system, they are reduced to a number equal to the atoms of a single four-continent world (*cāturdvīpaka*).
This is because as the principle becomes deeper, the stage becomes increasingly exalted; thus, those who reach it become progressively fewer. This is what is seen here.

The sharpness or dullness of the faculties is not uniform. A question is asked: "This sutra exclusively discusses the true mark (dharmatā) and directly awakens one to the Dharma-body, enabling an immediate ascent to the fruit of Buddhahood;
it does not speak of the gradual stages and levels of practice. To now explain it by means of these stages is it not a mistaken interpretation of the Buddha’s intent?
The answer is: "This is indeed the case as a matter of principle. The *Avataṃsaka* is the perfect and sudden teaching of the One Vehicle."
In this Dharma-gate, the forty-two stages that are taught all take faith as their foundation;

therefore, it is said that at the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), one attains Bodhi. Thus, the single thought-moment of the causal mind within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) already encompasses the ocean of fruition.

Therefore, it is said: "The cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause. This means that the entire sequence of stages from beginning to end resides fundamentally within the causal mind. This...
This is the gradual progression of that which is without gradual progression. As for the stages of progress described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it says:

"By means of the three progressive stages, one accomplishes the fifty-five positions. This is because, by relying on the perfection of the four fundamental precepts and the single mind, one enters into the three contemplations;
thus, through the three progressive stages, one awakens to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore, these fifty-five positions all rely upon [these foundations].

The threefold contemplation within a single mind merely delineates stages according to the depth of severing delusions; although various positions are enumerated, they are all subsumed within a single mind.
This, too, is not a gradual process characterized by sequential progression. The present sutra relies upon the four practices of peaceful dwelling.
This represents the ultimate mastery of the subtle principles of this sutra. Through hearing the discourse on the lifespan, one attains a wondrous realization of the Dharma-body;
this is identical in meaning to the principle of realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) through the three gradual stages as taught in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*.

However, while that sutra takes the "one mind and three contemplations" as its primary focus, this sutra takes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)—the fundamental Buddha-nature of sentient beings—as its primary focus, intending for them to gain entry through the realization of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Thus:

He is therefore named "Buddha. For this reason, the gradual stages of cultivation, abandonment, and practice are not discussed; rather, awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is taken as the foundation.

Now that one has attained a wondrous realization of the Dharma-body through these four practices and directly ascended to the stage of Buddhahood, the subsequent evaluation of merit is still explained by way of the various stages of the path.
This is because it relies upon the *pratyaya-buddhadhātu* (conditional Buddha-nature), and because conditions vary in their depth.

Because [the depth of realization] is profound, there are near and far degrees of awakening. However, this is spoken of solely in terms of awakening; it does not speak of severing ignorance by means of sequential stages.
This sutra discusses exclusively the true reality (*dharmatā*), as in the saying: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature. Therefore, there are no afflictions to be severed.
This is a matter of verifying awakening through stages; it is not that there are actually existing stages that can be designated by name. If...
To claim that it is difficult because of hierarchical stages is an error. As the ancient masters said: "Even the Noble Truths are not established; how then could there be any hierarchical stages?
This is truly the essence of the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These beings, referred to here simply as "those who have resolved their minds," are those who have not yet entered the Path.
The Buddha spoke thus of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas (up to the point where they) sang immeasurable verses in praise of all Buddhas.
This is the auspicious sign and proof of the Dharma of emptiness. Their lifespan is like space; they are inherently endowed with myriad virtues. Therefore, flowers rain down within emptiness.
Because their Dharma-bodies are identical, they made offerings to Śākyamuni, Prabhūtaratna, and the great assembly.

Furthermore, regarding the rain of fine powdered sandalwood, aloeswood, and other incenses: this signifies that all the supernatural powers and sublime practices inherent in the wondrous emptiness of the Dharma-body are fully perfected.
Reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven, it manifests that the Dharma-body pervades to the very limits of the realm of form. Emptiness.
From within [the assembly], voices arose praising the Buddha, saying: "The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is wondrous emptiness; the sound of the Dharma fills all places.
Thus they extolled the inconceivable merits of the Buddha.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat... (up to) ...joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"The Buddha spoke of a rare Dharma never heard before" (up to) "all have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind.
This verse of praise by Maitreya reveals that the benefits of this Dharma constitute the true cause for attaining Buddhahood in the future.

The eight lines following "The Buddha spoke of a rare Dharma" describe and praise the benefits of the Dharma. Alternatively, [it refers to] those dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression, etc., up to the twelfth [bhūmi].
The first four lines of the verse praise the initial entry into the Path up to the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the twelve lines following the "small chiliocosm" praise the third stage through to the eleventh stage. The final four lines praise the various classes of beings (*sattva*) and so forth.

The preceding verse describes how one obtains the true fruit of retribution by hearing of the lifespan [of the Buddha]. Furthermore, the section beginning with "In eight worlds below" describes sentient beings who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment] but have not yet entered the Path.
The World-Honored One has preached immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas (up to) the singing of praises for all Tathāgatas;
this verse is a portentous response. Because the Dharma-body is like space and its essence is endowed with myriad virtues, various portents appear within that space as offerings to the Buddhas.
"Such various events as these have never occurred before" (up to) "to assist the unsurpassed mind.
This is what is revealed by the following verse. Regarding the statement "such various auspicious signs as these have never occurred before":

it is because the teaching of the long duration of the lifespan was heard; thus, the wondrous response of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) assists in the arousal of the sublime mind, manifesting these various [signs].

This is an auspicious omen. The manifestation of this omen previously was to assist in revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); its manifestation now is to assist in inspiring the unsurpassed resolve (*anuttara-citta*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva... [up to] ...the merit attained shall be without limit.
These words refer to the further benefit resulting from hearing the comparison of lifespans. Regarding the immeasurable merit of a single moment of faith and understanding:
since the lifespan is like space, one who attains faith and understanding in a single thought-moment immediately enters the wondrous emptiness of the Dharma;
how could such merit have any limit?
If there were any son or daughter of good family who, having [attained] up to *samyak-saṃbodhi*, should fall back from it, such a thing is impossible.
These words refer to the lifespan of one who has faith and understanding; such a person immediately enters the Buddha-wisdom.

Therefore, practicing the five *pāramitās* for many eons while excluding *prajñā* constitutes entirely conditioned activity. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Skillful means without wisdom is bondage. This is why [it is so].

The meritorious practices performed over many kalpas do not equal the merit of the Buddha’s wisdom. Having entered the stage of the Dharma-position, one shall never again fall back into the cycle of birth and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom... (up to) "...the merit they gain is like this.

These four lines summarize and indicate the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*). "During all these kalpas... and the following twelve lines specifically praise the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
"Furthermore, if one maintains the prohibitive precepts... and the following four lines praise the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). If...

Furthermore, the eight lines beginning with "Again, practicing patience" eulogize the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). The four lines beginning with "If one further exerts diligent vigor" eulogize the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

The twelve lines beginning with "Moreover, throughout incalculable kalpas" eulogize the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). The four lines beginning with "This person, amidst hundreds of thousands...
eulogize the five perfections in total and all their merits. The eight lines beginning with "There are sons and daughters of good family... eulogize...
Comparing their merits: the merit of a single moment of faith and understanding regarding the lifespan [of the Buddha] exceeds that of one who practices the five perfections for many eons.
Because it severs all doubts and regrets and abides securely in true wisdom, transcending all conceptualization and external longing, its merit surpasses the former and is inconceivable.
"Those bodhisattvas who have practiced the path for immeasurable kalpas"—up to "the teaching of their lifespan is likewise.
This verse refers to those of superior faculties who, upon hearing the teaching of the lifespan, will certainly believe it without doubt.

The following sixteen phrases refer to those bodhisattvas who, having planted deep roots through practicing the path for immeasurable kalpas, will certainly [believe] upon hearing the teaching of their lifespan.
Because they are able to believe and accept it, they receive this sutra upon their heads. They vow that in the future they shall live long lives to deliver sentient beings;
just as the World-Honored One now preaches the Dharma of fearlessness, so too shall we preach such longevity when we attain Buddhahood in the future.
Because they believe with certainty and without doubt, the power of their vows is thus firm and steadfast.
If there are those with a profound mind who are pure and upright, they will have no doubt regarding this.
Such a verse must be believed by those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom; "profound mind" means to penetrate deeply into the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Purity ensures that the root of precepts is complete; uprightness ensures that one’s resolve and mindfulness are firm; extensive learning ensures that one serves many Buddhas;
dhāraṇī-retention ensures that one penetrates the treasury of the Dharma; and understanding according to the meaning ensures a wondrous accord with that which transcends words.
Only such a person can truly believe that this sutra shall not fall into the hands of other sentient beings.
Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear [the Buddha’s teaching] up to this point, they will be able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This refers to the meaning and purpose of the lifespan; it is the ultimate goal of the lifespan, which is the pinnacle of the Dharma-body.
Therefore, the merit attained is without limit. Because they skillfully enter the Buddha-wisdom, they are able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
"Arising" (*qi*) means "to open and develop.
How much more so for one who hears this sutra extensively, or teaches others to hear it—up to the point that they can give rise to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This demonstrates the benefit of hearing and upholding [the teaching]. The phrase "how much more so" (*he kuai*) is a term used for comparison with what precedes it; it refers to those who merely know the meaning and intent.
One will then give rise to the wisdom of a Buddha; how much more so when one hears extensively and teaches others in turn.
By upholding [the Dharma] in these six ways, one’s merit will be boundless, and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) will naturally arise.
Ajita, if a son or daughter of good family [up to] should know that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding—this refers to the mark of profound faith and understanding.

To say that one can, with a deep mind, believe and understand that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding means that the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly present, and the defiled land of Sahā is manifest as the Flower Treasury World (*kusumatalagarbha*). One who can contemplate in this manner [possesses this mark].

This constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding (*adhimukti*). Because one can suddenly transcend the ten stages (*bhūmi*) in a single thought-moment and thereby attain Buddhahood, it is called "profound faith and understanding.
In the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛivarta*), Śāriputra was permitted to enter by means of faith, and the four great disciples attained realization;
thus, that chapter is titled "Faith and Understanding. Although they received their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), their faith and understanding were not yet deep.
It was only because they believed the Buddha’s words that they were repeatedly admonished, saying: "What the Tathāgata has spoken is not false. Yet, they had not yet believed in the Buddha’s mind.

Even when the Jewel Stūpa appeared, and although they saw the many jewels and the three transformations of the Pure Land, they still did not know that Śākyamuni’s Dharma-body is eternally abiding and that the defiled land is fundamentally pure; this was because their own minds had not yet been opened.

He attained awakening. When the Buddha taught the four practices of peaceful bliss for upholding this sutra, he investigated them with diligent application; as the ground manifested before him, he awakened through his own mind.
Therefore, the Tathāgata himself spoke of the long duration of his lifespan to reveal that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and indestructible.
Reaching this point, he saw that the Dharma-body is forever without birth or extinction, and that purity and defilement are one and the same. Only then did he truly believe in the Buddha.
Therefore, the text states that when one contemplates the mind by joining the fingers, "if one can contemplate in this manner, it constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding.

Thus, the author previously stated that the chapter on Faith and Understanding extends as far as the *Pratītyasamutpāda-parivarta* (The Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa), wherein one attains understanding through faith.
From the *Devadatta-parivarta* up to this point, one realizes awakening through practice; therefore, this is called "profound faith and understanding" because of its thorough penetration.
The Dharma-body is the ultimate limit. Tiantai generally interprets the sutras through the three contemplations, and this is the core principle of his school.

By awakening to the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, one personally beholds the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were currently present; this is the mark of self-realized, profound faith and understanding.

It is not merely this; rather, it is because the wisdom of students is shallow and their minds coarse that they are unable to integrate [these teachings] into wondrous contemplation, and thus they consider them cumbersome.
How could they know the wondrous awakening of the ancients?
Furthermore, if after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa one hears this sutra (up to the point stated), such a person shall be considered as having borne the Tathāgata upon their crown.
The preceding section clarified the benefits of the "Chapter on the Lifespan"; this section clarifies the benefits of the entire sutra.

It says that merely being able to rejoice in this sutra already constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding; how much more so for those who read, recite, receive, and uphold it? Is this not so?
Is it because they bear the Tathāgata upon their heads? For this sutra is the entire body of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
After this good man, Ajita, has made such offerings for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas...
This means that if one is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, it constitutes making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha;
for this sutra is the Three Jewels in a single essence. Therefore, upholding the sutra is itself making offerings to the Three Jewels.
Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa [up to] one makes offerings to me and the community of bhikṣus,
this act of upholding the sutra— which is mentioned again here— constitutes an offering to the Triple Gem, because it demonstrates that the offering of the Dharma is supreme.

Therefore, when I speak of [the offerings] from "after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa" up to "building monasteries and making offerings to the Saṃgha," this formulation reveals that the offering of the Dharma is supreme.
It shows that one need not rely on stūpas, temples, and the like, because the practice of realizing the principle is supreme.
How much more so for a person who can uphold this sutra [up to] "quickly reach all-knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This statement implies that upholding the sutra while also concurrently practicing the six perfections results in immeasurable merit,
because such a person is able to quickly reach all-knowledge.
If a person reads, recites, receives, and upholds this sutra— up to the point of praising the merits of a bodhisattva—

the preceding statement [implied that] one need only uphold the sutra and does not need to further construct stupas, temples, or monastic dwellings, for fear that such activities would interfere with practice. Therefore,
it is stated here again that if one can both uphold the sutra and simultaneously engage in active practice, one should proceed to build temples and stupas.

A monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*). Furthermore, one can praise those who follow the three vehicles (*triyāna*). When such principles and practices are cultivated together, how could this not be even more sublime?
Moreover, for various reasons, others [should] all make offerings [to them] as if they were stupas (*stūpa*) of the Buddha.
Since this person is able to uphold the sutra, explain it, and fully cultivate numerous principles and practices,
will they not have already proceeded toward the site of enlightenment, drawn near to bodhi, sat beneath the tree of awakening, and be on the verge of attaining perfect enlightenment?
This explains the meaning of "swiftly attaining all-knowledge" mentioned above.

If there is a person who possesses such wondrous practice, then a stūpa should be erected and offerings made at all four postures of daily life; for this person has already fully realized the Buddha-mind and the Buddha-practice.
Since he is not far from the Buddha, he certainly deserves to be honored and supported. This is a summary of the merit of the marks of profound faith and understanding.

from the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter up to the six chapters ending with "Samantabhadra’s Exhortation" constitutes the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The preceding twenty-two chapters are collectively termed "Faith and Understanding," while the subsequent six chapters manifest "Practice and Realization. Therefore, [the text] uses Bhaiṣajyarāja...
"Clear conduct" is the entry. This differs entirely from the ancient interpretation; however, taking the meaning as the standard, one shall verify this for oneself when encountering the text.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty-one: "The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata."

The purpose of this chapter is as follows: Since the World-Honored One has previously expounded at length upon the merit of upholding this sutra and further demonstrated the practice of upholding it oneself, those present have attained perfect enlightenment to the ultimate degree and have fulfilled the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
Moreover, the assembly of earth-surging upholders of the sutra has been obtained; therefore, the Tathāgata rejoices and, exerting the full extent of his supernatural powers, provides certification.
Furthermore, this demonstrates the impartial Dharma-realm for those present, directly causing them to behold the Buddha’s realm before their eyes and see the Pure Land in the present moment.
This serves to manifest that the benefit of the Dharma is already perfected and is about to be entrusted as the family inheritance to the Dharma-king.
Subsequently, the emergence of the assembly from the earth signifies that the virtues of one's own mind-nature have reached fulfillment; only then does one become a [true] Dharma [heir].

The flower represents the whole body. When the Tathāgata immediately manifests his supernatural power, emitting light from every pore of his body and extending his tongue to the Brahma Heaven so that the entire earth trembles, this is what is meant by "revealing the whole body and overturning it to the very bottom."
The Buddhas all emit light together to manifest that the Way of each Buddha is identical.
The Buddhas of the ten directions sit together within the light, and a voice issues from the air, praising from afar Śākyamuni for preaching the Lotus Sūtra;
this manifests that the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions are mutually sealed. The worlds of the ten directions are pervaded without obstruction, as if they were a single buddha-field.
This is to illuminate and expand the true realm of the *dharmakāya*, thereby eliminating the limited and restricted minds of the followers of the two vehicles.
When the Tathāgata reaches this point, he exhausts his supernatural powers to proclaim the merits of this sutra;
that these merits are inexhaustible is because they encompass all the dharmas of the Tathāgata, all his sovereign supernatural powers, and all his secret treasuries. All...
These most profound matters have all been proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra; therefore, having long kept this essential point in silence, it is now being spoken.
Because it was difficult to believe and difficult to understand, there has now come a time of deep faith and deep understanding—namely, the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, the merit of upholding this is beyond the reach of thought or calculation; thus, the teaching has been revealed to this point.
The principles have been fully revealed and wondrous realization has reached perfection; thus, the Buddha’s spiritual power is exerted to seal and certify this.
Therefore, the sections prior to this chapter are judged to be the true causes for faith and understanding (*adhimukti*). Since the causal mind is now authentic, the wondrous fruit may be attained;

hence, the entrustment (*parindanā*) follows next. Regarding the purpose of this chapter: it reveals that the assembly emerging from the earth are all sons who have fulfilled their filial duties to the lineage.

The former judgment held that this chapter, along with the subsequent seven chapters, all belong to the section on the Propagation of the Teaching; it considered this chapter to be the "Initiation," as its meaning was not yet exhaustive.
Therefore, I, the ignorant one, judge that the Chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja, together with the following five chapters, constitutes the "Entry into the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision.
This is because only by proceeding from practice to the realization of the fruit does one fully exhaust the ritual framework of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
At that time, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a thousand worlds (up to) explained and transcribed [the sutra] and made offerings to it.
This assembly emerging from the earth requested that they uphold the sublime Dharma.

Yet, since this assembly emerging from the earth consists entirely of sons who have fulfilled their filial duties and have specifically come forth to uphold the sutra, why did they remain silent all along, waiting until now before finally requesting [it]?
This assembly had previously been dwelling in the space below, practicing the dhūta austerities and delighting in secluded places;
they seemed not yet to have mastered the work of engaging with the world to benefit sentient beings.

Therefore, they waited for the World-Honored One to distinguish the merits of upholding this sutra so as to strengthen their resolve and aspiration, and for him to speak of "Never-Disparaging" to demonstrate the practice of the two benefits. Thus, they have arrived here.

In the presence of the Buddha, he made a vow that after the parinirvāṇa, wherever his emanations might be or wherever they might attain parinirvāṇa, he wished for this sutra to be widely expounded in all those places.
Furthermore, he himself desired to obtain this truly pure Great Dharma; this was why he made his request.
The newly recorded assembly wished to propagate the sutra in other directions and did not dare remain in Sahā. Bhaiṣajyarāja, however, vowed to remain in Sahā.
"Venerable ones, you shall not dare to go to the ten directions.

Only those who have emerged from the earth, whose vows are great and whose minds are vast—equal to the Buddha-mind—should go to the places where their emanations reside and extensively preach this sutra; therefore, I specifically entrust it to them."
At that time, the World-Honored One caused the earth to shake in six ways from Mañjuśrī and the others [down to the ground].

This was because the Tathāgata had authorized them to uphold this sutra; thus he manifested great supernormal power to demonstrate that their original aspiration had been fulfilled, expressing a state of exultant joy.
Those who had long resided in Sahā—namely Mañjuśrī and the others in the assembly—along with those who had emerged from the earth...

This assembly was selected from among those gathered from other directions; he first manifested supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to alert them, for such power is the wondrous, effortless power of the *dharmadhātu*.
This constitutes the "Manifestation of Supernatural Transformations" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Regarding the "broad and long tongue":
among the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata, there is the mark of a tongue that can cover his face; here, it is said that he extends this broad and long tongue.
This is manifested through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Although the tongue is vast, it does not protrude from the mouth.

Now, when it is said that the broad and long tongue extends upward to the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*), the Brahma-world refers to the Sphere of Ultimate Form (*akaniṣṭha*). That it is said to "reach" there precisely demonstrates the locus where form exists.
All sounds and forms whatsoever are the sound of the Dharma. [The pores are] exceedingly...

Though the world is exceedingly vast, it is subtle. To say that "immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors issue from every pore, universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions" is intended to reveal that within each of the pores of the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*) and each of the atoms of the environmental retribution (*nirmāṇakāya*), the light of wisdom is fully pervasive;
these are all places where the Dharma is preached. This is the domain of this single Buddha, Śākyamuni.
The manifestation of such vast supernatural powers is as follows: the Buddhas beneath the various jewel trees are Buddhas who have gathered as clouds through the power of emanation.
The fact that the radiance from each of their tongue-attributes (*jihvā-vyañjana*) is equal to that of Śākyamuni, without any difference, reveals that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.
Regarding the manifestation of supernatural powers for a full hundred thousand years: the moment the light is emitted, time passes in this manner.

"Granting a long duration" reveals the equality of the three periods of time. Reaching as far as the Brahma-world signifies vertical exhaustion; pervading the ten directions signifies horizontal inclusion;

and "a hundred thousand years" signifies the three periods of time. This intends to reveal that this tongue-faculty vertically exhausts and horizontally encompasses the ten directions and the three periods of time, such that its spiritual power is all-pervasive and its Dharma-sound is spread everywhere.
The intention is to use this spiritual power to preach this sutra.

Even these merits cannot be fully exhausted. That even the smallest sounds—a cough or a snap of the fingers—can reach throughout the ten directions and cause the earth to tremble everywhere, signifies that the sound of the Dharma accords with the true Dharma-realm;
thus, wherever the sound reaches, it is a sign that the ignorance of all sentient beings who hear it is suddenly shattered. This is intended to manifest the merit of praising this sutra.
Therefore, he first manifested this supernatural power.
Among them, the sentient beings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas (and so forth), all rejoiced greatly at having attained what they had never experienced before.
These "sentient beings" refer to the eight classes of beings, each of whom was gathered through the reception of his supernatural power and opened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Among them...
The eight classes of sentient beings, all of whom dwell within the light pervading the worlds of the ten directions and are sustained by it,
were previously unable to see from afar with their physical eyes. Now, through the gathering of the Buddha’s light,

they all behold from a distance the Buddhas of the ten directions who have manifested as emanations, assembled like clouds in the sky of the Sahā world, as well as Śākyamuni, Prabhūtaratna, and the boundless [Buddhas].
The assembly surrounding Śākyamuni is what is called "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. They suddenly see the single assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were present before them;
thus, they all rejoice at having attained what they have never experienced before. This is due to being sustained by the Buddha's spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).
At that time, the various devas in the void [up to] attained unimpeded penetration as if it were a single buddha-field.
This means that the devas in the sky, by virtue of the illumination of the light, beheld the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa preaching the Lotus Sūtra.
"Turning the teaching to sentient beings so they may rejoice" means that one must first be able to enter the true emptiness of the *dharmatā* before one can awaken to this wondrous Dharma;
based on this, one is then able to turn the teaching to sentient beings so they may rejoice.
This precisely refers to sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat before one can propagate and uphold this sutra. When those sentient beings heard this voice, they all turned toward Śākyamuni...
"Proclaiming" refers to the turning of the teaching; thus, all who hear it each open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
"Scattering various necklaces and exquisite objects from afar toward Sahā" means dedicating each of one's wondrous practices toward the path of the Buddha.
"The scattered objects transform into jeweled canopies" signifies that principle (*li*) harmonizes with phenomena (*shi*), universally returning to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As for the phrase "the worlds of the ten directions are unimpededly pervasive as if they were a single Buddha-land":

when one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, then all realms of sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses become vast and free from obstruction; this is entirely brought about by the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattvas, beginning with Śikhin, saying: "The merits of this sutra cannot be fully exhausted.
This concluding statement reveals the excellence of the sutra; the various supernatural powers described above cannot be fully recounted.

For now, let us consider the mark of the tongue of Brahmā and the light from the pores illuminating the ten directions, as well as the assembly of emanated bodies gathered from the clouds of the ten directions.
The spiritual power of the Buddha, throughout a long duration of a hundred thousand years— vertically exhausting the three periods of time and horizontally pervading the ten directions,
shaking the great trichiliocosm and penetrating all Buddha-lands—

cannot exhaustively describe the merit of reciting this sutra even if such power were exercised for immeasurable kalpas; this most clearly demonstrates that this sutra is the entirety of the Dharma-realm.

Substance. Although the spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of all Buddhas is vast and beyond compare, it is nevertheless revealed only partially; it cannot yet exhaustively encompass the full measure of the *dharmadhātu*.
This is as it has been said: because it does not pervade even a single pore of Samantabhadra.

For the entire body of the *dharmadhātu*, every pore of the primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*) of all Buddhas and sentient beings, and every atom of the secondary retribution (*niśraya-phala*) world, are one.
A single [pore] encompasses the lands of the ten directions. The Great Sūtra says:
"Within each and every pore of Samantabhadra, unspeakably many lands enter in succession. The pores can receive all those Buddhas, yet the lands cannot pervade the pores."
As it is with one pore, so it is with every single pore; as it is with one atom, so it is with every single atom.

Although this sutra does not explicitly state that phenomena are mutually unimpeded (*shishi wuai*), this is because the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*) is the foundation of the four dharma-realms.
This is due to the fact that the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) expounded by this sutra is quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
The True Mind is the true aspect (*dharmatā*) of the one true dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*).
Therefore, even the supernatural powers manifested by all Buddhas cannot fully describe the merit of this sutra. As the *Avataṃsaka* states:
"Suppose there were a person who used empty space as paper, the great ocean as ink, and Mount Sumeru as a brush to write down even a single character of this sutra; its merit would not be exhausted."
This is precisely the meaning [of the word] "exhaustive.
To state it in brief: all that the Tathāgata has attained—up to and including his supernormal powers—he has proclaimed and fully expounded within this sutra.
This explains why his supernormal powers cannot be fully described. All that exists, throughout the entire dharma-realm...
It is that which possesses all things. It is the sovereign power of all spiritual transformations, the effortless great function pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It is the treasury of all secrets, the profound mystery encompassing the entire Dharma-realm. It is the most profound of all matters, penetrating to the very source and bottom of the Dharma-realm.
All of these are the total embodiment of the Dharmakāya; they can by no means be apprehended through the traces of seeing or hearing.
Seek it! This sutra now explains this clearly and distinctly. Although the aforementioned supernormal powers are vast and boundless, they still belong to that which can be seen and heard;
therefore, one cannot fully describe the merit of this sutra.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—[extending] until "all Buddhas shall attain parinirvāṇa herein"—this [passage] entrusts the assembly emerging from the earth to maintain this sutra.
This serves to conclude the preceding section by establishing the meaning that there is a complete body of the Tathāgata within [the stupa], and that stupas should be erected for it, and so forth.
As for the phrase "For what reason? and those that follow, they explain the underlying rationale.

Since all Buddhas—whether attaining enlightenment, delivering sentient beings, turning the wheel of Dharma, or entering nirvana—all emerge from this sutra, one should erect stupas to make offerings to it.
Therefore, you should propagate and uphold it so that the life of wisdom remains uninterrupted.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers... [until] they are certain and free from doubt."
The twelve lines beginning with "The Buddhas, saviors of the world" praise the matter of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
The twelve lines beginning with "Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" praise the fact that the merit of upholding this sutra cannot be fully described even by such supernatural power.

The six lines beginning with "One who can uphold this sutra" praises the fact that by upholding this sutra, one immediately beholds Śākyamuni, Prabhūtaratna, the various emanated Buddhas, and myself here now.
The Buddha’s teaching on the bodhisattva’s work—the manner in which the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas manifests—is entirely contained within this sutra;
therefore, one is able to see it. The eight lines beginning with “one who can uphold this sutra” praise the ability to uphold this sutra.
Because one sees the Buddhas, the Buddhas rejoice. The ten lines beginning with “the Buddhas sit at the site of enlightenment” praise [the benefits] arising from upholding this [sutra].

The sutra states that one immediately attains the secret and essential teachings of all Buddhas; thus, one obtains the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*). Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is the unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding their meanings (*artha*), there is the unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*). Regarding names and terminology (*nirukti*), there is the unimpededness regarding expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding inexhaustible joy in preaching, there is the unimpededness regarding joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). Therefore, it concludes by saying "all are without obstruction. This applies even after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
The final ten lines [of the verse] praise how, by attaining the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), he is able to preach the Dharma;

this constitutes the great benefit of teaching immeasurable bodhisattvas so that they all abide in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Therefore, the six lines beginning with "Thus, those who possess wisdom" conclude the verse and exhort [the audience] to uphold [the teaching].
Being about to entrust [the sūtra], he first manifests supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to demonstrate that it is impossible to fully expound this scripture.

Regarding these merits: this is intended to reveal that this sutra is the Dharma attained at the Tathāgata’s site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and its merits are vast and great, so as to inspire the firm power of aspiration in the bodhisattvas who uphold this sutra.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Two: Entrustment (*Parīndanā-parivarta*).

Regarding the purpose of this chapter's introduction: since the revelation of the revealed principle has been perfected from the preceding sections, the minds of those suited to the teaching have already attained thorough awakening, their faith and understanding are now authentic, and they are fully endowed with the true cause for attaining Buddhahood, the Tathāgata’s original intention for appearing in the world [is fulfilled].
It is already fulfilled. It is precisely like a patriarch who, having forgotten his paternal affection, would then entrust the family estate to his son;

therefore, the "Entrustment" (Parīndanā) is said to mark the conclusion of faith and understanding. Thus, this chapter follows; it is not for the purpose of severing [the teaching], but for its circulation.
These eleven chapters above constitute the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Together with the preceding twenty-one chapters, they collectively constitute "Faith" (Śraddhā).

Explanation: Generally, these belong to the category of manifesting the principle as the cause. The subsequent six chapters manifest the practice, taking clear realization and entry [into the path] as the fruit.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... (until) causing all sentient beings to universally hear and know.

When about to entrust [the teaching], he first rubbed their heads to comfort them and addressed them, thereby manifesting his compassionate pity so that they would not be startled or doubtful, but would certainly believe.
He rubbed their heads three times, demonstrating the utmost earnestness and sincerity.
Unsurpassed Bodhi is the most difficult-to-attain dharma; for kalpas upon kalpas, the Buddha practiced with diligent hardship, even throughout three thousand worlds.
There is not even a space the size of a mustard seed in this world that is not a place where a bodhisattva has sacrificed their body and life in pursuit of awakening.
It can only be accomplished through long-endured hardship; thus, it is said that unsurpassed awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) is difficult to attain.
That I now entrust [this teaching] to you, speaking again and again of its difficulty to attain, is just as a wealthy householder would want his son to know.
Regarding the hardships of its founding, I now entrust this Dharma to you, O Bodhisattvas. It is not merely that you should uphold it;
rather, I desire that you widely proclaim this Dharma so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it.
Because that which was entrusted to him is so weighty, his heart in proclaiming it is earnest. This is called the causal condition for the one great matter;
it is not a trivial thing.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion—[as far as the passage extends]—he has thereby repaid the grace of all Buddhas.
This commentary clarifies the intention behind his extensive proclamation. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions take all sentient beings as their own heart.
Whatever they themselves possess, they give entirely to sentient beings; because they possess great compassion, they have no sense of stinginess or regret.
Furthermore, they do not fear the vast number of sentient beings, for they are able to grant whatever is requested by those who seek it. This is the fundamental mind of all Buddhas.
...and is able to grant sentient beings the Buddha’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*).
Why, then, is it said that the Buddha’s wisdom consists of these three types? What is called the "Buddha’s wisdom" refers to that which sentient beings have been deluded about;
it is now granted, revealed, and shown so that they may awaken to and enter it. As for the "Tathāgata’s wisdom," it is that which [sentient beings...]
Birth is shared equally with the Buddhas; it is that which is realized only after cultivation. Natural wisdom, however, is the innate, wondrous nature;
it is fundamentally devoid of delusion or enlightenment, and does not belong to the realm of cultivation or realization. Wisdom is originally one.
It is only through being shown [the teaching] that one subsequently gains entry; through gaining entry that one subsequently practices;
and through practice that one realizes the originally existing, natural self-nature. Therefore, it is said that there are three stages.

Now, since the Buddha has already provided this instruction, he must certainly cause [beings] to realize, practice, and realize the originally existing [nature], which alone constitutes the ultimate goal. He bestows all of this upon them without stinginess; therefore, this is...
He is the great donor to all sentient beings; this mind of the Tathāgata takes sentient beings as its own mind.
Therefore, he teaches that all bodhisattvas should likewise follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata, bestowing everything upon others without giving rise to stinginess or parsimony.
Thus, in future ages, whenever there are those who have faith in the Buddha’s wisdom, one should immediately preach it for them.
This sutra enables one to attain the Buddha-wisdom. Previously, three kinds of wisdom were mentioned; now, in instructing the bodhisattvas, it speaks only of "Tathāgata-wisdom.
This is because [the Buddha] first revealed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings, so that they might personally awaken to, enter, cultivate, and realize it.
Therefore, revelation was treated as the urgent priority, which is why it is specifically mentioned here. Should it be...
There are sentient beings who do not believe in the Tathāgata’s wisdom; for them, one should provide instruction, benefit, and joy within the profound and wondrous Dharma.
That is to say, by means of the provisional teachings of the three vehicles and the secret Dharma, one should gradually lead and entice them, causing them to believe and accept it.
This is the true intent of this entrustment. Therefore it is said: "If you all can act in this way, then you will have already repaid the kindness of all the Buddhas.
At the end of the previous *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*, Śāriputra and the others were moved by the Buddha’s grace;
they even vowed to carry him upon their heads for dust-motes of kalpas and to offer their own bodies as seats throughout the trichiliocosm, yet in the end, they could not repay it.
This is the grace of the Buddhas; therefore, this exhortation concludes that if one can only propagate and proclaim this sutra, one has already repaid the grace of all Buddhas.
As it is said: "Even if one were to carry [the sutra] upon the crown of one's head for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, and offer one's body as a seat throughout the trichiliocosm."
"If one does not propagate the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, there will ultimately be no one capable of repaying their kindness.
At that time, the various Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas [said]: "So be it, World-Honored One; we pray that you have no further concern."
These bodhisattvas received their charge because of the Buddha’s entrustment. Because the Buddha stroked their heads and charged them three times, they received the charge three times in succession.
They comforted the World-Honored One, saying, "May you have no cause for concern; these are truly sons who can uphold the lineage."
This is sufficient to comfort the father’s heart.
At that time, from Śākyamuni Buddha down to the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha, all shall return to their former states.
Since this matter of entrustment is concluded, he causes the various emanated Buddhas to each return to their own lands. As for the aforementioned impoverished son—
This is an analogy. The elder thought of this son and intended to entrust him with the family estate. When the impoverished son returned, he was initially struck with alarm;
subsequently, he felt doubt; after a long time, he gained faith; and as more time passed, they became intimate.

Their father-son bond was so forgotten that the elder summoned his kinsmen, the king, and the ministers to entrust the family estate to him. Now, the appearance of Prabhūtaratna is likewise divided [into these stages].
The assembly has gathered in full. This was done to accord with the intentions of the kings and great ministers of the various realms;
thus, having now completed the entrustment, I have caused the emanated Buddhas to each return to their own lands.

Yet, I have left the Many-Treasures Stupa as it remains, for although they previously realized the Dharma-body, they had merely approached and conformed to it; now, I wish to manifest its definitive realization and entry.
Only when one wondrously accords with the Dharma-body can it be called deep entry and actual realization;

therefore, they left Prabhūtaratna behind, and his words caused the stupa to close as before, precisely manifesting that one has entered the secret treasury of the Dharma-body. Thus, he was left behind as a witness.
When these words were spoken, immeasurable [beings] throughout the ten directions (up to "having heard what the Buddha taught, all were greatly rejoiced").
They all rejoiced because they had received the entrustment of the Dharma through this realization.

As for the fact that the Buddhas who have manifested their bodies and the various bodhisattvas all rejoice, it is because they rejoice that Śākyamuni’s Dharma has something to be entrusted. Śāriputra and the newly ordained disciples...
As for "you disciples who rejoice": you rejoice because there are bodhisattvas who receive this entrustment, so that in the final age the assembly has someone upon whom to rely and take refuge.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata skillfully protects and cares for all bodhisattvas; he skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas. This is it.
I know that the Tathāgata’s appearing in the world was solely for the purpose of protecting and mindful of bodhisattvas, and specifically to entrust them with this matter.
For forty years I have sought such a person in vain; now, fortunately, I have found one and may entrust it to them.

Thus, the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world has been fulfilled, and the task of benefiting sentient beings is here completed. This is what is called "the teaching of the Dharma for bodhisattvas."
That which was protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness has now been fully disclosed. Therefore, it is now entrusted.

Those who receive this entrustment merely provide a seal of authentication for the mind; however, to realize the fruit of fruition, one must necessarily practice. This is what is meant by "first awakening, then practicing.
Thus, the final six chapters, through figures such as Bhaiṣajyarāja, correctly manifest that one must practice in accordance with the Dharma before [attaining realization]. Only then...
To realize and enter [this] is called "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. How could this be regarded as a mere empty reception?

Therefore, my humble judgment that it signifies "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" is intended to clarify its practice. If one speaks of its circulation, then this sutra serves as the general circulation for all the temporal teachings of a single lifetime.
Let the Wise examine this in detail.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Three: The Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. Regarding the purpose of this chapter’s inclusion:
since the preceding sections have already fully revealed the principle (*li*), this chapter now reveals the practice (*xing*) in order to clarify entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The former constitutes the teaching for bodhisattvas; the latter constitutes practicing according to that teaching to attain actual realization. Because...

Regarding the "Medicine King who Clarifies Practice": this means that although those of the Two Vehicles have awakened to the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*), they still possess subtle habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*) that have not yet been purified.

Consequently, it is difficult for them to engage with the secular world to benefit sentient beings; they must still pass through the service of many Buddhas and extensively cultivate various practices.

They necessarily rely on the medicine of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and the methods of its regulation and treatment, to thoroughly purify subtle ignorance and destroy [the obstacles of] co-arising [delusion].
The two attachments to birth and my Dharma are taken as "sublime practices," through which one may then realize entry [into the path].
Therefore, the opening question asks how the Medicine King wanders in the Sahā world and performs hundreds of thousands of millions of difficult and painful practices.

This precisely demonstrates that when those of the Two Vehicles first venture onto the perilous path of birth and death, they rely entirely upon the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; thus, he is called the Medicine King.
In the past, by hearing the Lotus Sūtra, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies.

Thereby, he was able to destroy the innate dual attachments to self and dharmas, and through his supernormal powers, he was able to make offerings to the Buddha and receive his entrustment. Thus, he made offerings to the Buddha with his very body.

O宿王華 (Sudr̥ṣṭiraśmi), this sutra can save all sentient beings [up to] it can untie all the bonds of birth and death.
These words describe the supreme efficacy of the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*). "Able to save all" means it is able to uproot the suffering of birth and death for sentient beings.

"Able to bring about freedom from suffering and affliction" refers to the causes of suffering, which are the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the results of suffering, which are the various forms of duḥkha-duḥkha. It brings benefit to sentient beings.
This immediately fulfills their aspirations. These three points highlight its superior efficacy.

Just as the twelve similes below that of the "Cooling Pond" specifically manifest this superior efficacy, so too do the sections from "This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*" onwards apply the Dharma to the aforementioned similes.
In brief, it enables sentient beings to leave behind all suffering, affliction, and illness, and to untie all the bonds of birth and death.
Furthermore, the suffering, pain, bondage, and attachment of sentient beings all arise from the conditioning and fettering of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision have opened, the light of wisdom manifests before him; being able to shatter ignorance, all sufferings are spontaneously extinguished—just as darkness is dispelled when one obtains a lamp.
If a person hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the merit they obtain will likewise be immeasurable.
This statement regarding "hearing" the sublime Dharma implies that because it possesses such superior efficacy, the merit of those who transcribe it is boundless,
and the merit of making offerings to it is immeasurable.

"O Rājagṛha-kusuma, if there be anyone who hears [this] (up to) 'after this woman's body is exhausted, she shall no longer receive [rebirth],' this means that if one hears even a single chapter, such as the 'Bhaiṣajyarāja,' one shall likewise attain immeasurable merit. This is like the hexagram Qian (乾) extending.
Qian is taken as Yang and Kun as Yin; thus Qian represents the male and Kun the female, because Qian is firm and Kun is yielding.
This Lotus Sūtra states that the Buddha-nature is a diamond seed, firm and indestructible;
therefore, when a woman upholds this sūtra, she enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and shall forever serve as the true cause for Prajñā. The seed of Buddha-nature persists through kalpas.
It is not worn away; therefore, one shall no longer receive a female body.
Furthermore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one shall likewise not be afflicted by the defilements of pride, jealousy, and other such impurities.
This statement means that the benefits obtained by women who practice according to the Dharma are even more excellent than those of men.

In the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, one is born through transformation from a lotus flower; this Buddha has taught that those who are able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha shall immediately attain rebirth there.
Now, if women in this degenerate age can practice according to what is taught in this sutra, they shall likewise attain rebirth.
Those who are born [there] enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, whereby they suddenly shatter ignorance and suddenly sever afflictions.
Because the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; this is the cause of the Pure Land.
Now, greed, anger, delusion, pride, and jealousy are the most prominent traits of women. Yet, by practicing according to the sutras, in a single moment—
They are severed instantaneously; being no longer afflicted by them, the body attains purity, and rebirth in the Pure Land becomes certain.
Regarding the "final five hundred years" after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa: in the first five hundred years, liberation is firm; in the second five hundred years, meditative concentration is firm;
in the third five hundred years, erudition is firm; and in the fourth five hundred years, merit and virtue are firm.
It is firm. The "final five hundred years" refers to the period when strife and contention are firmly entrenched;
that it is said women uphold [the Dharma] during this difficult time is why their attainment of benefit is most supreme.
As it is with women, so it should be understood for men.
Having attained the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, they achieve such power of merit and wisdom.

This refers to the merit of women who, by upholding this sutra, are born in the Pure Land. It is only upon attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*) that one realizes it;
having already realized the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*) and having already shattered false views, the faculty of the eye becomes pure.
Having already transformed the seven consciousnesses and their objects, one beholds seven million two hundred and twenty thousand *nayuta* Ganges-sands [of Buddhas].

The Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, manifest before one’s mind through the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas; therefore, they behold [the practitioner] from afar and praise them together, saying:
“You are able to [accomplish this], even down to the point where there is no one equal to you. These are all the words of praise from the Buddhas.
Because these are not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) merits, they cannot be burned or swept away; because they accord with the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, it is said that they can never be exhausted.

Regarding the phrase "destroying all demons and the like": the various demons refer to the demon of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*); the army of birth and death refers to the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*);
and the remaining enemies refer to the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*).

To say that one can destroy and utterly crush them means that by engaging in battle against the demons of the five aggregates, afflictions, and death, one achieves great merit and renown, transcends the three realms, and breaks the net of Māra; therefore, it is said that one "can."
"Breaks" means to destroy. Because one has attained the wisdom-life of all Buddhas, all Buddhas protect one together.

Because one has transcended the world, gods and humans cannot equal one. Because one has attained the Buddha-wisdom of the One Vehicle, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of the Three Vehicles cannot be equaled;
this is because those of the Three Vehicles have not yet attained the Buddha-wisdom. Therefore, it is concluded: "This Bodhi..."
Sādhana is endowed with such power of merit and wisdom; this is praised by means of the woman, and thus her great benefit is extensively established.
If there is anyone who hears of the merits obtained by this Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva (up to what has been described above), [they shall likewise obtain them].
The preceding statement spoke of being able to practice the entire sutra; this present statement speaks only of the benefit of being able to rejoice in a single chapter, that of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Because one can rejoice in and praise what is good, the faculty of the tongue becomes pure, and thus the mouth emits the fragrance of the blue lotus.
Because one has already realized that the physical body is itself the Dharma-body, the pores of the skin emit the fragrance of sandalwood. And as for this merit...
His virtues cannot be fully recounted. After Kumārajīva passed away, a single branch of a blue lotus sprouted before his stupa.
When the stupa was opened to examine it, the flower was seen to have emerged from the root of his tongue; this was the verification of his translation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Therefore, from "O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña" until "the illness will immediately be extinguished, leading to neither aging nor death," this single chapter is entrusted to Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña.
The intent is that the upholding of this sutra must take ascetic practice as its foundation.
During the final five hundred years, in Jambudvīpa at a time when Māras are powerful and the Dharma is weak, it cannot be widely propagated except through ascetic practice.
To proclaim this sutra, one cannot do so without being protected; therefore, he entrusts it to the Lord of the Night (Kṣitigarbha), lest various māras find an opportunity.

He specifically entrusts it to the Lord of the Night to protect it with his supernatural powers because this sutra is a sublime medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa, like the celestial nectar (amṛta).
Thus it is said: "Illness shall be extinguished, and there will be no aging."
The Immortal One did not [entrust this] to the assembly of those who emerged from the earth, though he intended for them to travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions to propagate it widely.
Furthermore, even though he entrusted the Medicine King specifically with the Sahā world, he was not yet satisfied.

Now, that he entrusts this chapter solely to the Constellation King (Nakṣatrarāja), charging him to cause it to be widely proclaimed and disseminated here in Jambudvīpa—how much more so, then, in Jambudvīpa?
It is but one of the four continents; its territory is extremely narrow and its people are exceedingly wicked. Why does the Buddha alone hold this place in such high regard?
Although the ten directions are vast, they are truly the Buddha’s fundamental concern. Because the Buddha transforms the Sahā world, beings are not born in the other three continents;
he manifests only in Jambudvīpa, which is the locus for the teaching of the body. Since many people therein encourage evil, he has specifically entrusted [the Dharma] to it.
This indicates that the people of Jambudvīpa have a karmic affinity with this sutra; therefore, it serves as an excellent medicine.
It is not that this sutra cannot transform and guide them, nor is it that ascetic practices cannot propagate its teachings; thus, this chapter alone is singled out for special emphasis.
“Ratnakusuma, if you see anyone who upholds this sutra... [as far as] ...you should give rise to such a mind of reverence.
This is an exhortation for Ratnakusuma to respectfully honor those who uphold the sutra. The blue lotus is a metaphor for the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind.

The powdered incense is a metaphor for subtle and wondrous supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). It signifies that those who uphold this sutra have already perfected its teachings; therefore, one scatters it over them.

This is because such individuals will before long sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), defeat the armies of Māra, preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, and emerge from the ocean of birth and death.
One must certainly revere them as if they were Buddhas.
When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva" was being preached—up to the "Dhāraṇī of Languages"—this refers to the benefits gained from hearing this chapter.

Because one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and deeply realizes the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one penetrates the fact that the languages of all sentient beings all enter into the dharma-nature;
thus, one attains the dhāraṇī gate of total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
It is said that when the Medicine King attains the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms, all forms are the Buddha-body.
Now, regarding the dhāraṇī of speech, all sounds and voices are the Dharma-sound.

This is because a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage, upon emerging from the concentration of True Suchness and advancing to the ninth stage, occupies the rank of a Dharma Master, manifesting physical forms to preach the Dharma. This...
In the seventh stage, it is already fully embodied yet subtle; therefore, it constitutes the mark of superior progress for the subsequent stages.
The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, within the jeweled stupa, [proceeds] to benefit immeasurable all sentient beings.
This is because it was explained that the Bodhisattva Medicine King, through his past practices of asceticism and his upholding of this sutra, had already perfectly realized the Dharma-body.
Therefore, Many Treasures praised the Bodhisattva Constellation King Flower and asked about this matter; he offered this praise for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The appearance of Prabhūtaratna was originally intended to authenticate this sutra; its underlying purpose was to find a person to perpetuate the life of wisdom.
Therefore, he now praises Bhaiṣajyarāja, and subsequently summons Gadgadasvara.
Having found the person, the final assembly shall not be seen again. Fascicle Six.
The General Meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree;
Expounded by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Mount Nanyue.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Four: The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.

The purpose of this chapter is to demonstrate that one who has truly ascended to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) through the Samādhi of the Lotus Sutra and realized the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*), then arises from the eighth stage to advance to the ninth stage, manifesting the function of True Suchness and attaining mastery over both form and mind. Thus, one attains [the state of] a *Tathāgata*.
The Samādhi of Illusion. Abiding in the rank of Dharma Master, he manifests emanated bodies to preach the Dharma through ultimate awakening;

responding without thought, he is specifically renowned by the name "Wonderful Sound" (Ghoṣadatta). This chapter follows because Wonderful Sound manifests bodies according to the various classes of beings to preach the Dharma.
This is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) of the self-nature of the Dharma of Perfect Enlightenment. The previous "Medicine King" was the mind-made body of the bliss of samādhi;
it exists when one enters meditative absorption and does not exist when one emerges from it.

This mind-made body manifests according to the various types [of beings] through the entry and emergence of samādhi, and because it is a transformation of karmic maturation (*vipāka*), it possesses the appearance of coming and going. As for Avalokiteśvara...
Thus, one should know that the Dharma-realm dependent origination is manifested through the universal gate.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [extended his light] to as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
This reveals that through the perfection of the causes—the sublime practices of upholding the sūtra—one is about to ascend to the fruition of awakening.

Therefore, light is emitted to summon Mañjughoṣa, thereby demonstrating the sign of the profound convergence of cause and fruit. Among the ninety-seven marks of a Great Man possessed by a Buddha, the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head is the foremost;
this is known as the "invisible crown" (*anavalokitamūrdha*). From this, light is emitted to demonstrate the dharma of the unsurpassed fruition.
This is the light flowing from the wisdom [of the Buddha]. The light from the white tuft between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*) demonstrates the light flowing from the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way.

Taking this wondrous wisdom as the fundamental causal mind, the simultaneous emission of these two lights now symbolizes the image of the true cause acceding to the fruit—the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) merging with the original source.
At the beginning of the sutra, when about to expound the wondrous Dharma, he first emits the light from his eyebrows to demonstrate this.

The true mark is the ultimate reality. It is intended for the practitioner to realize the essence of this light as the initial aspiration for awakening, thereby constructing the true mark and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Now that the two attachments have been shattered and wondrous practice is perfected, the two lights are emitted simultaneously to manifest the identity of cause and fruit.
Initially, it illuminated only eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction.

This manifests how, by means of awakening to the true reality (*dharmatā*), one transforms the realms of sense bases, objects, and consciousness—which are agitated and deluded by the ignorance of sentient beings—into that very reality.
Now, it illuminates throughout the eastern direction as many worlds as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* Ganges Rivers.

Although it says "illuminating throughout," this is merely a partial illustration used to demonstrate the perfect illumination of the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). For the Dharma-realm is boundless.
