Without departing from the restless roots and sense objects of sentient beings, one expands and fulfills [this light] until it is universally fused and unimpeded;
therefore, it first illuminates the eastern direction.
Beyond this number of worlds, there is a world where the light from the white tuft of hair shines everywhere throughout that land.

This statement regarding the illumination of the Buddha-land demonstrates that initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) possesses efficacy; it is the manifestation of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
The world is named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*), which is the land of eternal quiescent light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*), the realm inhabited by the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The Buddha’s name is Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Vimalapuṣpa-jyoti-rāja-jñāna*): "Pure Flower" symbolizes wondrous conduct as the cause, while "Constellation King Wisdom" [symbolizes the fruition].
This refers to the fruition-enlightenment (*phala-bodhi*). The intent is to clarify that this fruition-enlightenment is taken as the causal mind of the self;

therefore, he is titled the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Vimalasupratiṣṭhitaśrīcūḍarāja*). This fruition-Buddha of the *nirvāṇa-prabhāsvara* (tranquil light) realm had previously remained entirely unmanifest.
Now, because the white-hair radiance of Śākyamuni shines universally throughout his land—the white-hair radiance symbolizing the wisdom of the causal mind—it now illuminates that Buddha.

This section correctly demonstrates the aspect of the initial convergence of the source and the manifestation. Therefore, regarding the two lights, it mentions only the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*).
At that time, in the land of All-Pure Radiance Adornment (*Sarva-vimala-prabhā-saṃbhava*), [there appeared] great samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
These words state that the Bodhisattva of Initial Enlightenment attains all samādhis; this serves to manifest the sign of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Within the Land of Pure Light, there is a Bodhisattva named Wondrous Sound who, as a ninth-stage Bodhisattva, emerges from the Samādhi of True Suchness.
As if coming from the Land of Pure Light, he occupies the rank of Dharma Master and preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, teaching without deliberate thought.

It is like the sound of a celestial drum; therefore, it is called "Wondrous Sound. This arises from deeply realizing the true suchness (*tathatā*) of ultimate reality, giving rise to the function of great wisdom;
it is the sign of the stages from the ninth bhūmi up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). From the time this stage Bodhisattva first ascended to the bhūmis...

Having served many Buddhas, it is said that he has long planted the roots of virtue. Having drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas, he has already realized the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*) and has deeply entered the *dharmadhātu*;
thus it is said that he has accomplished profound wisdom. Regarding his attainment of the *Sudarśana-dhvaja-lakṣaṇa-samādhi* and others, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"A Bodhisattva of the ninth stage attains the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna*)."
Upon entering the stage of receiving office, they immediately attain ten million *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis.
What are now called the sixteen kinds of samādhis, such as the "Exquisite Banner" (*Sudhvaja*) and so forth, all emerge from the *tathatā-samādhi*.

They are given distinct names based on their specific functions; therefore, they are attained through the accomplishment of profound wisdom. Because this bodhisattva is well able to expound [the Dharma],...
The Dharma subdues heterodox paths and destroys the deviant to reveal the orthodox; thus it is called the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner.

Because one realizes the ultimate reality through upholding this sūtra, it is called the Lotus Samādhi. Because the Buddha’s knowledge and vision purify subtle ignorance, it is called the Samādhi of Pure Virtue.
Because it reveals original enlightenment, forever leaving behind all fetters and attaining great self-mastery...

Because he dwells [therein], it is called the Samādhi of the Play of the Sovereign King (*Rājaratnavikrīḍita*). Because he universally responds to the capacities of all beings through unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), it is called the Samādhi of Unconditioned Compassion.
Because the Dharma he preaches seals all phenomena with the seal of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), it is called the Samādhi of the Wisdom Seal (*jñānamudrā*).
Because all his speech accords with the True Dharma, it is called the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings.
Regarding samādhi: because True Suchness (tathatā) is the foundation of all practices, it is called the "Samādhi that Accumulates All Meritorious Qualities.

Because the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is manifested therein, it is called the "Pure Samādhi. Because one attains the function of great wisdom and is liberated from all fetters and attachments, it is called the "Samādhi of the Play of Supernatural Powers.
Because the light of wisdom destroys the darkness of ignorance, it is... [omitted].
It is called the Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom because it accords with reality and its wondrous function adorns the Dharma-body; hence it is called the Samādhi of the King of Adornments.
It is called the Samādhi of Pure Radiance because it is forever free from defilements and obstructions, and the light of wisdom shines constantly.

It is called the Samādhi of the Pure Treasury because the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is itself the Tathāgata-garbha. It is called the "Unshared" Samādhi because it does not belong to the three vehicles.
The "昧" (samādhi) refers to the Middle Way within every moment of thought through wisdom; therefore, it is called the "Sun-Swirling Samādhi.
This is a brief mention of the general name of the samādhi; in reality, one attains hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great samādhis, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
The light of Śākyamuni Buddha illuminates their bodies [extending] to Bodhisattva King of Adornment and Bodhisattva Superior Medicine.
This signifies that initial awakening (ādikṣānti-bodhi) possesses efficacy, while original awakening (mūla-bodhi) is its manifest aspect. The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The meaning of initial awakening is based upon original awakening. Thus, when Miaoyin addressed King of Hosts Wisdom, he sought to harmonize initial awakening with original awakening.
Awakening arises from the essence to manifest its function; therefore, he vows to go to the Sahā world to see Śākyamuni Buddha.

Because his fundamental causal mind was previously based on great wisdom, and because upon seeing Mañjuśrī he will gather all practices to enter the wondrous, perfect sea of fruition, he beholds Bodhisattvas such as Bhaiṣajyarāja, Śūradatta, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
At that time, from the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña up to the Tathāgata’s adornment of merit and wisdom,
[the text] shows the sublime practice of equality because Gadgadasvara requested to go to the Sahā world to visit Śākyamuni Buddha.
"Do not despise that land or give rise to thoughts of inferiority"— this is intended to reveal that the sublime practice of a Bodhisattva must necessarily involve [engagement with] defilement.
When purity is attained, subject and object are forgotten, and mental images are extinguished; only then does one enter the equal Dharma-realm.

As for the fact that the bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear small and humble, it is because they wish sentient beings to perceive the Dharma-body through their immediate manifestations and transformations; the intent lies in the fact that the essence is originally not small.
Your body, forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height, is due to the four immeasurable minds and the great vows made in response to the faculties and sense-objects.
This is what is accomplished. Six million eight hundred thousand yojanas is the transformation of the six sense organs and the eight consciousnesses into the wondrous, pure Dharma-body.

Regarding the phrase "all are the power of the Tathāgata," the activities of Bodhisattvas all rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom—which is unconditioned and non-active—yet they manifest transformations in infinite ways.
Therefore, it is said: "The merit and wisdom of the playful exercise of supernatural powers."
[The Buddhas] with wisdom and so forth.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat, [proceeded until he reached a platform made of] *candana* and *vaiḍūrya*, with *vaidūrya* and *tapanīya* gold, and *jāmbūnada* gold, and a base made of *cāmpeya* and *gośīrṣa* sandalwood, and a pedestal made of *candana* and *vaidūrya*.
This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, as he was about to arrive at the Sahā world, first manifested this auspicious sign of flowers as a precursor. By means of the wondrous state of non-action...

Because of this power, he did not rise from his seat. As for the manifestation of eighty-four thousand lotus flowers made of various jewels through the power of samādhi, it was to demonstrate the wondrous function of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Thus, the lotus flowers were manifested through the power of samādhi.
The Great Sūtra states: "A Bodhisattva of the ninth stage attains one million asaṃkhyeya samādhis.
The last of these samādhis is named 'Receiving the Supreme Position of All-Knowledge. When this samādhi manifests before them, a great precious lotus flower suddenly appears.
This flower is vast and expansive, its dimensions equaling those of a trichiliocosm."
"...adorned with various interspersed wondrous jewels," and so forth. Question: When the Wondrous Sound Bodhisattva came to see Śākyamuni, he had not yet received his office;
yet to explain it by this [example] is not particularly excessive? Answer: This is spoken by way of analogy.

Because the Bodhisattva has deeply realized the true mark (*dharmatā*) and entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because his practice has reached its ultimate fulfillment, at the moment when cause and effect converge—[this is what is meant].
At this juncture, there naturally arises inconceivable power that manifests as great transformative power. Since they are equal according to principle, the metaphors employed are likewise identical.

This is because the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* correctly explains the fulfillment of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), which—referring to the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—is when wondrous practice is already perfected and one is destined for profound union with the Truth.
Because the wondrous practice in this sūtra is non-abiding, it does not speak of gradual progression.
Furthermore, if we consider only the manifestation of the principle, it must certainly be so; what cause for doubt could there be?
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince (up to) also desired to make offerings and listen to the Lotus Sūtra.
In this passage, Mañjuśrī observes the flower and poses a question, intending to reveal the purpose of Gadgadasvara’s arrival; thus, the Buddha answers him.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, reality is established through wisdom. In the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, when Sudhana first sees Mañjuśrī, he is directed to visit spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
At the very end, Mañjuśrī reaches out his right hand from afar to stroke [the Bodhisattva’s] crown. This signifies that the fulfillment of wisdom is not different from the initial resolve.
This sutra likewise establishes its substance through wisdom; thus, at the beginning, a single ray of light is emitted to reveal the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Because it was initiated by Mañjuśrī, [the Bodhisattva] now enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Furthermore, Gadgadasvara comes to bear witness, again because of Mañjuśrī.
Thus it is elucidated. Since the essential purports of the two sūtras are identical, their symbolic representations are likewise equal.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "that bodhisattva has come so that I may behold him."
This was Mañjuśrī who, prompted by the capacity of the audience, posed the question; it may be understood from the text as it stands.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [up to] the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī said: "I wish to see your body."
This is Prabhūtaratna summoning Gadgadasvara. Gadgadasvara originally intended to draw near to Śākyamuni, as well as to behold Mañjuśrī and hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Yet, the reason he was summoned to appear by means of Prabhūtaratna is precisely to manifest that one who has entered the state of *samyaksambodhi* must rely upon the *dharmakāya* to come forth and receive him;
it is not a matter of the gate of provisional transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*). Thus, Prabhūtaratna summons Gadgadasvara.
Afterwards, he still remained in mid-air. As for why he did not speak from this point until the end of the assembly:

it is because those who practice by upholding this sutra have already wondrously harmonized with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and merged into the ocean of fruition (*phala-samudra*). Having realized that there are no two distinct aspects, they are free from the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).

Since the Dharma-body has neither "this" nor "that," there is no mutual seeing of one another. Therefore, they see him at the time of his awakening; once they have entered [the state of non-duality], they do not see him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land (until: "a hundred thousand celestial instruments played spontaneously without being struck").

This was the manifestation of Gadgadasvara’s arrival. As for his coming together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, it signifies that by means of the wondrous practice of upholding this sutra, he had entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
thus, having integrated the eighty-four thousand afflictions, he had attained spiritual transformation.
This is the penetration of wondrous function. Through the course of wondrous practice, ignorance is suddenly shattered; therefore, as he passes through various lands, the earth quakes in six ways.
Whatever he does is entirely a true cause; therefore, lotus flowers rain down everywhere, and the natural sound of the Dharma resounds.
Therefore, celestial music resounded spontaneously. All these were manifestations of virtue based upon his conduct; thus, the auspicious signs responded accordingly.

This Bodhisattva’s eyes were like the broad petals of a vast blue lotus flower (*utpala*)... [omitted] ...he prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet and presented him with a necklace of pearls.
This is the ritual for when this [Bodhisattva] of Wondrous Sound has arrived.
"Eyes like vast blue lotuses" and so forth describe the physical marks and signs of the body of Wondrous Sound, clarifying that his body measures forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height.
Entering the seven-jeweled platform signifies entering the platform within the flower. Ascending into the void represents ascending into the emptiness of the *dharmatā*. By means of necklaces...
Regarding "Adorned and honoring Śākyamuni": this signifies that the Dharma-body is adorned with sublime conduct.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...are you at peace, free from affliction, and able to endure as you dwell for a long time?"
This is the message of inquiry from the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, respectfully addressed by Gadgadasvara to his original teacher.

The matters of inquiry concern the hardships of this Sahā world of endurance; it is because the World-Honored One has manifested his body to share the sufferings of the people that he asks these questions.
His inquiry regarding Prabhūtaratna likewise uses the phrase "little affliction," which clearly demonstrates that the Sahā world is not easily entered.
It is the ground.
World-Honored One, I have now come here desiring to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna...

This vision of the two World-Honored Ones by Gadgadasvara is the manifestation of the initial awakening (prathama-abhisambodhi) coinciding with the fundamental awakening (mūla-abhisambodhi). Furthermore, listen to...
To behold both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and Mañjuśrī is the sign of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) and the merging of the two wisdoms in profound stillness.

To see both the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of Prabhūtaratna and the reward and transformation bodies (*saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni signifies that once original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣājñāna*) is manifested,
the three bodies are one essence— non-dual and indivisible.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue (up to the point where he asks): "By cultivating what merit does one possess such supernatural power?
This question concerns the original cause of Gadgadasvara. He asks by means of "Flower Virtue" because the flower symbolizes the root of wondrous conduct.
This reveals that such powers of samādhi and supernormal faculties of Gadgadasvara are all accomplished based upon sublime conduct;
therefore, he poses his question by way of a pretext.
The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva: "...In this present life, in the land of the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (Śubhavyūha), he possesses such supernormal powers."
This response recounts the original cause of Gadgadasvara. The Buddha whom he originally served was named Meghasvararāja (Cloud-Thunder-Voice King).

Because dense clouds were about to rain down moisture upon all beings, thunder must first issue as a warning; thus, his voice responded with sovereign mastery to the capacities of sentient beings, and he was named Cloud-Thunder-Voice King.
This was a title bestowed according to his manifestation of the Dharma. That Gadgadasvara took him as his teacher was indeed for a specific reason.
Because all worlds do not depart from the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the land is named "Manifesting All Worlds.
This is the true land that serves as the basis. Because sentient beings have aspirations, it manifests in accordance with their perceptions;

thus it is named "Joyful Vision," which refers to the moment when the transformation [of the Buddha] accords with the capacities of those to be taught. The number twelve thousand represents the image of the mutual correspondence between the sense faculties and their objects.
"One hundred thousand" refers to the great number of one hundred thousand. "Music and dance" symbolize conduct that is subtle, wondrous, and pleasing.

"Eighty-four thousand" is the enumerative number representing the mutual relationship between the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the Dharma-gates. A "bowl" (*pātra*) is called a "vessel of appropriate measure" (*pramāṇika-bhājana*);

it symbolizes the Dharma that accords with the capacities and measures of sentient beings. By means of this, the Bodhisattva, in the past, at the gateway of the faculties and their objects, by means of one hundred thousand...

Through subtle and wondrous conduct, he extensively transforms sentient beings; he is able to transform afflictions into Dharma-gates, and he is able to know the faculties of sentient beings to respond universally and teach them according to the times.

Because he possessed such causes of wondrous conduct in the past, he has now realized the fruit and received the name "Wonderful Sound" (Ghoṣadatta), and thus possesses such matters of samādhi and supernormal powers. This is indeed...
This was realized upon entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, it is said that he possesses such supernatural power.
What do you think, Flower Virtue, regarding [the Buddhas] up to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas?
This inquiry clarifies that past causes serve as proof for present conditions. Thus it is said:
"He who offered musical performances and presented precious vessels was none other than this present Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.
Because he has long made offerings to the Buddhas with exquisite sounds and has deeply planted roots of virtue, the power of his retributive response is such as this.
"Śubhavyūha, you have merely seen the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara (up to) preaching this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings.
This was intended to speak of the manifestations of Gadgadasvara, so that you might witness his vast and great supernormal powers; yet his body remains here."

Manifesting various bodies and preaching this sutra for the sake of sentient beings everywhere, he has entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the cause of wondrous sound and the wondrous Dharma.
Having destroyed the two attachments and purified the two obstacles, he has already realized the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Now, arising from the samādhi of True Suchness, he enters the nine stages up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and dwells therein.

Regarding the stage of the Dharma Master: by the power of samādhi, he manifests bodies within the ten realms. Since he is about to explain these manifested forms, he first indicates their general characteristics.
He may manifest the body of a Brahmā King, or the body of Śakra (the Lord of Devas), and so on, even transforming into a female body to preach this sūtra.

This statement refers to manifesting bodies within the ten realms to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate. It first cites the Brahma heavens and extends down to the states of the three miserable paths.
Those among the six destinies who reside in the good realms are able to hear the Dharma; therefore, it says, "he preached this sutra.
As for those in the three miserable paths, they are unable to hear the Dharma; he merely provides relief from their suffering.
"Flower Virtue" refers to the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*). [The phrase] "even so in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" likewise applies to all such realms.
This passage reiterates the aforementioned supernatural powers to extensively manifest their wondrous functions.

To say that he can manifest his body within the six destinies and possesses these various kinds of supernormal transformations without any diminution of his wisdom is like dividing a single lamp into hundreds of thousands.
The lamp remains as it was originally. Having already acted for the sake of others, one possesses all the more; having already given to others, one possesses all the more.

To "illuminate the Sahā world with a certain measure of wisdom" means that by means of the various samādhis of Buddha-wisdom, one is able to enter the mental activities of all sentient beings; therefore, it is said that each obtains what they know.
"Regarding the fact that it is likewise so in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions":

this means that it is not only in the Sahā world, but he is able to manifest divided bodies in immeasurable worlds. This also indicates the manifestation of the bodies of the four types of noble beings.
If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a śrāvaka—up to the power of wisdom, such are its workings.
This is the manifestation of the bodies of the four types of noble ones to preach the Dharma. By manifesting such bodies, he preaches the Dharma according to the various classes of beings.
Although this is the power of samādhi and supernatural faculties, it is actually due to the power of entering the Buddha’s wisdom that it occurs.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "[Up to] 'you are thus able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings. [The questioner asks:

"In what samādhi does this Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound (Ghoṣadatta) abide, such that he is able to respond so wonderfully? The Buddha replied: "It is called the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies (*sarvarūpakāyasaṃdarśana-samādhi*).
This is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) whose intrinsic nature is the very essence of the Dharma of Perfect Enlightenment. — *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*
It is asked: What is the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) that realizes the self-nature of dharmas?
It refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), wherein one observes and realizes that all phenomena, such as illusions and the like, are entirely non-existent.

Thereupon, the body and mind undergo transformation, and one attains the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) as well as other gateways of samādhi, immeasurable marks, powers, masteries, and clarities, which are adorned like exquisite flowers and are as swift as one’s will.

It is like a magical illusion, a dream, the moon in water, or a reflection in a mirror; it is neither the primary elements nor their derivatives, yet it possesses all the various limbs and features of the primary and derivative elements in full adornment.
Because it penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*), it enters into all Buddha-fields and great assemblies.
This is called the "mind-made body born of the realization of the nature of phenomena" (*dharmasvabhāvavabodhamanomaya-kāya*). Commentary: This refers to the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage...

The Bodhisattva realizes the *tathatā* (true suchness) of the one mind and advances to the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), where he gives rise to the functioning of *tathatā* and attains the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi).
Within this single mind, through its transformative power, he can manifest immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) that arise simultaneously, like flowers blooming.
Just as he travels at will without obstruction through stone walls, it is said that his swiftness is "like that of the mind. He thus advances to the tenth [stage].
The Ground. Because one transforms all sentient beings according to whatever is recollected, it is said that one "enters accordingly into the great assemblies of all Buddha-fields.

This refers to the Bodhisattva’s cultivation; the former [stage] concerns the attainment of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedyāryajñāna*), while this concerns entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) to sever delusions and realize the truth.
Upon reaching this point, there spontaneously arises inconceivable karmic activity, which corresponds directly to the essence of reality. It is not...

This is because it is delimited by specific stages and positions. If one does not constrain oneself by practicing to achieve virtue, but merely speaks of "circulation," then why were there the names "Wondrous Sound" and "Avalokiteśvara"?
Moreover, it would be of no benefit even for entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision.
When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, [the assembly] also attained this samādhi and dhāraṇī.
These words describe the wondrous benefits of the vehicle of the Dharma; therefore, those who hear it are identical in both their severance of afflictions and their realization of the fruit.
At that time, from the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara until the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa, they attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

This means that the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara returned to his own land to report back to his original teacher, withdrawing his manifested functions back into his essential nature; thus, he returned to his native country.

Because they have not yet entered the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Suyukta-bodhi) and still abide in the causal state, they enter and emerge from samādhi; thus, there are signs of coming and going.

All this coming and going relies upon the wondrous power of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra), whereby all deeds are perfected as sublime practices. Therefore, they rain down precious lotus flowers and perform various kinds of musical arts.
Because they practice together and realize together, they cause their companions—eighty-four thousand people—to all attain [enlightenment].
Through the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms, forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas upon hearing the Dharma.
Because Puṣpadatta had posed a question, he attained the Lotus Samādhi; furthermore, he entered it through the practice of actual realization.
The Universal Gate Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Regarding the intent of this chapter: it describes how, by means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Samādhi*, one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus, the cause of initial awakening (*ādi-bodha*) becomes perfected, and one wondrously enters the ocean of fruition.
Flowing against the current, one manifests bodies within the ten realms, responding without volition—this is what is called the "Noble Seed."
The simultaneous manifestation of bodies of similar kind brings forth the image of the "spontaneously born body produced by mental attention" (*manomaya-kāya*) that arises together with its class;
this serves to reveal the ultimate consummation of the Samādhi of the Sublime Dharma. Therefore, this chapter follows.

By extinguishing the ignorance of the fundamental characteristic of arising, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom manifests in equality; thus, it is provisionally designated as the "Universal Gateway" of Avalokiteśvara.

I shall now clarify this for you. Because Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, through the power of the Vajra Samādhi cultivated by hearing and practicing that which is heard—which is like an illusion—both arising and ceasing have been extinguished and quiescent extinction has manifested.

Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, he immediately attains a compassionate power identical to that of the Buddhas of the ten directions above, and [a power] for the sentient beings of the six realms below.

Because they share a common birth and look upward with shared compassion, they are able to respond universally to all beings with a single body, such that there is nothing to which their response does not reach.
This is the successful accomplishment of the Lotus Samādhi, in which wondrous practice is perfected; it reaches its ultimate subtlety here.

Therefore, from the chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja onwards up to these three chapters, the virtues of accomplished practice are realized by means of the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). If...

Thus, it shall be circulated. If the preceding sutra contains only faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) but lacks practice and realization (*pratipatti-sākṣātkriyā*), then such understanding would be a "vain understanding.
Furthermore, how could newly recorded bodhisattvas, who must in the future attend to many Buddhas, reach the fruit of Buddhahood?

The Sage’s intent is clear and can be seen through deep contemplation; his meaning is that although the wondrous practices are perfected, he truly fears that practitioners may still possess residual habits (*vāsanā*).
The reflections of conditions are difficult to exhaust; therefore, it is further taught that through three kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one may achieve the wondrous fruit.
Thus, the final three chapters conclude [the discourse].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati [asked]: "By what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara?"
This reveals that the Lotus Samādhi is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the wondrous realization of the ultimate fruit.

Therefore, it is elucidated through the universal gate manifestations of Avalokiteśvara. As for the inquiry made by Akṣayamati, it is because the Tathāgatagarbha, when deluded, becomes the ālayavijñāna;
its functions reside in five aspects, and thus there exists inconceivable karmic power. Now, this is transformed...
Consciousness becomes wisdom, and the five consciousnesses together achieve inconceivable divine powers and wondrous functions.
The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara manifests based upon this; therefore, it is initiated by the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
As for why he specifically inquires about the name "Avalokiteśvara," it is because he wishes to verify the reality through the name. Thus, the World-Honored One answers with the actual facts.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to the point where it says): "At that moment, by observing their sounds, they all attained liberation.
This answers the reason for the name Avalokiteśvara. Regarding the term "observing" (*avalokita*) applied to sound, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Because I do not observe my own ears, but observe the observer, I cause those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions to observe..."
Through sound, one immediately attains liberation; thus, the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

This arises from the ear-faculty’s illusory-like hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation through the Vajra Samādhi. By the power of contemplative illumination, one attains the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
To say "not observing the sounds themselves, but observing the observer" means to turn back and observe the nature of hearing itself, rather than that which arises from external objects.

Because of this knowledge and vision, once the object of sound has ceased, the nature of hearing becomes perfectly pervasive. Since one enters through sound, one receives the name "Avalokiteśvara" (The One Who Observes Sounds).
That sutra states that one receives the name by means of the faculty of the ear observing and illuminating;
here it is said that when sentient beings in immeasurable suffering and affliction single-mindedly invoke the Bodhisattva's name, they all attain liberation by the Bodhisattva observing their sounds.
This is a name derived according to the capacity [of the practitioner].

Because the Bodhisattva shares the same compassion and longing as the sentient beings of the six realms below, this arises from contemplating the perfect penetration of one's own nature; thus, the nature of all sentient beings is equal.
Therefore, sentient beings are precisely the sentient beings within the Bodhisattva’s own mind. Consequently, the suffering of sentient beings is [the suffering of] the Bodhisattva...

The suffering of sentient beings—if their cries of distress move the Bodhisattva’s heart, then the Bodhisattva contemplates the silence and extinction of those sounds and immediately enters into the *dharmatā*.
When empowered by such spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*), the sufferings of sentient beings are liberated of their own accord, without even being expected to be so.
This is the power of wisdom and compassion that simultaneously benefits both oneself and others. This is a general enumeration of the names.
The manifestation of its power and function is explained separately below:
"If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara" (up to) "...for this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara."
This specifically reveals the virtuous functions of Avalokiteśvara, namely the fourteen kinds of fearlessness, as fully elucidated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The Sūtra states:
"By the reversal of cognitive vision (*jñāna-darśana*), even if sentient beings enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.

By the reversal of hearing and listening (*śravaṇa-śruti*), even if sentient beings are adrift on a great flood, the water cannot drown them. This is because cognitive vision belongs to the element of fire, and hearing..."

The faculty of hearing belongs to water. Because the Bodhisattva’s seeing and hearing have both subsided and his sense organs and their objects have both been extinguished, he bestows his protection upon sentient beings such that neither water nor fire can harm them.
Because he has severed and eliminated deluded thoughts and his mind is free from killing or harming, he causes all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts;
through the power of contemplative illumination, he bestows his protection upon those people, so that the ghosts cannot cause them harm.
Furthermore, if there is someone who is on the verge of being harmed, [and so forth, until] they are immediately broken into pieces and yet attain liberation.
This is because the Bodhisattva has dissolved their form to become identical with sound; since there is no dust (resistance) to confront, there is nothing at all that can be touched.
Therefore, swords and staves cannot inflict harm.
If even the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system [cannot do so], they would certainly not be able to look upon him with evil eyes, much less inflict harm.

This is liberation from the calamity of rākṣasa demons. Since rākṣasas take darkness as their nature, when one’s wisdom-nature emits light through the cultivation of hearing and the clarity of the spirit, then all dark appearances can never again cause obscuration; thus, the rākṣasas dare not look upon one with evil eyes.

Furthermore, if there should be another person—whether guilty or innocent—[who undergoes this], all fetters and shackles will be completely severed and destroyed, and they shall immediately attain liberation.

This is because the nature of sound has been perfectly dissolved; as hearing is turned back inward, one becomes detached from all worldly burdens and entanglements. Therefore, all shackles and locks can be [severed].
It completely cuts off and destroys them all.
If the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with hostile bandits... [the power of] his majestic spiritual authority is as sublime as this.

This is because, through the cessation of sound and the perfect hearing, he universally generates the power of compassion; thus he is able to cause sentient beings to be free from all hostile bandits.
Because robbery arises from opposition, now that sound has ceased and hearing is perfected, the sensory objects are suddenly empty and there is no longer any counterpart;
thus, the thief cannot rob. The above has removed external difficulties; below, one purifies internal karma.
If there are sentient beings who are excessive in lustful desire, when they contemplate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they immediately become free from desire.
This is because, through the cultivation of hearing, they have detached from sensory objects; since they are not plundered by forms, they are thus able to leave desire behind.
Greed and desire arise from the grasping of love for sensory objects; now that they have detached from objects and do not grasp, desire is likewise far removed.
If those with much anger constantly contemplate and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will immediately be freed from anger.
This is because, through pure sound and the absence of sensory dust, the faculties and their objects are perfectly integrated; being free from all opposition, one is thus able to leave anger behind.
If those with much ignorance constantly keep in mind and pay respect to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will immediately be freed from delusion.
This is due to the power of his unimpeded, luminous illumination that dispels dust and turns back turbidity; thus, they are liberated from all the darkness of ignorance.
However, the nature of ignorance acts as an obstruction arising from darkness; now that illumination has appeared, one is thus freed from delusion.
[From] the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Inexhaustible Intent... [up to] the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such power.
This was because she had merged her form with the world and served all Buddhas extensively; having surpassed the ranks of the Dharma Princes (*dharmaputra*), she was thus granted a son.
This is because a man possesses the capacity for administrative action, which constitutes the virtue of a Dharma Prince’s ability to manage affairs.
Furthermore, while he is able to receive and uphold the Dharma-gates of the Buddhas of the ten directions, a woman possesses the quality of compliant acceptance and integration.
Because of this merit, one shall immediately give birth to a daughter.
If there are sentient beings who pay respectful homage [and so forth], it shall not be exhausted even throughout hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.

This is the fourteenth merit of fearlessness. In this Sahā world, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers who benefit sentient beings through skillful means.
Yet, if one holds even the single name of Avalokiteśvara, one becomes equal to those sixty-two billion.
Because Avalokiteśvara has perfectly realized the equal Dharma-realm, a single name is equal to the multitude.

These names are numerous. These fourteen fearlessnesses are all actual realities. If explained merely from the perspective of doctrinal understanding, they do not manifest the divine power of the Great Being to uproot suffering.
"Akṣayamati, by upholding [the name of] Avalokiteśvara, one obtains immeasurable and boundless merit and benefit.
This verse concludes that by upholding [the name], one attains the virtue of the fourteen fearlessnesses.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] ...what are the matters of the power of skillful means?
This question is intended to reveal the virtue of the thirty-two manifestations. The Sūtra says:
"Because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I was granted by that Tathāgata the Vajra-samādhi of hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation, which is like an illusion."
Because the Buddha-Tathāgata shares the same power of compassion, my body manifests in thirty-two forms to enter all lands,
beginning with the body of a Buddha and ending with humans and non-humans, totaling thirty-two. This precisely clarifies the "spontaneously born, effortless,
and mentally produced body" (*manomaya-kāya*) that arises together with its various types.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to): "He immediately manifests in the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.
This refers to manifesting the bodies of the four types of noble ones; it does not mention the body of a bodhisattva because that has already been manifested.
To those who should be saved by the body of Brahmā King, [the Buddha] manifests as that very body and preaches the Dharma for them.
This constitutes the manifestation of the bodies of the six classes of ordinary beings; first, he mentions the sovereign lord of the heavenly realm. Brahmā is the celestial lord of the First Dhyāna;
Śakra is the celestial lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; Maheśvara and Mahāmaheśvara dwell at the summit of the Desire Realm. These are the heavens.
The Great General commands the ghosts and spirits; the Four Heavenly Kings command the world. Vaiśravaṇa resides in the north as the honored one.
Brahmā and Śakra are among the assembly who constantly follow the Buddha. The others represent those who lead their respective groups.
For those who are to be saved by the body of a minor king, [the Buddha] manifests as a brahmin and preaches the Dharma to them.
This is the manifestation in the human realm, occurring through kings, ministers, and commoners alike.

Although *Miaoyin* (Ghoṣadatta) first mentions the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), there are four types of such monarchs—of gold, silver, copper, and iron—each ruling over four, three, two, or one world-realm respectively.
Those whom they govern are called "scattered-rice" kings; what are now termed "lesser kings" are these very scattered-rice kings.

They are not called "wheel-turning kings" (cakravartin), which is an abbreviation, or perhaps a way of including them by implication. These lesser kings rule over states and nations; the elders (gṛhapati) represent their clans;

the householders (vaiśya) maintain themselves through pure integrity; the officials (kṣatriya) adjudicate matters for the districts and cities; and the brahmins provide protection through their arts and sciences. As for those...
In truth, the hundred artisans and the four classes of people are all capable of manifesting this; I have merely cited the most prominent among them.
One should preach the Dharma by appearing in the forms of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
This manifests four kinds of bodies.
One should preach the Dharma by assuming the forms of elders, lay devotees, officials, and so forth, down to boys and girls.
This manifests the bodies of women and youths; that is to say, [the forms of] elders, lay devotees, officials, and brahmins.
These are the women of the gates.
He should preach the Dharma to them by manifesting as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, up to and including vajrapāṇi spirits;
this is the manifestation of the eight classes of beings. The vajrapāṇi spirit is one who wields the vajra-pestle to protect the Dharma.
"O Akṣayamati, this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... [omitted] ...all address him as the Bestower of Fearlessness.
This concludes the thirty-two manifestations, which should be honored accordingly. Regarding the six realms of existence, only the three fortunate paths are mentioned;

the three miserable paths are not discussed because those realms of suffering are not places where the Dharma is preached. Nevertheless, he does not fail to rescue them, as seen in the case of Jvālāmukha (the Flaming Face).
"O Mahāsattva, this too is a manifestation of the body; it is simply that [the previous case] was not categorized as such.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Benevolent One, please accept this precious necklace as an offering of the Dharma."
This inexhaustible offering is a sign of progress through hearing the Dharma. Necklaces are the adornments of Bodhisattvas, and the neck is the place where they are bound.
Now, having untied them to offer to Avalokiteśvara, one responds universally according to what is heard;
one awakens to wondrous practice that accords with conditions and suddenly abandons attachment to dharmas. Therefore, untying these to present as an offering is called the "gift of Dharma."
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva was unwilling to accept it (up to the point where) one portion was offered to the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
Avalokiteśvara did not accept it, thereby symbolizing that within the nature of the Dharma-realm there is fundamentally neither receiving nor relinquishing. The Buddha exhorted him to accept it.

The outer seal signifies not abandoning a single dharma. Turning [the merit] to serve the Two Honored Ones signifies dedicating it toward the three destinations, thereby merging them into the identical ocean of fruition.
From the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Infinite Intent... to... wandering in the Sahā world.
This is the formal conclusion that answers the intent of the question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati asked in verse:
"World-Honored One, you who are endowed with wondrous marks, I now ask again: for what causes and conditions is this son of the Buddha named Avalokiteśvara?"
This Akṣayamati again questioned him in verse.
The World-Honored One, who is fully endowed with wondrous marks, answered Akṣayamati in verse (up to): "He is able to extinguish all suffering of existence.
This was the World-Honored One’s summary response describing the virtues of Avalokiteśvara; because he possesses profound vows, he delivers beings from suffering.
Sentient beings receive their name from the cessation of suffering. "All existences" refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Even if one were to harbor a malicious intent to push them into a great pit of fire, they would not be submerged by the waves.

The following section provides a specific verse for rescuing from calamities; it consists of the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). However, as these various calamities are merely cited incidentally, the textual sequence is not strictly ordered.
These eight lines first cite the calamities of the three disasters (*trividha-vyasanāni*).
Or, if one were on the peak of Mount Sumeru and pushed over by someone— [down to] the point where not even a single hair could be harmed—
this refers to the peril of being cast down from a height.

Or, if one encounters hostile bandits surrounding them, each brandishing a blade to inflict harm, yet through the power of contemplating Avalokiteśvara, they all immediately give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
This verse concerns the hardship of hostile bandits.
Or, when encountering the suffering of royal punishment and facing execution at the point of death, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the blade is instantly shattered into pieces.
This verse concerns the hardship of execution.
Or if one is imprisoned and shackled, with hands and feet bound by cangues and fetters, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one will be released and set free.
This verse concerns the hardship of imprisonment.
As for curses and various poisonous drugs intended to harm the body, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall return to the person who sent them.
This verse concerns the peril of poisonous spells.
Should one encounter evil rākṣasas, venomous nāgas, various ghosts, and the like, at the moment one calls upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will all dare not cause harm.
This verse concerns the peril of rākṣasa ghosts.
"If surrounded by fierce beasts with fearsome sharp teeth and claws... (until)... they turn back upon hearing the sound.
This verse concerns the perils of venomous insects.
"When clouds and thunder roll, lightning flashes, and hail falls in torrential rain—by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, these shall dissipate at that very moment."
This verse concerns the hardships of calamities and disasters. All that precedes is the salvation from external difficulties; what follows is the salvation from internal difficulties.
Sentient beings are beset by perils and their bodies are oppressed by immeasurable sufferings; yet through the wondrous power of wisdom, Avalokiteśvara can rescue the world from its suffering.
This verse summarizes lust, anger, and delusion; these are all the internal karmic sufferings of sentient beings.
"Possessing the power of supernormal faculties and extensively cultivating the skillful means of wisdom" (up to) "gradually causing them all to be extinguished."
This is a summary verse concerning the manifestation of the body and the preaching of the Dharma. The prose version does not mention the evil realms; they are brought forth here in the verse.

"The contemplation of reality, the pure contemplation, the contemplation of vast wisdom, the contemplation of compassion, and the contemplation of loving-kindness—may I always aspire to and gaze upon them."

This verse concludes by clarifying the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). It reveals that there are five modes of contemplative observation through which a Bodhisattva responds to sentient beings.

"True Contemplation" (*tathatā-vipaśyanā*) means observing that all sentient beings are fundamentally the one true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), devoid of any differentiated characteristics; hence it is called "True Contemplation.

"Pure Contemplation" (*viśuddha-vipaśyanā*) means that the nature of the minds of sentient beings is originally pure and free from all defilements; hence it is called "Pure Contemplation. By means of great wisdom...
Wisdom illuminates and shatters the darkness of ignorance; hence it is called the contemplation of wisdom (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*). There is no suffering from which one does not deliver others;

hence it is called the contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā-vipaśyanā*). There is no joy that one does not bestow upon others; hence it is called the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-vipaśyanā*). By means of these five contemplations, the Bodhisattva constantly illumines sentient beings;
thus, responding to their conditions, sentient beings always aspire to gaze up upon him with reverence.
"The stainless, pure light of the sun of wisdom destroys all darkness, subdues the calamities of wind and fire, and shines universally upon the world.
This speaks to the function of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). "Stainless, pure light" refers to the three virtues of the *dharmakāya*. "Stainless" [refers to]...
Liberation is the virtue of *vimukti*; purity is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; and radiance is the virtue of *prajñā*.
Having already realized these three virtues, the Bodhisattva uses their power to universally illuminate the world; thus, like the sun of wisdom, they are able to destroy all darkness.
The three calamities (*trīṇi upadravāṇi*) arise from the transformation of deluded nature-virtue; now that the three virtues are perfected, they are able to subdue them.
"Disaster" means being far removed from all calamities. Through this wisdom of contemplation, which is universally luminous, it constantly illuminates the world.
Thus we know that a bodhisattva has never, even for a single thought-moment, abandoned sentient beings.

"The thunderous roar of the precepts, whose essence is compassion, and the wondrous great cloud of a benevolent mind pour down the nectar-like rain of the Dharma, extinguishing the flames of affliction.

This verse describes the manifestation of teaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. Having already realized the Dharmakāya and being fully endowed with the three virtues, yet the Dharmakāya is quiescent and transcendent;
that it is nevertheless able to manifest and teach the Dharma for the benefit of living beings is due to the power of unconditioned great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*).
Furthermore, the Dharma-body has no substance; it takes compassion as its substance. As for the precepts, they are the teachings and prohibitions that flow forth from the Dharma-body.

Therefore, when about to preach the Dharma, one first uses the thunder to startle and awaken the various capacities of sentient beings, and with a mind of loving-kindness, raises the vast clouds of the Great Dharma.
Only then does one pour down the nectar-rain of the Dharma, thereby extinguishing and removing the afflictions of sentient beings.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The object of focus for bodhi is suffering sentient beings.
If there were no compassion, then even a Buddha would not appear in the world, nor would there be any Dharma to be taught."
"In the midst of legal disputes before officials, or amidst the terrors of battle arrays, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, all enemies shall utterly disperse.
This verse indicates that because it extinguishes afflictions (*kleśa*), it can scatter all enemies; this is the power of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*).
"Exquisite Sound, Avalokiteśvara, Brahma-sound, Tide-sound" (up to) "In every thought-moment, do not give rise to doubt.
This verse establishes names based on virtues and exhorts one to uphold [the name] to obtain benefit. Because it is spoken without [deliberate] mental effort, it is called "Exquisite Sound."
He knows without deliberation; therefore, he is called "Avalokiteśvara" (The One Who Observes Sounds). He is pure and unattached; therefore, he is called "Brahma-sound.
His responses do not miss their proper time; therefore, he is called "Sound of the Ocean Tide. These are all not sounds of the mundane world.
Thus, one must constantly recite his name with sincere faith and without doubt.
"Avalokiteśvara, the Pure and Holy One, [is the refuge] for those in suffering, affliction, and the perils of death... therefore, one should pay him homage.
This eulogy of virtues encourages taking refuge to manifest his benefits. Because he has already realized the Dharmakāya, he is called "Pure and Holy.

Because he universally covers all sentient beings, he acts as a protector and reliance for those in suffering, affliction, birth, and death. This is because he is endowed with all meritorious virtues.

Therefore, he possesses the fourteen fearlessnesses; with eyes of compassion, he gazes upon all sentient beings. Thus, he is able to manifest thirty-two transformations for the sake of sentient beings, providing a mass of merit as vast and immeasurable as the ocean. For these reasons, he should be prostrated to.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Earth-Holder rose from his seat... [up to] ...one should know that this person’s merit is not small.
This concludes the praise for the merit of hearing this chapter. Regarding the attribution of these virtues to Earth-Holder:

because Avalokiteśvara has realized the ultimate Dharmakāya and perfected the ground of the single reality (ekajñatā-bhūmi), he is able, with a mind like the great earth, to sustain all sentient beings and bring them forth.

Because of these merits, he concludes with the praise of "Holding the Earth. Guanyin responds to all sentient beings through unconditioned, wondrous activity; hence it is called "the karma of mastery.

Because there is nowhere he does not manifest, it is called "manifestation through the Universal Gate. Because there is no suffering from which he does not deliver, it is called "the power of spiritual penetrations.
This Guanyin has already realized Wondrous Enlightenment; although he dwells in the stage of fruition, [he continues to act for the sake of others].
Without abandoning the practice of causes, one has already attained Buddhahood; thus, manifesting the cloud-like body of the Dharma-realm, it is called the "Universal Gate.
If the previous [chapter on] "Wondrous Sound" refers to the practices prior to Equal Enlightenment, then by relying on the power of samādhi, there still remains the appearance of coming and going.
The Buddha’s intention in teaching these three chapters lies in entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; one must necessarily shatter the two attachments and purify the two [obstructions].

Obstacles are exhausted at the limit of true suchness (*tathatā*), and through the manifestation of great spiritual efficacy, one enters wondrous enlightenment. When cause and effect are as one, this constitutes the ultimate realization.
Therefore, [the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*] specifically employs the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) to explain this, clarifying the sequence of realization and entry.
Since this sutra does not describe the gradual stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*), it specifically relies on these [three bodies] to manifest actual practice.
This is presented to the newly recorded bodhisattvas as a verification for those who will enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision in the future.
How could the profound intent behind the Tathāgata’s teaching be regarded with superficial understanding?
When the Buddha preached this "Universal Gate" chapter (up to the point where they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), this concludes the practice resulting from hearing this chapter.
The fruit of Buddhahood, *bodhi*, is called "the peerless equal" (*asama-sama*);
it means that there is nothing equal to it, yet it is able to equalize all things. Because Avalokiteśvara has realized this, those who hear [this teaching] all give rise to this mind. Thus...
Thus, one accomplishes sublime conduct.
Regarding the intention for the arrival of this chapter, "The Chapter on Dharanis," the twenty-sixth of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
since the preceding sublime conduct has already been perfected, one should now realize the sublime fruit. This applies especially to those of the highest capacity.

There is the "Direct Entry by Leaping Over," which is for those of middling and lower capacities. However, because the *ālayavijñāna* has been deeply conditioned over many kalpas, residual habits lie latent within it.
Thus, even if one possesses the merit of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are instances where wisdom encounters obstacles and the spirit fails to reach its goal;
such defilements cannot be severed easily without the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). It is for this reason that the final three grades are taught. By means of these—
This chapter appears in order to manifest the signs of the three kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). These three kinds of empowerment are:

the empowerment of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), the empowerment of the Dharma (*dharma*), and the empowerment of manifesting one's physical form, countenance, and speech. In the *Laṅkāvatāra*, there are only two; here, it is primarily the empowerment of the Dharma.

This present chapter, however, concerns the empowerment of supernormal power. Mantras are the secret heart-seals (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas, like the secret insignia of a celestial sovereign. Great...

When one seizes them, their hardness is crushed and their sharpness broken; there is no enemy that cannot be overcome. The *ālaya-vijñāna* is the cavern of birth and death, most profoundly deep and obscure;
therefore it is said that "the treasury of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is profound, firm, and remote, such that no one can reach it.
As for those habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that lie latent and remain beyond the reach of the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one must rely upon the secret mind of the Tathāgata.

One should attack it with the power of the mudrā. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "If a practitioner has not yet eliminated their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they should single-mindedly recite my divine mantra.
This is precisely for that reason. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:

"If one does not establish oneself through the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi-bala*), one will fall into the evil views and deluded imaginings of external paths, as well as the hopes of the various śrāvakas and māras. Therefore...
If one does not apply [this practice] prior to the seventh stage, one falls into the ranks of the external paths. If one does not apply it at the eighth stage, one falls into the two vehicles.

From the ninth stage up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, if one does not apply it, one cannot enter the Subtle. This is because the ālayavijñāna has not yet been shattered prior to the seventh stage.
Prior to equal enlightenment (*sambodhi*), the retributive fruit (*vipāka*) has not yet been emptied; therefore, it is necessary to apply [the empowerment].

However, the three types of mind-born bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) serve to verify what has already been attained, while the three types of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) serve to awaken that which has not yet been reached.
Such is the general principle of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma. It does not mean that empowerment occurs only after the mind-born bodies have arisen. By no means should one...
Viewing it from both the beginning and the end:
at that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat... [and] immediately spoke a mantra.
This speaks of the merit of upholding the sutra, which is intended to reveal the great benefit of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Because of Bhaiṣajyarāja—

As for the initiator: Previously, Bhaisajyaraja was taken as the symbol of śamatha and vipaśyanā, and he was the foremost among those who practice asceticism while upholding the sutra and the first to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

therefore, he asks this question to demonstrate to the newly recorded bodhisattvas how to first regulate the mind through śamatha and vipaśyanā, and finally to eliminate habitual tendencies through secret mantras. This is according to the Buddha’s teaching on cultivation.
There are two modes of practice: the exoteric and the esoteric. Thus, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* constitute the exoteric practice, while mantras constitute the esoteric practice.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If a practitioner has not yet eliminated their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they should single-mindedly recite my divine mantra.
Therefore, when practitioners are about to ascend to the stage of enlightenment, those who are occasionally ruined by the power of Māra do so because of these habitual tendencies.
Therefore, in the final age, those who uphold this sutra must rely on the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of divine mantras to ensure they remain free from peril.
This is why the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that before the seventh stage, if one is not empowered, one will fall into the hopes and desires of various demons.

This chapter is judged to be an exposition of the empowerment of supernatural power; yet, as for the initial inquiry regarding the merit of upholding the sutra, it refers back to what was previously said concerning the benefits of upholding the sutra.

Most [teachings] concern the benefit of others (*parārtha*) for the sake of those to be converted; now, however, it speaks of their merit (*puṇya*), specifically clarifying that self-benefit (*svārtha*) resides within oneself.
Because this sutra provides such great benefit, one who does not possess profound merit cannot bear its weight. It is like hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
one has not planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas—meaning that without merit, one cannot carry the wisdom. Thus it says "to read."
Recite [the sutra] until it is thoroughly mastered. This constitutes entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, it is said that one should "practice according to the teaching.
Because the merit of upholding this sutra with great wisdom cannot be fully preserved without supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), it is necessary to receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Thus, while the previous comparisons of merit spoke only of the seven treasures, the present instance specifically concerns the merit of making offerings to the Buddha; this is the blessing inherent in wisdom itself.
Therefore, the Buddha sealed it, saying: "The merit of practicing according to what has been taught is exceedingly great.
From *an-er* (1) to *ma-n-er* (2), up to *a-mo-ruo-na-duo-ye* (43)—this secret divine mantra is the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas;
it has never before been translated. [This concludes] the translation from Sanskrit into Chinese.
There are five reasons for not translating [certain terms]: first, secrecy, as in the case of mantras; second, multiple meanings, as in the term *bhagavān*;
third, non-existence in this land, as in the case of the Jambu tree; fourth, following ancient tradition, as in the case of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and fifth, reverence, as in the case of *prajñā*. This mantra is one such instance among these five reasons for not translating.
It is like a secret code within an army; it serves only to accomplish the task and must not be known by others.
If one [violates this], the World-Honored One’s dhāraṇī-mantra (up to the point where it says) "it would constitute an offense against and destruction of all these Buddhas."
All mantras are termed *dhāraṇī*, which is translated here as "total retention" (*saṃgraha-dhāraṇa*). This signifies that they encompass all phenomena and sustain immeasurable meanings;
it is a designation for the meaning of the "mind-seal" (*citta-mudrā*). This mantra was spoken by sixty-two billion Buddhas and is thus the mind-seal of all Buddhas.
It is entrusted to the Dharma-master who upholds this sutra; therefore, this mantra is required for protection and sustenance.
As for Bhaiṣajyarāja being mentioned first, it is because he is the foremost of both the exoteric and esoteric practices.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised Bhaiṣajyarāja (up to the point where it says) he brings great benefit to all sentient beings.
This was the seal of approval from the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīradatta addressed the Buddha, saying (up to): "He then spoke a mantra before the Buddha, saying:
*Cule* (1), *mahācule* (2) ... (up to) ... *nirleḍhipati* (13)."
"World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī mantra (up to) would constitute an offense against and destruction of all these Buddhas.
This Vīradatta, who speaks the mantra for protection, suddenly severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); none but a hero could do so.

Because this assists in accomplishing sublime conduct, the mantra is spoken next by Bhaiṣajyarāja. The yakṣas and others are all malevolent spirits who cause affliction and harm; they [are those who] uphold the sūtra.

"O Dharma Master, in the final age there will be much harm. Without relying on the power of mantras, one cannot avoid such harm and accomplish one's practice; therefore, it is necessary to perform empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
At that time, Vaiśravaṇa, the World-Protecting Heavenly King (up to), spoke this mantra, saying:"
A-li (1) na-li (2) [to] na-li (5) ku-sui-li (6).
By means of this divine mantra, the World-Honored One protects the Dharma Master [to] ensure that within a hundred yojanas there shall be no calamities or afflictions.
Vaiśravaṇa is the Heavenly King of the North. Among the Four Kings who protect the world, he presides over spirits and deities as the lord of the realm of birth and death.
As for why the mantra is recited first for the North: the trigram of the North is Kan; Kan signifies "to sink" or "to be trapped."
By placing one *skandha* between two other *skandhas*, it demonstrates the image of the perils and difficulties of birth and death.

For a practitioner who, amidst these perils and difficulties of birth and death, desires to suddenly realize *bodhi*, how could they overcome these dangers and transcend birth and death without the empowerment of supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*)?
Since Vaiśravaṇa is the lord of these perils and difficulties, he is mentioned first.
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, being present in this assembly, spoke a mantra, saying:
*Agaṇe* (1), *Gaṇe* (2), ... [up to] ... *Phuḷusvāhā* (8), *Adhi* (9).
The World-Honored One is this *dhāraṇī* divine spell... (up to) "it would constitute an offense against and destruction of all these Buddhas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the Heavenly King of the East. The trigram of the East is Zhèn; Zhèn signifies movement.
The East is the source of all movement. The *Yī Jīng* says: "Good fortune, misfortune, regret, and shame arise from movement. The *Lùn* says: "Movement must necessarily..."
Suffering. Thus, it is that the practitioner performs the practice of ultimate stillness amidst the turbulence of birth and death.
Were it not for the empowerment of spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), how else could one reach the realm of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*)?
As for the trigram of the south, it is Li; "Li" means attachment. It is the symbol of empty luminosity. The trigram of the west is Dui; "Dui" means...
It is said that if there were no realm of empty clarity and joyful serenity, there would be no need for empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*);
therefore, those two Heavenly Kings did not need to speak.
At that time, there were rākṣasīs and others who, [having arrived] before the Buddha, spoke this mantra, saying:
Iti-li (1), Iti-min (2) ... [through] Dohi (18), Rāuhi (19).
Do not trouble the Dharma-preacher upon my head! (Through) he then spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"If you do not comply with my spell and instead harass and disturb those who preach the Dharma, you shall incur such calamities as these.
After the rākṣasīs had spoken this verse, they said, "We shall provide protection for such Dharma-preachers."
This rākṣasī is governed by Vaiśravaṇa; therefore, she is also said to recite mantras to protect the Dharma-preacher who upholds this sūtra.
Rākṣasīs are ghosts of profound obscurity, and like Hārītī, they all fly about devouring human flesh.
These women represent the ultimate in yin-deviance; this demonstrates how the karmic habits of the rākṣasa of ignorance cause destruction and harm.
The Dharma-body. Now, by investigating and exhausting [reality] through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one transforms ignorance into the wondrously luminous light of the mind.

Therefore, even the rākṣasī protects those who uphold, receive, read, recite, and practice this sutra with her own body, suddenly causing their ignorance and the three poisons to be purified and exhausted without remainder—what is called "causing the various poisonous medicines to be digested. If at night...
The *kṣapaṇakas* and others are all malevolent spirits under their command; if none of these are to cause affliction, then there will be nothing that can cause affliction.
The Buddha praised and authorized this. Yet, the merit of merely protecting and upholding the name of this sutra is already immeasurable;
how much more so for those who fully receive, uphold, and make offerings to it—their merit is truly inconceivable. That one must necessarily offer incense and lamps to the Buddha is to symbolize—
It wondrously accords with the Dharma-body and secretly penetrates the Dharma-realm; therefore, the offering of incense is most honored.
All afflictions, upon a single thought, are transformed into supreme awakening; therefore, the various offerings of lamps are considered foremost.
When this "Chapter on the Dhāraṇī" was being spoken, sixty-eight thousand people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This refers to the practice accomplished through hearing this chapter. By cultivating both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings simultaneously, one immediately attains the purification of the six sense faculties and the perfect clarity of the eight consciousnesses.
Therefore, these sixty-eight thousand people all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; this is due to the empowerment of spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This is its benefit.
Regarding the twenty-seventh chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha":

the purpose of this chapter is to illustrate the phenomenon of the transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*vijñāna-parāvṛtti-jñāna*), thereby manifesting the empowerment of the Dharma-power (*dharmabala-adhiṣṭhāna*).
King Wondrous Adornment is the Tathāgatagarbha; while enshrouded in afflictions, it manifests as the eight consciousnesses, the sovereign mind-kings.
Now that its original reality has been revealed, it is called the "Original Matter. The two sons, Pure Treasury and Pure Eye, are the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
This is a symbol of transforming defilement into purity. The lady’s gentle compliance and internal assistance is a symbol of the internal permeation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Because she purifies ignorance, she is called "Pure Virtue" (*Śuddhaguṇā*). Since the sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform within the causal stage, the two sons first requested to leave the household life.

The two sons transformed their father’s heterodox mind, and they all left the household life together; this correctly reveals the emergence of original enlightenment (*mūlabodhi*) from its entanglements.
This power of śamatha and vipaśyanā is that by which Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body attain a non-discriminative mind and accord with the wisdom and function of all Buddhas.
Through the spontaneous practice of the Dharma-power and the permeation of True Suchness (tathatā), they extinguish ignorance.
This chapter appears because of what is called the empowerment of the Dharma-power (*dharmabala-adhiṣṭhāna*). Its meaning is as follows:

through the empowerment of spiritual power (*ṛddhibala-adhiṣṭhāna*), external māras are eliminated; then, the Dharma-power internally perfumes the mind, purifying the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and realizing the two transformations of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Therefore, it recounts the fundamental history of King Subhavyūha. The aforementioned empowerment of spiritual power represents the stage prior to the seventh bhūmi, whereas the [empowerment of] Dharma-power...

Through the empowerment of power (*balādhiṣṭhāna*), he emerges from the *tathatā-samādhi* of the eighth stage; this represents the progression through the ninth stage up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly: [omitted] "The land is named Radiant Adornment (*Prabhāsa-vyūha*), and the eon is named Joyful Vision (*Priyadarśana*)."
This will reveal the fundamental history of the Sublime Adornment (*Ghanavyūha*). First, it recounts the Buddha of the female teacher.
The Buddha’s name is Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower (*Meghadundubhisvararāja-puṣpa*). Dense clouds precede the rain, and thunder heralds it; hence, he is called "Cloud-Thunder-Sound.

"Constellation" refers to the fruition-enlightenment, and "flower" refers to causal practice; thus, the wisdom of fruition-enlightenment serves as the mind of the causal stage, progressing up to the ninth [stage].
The ground [of this land] is such that it can fully receive the Dharma-clouds and Dharma-rains of all Buddhas;

therefore, the Buddha who serves as its teacher is named Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom (Meghadundubhisvararāja-puṣpadhvaja-jñāna). The Land of Eternal Quiescent Light uses light as its adornment, and is thus called "Adorned with Radiance.
As a Pure Land, it is the place where all sages return, and is thus called "Joyful to Behold" (Sudarśana). This refers to the Buddha of that time.
In that Buddha-dharma, there was a king named *Su-vyūha* (Wondrous Adornment), who had two sons named *Viśuddha-garbha* (Pure Treasury) and *Viśuddha-cakṣus* (Pure Eye).
Regarding the king named *Su-vyūha*: it refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is fundamentally the essence of the wondrously adorned fruition-body (*phala-kāya*).

Now, being deluded regarding this, it becomes the *ālayavijñāna*, termed the sovereign mind-king of the eight consciousnesses; because of this, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses arise as its transformations.

The consciousnesses create various karmas and undergo various sufferings. If the seven consciousnesses are transformed into the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), then the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) will have no defilement to undergo; hence it is called the "Pure Store.

If the six consciousnesses are transformed into the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), then discriminative views are immediately eliminated and the objective aspect (*dṛśya-bhāga*) also vanishes, whereby one attains the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Therefore, it is called the "Pure Eye. This is a symbol of transforming defilement into purity.
These two sons possess great supernatural power (up to) they have all fully understood and attained thorough penetration.
These two sons possess great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to manifest the two wisdoms (*jñāna*) and to exercise vast functional efficacy.

All the Bodhisattva’s practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and ten thousand deeds, the Buddha’s [four immeasurables of] compassion, mercy, joy, and equanimity, and even the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), all rely upon the power and efficacy of these two wisdoms; therefore, it is said that they are "all clearly understood."

One thoroughly penetrates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path. The practices for achieving [enlightenment] do not generally exceed these.
