Taking the four immeasurable minds as their essence, the six perfections as their function, and the factors of the path as their support, all are cultivated by the transformed wisdom of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
Because they practice, they further attain the Bodhisattva’s Pure Samādhi (up to) fully penetrating this samādhi as well;
these refer to the two sons’ samādhis. By means of the two wisdoms, they contemplate and illuminate, purifying ignorance in every thought-moment.
Therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Purity. The sun represents fundamental wisdom, while the stars represent subtle observation; hence, it is called the Samādhi of the Sun and Stars.
It illuminates the three bodies; hence, it is called the Samādhi of Pure Light. It thoroughly understands the sense faculties and their objects; hence, it is called the Samādhi of Pure Form.
It penetrates and contemplates the body, mind, world, and all internal and external phenomena; hence, it is called the Samādhi of Pure Illumination.
In every thought-moment, it adorns the *dharmakāya*; hence it is called the "Samādhi of Long-Adornment. It can destroy the hindrances of afflictions and various māras;
hence it is called the "Samādhi of the Treasury of Great Majestic Virtue. These are all manifestations of the cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) of the two wisdoms.
At that time, that Buddha desired to guide King Subhavyūha [to the Buddha's presence], or else to permit us to go to the Buddha's abode.
This describes the causes and conditions for the two sons' transformation of their father; it is not the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle.
Because one cannot transform that karmic consciousness, it is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached in order to guide King Miaozhuangyan.
It is not through the power of the wisdom and function of the two consciousnesses that one can open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

therefore, the two sons said to their mother, "We wish for our mother to see the Buddha and hear the sutra. The merit of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is specifically for the purpose of transforming the perverse. Thus...
He ordered them to go and inform their father so that they might depart together. These two consciousnesses are fundamentally the wondrously luminous Buddha-wisdom;

now, functioning as [ordinary] consciousness, they are said to have been born into a family of false views. Only by using *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to permeate and transform ignorance can one turn defilement into purity.
Therefore, the mother had the two sons observe the divine transformations, so that if the father were to see them, his mind would surely become pure.
Thereupon, the two sons, out of consideration for their father, caused the heart of their royal father to attain pure faith and understanding.

These two sons manifested supernatural transformations to awaken their father’s mind; that is to say, by purifying the essence of their own minds through non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), they surged upward into the void.
Earth, water, fire, and wind are all the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eight consciousnesses, which [the father] had previously grasped.
They grasp at things as "I" and "mine. Only when each of these manifestations is now dissolved and integrated without obstruction will they be free from the mind of grasping;
thus, he caused his father to see the divine transformations so that his mind would become pure and attain faith and understanding.
At that time, the father saw that his son’s supernatural powers were such as this, and his heart was filled with great joy. [The passage continues: "We may go together.
This father, seeing the supernatural power and feeling great joy in his heart, gave rise to the aspiration to see the Buddha;

this is because the *ālayavijñāna* has been perfumed by the functions of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, and thus possesses the mechanism for transformation. Therefore, he inquired about the teacher from whom [the son] had learned, wishing to go together with him.
They went to see him.
Thereupon, the two sons descended from the sky and, wishing to further declare their intent, addressed their mother in verse:
"We pray that our mother will release us so that we may go forth and see the śramaṇa... [we pray] that she will grant permission for our renunciation."
The mother then said, "I grant you permission to leave the household life. Why is this? Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter.

When the two sons saw that their father had already gained faith, they addressed their mother, requesting permission to leave the household life. This was because they had undergone transformation through six or seven causal stages;

thus, they requested ordination first. However, it is not possible to realize [the truth] directly without the power of internal cultivation through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Because of the Buddha’s wisdom, the mother permitted her two sons to leave the household life, thereby manifesting that a Buddha is difficult to encounter.
Only those who possess deep-seated faith and understanding can enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Thereupon, the two sons said to their parents: "The appearance of the Buddhas is rare, and such a time is likewise difficult to encounter.

When these two sons requested that their parents go together to see the Buddha, their intention was to manifest that through the transformative cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), one must necessarily achieve the identity of mind and object (*citta-viṣaya-ekalakṣaṇa*) before one can enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, they wished to go together to see the Buddha. Thus it is said.

"The Buddha is extremely difficult to encounter, and his appearance in the world is likewise rare. This means that if one wishes to understand the meaning of the Buddha-nature, one must contemplate the conditions of time and season.
At that time, King Subhavyūha’s harem [members]... [the King] taught, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, and the Great King was filled with immense joy.
This passage describes how the entire palace possesses the potential for transformation.

It signifies that the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which contains the seeds, habitual tendencies, and afflictions, is transformed from defilement to purity through the power of being perfumed by *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Thus, the eighty-four thousand members of the King’s inner harem are all capable of upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. However, as for the Tathāgata...
The reason why the *ālayavijñāna* does not follow the painful realms of birth and death is that it is bound and entangled by the karmic forces produced by the six consciousnesses.
Now, when the seventh consciousness (*manas*) no longer clings, the six consciousnesses are likewise transformed, and the cause of birth and death within the eighth consciousness is severed.
Being inherently undefiled, one immediately enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhacakṣus attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

[This is] the Samādhi of Penetrating and Departing from All Evil Destinies attained by the Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha. Because initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*) possesses efficacy, fundamental awakening (*mūlakṣaya*) is then manifested;
thus, the king and his consort attained the Samādhi of the Gathering of All Buddhas and were able to know the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
Since the sixth and seventh consciousnesses have already been transformed, the five [sensory] consciousnesses and the eighth [consciousness] are simultaneously [transformed].
"Transformation" means that there is nothing among the four great elements, the faculties, the sense objects, or all afflictions that does not undergo transformation.

Therefore, the king, his ministers, and forty-two thousand people went together at once to the place where the Buddha was. Upon arriving there, they realized that all phenomena are none other than the Buddha-dharma;
thus, the Buddha preached the Dharma for the king, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
At that time, King Subhavyūha and his consort (up to) accomplished the foremost, most subtle Dharma.

This was the benefit of making offerings to the Buddha with such sublime adornment. Because they transformed defilement into purity and were liberated from their fetters, they untied the necklaces of genuine pearls from around their necks and scattered them over the Buddha.
This was because they had wondrously realized the eternal, blissful, self, and pure nature of the Dharmakāya.
Because Nirvāṇa possesses the sublime virtue of wondrousness, it transforms into a precious four-pillared pavilion.

Within the pavilion is a great precious throne, spread with hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial robes. Upon it sits a Buddha in the full lotus posture. That the void is eternally one represents the virtue of true permanence;
that the celestial robes fit the body perfectly represents the virtue of true bliss; and that there is a Buddha sitting cross-legged represents the virtue of true self.
It emits great radiance; this is the virtue of true purity. Since the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has become empty, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) manifests.
Therefore, one recollects the Buddha’s body with its rare and subtle color; this is the sign of wondrously accords with the Dharma-body.
At that time, the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña—[the extent of] the merit of the level and upright nature of his land was such as this.
As for this Buddha’s bestowing of the prediction upon Subhavyūha: it is because he realized that the nature of the treasury is fundamentally empty and opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
this is the true cause of attaining Buddhahood, and thus he was granted the prediction. Because he universally shades all living beings, the Buddha’s name is Vairocana (Universal Radiance).

Because the King has forever shattered the dark ignorance of delusion, the land is named Great Radiance (*Mahāprabha*). Because he has suddenly transcended all realms of existence (*bhava*), the eon is named Great High King (*Mahocchrayarāja*).
These are both symbols of the eight consciousnesses emerging from their entanglements.
The king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother... [until] "...because he came to be born into my family for the sake of bringing me benefit.
These words refer to the benefit of Miaoyan’s renunciation of the world. By transforming the *ālayavijñāna* into wisdom, it merges identically with the *dharmakāya*;

by responding to conditions through expedient wisdom (*upāyaprajñā*), he is said to have "entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother. As for the mention of "the consort and others," the intent is to manifest cessation (*śamatha*).

When the contemplation of merit is perfected and one simultaneously transcends the entanglements, then all functions of omniscience—the faculties, objects, and all phenomena—simultaneously become sublime functions.

Therefore, together with his wife, two sons, and all their retinue, he diligently cultivates the Way within the Buddha-dharma, whereby all afflictions are transformed into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus, during the eighty thousand...
For three thousand years, he diligently practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Upon reaching this stage, all practices become pure and wondrous merit, serving as the adornment of the Dharma-body.
Therefore, it is said that he attained the "Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits. Having realized the non-abiding body and entered the emptiness of the Dharma-nature, he ascends into the void.

Emptiness. Only when fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is manifested does one perceive the efficacy of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). Thus, when King Wen saw the Buddha, he was moved to regard his two sons as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

This is because they were attained through cultivation, with the True Suchness (*tathatā*)—perfumed by the power of the Dharma—serving as the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) for the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, it is said: "The two sons turned my perverse mind and enabled me to dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma."
Therein he was able to see the World-Honored One. These two sons are my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Desiring to arouse the roots of goodness from past lives, they have been born into my household. These spiritual friends are the great causal conditions;
it is for this reason that they have transformed and guided me so that I might see the Buddha. All of this demonstrates the power of the conditioning force of auxiliary causes and conditions.
At that time, from the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña... up to [the attainment of] *samyaksaṃbodhi*.

This mutual certification by the Buddhas regarding the "Exquisite Adornment" (*miāoyán*) clearly reveals the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause (*yuán-yīn*). Therefore, the emphasis is placed upon the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

The underlying meaning is that while the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*zhèng-yīn*) is inherently possessed by every person, it nevertheless requires the support of roots of goodness from past lives. Thus, one must rely upon [a spiritual friend].

Through the conditions and causes provided by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they are brought forth; through the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they are then manifested. As it is said, "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions.
Therefore, reliance upon spiritual friends is emphasized as the great causal condition. For this reason, the preceding sections have recounted the fundamental cause of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū;
now, by means of the seeds of conditions for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), one is finally able to attain this wondrous [state] from here.

This is because they enter into the realization of the Dharma. Therefore, the Dharma masters who uphold the sutras are all the causes and conditions for the Buddha-nature of sentient beings in the final age.
Thus, the reason one dares not violate or destroy them is precisely that the seeds of Buddha-nature held by these spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are of such great importance.
"Great King, do you see these two sons? [This continues until: "...to take pity on sentient beings of wrong views and cause them to abide in right view.

This explains the fundamental cause for the emergence of the two sons. "Having already made offerings to the sixty-five hundred [deities]" refers to the six consciousnesses giving rise to contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), which, at the gates of the five sense faculties, clearly penetrates each one without being obstructed by the sense organs or their objects.

Whatever he does is entirely a sublime practice. Therefore, it is said that he made offerings to, drew near to, and reverently served as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in sixty-five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of Ganges Rivers.

From those Buddhas, he received and upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, out of compassion for sentient beings with wrong views, causing them to abide in right view. Thus, one knows that upholding this sutra [is the source of these merits].
Dharma Master, you take the cultivation of contemplative insight as your primary foundation.
Yet the efficacy of such cultivation has been realized over many kalpas, and is not the result of a single moment.
King Wondrous Adornment immediately descended from the midst of space... [as previously stated] ...having spoken these words, he prostrated to the Buddha and departed.

This "Wondrous Adornment" praises the Buddha to manifest the image of his wondrous accord with the *dharmakāya*. Therefore, he first praises the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the *saṃbhogakāya*, and subsequently praises the merits of the *dharmakāya*.
For the Dharma of the Tathāgata is fully and perfectly accomplished and is... [inexpressible].
The inconceivable and subtle merits, the practices of the teachings and precepts, and all that is peaceful, secure, and wholesome—these are all the merits of the Dharma-body.

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "It is like refining gold ore; the gold does not exist because of the refining, yet although it was originally gold, it is only through refining that it is perfected.
Once it has become the substance of pure gold, it can never again become ore. Therefore, it is wondrous.
Miaoyan said: "From this day forward, I shall no longer act according to my own whims;
I shall not give rise to any evil thoughts such as false views, arrogance, or anger. Thus, Miaoyan thoroughly perceived his own mind and reached the stage of non-doubt.
All of this is the merit of the Sublime Dharma; that is to say, the benefit of the empowerment of the Dharma’s power.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "What do you think? [and so on, until] "the devas and human beings should also pay homage."
This demonstrates the present circumstances of the two sons, Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra.

It reveals that their ability to transform the minds of those with perverse views through wondrous adornments, as well as their conversion of the queen and her retinue so that they all entered the Buddha-dharma, was entirely due to the power of the sons' cultivation of the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), which transformed and refined them.
This is the karmic cause from past lives of Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata; for by means of all bodhisattvas...
Regarding spiritual practice: there has never been one who practiced without relying on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Nor has there ever been any Tathāgata who attained perfect enlightenment without being dependent upon *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

It is because these two Bodhisattvas, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, have accomplished such great merits and have planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable Buddhas that they are thus able to achieve [these results].

This is the inconceivable power [of the Buddha]. The intent lies in returning through contemplation of the mind to exhaustively fulfill the wondrous practice of upholding the sutra, thereby manifesting the merit of the empowerment of the Dharma-power.
Therefore, one should prostrate to the names of these two bodhisattvas.

When the Buddha preached this "Chapter on the Former Deeds of King Subhavyūha" (up to the point where they attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena), this concludes the section on hearing the teaching and bringing it into practice.
It signifies that when the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is perfected, all afflictions (*kleśa*) become pure upon mere thought;
thus, eighty-four thousand people became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Encouragement of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Regarding the intent of this chapter’s inclusion:
following the preceding stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), one is thereby supported in wondrous practice (*caryā*). When practice is perfected, the fruit is attained;

it is now at the point of realization and entry that [the Buddha] manifests his physical presence, countenance, speech, and empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The sūtra states: "If such a person sits and contemplates this..."
Sūtra: At that time, I shall again mount the six-tusked white elephant king and appear before that person.
Should that person forget even a single word or a single verse, I shall instruct them and provide them with the text for recitation. Furthermore, it says:
"If there are those who receive, read, recite, correctly contemplate, practice, or transcribe this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that such persons..."
Then one sees Śākyamuni Buddha, as if hearing this sutra directly from the Buddha’s own mouth;
this is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of his manifest body, face, and speech. For even a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment cannot enter the Sublime without such empowerment.

Because there is the Dharmakāya that comes to receive [the practitioner], it is necessary to receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in order to attain realization and entry; for this reason, this chapter follows.
This sutra establishes its essence through wisdom; therefore, Mañjuśrī initiates the discourse to support faith and understanding, while practice is used to perfect virtue.

Therefore, Samantabhadra completes the process by clarifying the realization through entry. Thus, it constitutes the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. There are two aspects to Samantabhadra: first, that which precedes the Way and belongs to the cause;
second, that which follows the Way and belongs to the fruit. To say that one's practice pervades the Dharma-realm is called "Universal" (Samanta).

To be adjacent to the ultimate and nearly equal to a sage is called "Worthy" (Bhadra). This refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, where it belongs to the cause. To fully encompass the true Dharma-realm is called "Universal. To pervade and interweave [all things]—*mili*—is the meaning of its name.
The myriad transformations are called "sagehood. This belongs to the fruit within the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

Because this Samantabhadra is the entire substance of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and serves as the vow-body (*praṇidhāna-kāya*) of Vairocana’s ten bodies, the Bodhisattva relies upon this to give rise to the mind, cultivate faith, understanding, and practice, and thereby realizes this very essence.
Therefore it is said: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm; there is nothing that does not return to it."

The Dharma-realm. However, once a bodhisattva has perfected the causes and reached the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they must rely on the reception of the fruition-enlightenment (*phala-bodhi*) before they can enter the Subtle [Dharma].
Therefore, this chapter constitutes the conclusion of the entry into realization. Furthermore, Samantabhadra, through the power of his vows, ensures that one will certainly obtain this sutra.
Because it is by relying on Samantabhadra that one attains entry into realization, it is called "Exhortation and Inspiration" (*samādāpana*).
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (up to) came from the east, in numbers immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.

This refers to the arrival of Samantabhadra. Since Samantabhadra was not present in the assembly during the first chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, his arrival now from the east is significant;
for the east is the realm of all movement, and the wondrous practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* accords with ultimate truth.
The Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) pervades the deluded and agitated minds of all sentient beings.
Now, by entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the essential nature of the Dharma-realm finally manifests before one. Therefore, this is the ultimate convergence.
Samantabhadra comes from the east; at the beginning, light illuminates the east, and at the end, Samantabhadra comes from the east—this precisely demonstrates the practice of wisdom.
This is the image of profound unity. By means of this *dharmatā*, it universally enters into the bodies of all sentient beings without being obstructed by afflictions;
hence it is called "the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations" (*vibhutva-abhijñā*).

Because the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the *dharmakāya* transcends the sphere of mind and thought, it is called "majestic virtue. Because there is nothing it does not possess, it is called "renown. This constitutes the ten thousand...
As the very foundation of practice, he was accompanied by immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable great bodhisattvas.
All the lands through which they passed were universally shaken, [and there arose] hundreds of thousands of billions of various kinds of musical performances.
This means that in all of Samantabhadra’s movements and actions, he invariably shatters ignorance to accomplish wondrous conduct, thereby nourishing the joy of the Dharma;
thus it is said that "all are universally shaken," raining down precious lotus flowers and performing various kinds of musical performances.
Furthermore, together with countless devas and nāgas (up to) they paid homage to Śākyamuni Buddha and circumambulated him seven times to the right.
These words refer to the following of the eight classes of divine beings of Samantabhadra;

as they all rely upon wondrous conduct to protect the Dharma, it is said that each manifests the power of their majestic virtue and supernatural penetrations, circumambulating seven times to the right, displaying the reverent etiquette of seeing the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... how can one obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa?
This is the inquiry into the Dharma by Samantabhadra, intended to reveal his underlying purpose. He takes the wondrous conduct of Samantabhadra as the entirety of the Dharmakāya.

The essence possesses great majestic power; therefore, it is called the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja. Because the mind-hearing penetrates through all, it is called "hearing from afar.
Since it is called "hearing from afar," he specifically requests, "I pray only that you would explain it.
That the World-Honored One did not utter a single word in reply precisely reveals that the Way beyond words does not admit of sound. When the World-Honored One preached the Prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti...
While he sat in meditative composure within a rocky cave, Śakra scattered flowers and exclaimed, "Venerable One, you have skillfully heard the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti replied, "I have not heard it. Śakra said, "The World-Honored One has taught by means of non-teaching; you, Venerable One, have heard by means of non-hearing."
One day, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Mañjuśrī struck the mallet and said: "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. Now, Samantabhadra specifically requests that you speak of it.
The World-Honored One did not answer. Samantabhadra then asked: "How can this sutra be obtained? This was intended to reveal that the wondrous Dharma is a path beyond words. It is without...
It is taught as non-explanation; it can only be realized through wordless, silent testimony. Therefore, it is said that one can obtain this sutra.
The Buddha told Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (up to): "After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you will certainly obtain this sutra."
This Buddha correctly demonstrates the sublime conduct of Samantabhadra in order to provide the support for realization and entry [into the Dharma].

Because Samantabhadra has specifically come to hear this sutra, he requests, "I only pray that you will speak of it. The World-Honored One does not offer a single word in reply, intending to show that the path of silence beyond words cannot be expressed in speech.
Therefore, [Samantabhadra] follows up by asking, "How can one obtain this sutra? Thus, the Buddha—
It is said that by accomplishing four dharmas, one shall obtain this sutra: first, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, planting the roots of all virtues;
third, entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*); and fourth, giving rise to the mind that seeks to save all sentient beings.

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "When faith is accomplished, three kinds of minds arise: the first is the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*), because it correctly contemplates the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore...
First is being protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Second is the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), because one delights in accumulating all virtuous practices;
therefore it is said, "planting the roots of all virtues. Third is the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*), because one desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings;
therefore it is said, "arousing the mind to rescue all sentient beings. Furthermore, it is said that when such faith is perfected, one attains the arousal of the bodhicitta.

This refers to entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Therefore, it is said that one "enters the stage of right determination. However, while this chapter speaks of realization, it describes it as the "accomplishment of faith" (*śraddhā-sampanna*).
This means that first, through Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom, one gives rise to faith; based on faith, understanding arises; based on understanding, practice is initiated;

and when practice begins, conceptual understanding ceases. Thus, it constitutes entry into realization. This is precisely what is meant by the accomplishment of faith. That which is called "arousing... [is thus explained].
The two minds are ultimately no different; yet between these two minds, the former mind is more difficult. Nevertheless, faith must rely upon practice to achieve fulfillment.
Thus, Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom necessarily requires Samantabhadra’s exhortation and inspiration. Therefore, it is concluded that by means of the four dharmas, one will certainly attain this sutra.
The treatise speaks according to the initial arousal of the mind, whereas this [passage] speaks in terms of fulfillment. This is sufficient to demonstrate [the distinction].
The practice of wisdom and its basis are non-dual from beginning to end.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "...all those who cause affliction shall find no opportunity."
This clearly demonstrates the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Because there is the power of empowerment and protection, all demons, malevolent spirits, and those who afflict people are unable to find an opportunity. Although this eliminates external calamities, it truly purifies internal obstacles;
for the sublime conduct of Samantabhadra enables all afflictions and demons to remain unable to manifest. Not...
To cause harm to the Dharma-body is to damage the life-force of wisdom; [I shall act] so that they may attain peace and enter [realization].
Whether this person is walking or standing still (up to: "I shall instruct them and recite with them until they have mastered it thoroughly").
This is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of manifesting the true body, face, and speech.

It is said that if a person—whether walking, standing, or sitting—contemplates this sutra, then throughout the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), they will enter deeply into the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* in every thought-moment, remaining neither forgetful nor deluded.
Should they ever forget or lose even a single phrase or a single verse, then the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, mounted upon his six-tusked...
A white elephant appears before that person, instructing them to recite together until they have mastered it;
it ensures they will certainly realize and enter [the truth] before ceasing. This is the empowerment through body, face, and speech.
At that time, those who receive, uphold, read, and recite the Lotus Sūtra shall attain such dhāraṇīs as these.
This means that by the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), through seeing the body and face [of the Buddha], they immediately attain samādhi and dhāraṇī.
*Dhāraṇī*—here translated as "Total Holding" (*saṃgraha*)—is another name for the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the single mind.

Regarding the meaning of the three types of *dhāraṇī* as cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*): "revolving" refers to the revolving of the inverted auditory faculty as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, like the eddies in a rapid current.
This means that all phenomena ultimately converge within the single mind; therefore, it is called True Suchness, which is profoundly serene and eternal.
Quiescence (*śamatha*) is the *dhāraṇī* of revolving; this is called "stopping" (*śamatha*). The true suchness of the single mind possesses the function of great wisdom;
without departing from the single mind, it manifests as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs* of revolving—this is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

Since essence and function are non-dual and are but the single mind, the simultaneous operation of stopping and contemplation is called the Middle Way. It is the simultaneity of negation and illumination, wherein existence and cessation are one.
It is unimpeded. It is the *dhāraṇī* of skillful means for the sound of the Dharma; it is called *samādhi*.

Because one enters the nature of the Dharma-realm upon seeing Samantabhadra, it is attained instantaneously in a single thought-moment. Therefore, it is said: "By seeing me, one immediately attains *samādhi*," and so forth.
"World-Honored One, in a future age, during the final five hundred years," [and so forth], "he spoke a mantra before the Buddha.
This is the mantra spoken by Samantabhadra for protection, through which the power of empowerment is fully realized.
In the final five hundred years, it is a time when strife is firm and difficult to sustain; without the power of empowerment, there is no way to achieve victory."

Therefore, one must apply oneself with effort. While it was previously stated that one should contemplate in every thought-moment throughout the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—it is now said that one should cultivate this sutra with single-minded diligence.
This indicates that it is not through mere recitation alone that one may hope for a spiritual response.
When the twenty-one days are complete, [the Buddha] appears with a body that all sentient beings joyfully behold.
The manifestation before that person occurs because their contemplation has become increasingly clear, like the moon appearing in clear water.
Since the mind of the practitioner and the *dharmadhātu* have merged into one, the Bodhisattva manifests their form; this is the natural principle of the mutual resonance between cause and response.
In order to purify the practitioner of the habitual tendencies of ignorance, he utters this empowered mantra:
*Ātānāti* (1), *Dantapāti* (2), [and so on] up to *Sindhāvikhilete* (19).
By the empowerment of the power of this mantra, may his merit be swiftly accomplished. Since this mantra can destroy obstacles, for all who practice...

For those whose power of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is insufficient, it is necessary to rely on the empowerment of divine mantras (*vidyā-mantra*), so that their merit may be easily accomplished.
World-Honored One, as for the Bodhisattvas (up to...)— all this is due to the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra.
This reveals that the mantra is the entire body of the Dharma-realm; hence it is said: "One should know this to be the supernatural power of Samantabhadra.
If one contemplates the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra, then the great function of the Dharma-realm manifests before one.
Thus, when the mind merges with the mantra, the Bodhisattva’s response is like an echo.
"If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and correctly contemplate [the sūtra]... they shall have their heads stroked by all the Tathāgatas.
This statement indicates that the essential practice for upholding the sūtra takes correct mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) as its primary focus.

While the preceding section merely spoke of "receiving and upholding," here Samantabhadra specifically mentions "contemplating, practicing, and correctly contemplating. From this, one knows that upholding the sūtra [requires such mental engagement].
Taking contemplative observation as the essential practice means not merely following along with the text or counting characters.

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "When the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic; because it is far removed from subtle thoughts, one attains the vision of the nature of the mind. It further states:
"One who can contemplate non-thought may be said to be heading toward Buddha-wisdom. Herein, right mindfulness is precisely non-thought.
In the cultivation through contemplation, one must observe non-thought (*amanasikāra*) to correspond with the *dharmadhātu* of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Consequently, this evokes the manifestation and empowerment of Samantabhadra, as the Tathāgata’s hand touches the crown of one's head. Therefore, the subsequent passage explains the meaning and significance of "right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*).
Thus, it is known that entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision necessarily takes right mindfulness as the essential practice.

If one merely transcribes [this text], at the end of that person's life—up to the point where they understand its meaning and practice according to the teaching—this is the benefit of such superior practice.
If one merely transcribes it without understanding the meaning at all, one will still receive the retribution of rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
how much more so for one who, with right mindfulness, understands the meaning and practices accordingly—would such a person not receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata?
If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, [and] correctly contemplate [this teaching], practicing according to what is taught,

this reveals the superior benefits of understanding the meaning in order to encourage its practice and upholding. Whereas previously it was stated that merely copying it down would result in rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
the merit and benefit of now understanding the meaning is that at the time of death, one will certainly be met by the hands of a thousand Buddhas.
One shall be guided to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, where one will dwell together with Maitreya, the Bodhisattva who is next to attain Buddhahood.
This constitutes participation in the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower Tree in the future; furthermore, it serves as the causal seed for the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle.
Therefore, the wise should single-mindedly maintain right mindfulness and practice according to the teachings; this is what constitutes sublime conduct.
"World-Honored One, by means of my supernormal powers, I shall cause this [sūtra] to be widely circulated so that it shall never be interrupted.
This is the vow of Samantabhadra for the circulation of this sūtra; he pledges to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas shall never be severed."
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised [them], saying: "Those who are able to receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva...
This is the Tathāgata’s praise for the merit of Samantabhadra’s protection and assistance in upholding this sutra.

The Tathāgata shall likewise protect through his supernatural power those who receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra, because this sutra is the Dharma protected by the mindfulness of the Tathāgata. Universal...
When the virtuous Upāli, as a holder of this sutra, possesses it, then the sutra resides within Samantabhadra;

likewise, when the Tathāgata protects and upholds the name of Samantabhadra, then the sutra also resides within the person who holds that name. This is because whatever thought is raised manifests the nature of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) with clear and manifest presence.
"Samantabhadra, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra]— up to being covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha—
this refers to the sublime realization of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the cultivation of correct mindfulness.
Since this sutra already contains the entire body of the Tathāgata, one thereby beholds the wondrous Dharma-body of Śākyamuni, as if hearing it directly from the Buddha’s own mouth."
Upon hearing [the Dharma], one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision in every thought-moment; therefore, one seals and makes offerings to the Buddha.

This is praised as "good" by the Buddha, for it is the true seed of attaining Buddhahood and will inevitably lead to the bestowal of a prophecy of enlightenment. Thus, when the Buddha strokes one's head with his hand, all practices become the practice of a Buddha.
Therefore, they are covered by robes; this is the sublime realization of practicing right mindfulness.
Such persons no longer crave worldly pleasures (up to) being able to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra.
This statement concerns the successful accomplishment of the sublime realization through upholding this sutra.

In the preceding "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct," it was prescribed that those who uphold the sutra should not associate with the scriptures of non-Buddhists, nor approach women who observe improper vows, and should not give rise to afflictions such as the three poisons.
This is because all such precepts are intended to prevent the arousal of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that might hinder right mindfulness.
Therefore, one distances oneself from them so that they do not cause harm. Now, having entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), all evil habits are purified and exhausted;
naturally, there is no greed or delight, and one is not troubled by them. Whatever is cultivated and practiced is entirely the sublime conduct of Samantabhadra.
If knowledge and vision have not yet opened, then every movement results in agitation and confusion. Now that one has realized this entry, there is none.
Because the Dharma is not inferior, the mind becomes distant of its own accord without depending on physical seclusion.
Samantabhadra, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata... [until] ...shall sit upon the lion Dharma-seat amidst the great assembly of devas and humans.

This statement regarding "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" means that one immediately attains bodhi. Therefore, upon seeing those who uphold this sutra, one should conceive the thought that they will attain Buddhahood.
Since the time for realizing the fruit is near, it is said that "before long they shall proceed to the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and so forth.
The passage concerning the "subduing of all Māras" refers entirely to the matter of attaining Buddhahood.
"Samantabhadra, if in future ages one upholds, receives, reads, and recites [this sutra]... (up to) one shall likewise obtain its meritorious retribution in the present life.
These words refer to the immediate blessings brought about by upholding the sutra. Because one is nourished by the flavor of the Dharma, one does not greedily cling to worldly enjoyments.
Because this is merit that is inseparable from wisdom, one's vows are not in vain, and the three obstacles are daily diminished.
Therefore, their merit becomes increasingly profound. If the retribution in the present life is such as this, then the excellence of future rebirth in the heavens can be known.

There is a distinction between the prior and subsequent benefits of upholding the sutra: by means of right mindfulness and practicing according to the teaching, one will attain Buddhahood before long;
whereas by merely receiving, upholding, reciting, and transcribing it, one receives the karmic reward of heavenly bliss.

If there are those who speak words of contempt and disparagement—[extending] to such severe and evil illnesses as dropsy and shortness of breath—this generally states that the retribution for praise and disparagement is as manifest as a shadow or an echo.
To disparage one who upholds this sutra is to act like a madman;
thus, one loses right knowledge and vision, and consequently experiences blindness life after life. If, however, one makes offerings and offers praise...
If a person encounters such a case, they will obtain an immediate retribution. If one exposes another's faults and evils—regardless of whether they are true or false—one will contract leprosy;
this is because one has injured and defiled the Dharma-body, and thus incurs this retribution.

If one treats such a person with derisive laughter, one will incur retributions such as having teeth that are sparse and missing throughout successive lifetimes; this is because one has injured the sublime Dharma through the karma of speech.
Because the entire body [of the Dharma] is thus affected, it brings about all manner of severe and grievous illnesses throughout the body.

As for the detailed account of the retribution for disparaging the sutra at the end of the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) chapter, this was spoken because the preceptor failed to discern the capacity of the recipient, thereby causing those without wisdom to treat it with contempt, disparage, and slander it;
this refers specifically to those who slander the sutra. Furthermore, from the "Dhāraṇī" (Dharanī) chapter onwards, there are detailed accounts of disparaging those who uphold [the Dharma].

The passage concerning the "Dharma Master" refers specifically to those who slander him; it is said out of fear that if people hear of such slanders, they will lose faith in the Dharma Master, and thus the lineage of the Buddha would be severed from this point onward.
Now, when it says "one who upholds the sutra," the intent is to refer to a person who maintains right mindfulness and practices according to the teaching.
Such a person has already entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and has attained the wondrous realization of the Dharmakāya. To disparage them is to wound the Dharmakāya itself.
This constitutes the whole. Thus we know that the retributions for slandering the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the past and future each have their respective basis;

it does not mean that this section concludes the preceding text. Nevertheless, the Buddha, through the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, expounds the Dharma with equanimity, perfectly illuminating the entire dharma-realm.

From beginning to end, it is a single consistent thread, manifested in accordance with the nature of reality to fully exhaust the various dispositions of sentient beings; fundamentally, there is no conceptual deliberation involved.

Analysis: If one seeks [the meaning] by following the rises and falls of the literary composition and its structural correspondences, it seems to involve deliberate mental calculation and the crafting of mere words;
thus, one falls into the common parlance of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This is not the teaching of great wisdom, which is beyond thought and accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, it is said: "The student should be skillful regarding the meaning and not cling to verbal expressions."
Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra, you should rise to welcome them from afar, as you would show reverence to the Buddha.
This concludes the section on revering those who uphold the sutra, which generally summarizes the meaning of the profound importance of the Dharma.

The preceding text has repeatedly stated that one who reveres the upholder of the sutra should be revered as the Buddha, for by practicing according to the teaching, they enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision before long.
One immediately attains Bodhi because one's sublime practices have already been perfected; "one should serve them with reverence as if they were the Buddha" refers precisely to this.
The phrase "therefore" (is-ho) is a term used to conclude the preceding passage.

When this "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra" was being preached (up to the point where) bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms attained the path of Samantabhadra, this concludes the realization of practice through hearing this chapter.
By entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, all dharmas universally converge within the Dharma-realm;
thus, one attains hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs* of revolution, whereby each and every practice accords with the true Dharma.
Because it is the realm (*dhātu*), it is said that one attains the path of Samantabhadra. By hearing this universal Dharma (*sarvadharma*), one achieves this great benefit;
the wondrous benefit of the Sublime Dharma culminates herein. The sublime practice of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* culminates in non-attainment.

After the youth Sudhana of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* had visited all his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and entered the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he saw only Samantabhadra, because within the nature of the Dharma-realm, [it is originally...]
There is nothing to be realized; therefore, only Samantabhadra accords with the measure of the dharmadhātu.
Thus, the essential purports of these two sutras are mutually required and form a single, coherent whole, through which one may perceive the intent of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Samantabhadra and the other bodhisattvas (up to) received and upheld the Buddha’s words, prostrated, and departed.
This constitutes the final section on the dissemination of the teaching. Although Mañjuśrī initiated the discourse, his name is not mentioned in the conclusion;
this is because he is merged with and identical to the ocean of fruition. It is like the *Avataṃsaka* assembly, where conditions are integrated into reality, such that there is no [distinction].
Mañjuśrī simply returns to Samantabhadra; their significance is equal. This sutra is specifically intended to attract and guide those of the two vehicles;
therefore, the śrāvakas accept it with faith and practice it.
[The Verse of Dedication]
I prostrate to the Lord of the Dharma-realm, whose body is radiant with the marks and signs of perfection;
who, in accordance with conditions, responds to sentient beings by expounding the subtle and wondrous Dharma, causing all sages and worthies to fully open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
With the wisdom of a single hair, I measure the emptiness of the Dharma-nature, like drinking but a single drop from the ocean.

If one wishes to know the flavor of the hundred rivers— The dharma of quiescence that transcends words, Which is difficult to seek through discursive thought— One must rely on profound wisdom and skillful means to attain penetration.
May all who see, hear, or rejoice in this, Suddenly open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; The inconceivable seed of Buddhahood Shall ultimately never be severed.
Together entering the city of Nirvāṇa, Abiding peacefully in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Verified by Fang Yu, disciple of Mount Nanyue.
The Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra, Fascicle Seven (End).
